Dale harbour is a ready outlet for small vessels, where they may ride in two or three fathoms at low <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>.—In the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, before the Spanish invasion, two forts were begun at the entrance of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILFORD">Milford</a> Haven, one on each side, called Nangle and Dale blockhouses; but they were not then finished.—The Stack rock rises here above water, lying near the middle of the entrance between Nangle and Dale. Penemouth is the opening of that branch of the haven on which the town of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEMBROKE">Pembroke</a> is seated, and where the customhouse of Milford is kept. The breadth of the entrance between rock and rock is but 220 yards at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> water, and 112 at low water. There is a ridge of rocky ground that has the name of Carrs, which runs almost across Milford Haven, from <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> towards Llandstadwell, where it renders the landing <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> difficult to strangers, from its not appearing at low water. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> convenience of this harbour is, that in an hour's time a ship may be in or out of it, and in the way between the Milford <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">Land</a>'s End and Ireland. As it lies near the mouth of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEVERN">Severn</a>, a ship in eight or ten hours may be over on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Ireland, or off the Land's End in the English channel; and a vessel may get out hence to the west much sooner than from either <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLYMOUTH">Plymouth</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FALMOUTH">Falmouth</a>. This harbour has been greatly improved by new works, at the expense of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> on April 14, 1759 granted 10,000l. for fortifying the harbour of Milford, all of which was expended on the fort at Neyland, which, however, still remains unfinished.

MILIO

Pages 146-148

a celebrated <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol2.html#article-ATHLETE">athlete</a> of Crotona in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. His father's name was Diotimus. He early accustomed himself to carry the greatest burdens, and by degrees became a prodigy of strength. It is said that he carried on his shoulders a young bullock, four years old, for above forty yards; and afterwards killed it with one blow of his fist, and eat it up in one <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>. He was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> times crowned at the Pythian games, and six at the Olympian. He presented himself a seventh <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; but no one had the courage <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> boldness to enter the lists against against him. He was one of the disciples of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYTHAGORAS">Pythagoras</a>; and to his uncommon strength, it is said, the learned preceptor and his pupils owed their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>: The pillar which supported the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> of the school suddenly gave way; but Milo supported the whole <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, and gave the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> and his auditors time to escape. In his old <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, Milo attempted to pull up a tree by the roots, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> it. He partly effected it; but his strength being gradually exhausted, the tree when half clef t re-united, and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> remained pinched in the body of the tree. He was then alone; and, being unable to disentangle himself, he was devoured by the wild beasts of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, about 500 years before the Christian era. Milo, T. Annus, a native of Lanuvium, who attempted to obtain the consulship at Rome by intrigue and seditions tumults. Clodius the tribune opposed his views; yet Milo would have succeeded but for the following event: As he was going into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, attended by his wife and a numerous retinue of gladiators and servants, he met on the Appian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> his enemy Clodius, who was returning to Rome with three of his friends and some domestics completely armed.—A quarrel arose between the servants. Milo supported his attendants, and the dispute became general.—Clodius received many severe wounds, and was obliged to retire to a neighbouring cottage. Milo pursued his enemy in his retreat, and ordered his servants to despatch him. The body of the murdered tribune was carried to Rome, and exposed to public view. The enemies of Milo inveighed bitterly against the violence and barbarity with which the sacred person of a tribune had been treated. Cicero undertook the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of Milo; but the continual clamours of the friends of Clodius, and the sight of an armed soldiery, which surrounded the seat of judgment, so terrified the orator, that he forgot the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his arguments, and the defence he made was weak and injudicious.—Milo was condemned, and banished to Massilia. Cicero soon after sent his exiled friend a copy of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORATION">oration</a> which he had prepared for his defence, in the form in which we have it now; and Milo, after he had read it, exclaimed, O Cicero, hadst thou spoken before my accusers in these terms, Milo would not be now eating figs at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARSEILLES">Marseilles</a>. The friendship and cordiality of Cicero and Milo were the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> intimacy and familiar intercourse. It was to the successful labours of Milo that the orator was recalled from banishment, and restored to his friends. Milo, (anciently <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MELOS">Melos</a>), an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the Archipelago, about 50 miles in circumference, with a harbour, which is one of the largest in the Mediterranean. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> town is of the same name as the island, and was prettily built, but abominably nasty: the houses are two stories <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, with flat roofs; and are built with a sort of pumice <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, which is hard, blackish, and yet very <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>. This island was formerly rich and populous. From the earliest times of antiquity it enjoyed pure <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>. The Athenians, not being able to persuade the Melians to declare in their favour in the Peloponnesian <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, made a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> upon the island, and attacked them vigorously. In two different expeditions they failed of their purpose: but returning with more numerous forces, they laid siege to Melos; and obliging the besieged to surrender at <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a>, put to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> all the men who were able to bear arms. They spared only the women and children, and these they carried into <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of cruelty puts <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> to the blush, and disgraces the Athenian name. But war was then carried on with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of wild rage, unexampled in the present times. Republics know not how to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a>, and always carry their vengeance to an extravagant height. When Lysander, the Lacedaemonian general, came to give <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a> to the Athenians, he expelled the colony which they had sent to Melos, and re-established the unfortunate remains of its original inhabitants. This island lost its liberty when Rome, aspiring to the empire of the world, conquered all the isles of the Archipelago. In the partition of the empire, it fell to the share of the eastern emperors, was governed by particular dukes, and was at last conquered by Soliman II. Since that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, it has groaned under the yoke of Turkish despotism, and has lost its opulence and splendour. At the commencement of the present century, it boasted of 17 churches and 11 chapels, and contained more than 20,000 inhabitants. It was very fertile in corn, wine, and fruits; and the whole space from the town to the harbour, which is nearly two miles, was laid out in beautiful gardens. M. Tournefort, who visited it in the year 1700, gives a fine <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of it. "The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, being constantly warmed by subterraneous fires, produced almost without interruption plenteous crops of corn, barley, cotton, exquisite wines, and delicious melons. St Elias, the finest <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> in the island, and situated on the most elevated spot, is encircled with <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CITRON">citron</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CEDAR">cedar</a>, and fig trees. Its gardens are watered by a copious <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>. Olive trees, of which there are but few in the other parts of the island, grow in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> numbers around this monastery. The adjacent vineyards afford excellent wine. In a word, all the productions of the island are the very best of their kinds; its partridges, quails, kids, and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LAMBS">lambs</a>, are highly valued, and yet may be bought at a very cheap price." Were M. Tournefort to return to Milo, M. Savary assures us, he would no longer see the fine island which he has described. "He might still see <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a>, in the form of feathers, and fringed with silver thread, hanging from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> of the caverns; pieces of pure sulphur filling the cliffs of the rocks; a variety of mineral <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>; hot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a> (though these are now only a set of small dirty caves); the same subterraneous fires which in his days warmed the bosom of the earth, and were the cause of its extraordinary fertility: but instead of 5000 Greeks, all paying the capitation tax (A), he would now find no more than about 700 inhabitants. (A) Grown up men are the only persons who pay the capitation tax. Therefore, by adding to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of 5000 who paid the tax, the women, boys, and girls, we find that Melos, in the days of Tournefort, contained at least 20,000 souls. inhabitants on an island 18 leagues in circumference. He would sigh to behold the finest lands lying uncultivated, and the most fertile valleys converted into marshes; of the gardens scarcely a vestige is left; three-fourths of the town in ruins, and the inhabitants daily decreasing. In short, during the last 50 years, Melos has assumed a quite different appearance. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a>, which the Turks propagate everywhere, has cut off one part of its inhabitants; the injudicious administration of the Porte, and the oppressive extortions of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> pacha, have destroyed the rest. At present, for want of hands, they cannot cut out a free channel for their waters, which stagnate in the valleys, corrupt, and infect the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> with their putrid exhalations. The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> marshes, of which there are numbers in the island, being equally neglected, produce the same effects. Add to these inconveniences, those sulphurous exhalations which arise all over the island, and by which the inhabitants of Melos are afflicted with dangerous fevers during three-fourths of the year. Perhaps they may be obliged to forsake their country. Every countenance is <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a>, and livid; and none bears any marks of good <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>. The prudent traveller <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> be careful to spend but a very short time in this unwholesome country, unless he chooses to expose himself to the danger of catching a fever. To <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> over night, or to spend but one day in the island, is often enough to occasion his being attacked with that distemper. "Yet (continues our author) a judicious and enlightened <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> might expel those evils which ravage Melos. Its first care would be to establish a lazaret, and to prohibit vessels whose crews or cargoes are infected with the plague from landing. <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CANALS">Canals</a> might next be cut, to drain the marshes whose exhalations are so pernicious. The island would then be repopulated. The sulphurous vapours are not the most noxious. These prevailed equally in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> times, yet the island was then very populous. M. Tournefort, who travelled through it at a time less distant from the period when it was conquered by the Turks, and when they had not yet had time to lay it waste, reckons the number of its inhabitants (as we have said) at about 20,000. The depopulation of Melos is therefore to be ascribed to the despotism of the Porte, and its detestable <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol18.html#article-POLICE">police</a>." The women of Milo, once so celebrated for their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, are now sallow, unhealthy, and disgustingly ugly; and render themselves still more hideous by their dress, which is a kind of loose jacket, with a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> coat and petticoat, that scarcely covers two-thirds of their thighs, barely meeting the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STOCKING">stocking</a> above the knee. Their hind <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> hangs <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the back in a number of plaits; that on the fore part of the head is combed down each side of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a>, and terminated by a small stiff curl, which is even with the lower part of the cheek. All the inhabitants are Greeks, for the Turks are not fond of trusting themselves in the small <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>; but every <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> the captain <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BASHAW">bashaw</a> goes round with a squadron to keep them in subjection, and to collect the revenue. When the Russians made themselves masters of the Archipelago, many of the islands declared in their favour; but being abandoned by the peace, they were so severely muleted by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> signior, that they have professed a determination to remain perfectly quiet in future. As the Turks, however, do not think them worth a garrison, and will not trust them with arms and ammunition, all those which the Russians may choose to invade will be obliged to submit. The two <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> which form the entrance of the harbour, crossing each other, render it imperceptible until you are <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to it. Thus, while you are perfectly secure within it, you find great difficulty in getting out, particularly in a northerly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>; and as no trade is carried on except a little in corn and salt, Milo would scarcely ever be visited, were it not that, being the first island which one makes in the Archipelago, the pilots have chosen it for their residence. They live in a little town on the top of a high rock, which, from its situation and appearance, is called the Castle.—Partridges still abound in this island; and are so cheap, that you may buy one for a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of powder only. The peasants get them by standing behind a portable screen, with a small aperture in the centre, in which they place the muzzle of their piece, and then draw the partridges by a call. When a sufficient number are collected, they fire among them, and generally kill from four to seven at a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SHOT">shot</a>; but even this method of getting them is so expensive, from the scarcity of ammunition, that the people can never afford to shoot them, except when there are gentlemen in the island, from whom they can beg a little powder and shot. Milo is 60 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of Candia; and the town is situated in E. Long. 25° 15' N. Lat. 36° 27'. MILSTONE. See MILLSTONE.

MILITANT

Pages 131-131
or Church-Militant, denotes the body of Christians while here on earth.

MILITARY

Pages 131-134

something belonging to the soldiery <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITIA">militia</a>. MILITARY <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">Discipline</a>, the training of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, and the due enforcement of the laws and regulations instituted by authority for their conduct. Next to the forming of troops, military discipline is the first object that presents itself to our notice; it is the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> of all armies; and unless it be established amongst them with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a>, and supported with unshaken <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>, they are no better than so many contemptible heaps of rabble, which are more dangerous to the very state that maintains them than even its declared enemies. MILITARY Execution, the ravaging or destroying of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, or town, that refuses to pay the contribution inflicted upon them. MILITARY <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">Exercise</a>. See Exercise and Words of Command. MILITARY State, in British polity, one of the three divisions of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAITY">laity</a>. See Laity. This state includes the whole of the soldiery, or such persons as are peculiarly appointed among the rest of the people for the safeguard and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the realm. In a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, it is extremely dangerous to make a distinct order of the profession of arms. In <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> monarchies, this is necessary for the safety of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>; and arises from the main principle of their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, which is that of governing by fear; but, in free states, the profession of a soldier, taken singly and merely as a profession, is justly an object of jealousy. In these no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> should take up arms but with a view to defend his country and its laws: he puts not off the citizen when he enters the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>; but it is because he is a citizen, and would wish to continue so, that he makes himself for a while a soldier. The laws therefore, and constitution of these kingdoms, know no such state as that of a perpetual standing soldier, bred up to no other profession than that of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>; and it was not till the reign of Henry VII. that the kings of England had so much as a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> about their persons. In the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the Anglo-Saxons, as appears from Edward the Confessor's laws, the military force of England was in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the dukes or heretochs, who were constituted through every <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>; being taken out of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, and such as were most remarkable for be- Military ing sapientiae, fideles, et animosi. Their duty was to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> and regulate the English armies with a very unlimited power; prout eis visum fuerit, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AD">ad</a> honorem coronae et utilitatem regni. And because of this great power they were elected by the people in their full <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>, or folkmote, in the same manner as sheriffs were elected: following still that old <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FUNDAMENTAL">fundamental</a> maxim of the Saxon constitution, that where any officer was entrusted with such power, as, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> abused, might tend to the oppression of the people, that power was delegated to him by the vote of the people themselves. So too, among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Germans, the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> of our Saxon forefathers, they had their dukes, as well as kings, with an independent power over the military, as the kings had over the civil state. The dukes were <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTIVE">elective</a>, the kings <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a>: for so only can be consistently understood that passage of Tacitus, Reges ex nobilitate, duces ex virtute sumunt. In constituting their kings, the family or blood <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> was regarded; in choosing their dukes or leaders, warlike merit: <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> as Caesar relates of their ancestors in his time, that whenever they went to war, by way either of attack or defence, they elected leaders to command them. This <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> share of power, thus conferred by the people, though intended to preserve the liberty of the subject, was perhaps unreasonably detrimental to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREROGATIVE">prerogative</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>: and accordingly we find a very ill <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> made of it by Edric <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Mercia, in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Edmund Ironside; who, by his office of duke or heretoch, was entitled to a large command in the king's <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, and by his repeated treacheries at last transferred the crown to Canute the Dane. It seems universally agreed by all historians, that King Alfred first settled a national militia in this kingdom, and by his prudent discipline made all the subjects of his dominions soldiers: but we are unfortunately left in the dark as to the particulars of this his so celebrated regulation; though, from what was last observed, the dukes seem to have been left in possession of too large and independent a power: which enabled Duke Harold, on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Edward the Confessor, though a stranger to the royal blood, to mount for a short space the throne of this kingdom, in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a> of Edgar Etheling the rightful heir. Upon the Norman conquest, the <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol9.html#article-FEUDAL_LAW">feudal <a </a>class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a> was introduced here in all its rigour, the whole of which is built on a military <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> thereof, all the lands in the kingdom were divided into what were called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a>'s fees, in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> above 60,000; and for every knight's fee, a knight or soldier, miles, was bound to attend the king in his wars, for 40 days in a year; in which space of time, before war was reduced to a science, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a> was generally finished, and a kingdom either conquered or victorious. By this means the king had, without any expense, an army of 60,000 men always ready at his command. And accordingly we find one, among the laws of William the Conqueror, which in the king's name commands and firmly enjoins the personal attendance of all knights and others; quod habeant et teneant se semper in armis et equis, ut decet et portet: et quod semper sint prompti et parati ad servitium suum integrum nobis explendum et peragendum, cum opus adfuerit, secundum quod debent de feudis et tenementis suis de jure nobis facere. This personal <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of time degenerated into pecuniary commutations or aids; and at last the military <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the feudal system was abolished at the Restoration, by stat. 12 Car. II. c. 24. See Feudal System. In the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time, we are not to imagine that the kingdom was left wholly without defence in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> insurrections, or the prospect of foreign invasions. Besides those who by their military tenures were bound to perform 40 days service in the field, first the assize of arms, enacted 27 Hen. II. and afterwards the statute of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINCHESTER">Winchester</a>, under Edward I. obliged every man, according to his estate and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, to provide a determinate <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of such arms as were then in use, in order to keep the peace; and constables were appointed in all <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a> by the latter statute, to see that such arms were provided. These weapons were changed, by the statute 4 and 5 Ph. and M. c. 2, into others of more <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> service; but both this and the former <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> were repealed in the reign of James I. While these <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in force, it was usual from time to time for our princes to issue commissions of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARRAY">array</a>, and send into every county officers in whom they could confide, to muster and array (or set in military order) the inhabitants of every district; and the form of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> of array was settled in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> in the 5 Hen. IV. But at the same time it was provided, that no man should be compelled to go out of the kingdom at any rate, nor out of his shire, but in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of urgent <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a>; nor should provide soldiers unless by consent of parliament. About the reign of King Henry VIII., and his children, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a>-lieutenants began to be introduced, as standing representatives of the crown, to keep the counties in military order; for we find them mentioned as known officers in the statute 4 and 5 Ph. and M. c. 3, though they had not been then <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> in use; for Camden speaks of them in the time of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> as extraordinary magistrates, constituted only in times of difficulty and danger. In this state things continued till the repeal of the statutes of armour in the reign of King James I.; after which, when King <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. had, during his northern expeditions, issued commissions of lieutenancy, and exerted some military powers which, having been long exercised, were thought to belong to the crown, it became a question in the long parliament, how far the power of the militia did inherently reside in the king; being now unsupported by any statute, and founded only upon immemorial usage. This question, long agitated with great <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> and resentment on both sides, became at length the immediate cause of the fatal rupture between the king and his parliament: the two houses not only denying this prerogative of the crown, the legality of which claim perhaps might be somewhat doubtful; but also seizing into their hands the entire power of the militia, the illegality of which step could never be any doubt at all. Soon after the restoration of King Charles II., when the military tenures were abolished, it was thought proper to ascertain the power of the militia, to recognize the sole <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of the crown to govern and command them, and to put the whole into a more regular method of military subordination: and the order in which the militia now stands by law, is principally built upon the statutes which were then enacted. It is true, the two last of them are apparently repealed; but many of their provisions provisions are re-enacted, with the addition of some new regulations, by the present militia laws; the general scheme of which is to discipline a certain number of the inhabitants of every county, chosen by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a> for three years, and officered by the lord-<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a> lieutenants, and other principal landholders, under a commission from the crown. They are not compellable to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a> out of their counties, unless in case of invasion or actual rebellion, nor in any case compellable to march out of the kingdom. They are to be exercised at stated times: and their discipline in general is liberal and easy; but, when drawn out into actual service, they are subject to the rigours of martial law, as necessary to keep them in order. This is the constitutional security which our laws have provided for the public peace, and for protecting the realm against foreign or domestic violence; and which the statutes declare as essentially necessary to the safety and prosperity of the kingdom. When the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> was engaged in war, more veteran troops and more regular discipline were esteemed to be necessary, than could be expected from a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> militia; and therefore at such times more rigorous methods were put in use for the raising of armies and the due regulation and discipline of the soldiery, which are to be looked upon only as temporary excrescences bred out of the distemper of the state, and not as any part of the permanent and perpetual laws of the kingdom. For martial law, which is built upon no settled principles, but is entirely arbitrary in its decisions, is, as Sir Matthew Hale observes, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> and reality no law, but something indulged rather than allowed as a law. The necessity of order and discipline in an army is the only thing which can give it countenance; and therefore it ought not to be permitted in time of peace, when the king's courts are open for all persons to receive <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> according to the laws of the land. Wherefore, Thomas <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANCASTER">Lancaster</a> being convicted at Pontefract, 15 Edward II. by martial law, his attainder was reversed 1 Edward III. because it was done in time of peace. And it is laid <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, that if a lieutenant, or other, that hath commission of martial authority, doth in time of peace hang or otherwise execute any man by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of martial law, this is <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>; for it is against <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MAGNA_CHARTA">magna <a cla</a>ss="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CHARTA">charta</a>. And the petition of right enacts, that no soldier shall be quartered on the subject without his own consent; and that no commission shall issue to proceed within this land according to martial law. And whereas, after the Restoration, King Charles II. kept up about 5000 regular troops, by his own authority, for guards and garrisons, which King James II. by degrees increased to no less than 30,000, all paid from his own civil <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIST">list</a>; it was made one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BILL">bill</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a>, that the raising or keeping a standing army within the kingdom in time of peace, unless it be with consent of parliament, is against law. But as the fashion of keeping standing armies (which was first introduced by Charles VII. in France 1445) has of late years universally prevailed over <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> (though some of its potentates, being unable themselves to maintain them, are obliged to have recourse to richer powers, and receive subsidiary pensions for that purpose), it has also for many years past been annually judged necessary by our legislature for the safety of the kingdom, the defence of the possessions of the crown of Great <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, and the preservation of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a> of power in Europe, to maintain even in time of peace a standing body of troops, under the command of the crown; who are however ipso facto disbandished at the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EXPIRATION">expiration</a> of every year, unless continued by parliament. And it was enacted by statute 10 William III. c. 1. that not more than 12,000 regular forces should be kept on foot in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, though paid at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of that kingdom: which permission is extended by statute 8 Geo. III. c. 13, to 16,235 men in time of peace. To prevent the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-EXECUTIVE_POWER">executive power</a> from being able to oppress, says Baron Montesquieu, it is requisite that the armies with which it is intrusted should consist of the people, and have the same spirit with the people: as was the case at Rome, till Marius new-modelled the legions by enlisting the rabble of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and laid the foundation of all the military tyranny that ensued. Nothing then, according to these principles, ought to be more guarded against in a free state, than making the military power, when such a one is necessary to be kept on foot, a body too distinct from the people. Like ours, therefore, it should wholly be composed of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> subjects; it ought only to be enlisted for a short and limited time; the soldiers also should live intermixed with the people; no separate camp, no <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARRACKS">barracks</a>, no inland fortresses should be allowed. And perhaps it might be still better, if, by dismissing a stated number, and enlisting others at every renewal of their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a>, a circulation could be kept up between the army and the people, and the citizen and the soldier be more intimately connected together. To keep this body of troops in order, an annual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of parliament likewise passes, "to punish <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUTINY">mutiny</a> and desertion, and for the better payment of the army and their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>." This regulates the manner in which they are to be dispersed among the several inn-keepers and victuallers throughout the kingdom; and establishes a law martial for their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. By this, among other things, it is enacted, that if any officer or soldier shall excite, or join any mutiny, or, knowing of it, shall not give notice to the commanding officer, or shall <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a>, or list in any other regiment, or <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> upon his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POST">post</a>, or leave it before he is relieved, or hold correspondence with a rebel or enemy, or strike or use violence to his superior officer, or shall disobey his lawful commands; such offender shall suffer such <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> as a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> martial shall inflict, though it extend to death itself. However expedient the most strict regulations may be in time of actual war, yet in times of profound peace, a little relaxation of military rigour would not, one should hope, be productive of much inconvenience. And, upon this principle, though by our standing laws (still remaining in force, though not attended to) desertion in time of war is made felony without benefit of clergy, and the offence is triable by a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JURY">jury</a>, and before the judges of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> law; yet, by our militia laws before mentioned, a much <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> punishment is inflicted for desertion in time of peace. So, by the Roman law also, desertion in time of war was punished with death, but more mildly in time of tranquillity. But our mutiny act makes no such distinction: for any of the faults above mentioned, are equally at all times, punishable with death itself, if a court martial shall think proper. This discretionary power of Military, the court martial is indeed to be guided by the directions of the crown; which, with regard to military offenses, has almost an absolute legislative power. "His Majesty (says the act) may form articles of war, and constitute courts martial, with power to try any crime by such articles, and inflict such penalties as the articles <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a>." A vast and most important trust! an unlimited power to create crimes, and annex to them any punishments not extending to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> or limb! These are indeed forbidden to be inflicted, except for crimes declared to be so punishable by this act; which crimes we have just enumerated, and among which, we may observe, that any disobedience to lawful commands is one. Perhaps in some future revision of this act, which is in many respects hastily penned, it may be thought worthy the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> of parliament to ascertain the limits of military subjection, and to enact express articles of war for the government of the army, as is done for the government of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>; especially as, by our present constitution, the nobility and gentry of the kingdom, who serve their country as militia officers, are annually subjected to the same arbitrary rule during their time of exercise. One of the greatest advantages of our law is, that not only the crimes themselves which it punishes, but also the penalties which it inflicts, are ascertained and notorious; nothing is left to arbitrary <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a>: the king by his judges dispenses what the law has previously ordained, but is not himself the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEGISLATOR">legislator</a>. How much, therefore, is it to be regretted, that a set of men, whose bravery has so often preserved the liberties of their country, should be reduced to a state of servitude in the midst of a nation of freemen; for Sir Edward <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COKE">Coke</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> inform us, that it is one of the genuine marks of servitude, to have the law, which is our rule of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, either concealed or precarious; Misera est servitus, ubi jus est vagum aut incognitum. Nor is this state of servitude quite consistent with the maxims of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> policy observed by other free nations. For the greater the general liberty is which any state enjoys, the more cautious has it usually been in introducing <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a> in any particular order or profession. These men, as Baron Montesquieu observes, seeing the liberty which others possess, and which they themselves are excluded from, are apt (like cunuchs in the eastern seragllos) to live in a state of perpetual envy and hatred towards the rest of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a>, and indulge a malignant <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> in contributing to destroy those privileges to which they can never be admitted. Hence have many free states, by departing from this rule, been endangered by the revolt of their slaves; while, in absolute and despotic governments, where no real liberty exists, and consequently no injurious comparisons can be formed, such incidents are extremely rare. Two precautions are therefore advised to be observed in all prudent and free governments: 1. To prevent the introduction of slavery at all; or, 2. If it be already introduced, not to intrust those slaves with arms who will then find themselves an overmatch for the freemen. Much less ought the soldiery to be an exception to the people in general, and the only state of servitude in the nation. But as soldiers, by this annual act, are thus put in a worse condition than any other subjects; so, by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> of our standing laws, they are in some cases put in a much better. By statute 43 Eliz. c. 3; a weekly allowance is to be raised in every county for the relief of soldiers that are sick, hurt, and maimed: not forgetting the royal <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a> at Chelsea for such as are worn out in their duty. Officers and soldiers, that have been in the king's service, are by several statutes, enacted at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of several wars, at liberty to use any trade or occupation they are fit for, in any town in the kingdom (except the two <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>), notwithstanding any statute, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> to the contrary. And soldiers in actual military service may make nuncupative wills, and dispose of their goods, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WAGES">wages</a>, and other personal chattels, without these forms, solemnities, and expences, which the law requires in other cases. Our law does not indeed extend this privilege so far as the civil law, which carried it to an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> that borders upon the ridiculous: for if a soldier, in the article of death, wrote anything in bloody letters on his shield, or in the dust of the field with his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, it was a very good military <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TESTAMENT">testament</a>. MILITARY COURT. See CHIVALRY, Court of. MILITARY <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TENURE">TENURE</a>. See TENURE, FEUDAL System, and KNIGHT.

MILITARY WAYS

Pages 134-134

are the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a> which Agrippa procured to be made through the empire in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Augustus, for the more convenient marching of troops and conveyance of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a>. N. Bergier has written the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the origin, progress, and amazing <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, of these <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> roads, which were paved from the gates of Rome to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> parts of the empire. See WAY.

MILITIA

Pages 134-134

in general, denotes the body of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> those who make profession of arms. In a more restrained <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, militia denotes the trained bands of a town or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, who arm themselves, upon a short warning, for their own <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>. So that, in this sense, militia is opposed to regular or stated troops. See <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">MILITARY</a> State, and FEUDAL System.

MILIUM

Pages 134-134

MILLET, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, belonging to the triandra class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 4th order, Graminae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MILK

Pages 134-142

a well-known fluid, prepared by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> in the breasts of women, and the udders of other animals, for the nourishment of their young.—According to Dr <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CULLEN">Cullen</a>*, milk is a connecting and intermediate substance between animals and vegetables. It seems immediately to be secreted from the chyle, both being a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> liquor of the same consistence: it is most copiously secreted after meals, and of an acescent nature. In most animals who live on vegetables, the milk is acescent; and it is uncertain, though at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> no observation proves the contrary, whether it is not so likewise in carnivorous animals. But, whatever be in this, it is certain, that the milk of all animals who live on vegetables is acescent. Milk being derived from the chyle, we thence conclude its vegetable nature; for in those who live on both promiscuously, more milk is got, and more quickly, from the vegetable than the animal food. Milk, however, is not purely vegetable; though we have a vegetable liquor that resembles its <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, consistence, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, acescence, and the separability of the oily <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>, viz. an emulsion of the nuces oleosae and farinaceous substances. But these want the coagulable part of milk, which seems Milk to be of animal nature, approaching to that of the coagulable lymph of the blood. Milk, then, seems to be of an intermediate nature, between chyle taken up from the intestines and the fully elaborated animal fluid. Its contents are of three kinds: 1st, An oily part, which, whatever may be said concerning the origin of other oils in the body, is certainly immediately derived from the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> of the vegetables taken in; as with these it agrees very exactly in its nature, and would entirely, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we could separate it fully from the coagulable part. Another mark of their agreement is the separability, which proves that the mixture has been lately attempted, but not fully performed. 2dly, Besides this oily, there is a proper coagulable part: And, 3dly, Much <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> accompanies both, in which there is dissolved a saline saccharine substance. These three can be got separate in cheese, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>, and whey; but never perfectly so, a part of each being always blended with every other part. Nothing is more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a>, from what has been said of its immediate nature, than to suppose that it requires no <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSIMILATION">assimilation</a>; and hence has been deduced the reason of its <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXHIBITION">exhibition</a> in the most weakly state of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> body. But wherever we can examine milk, we always find that it coagulates, suffers a decomposition, and becomes acescent. Again, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INFANTS">Infants</a>, who feed entirely on milk, are always troubled with evacuations, which every body observes are not of the same <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> with the food taken; and therefore it appears, that, like all other food, milk turns naturally acescent in the stomach, and only enters the chyle and blood in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of a new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>. It approaches then to the nature of vegetable aliment, but is not capable of its noxious venous <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERMENTATION">fermentation</a>, and therefore has an advantage over it; neither from this quality, like animal food, is it heating in the stomach, and productive of fever; though at the same time, from its <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of coagulable <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, it is more nourishing than vegetables. Milk is the food most universally suited to all ages and states of the body; but it seems chiefly designed by nature as the food of infants. When animals are in the foetus state, their solids are a perfect jelly, incapable of an assimilatory power. In such state nature has perfectly assimilated food, as the albumen ovi in the oviparous, and in the viviparous animals certainly somewhat of the same kind, as it was necessary the vessels should be filled with such a fluid as would make way for an after assimilation. When the infant has attained a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of firmness, as when it is separated from the mother, yet such a degree of weakness still remains as makes somewhat of the same indication necessary; it behoves the infant to have an alkalescent food ready prepared, and at the same time its noxious tendency to be avoided. Milk then is given, which is alkalescent, and, at the same time, has a sufficient quantity of acidity to correct that alkalescence. As the body advances in growth, and the alkalescent tendency is greater, the animal, to obviate that tendency, is led to take vegetable food, as more suited to its strength of assimilation. Dr Cullen observes, that milk is suited to almost all temperaments; and it is even so to stomachs disposed to acescenty, more than those substances which have undergone the venous fermentation; nay, it even cures the heartburn, checks venous fermentation; and precipitates the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LEES">lees</a>, when, by renewal of fermentation, the wine happens to be fouled. It therefore very properly accompanies a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of vegetable aliment: although sometimes its acescenty is troublesome, either from a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> proportion taken in, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> from the degree of it; for, according to certain unaccountable circumstances, different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a> are formed in the stomach in different states of the body; in a healthy body e.g. a mild one; in the hypochondriac <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> sometimes, one of a very acid quality. When the acidity of milk is carried to a great degree, it may prove remarkably refrigerant, and occasion <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> crudities, and the recurrence of intermittent fevers. To take the common notion of its passing unchanged into the blood, it can suffer no solution. But if we admit its coagulum in the stomach, then it may be reckoned among soluble or insoluble foods, according as that coagulum is more or less tenacious. Formerly rennet, which is employed to coagulate milk, was thought an acid; but, from late observations, it appears, that, if it be an acid, it is very different from other acids, and that its coagulum is stronger than that produced by acids. It has been imagined, that a rennet is to be found in the stomachs of all animals, which causes coagulation of milk; but according to Dr Cullen the coagulation of milk seems to be owing to a weak acid in the stomach, the relics of our vegetable food, inducing, in healthy persons, a weak and soluble coagulum: but in different stomachs this may be very different, in these becoming heavy and less soluble food, and sometimes even evacuated in a coagulated undissolved state both by stomach and stool. As milk is acescent, it may be rendered sometimes purgative by mixing with the bile; and some examples of this have been remarked. More <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a>, however, it is reckoned among those foods which occasion costiveness. Hoffman, in his experiments on milk, found that all kinds of it contained much water; and when this was dissipated, found the residuums very different in their solubility. But we must not thence conclude, that the same insolubility takes <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the stomach; for extracts made from vegetables with water are often very insoluble substances, and hardly diffusible through water itself: therefore, in Hoffman's extracts, if we may so call them, of milk, somewhat of the same kind might have appeared; and these substances, which in their <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> state were not so, might appear very insoluble. However, we may allow that milk is always somehow insoluble in the intestines, as it is of a drying nature, and as cheese, &c. is very costive. And this effect shows that milk is always coagulated in the stomach; for if it remained fluid, no feces would be produced, whereas sometimes very hard ones are observed. In the blood vessels, from its animal nature, it may be considered as nutritious; but when we consider its vegetable contents, and acescenty in the prime <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-VIRE">vire</a>, we find that, like animal food, it does not excite that degree of fever in the time of digestion, and that from its acescenty it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> resist <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUTREFACTION">putrefaction</a>. Hence its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in hectic fevers, which, whatever be their cause, appear only to be exacerbations of natural feverish paroxysms, which occur twice every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, commonly after meals, and at night. To obviate these, therefore, we give such an aliment as produces the least exacerbation of these fevers; and of this nature is milk, on account of its accecent vegetable nature. There appears also somewhat peculiar to milk, which requires only a small exertion of the animal powers in order to its assimilation; and besides, in hectic complaints there is wanted an oily, bland food, approaching to the animal nature; so that on all these accounts milk is a diet peculiarly adapted to them, and, in general, to most convalescents, and to those of inflammatory temperaments. So far of milk in general. We shall now speak of the particular kinds which are in common use. The milks of women, mares, and asses, agree very much in their qualities, being very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DILUTE">dilute</a>, having little <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> contents, and, when evaporated to dryness, having these very soluble, containing much saccharine matter, of a very ready accecenty, and, when coagulated, their coagulum being tender and easily broke <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>. From this view they have less oil, and seem to have less coagulable matter than the rest. The milks of cows, sheep, and goats, agree in opposite qualities to the three <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> mentioned; but here there is somewhat more of gradation. Cows milk comes nearest to the former milk: goats milk is less fluid, less sweet, less flatulent, has the largest proportion of insoluble part after coagulation, and indeed the largest proportion of coagulable part; its oily and coagulable parts are not spontaneously separable, never throwing out a cream, or allowing butter to be readily extracted from it. Hence the virtues of these milks are obvious, being more nourishing, though at the same time less easily soluble in weak stomachs, than the three first, less accecent than these, and so more rarely laxative, and peculiarly fitted for the diet of convalescents without fever. The three first again are less nourishing, more soluble, more laxative, as more accecent, and adapted to the convalescents with fever. These qualities, in particular milks, are considerably diversified by different circumstances. First, Different animals, living on the same diet, give a considerably different milk; for there seems to be something in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, abstracting from the aliment, which constitutes a considerable diversity of milk, not only in the same <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of animals, but also in the same animal, at different ages, and at different distances after delivery: this applies to the choice of nurses. Secondly, Milk follows the nature of the aliment more than any other juice in the human body, being more or less fluid and dilute, more or less solid and nourishing, in proportion as these qualities are more or less in the aliment. The nature of the aliment differs according to its time of growth, e.g. old grass being always found more nourishing than young. Aliment, too, is always varied according to the season, as that is warm or dry, moist or cloudy. The milk of each particular kind of animal is fitter for particular purposes, when fed on proper food.—Thus the cow delights in the succulent herbage of the vale: if the sheep be fed there he certainly rots, but on the higher and more dry side of the mountain he feeds pleasantly and healthy; while the goat never stops near the bottom, but ascends to the craggy summit: and certainly the milks of these animals are always best on their proper <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, and that of goats is best on a mountainous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. From a dissertation of Linnæus, we have many observations concerning the diversity of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> on which each animal chooses to feed. All the Swedish plants which could be collected together, were presented alternately to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> animals, and then it appeared that the goat lived on the greatest variety, and even on many which were poisonous to the rest; that the cow chose the first succulent shoots of the plant, and neglected the fructification; which last was preferred by the goat. Hence may be deduced rules concerning the pasturage of different animals; e.g. Farmers find, that, in a pasture which was only fit to feed a certain <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of sheep, an equal number of goats may be introduced, while the sheep are no less nourished than before. It is not easy to assign the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between milk fresh drawn and that detained in the open <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> for some time: but certainly there is some material one, otherwise nature universally would not have directed infants to sucking; and indeed it seems better than the other, fitted for digestion and nourishment. Physicians have supposed that this depended on the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVAPORATION">evaporation</a> of some spirit rector: but our author cannot conceive any such, except common water here; and besides, these volatile parts can hardly be nutritious. A more plausible account seems deducible from mixture: milk new drawn has been but lately mixed, and is exposed to spontaneous separation, a circumstance hurtful to digestion; none of the parts being, by themselves, so easily assimilated as when they are all taken together. Hence, then, milk new drawn is more intimately blended, and therefore then is most proper to the weakly and infants. Another difference in the use of milk exposed for some time to the air, is taking it boiled or unboiled. Physicians have generally recommended the former; but the reason is not easily assigned. Perhaps it is this: Milk kept for some time exposed to the air has gone so far to a spontaneous separation; whereas the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> thoroughly blends the whole, and hence its <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> is not so easy in the stomach; and thus boiled milk is more costive than raw, and gives more feces. Again, When milk is boiled, a considerable quantity of air is detached, as appears from the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FROTH">froth</a> on the surface; and air is the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> of fermentation in bodies; so that after this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> it is not liable to accecenty: for these reasons it is proper for the robust and vigorous. Another difference of milk is, according as it is fluid or coagulated. The coagulated is of two kinds, as induced by rennet, or the natural accecenty of the milk. The former <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> makes the firmer and less easily soluble coagulum; though, when taken with the whey unseparated, it is less difficult of solution, though more so than any other coagulum in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>. Many nations use the latter form, which is easier soluble, but very much accecent, and therefore, in point of solution, should be confined to the vigorous, in point of accecenty, to those who live on alkaloescent food; and in the last case, the Laplanders use it as their chief MILK Milk by evaporation yields a sweet saline matter, of which Dr <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> gives the following proportion: | Twelve ounces of | Left of dry matter | From which water extracted a sweet saline substance amounting to | |------------------|--------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------| | Cows milk | 13 drachms | 1½ drachms | | Goats milk | 12½ | 1½ | | Human milk | 8 | 6 | | Asses milk | 8 | 6 | The saline substance extracted from asses milk was white, and sweet as <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>; those of the others <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, and considerably less sweet; that from cows milk had the least sweetness of any. On distilling 12 quarts of milk in balneo mariae, at least <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> quarts of pure phlegm were obtained; the liquor which afterwards arose was acidulous, and by degrees grew sensibly more and more acid as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a> was <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a>. After this came over a little spirit, and at last, the empyreumatic oil. The remaining solid matter adhered to the bottom of the retort, in the form of elegant shining <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, which being calcined and elixated yielded a portion of fixed alkaline <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>. Milk set in a warm place, throws up to the surface an unctuous cream, from which, by agitation, the butter is easily separated. The addition of alkaline salts prevents this separation, not (as some have supposed) by absorbing an acid from the milk, but by virtue of their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of intimately uniting oily bodies with watery liquors. Sugar, another <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> intermedium betwixt oils and water, has this effect in a greater degree, though that concrete is by no means alkaline, or an absorbent of acids. The sweet saccharine part of the milk remains dissolved in the whey after the separation of the curd or cheesy matter, and may be collected from it in a white crystalline form, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> the whey till all remains of the curdled substance have fallen to the bottom; then filtering, evaporating it to a due consistence, setting it to shoot, and purifying the crystals by solution in water and a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CRYSTALLIZATION">crystallization</a>. Much has been said of the medicinal virtues of this sugar of milk, but it does not seem to have any considerable ones: It is from cows milk that it has been generally prepared; and the crystals obtained from this kind of milk have but little sweetness. When milk is suffered to coagulate spontaneously, the whey proves acid, and on standing grows more and more so till the putrefactive state commences. Sour whey is used as an acid, preferable to the directly vegetable or the mineral acids, in some of the chemical arts; as for dissolving <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> in order to the staining of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>. This acid was commonly made use of in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLEACHING">bleaching</a> of linen, for dissolving and extracting the earthy particles left in the cloth by the alkaline salts and lime employed for cleansing and whitening it. Butter milk is preferred to plain sour milk or sour whey: This last is supposed to give the cloth a yellow colour. Dr Home, in his ingenious treatise on this subject, recommends water acidulated with sulphuric acid (in the proportion of about half an ounce, or at most three <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of an ounce, to a gallon), as preferable in many respects to the acid of milk, or of the more directly vegetable substances. He observes, that the latter are often difficulty procurable, abound with oleaginous particles, and hasten to corruption; whilst the vitriolic acid is cheap, and pure, and indisposed to putrefy: That milk takes five days to perform its office, whilst the vitriolic acid does it in as many hours, perhaps in as many minutes: That this acid contributes also to whiten the cloth, and does not make it weaker though the cloth be kept in it for months. He finds, that acid, as well as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALKALIES">alkalies</a>, extract an oily matter from the cloth, and lose their acidity and alkalinity. Since this treatise appeared, the use of sour milk is very generally superseded by oil of vitriol. It is observable, that asses milk is greatly disposed, on standing for a little time, to become thick and ropy. In the Breslaw collection for the year 1729, there is a remarkable account of milk (which probably was that of the ass) grown so thick and tenacious as to be drawn out into <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> strings, which, when dried, were quite brittle. New cows milk, suffered to stand for some days on the leaves of butterwort or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEW">dew</a>, becomes uniformly thick, slippery, and coherent, and of an agreeable sweet taste, without any separation of its parts. Fresh milk, added to this, is thickened in the same manner, and this successively. In some parts of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, as we are informed in the Swedish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a>, milk is thus prepared for food. New milk has a degree of glutinous quality, so as to be used for joining broken <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARE">ware</a>. There is a far greater tenacity in cheese properly prepared. Milk, when examined by a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MICROSCOPE">microscope</a>, appears composed of numerous globules <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWIMMING">swimming</a> in a transparent fluid. It boils in nearly the same degree of heat with common water; some sorts rather sooner, and some a little later: after boiling, it is less disposed to grow sour than in its natural state. It is coagulated by acids both mineral and vegetable, and by alkalies both fixed and volatile. The coagulum made by acids falls to the bottom of the serum; that made by alkalies swims on the surface, commonly forming (especially with volatile alkalies) a thick coriaceous skin. The serum, with alkalies, proves green or saurious; with acids, it differs little in appearance from the whey that separates spontaneously. The coagulum formed by acids is dissolved by alkalies, and that formed by alkalies is redissolved by acids; but the milk does not in either case resume its original properties. It is coagulated by most of the middle salts, whose basis is an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> or a metallic body; as solution of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a>, fixed sal ammoniac, sugar of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, green and blue vitriol; but not by the chalybeate or purging mineral waters, nor by the bitter salt extracted from the purging waters. Among the neutral salts that have been tried, there is not one that produces any coagulation. They all dilute the milk, and make it less disposed to coagulate with acids or alkalies: Nitre seems to have this effect in a greater degree than the other neutral salts. It is instantly coagulated by highly rectified rectified spirit of wine, but scarcely by a phlegmatic spirit. It does not mingle with expressed oils. All the coagula are dissolved by <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GALL">gall</a>. It has generally been supposed by medical authors, that the milk of animals is of the same nature with chyle, and that the human milk always coagulates in the stomach of infants; but in a late dissertation upon the subject by Mr Clarke, member of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> Irish Academy, we find both these positions controverted. According to him, women's milk, in a healthy state, contains no coagulable, mucilaginous, or cheesy principle, in its composition; or it contains so little, that it cannot admit of any sensible <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>. Dr Rutty states, that it does not afford even a sixth part of the curd which is yielded by cows' milk; and Dr Young denies that it is at all coagulable either by rennets or acids. This is confirmed by Dr Ferris, who in 1782 gained the Harveian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a> medal at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a> by a dissertation upon milk. Mr Clarke informs us, that he has made a vast number of experiments upon women's milk with a view to determine this point. He made use of ardent spirits, all the different acids, infusions of infants' stomachs, and procured the milk of a great many different women; but in no instance, excepting one or two, did he perceive anything like curd. This took place in consequence of a spontaneous acæcency; and only a small quantity of soft flaky matter was formed, which floated in the serum. This he looked upon to be a morbid appearance. The general <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that women's milk is coagulable has arisen from a single circumstance, viz. that infants frequently vomit the milk they suck in a state of apparent coagulation. This greatly perplexed Dr Young; who, after having tried in vain to coagulate human milk artificially, concluded, that the process took place spontaneously in the stomach; and that it would always do so if the milk were allowed to remain in a degree of heat equal to about 96 degrees of Fahrenheit. Mr Clarke took equal quantities of three different kinds of milk, and put them into bottles slightly corked, and these bottles into water, the temperature of which was kept up by a spirit of wine <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-LAMP">lamp</a> as near as possible to 96° of Fahrenheit: but after frequently examining each bottle during the course of the experiment, at the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EXPIRATION">expiration</a> of several hours there was not the smallest tendency towards coagulation to be perceived in any of them; the cream was only thrown to the surface in a thick and adhesive form, and entirely separated from the fluid below, which had something of a gray and wheyish appearance. As the matter vomited by infants is sometimes more adhesive than we can suppose cream to be, Mr Clarke supposed that the curd might be so entangled with the cream, as to be with difficulty separated from it; but having collected a quantity of rich cream from the milk of different women, he repeated the experiment with precisely the same event, not being able in any one instance to produce the smallest quantity of curd. To determine, however, what effects might be produced upon milk by the stomach of an infant, Mr Clarke made the following experiment: Having taken out the stomach of a fetus which had been deprived of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> by the use of instruments, he infused it in a small quantity of hot water, so as to make a strong infusion. He added a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEA">tea</a>-spoonful of this infusion to equal quantities of cows and human milk; the consequence of which was, that the cow's milk was firmly coagulated in a short time, but the human milk was not altered in the least; neither was the least coagulation produced by adding a second and third spoonful to the human milk. "Upon the whole, then, (says Mr Clarke), I am persuaded it will be found, that human milk, in a healthy state, contains little or no curd, and that the general opinion of its nature and properties is founded upon fallacious <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a> and superficial observations made on the matter vomited by infants.
