Greater reliance is to be placed on the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NARRATION">narration</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a>, whose veracity is confirmed, and who was indisputably better informed and more capable of giving an account of the life and exploits of men who flourished in his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and of which he could see the living monuments. Herodotus was born about six years after the famous battle of Marathon; and C. Nepos, as a writer of the Augustan age, flourished about 450 years after the age of the father of history. <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILTON">Milton</a>, John, the most illustrious of the English poets, was descended of a genteel family, seated at a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of their own name, viz. Milton, in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORDSHIRE">Oxfordshire</a>. He was born <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 9, 1608, and received his first <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> under the care of his parents, assisted by a private <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a>. He afterwards passed some time at St Paul's school, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>; in which <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> his father had settled, being engaged in the business of a scrivener. At the age of 17, he was sent to Christ's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>; where he made great progress in all parts of academical learning; but his chief delight was in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>. In 1628, he proceeded bachelor of arts, having performed his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> for it with great applause. His father designed him for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>; but the young <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>'s <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSES">Muses</a> was so strong, that it became impossible to engage him in any other pursuits. In 1632, he took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of arts; and having now spent as much time in the university as became a person who determined not to engage in any of the three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROFESSIONS">professions</a>, he left the college, greatly regretted by his acquaintance, but highly displeased with the usual method of training up youth there for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>; and being much out of humour with the public administration of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> affairs, he grew dissatisfied with the established form of church government, and disliked the whole <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of education practised in the university. His parents, who now dwelt at Horton, near Colnbrook, in Buckinghamshire, received him with unabated affection, notwithstanding he had thwarted their views of providing for him in the church, and they amply indulged him in his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of retirement; wherein he enriched his mind with the choicest stores of Grecian and Roman literature; and his poems of Comus, Allegro, Il Penseroso, and Lycidas, all wrote at this time, would have been sufficient, had he never produced any thing more considerable, to have transmitted his fame to the latest posterity. However, he was not so absorbed in his studies as not to make frequent excursions to London; neither did so much excellence <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> unnoticed among his neighbours in the country, with the most distinguished of whom he sometimes chose to relax his mind, and improve his acquaintance with the world as well as with books.—After five years spent in this manner, he obtained his father's permission to travel for farther improvement. At <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> he became acquainted with the celebrated Hugo Grotius; and from thence travelling into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, he was everywhere caressed by persons of the most eminent <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> and learning. Upon his return home, he set up a genteel academy in Aldersgate street.—In 1641, he began to draw his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEN">pen</a> in defence of the Presbyterian party; and the next year he married the daughter of Richard Powell, Esq., of Forest Hill in Oxfordshire. This lady, however, whether from a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> on account of party, her father being a zealous royalist, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> some other cause, soon thought proper to return to her relations; which so incensed her husband, that he resolved never to take her again, and wrote and published several tracts in defence of the doctrine and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> of divorce. He even made his addresses to another lady; but this incident proved the means of a reconciliation with Mrs Milton. In 1644, he wrote his Tract upon Education; and the restraint on the liberty of the press being <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, he wrote boldly and nobly against that restraint. In 1645, he published his juvenile poems; and about two years after, on the death of his father, he took a smaller house in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">High</a> Holborn, the back of which opened into <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>'s-Inn Fields.—Here he quietly prosecuted his studies, till the fatal catastrophe and death of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I.; on which occasion he published his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TENURE">Tenure</a> of Kings and Magistrates, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTIFICATION">justification</a> of the fact. He was now taken into the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the commonwealth, and made Latin secretary to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of state, who resolved neither to write to others abroad, nor to receive any answers, except in the Latin tongue, which was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to them all. The famous Exon Ebrarius coming out about the same time, our author, by command, wrote and published his Iconoclastes the same year. It was also by order of his masters, backed by the reward of 100l. that in 1651 he published his celebrated piece, entitled Pro Populo Anglicano Defensio; "A Defence of the people of England," in answer to Salmasius's Defence of the King; which performance spread his fame over all <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. He now dwelt in a pleasant house with a garden in Petty France, Westminster, opening into St James's <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARK">Park</a>. In 1652 he buried his wife, who died not long after the delivery of her fourth child; and about the same time he also lost his eyesight, by a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUTTA">gutta</a> serena, which had been growing upon him many years. Cromwell took the reins of government into his own <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> in the year 1653; but Milton still held his office. His leisure hours he employed in prosecuting his studies; wherein he was so far from being discouraged by the loss of his sight, that he even conceived hopes this misfortune would add new vigour to his genius; which in fact seems to have been the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>.—Thus animated, he again ventured upon matrimony: his second lady was the daughter of Captain <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOODSTOCK">Woodstock</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HACKNEY">Hackney</a>: she died in childbirth about a year after. On the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEPOSITION">deposition</a> of the protector, Richard Crom- well, and on the return of the long parliament, Milton being still continued secretary, he appeared again in print; pleading for a farther reformation of the laws relating to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>; and, during the anarchy that ensued, he drew up several schemes for re-establishing the commonwealth, exerting all his faculties to prevent the return of Charles II. England's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESTINY">destiny</a>, however, and Charles's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a> prevailing, our author chose to consult his safety, and retired to a friend's house in Bartholomew <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">Close</a>. A particular prosecution was intended against him; but the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> esteem to which his admirable genius and extraordinary accomplishments entitled him, had raised him so many friends, even among those of the opposite party, that he was included in the general amnesty. This storm being over, he married a third wife, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, daughter of Mr Minshall a Cheshire gentleman; and not long after he took a house in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTILLERY">Artillery</a> Walk, leading to Bunhill Fields. This was his last stage: here he sat <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> for a longer continuance than he had been able to do anywhere; and though he had lost his fortune (for every thing belonging to him went to wreck at the Restoration), he did not lose his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for literature, but continued his studies with almost as much ardour as ever; and applied himself particularly to the finishing his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, the Paradise Lost; one of the noblest poems that ever was produced by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> genius. —It was published in 1667, and his Paradise Regained came out in 1670.—This latter work fell short of the excellence of the former production; although, were it not for the transcendent merit of Paradise Lost, the second <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> would doubtless have stood foremost in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of English epic poems. After this he published many pieces in prose; for which we refer our readers to the edition of his Historical, Poetical, and Miscellaneous Works, printed by Millar, in 2 vols. 4to, in 1753. In 1674, this great man paid the last debt to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> at his house in Bunhill Fields, in the 66th year of his age; and was interred on the 12th of November, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCEL">chancel</a> of St Giles's, Cripplegate.—A decent monument was erected to his memory, in 1737, in Westminster <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">Abbey</a>, by Mr Benson, one of the auditors of the impress.—Milton was remarkably handsome in his person; but his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> was tender, and by no means equal to his incessant application to his studies.—Though greatly reduced in his circumstances, yet he died worth 150l. in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, besides his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a> goods.—He had no son; but left behind him three daughters, whom he had by his first wife. Milton, the name of several places in England; particularly, Milton, or Middleton, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DORSETSHIRE">Dorsetshire</a>, south-west of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLANDFORD">Blandford</a>, near the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DORCHESTER">Dorchester</a>, 114 miles from London. It is chiefly noted for its abbey, built by King Athelstan. The church stands near the south side of the abbey. It is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and magnificent pile of Gothic <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, and contains several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> monuments. Here is an almshouse for six people, who have 12s. a-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a>, and three yards of cloth for a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOWN">gown</a>, one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of shoes and stockings, and 10s. each on St Thomas's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> yearly. Here is a free school, and a market on Tuesdays. Milton, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>, near Sittingbourne and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of Sheppey, 6 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-west of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEVERSHAM">Feversham</a>, and 40 from London. It is also called Middleton from its situation near the middle of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>, i.e. from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEPTFORD">Deptford</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWNS">Downs</a>. The kings of Kent had a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> here, which was castellated, and stood below the church; but was burnt down in Edward the Confessor's time by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">Earl</a> Goodwin, &c. Its church stands near a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> off. On approaching the town up the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>, by the East Swale, it seems hid among the creeks: yet it is a large town; and has a considerable market on Saturdays, and a fair on <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 24. The oysters taken here are the most famous of any in Kent. This town is governed by a portreeve, chosen yearly on St James's day, who supervises the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-WEIGHTS_AND_MEASURES">weights and measures</a> all over the hundred. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">Population</a> 2470 in 1811.

MILTON

Pages 680-686

book i. The following passage from Shakespeare falls not much short of that now mentioned in particularity of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>: O you hard hearts! ye cruel men of Rome! Knew you not Pompey? Many a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> and oft Have you climb'd up to walls and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BATTLEMENTS">battlements</a>, To towers and windows, yea, to chimney tops, Your <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INFANTS">infants</a> in your arms, and there have sat The live-<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> with patient <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a> To see <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> Pompey <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> the streets of Rome; And when you <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> his chariot but appear, Have you not made an universal shout? That Tyber trembled underneath his banks, To hear the replication of your sounds, Made in his concave shore? Julius Caesar, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> i. sc. 1. The following passage is scarcely inferior to either of those mentioned: "Far before the rest, the son of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OSSIAN">Ossian</a> comes: bright in the smiles of youth, fair as the first beams of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>. His long <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> waves on his back; his dark brow is half beneath his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HELMET">helmet</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> hangs loose on the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERO">hero</a>'s side; and his spear glitters as he moves. I fled from his terrible eye, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> Temora." Fingal. The Henriade of Voltaire errs greatly against the foregoing rule: every incident is touched in a summary way, without ever descending to circumstances. This manner is good in a general <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, the purpose of which is to record important transactions: but in a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> it is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> and uninteresting; because it is impracticable to form distinct images of persons <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> things represented in a manner so superficial. It is observed above, that every useless circumstance ought to be suppressed. The crowding such circumstances is, on the one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, not less to be avoided than the conciseness for which Voltaire is blamed, on the other. In the Æneid, Barce, the nurse of Sichæus, whom we never hear of before nor after, is introduced for a purpose not more important than to call <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNA">Anna</a> to her sister Dido: and that it might not be thought unjust in Dido, even in this trivial circumstance, to prefer her husband's nurse before her own, the poet takes care to inform his reader, that Dido's nurse was dead. To this may be opposed a beautiful passage in the same book, where, after Dido's last speech, the poet, without detaining his readers by describing the manner of her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, hastens to the lamentation of her attendants: Dixerat: atque illam media inter talia ferro Collapsam aspicit comites, ensimque cruro Spasmantem, sparsaque manus. It clamor <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AD">ad</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTA">alta</a> Atria; concussam bacchatur fama per urbem; Lamentis gemitique, et foemineo ululatu Tecta fremunt, resonat magnis plangoribus aether. Lib. iv. 663. As an appendix to the foregoing rule, may be added the following observation. That to make a sudden and strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a>, some single circumstance, happily selected, has more power than the most laboured description. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MACBETH">Macbeth</a>, mentioning to his lady some voices he heard while he was murdering the King, says, There's one did laugh in's <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a>, and one cry'd <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">Murder</a>! They wak'd each other; and I stood and heard them: But they did say their prayers, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> them Again to sleep. Lady. There are two lodg'd together. Macbeth. One cry'd, God bless us! and, Amen! the other; As they had seen me with these hangman's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, Listening their fear. I could not say Amen, When they did say, God bless us. Lady. Consider it not so deeply. Macbeth. But wherefore could not I pronounce Amen! I had most need of blessing, and Amen Stuck in my throat. Lady. These deeds must not be thought After these ways; so, it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> make us mad. Macbeth. Methought, I heard a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> cry, Sleep no more! Macbeth doth murder sleep, &c. Act ii. sc. 2. Describing <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Henry: I saw young Harry, with his beaver on, His cuisses on his thighs, gallantly arm'd, Rise from the ground like feather'd <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a>; And vaulted with such ease into his seat, As <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> an angel dropt <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a>, To turn and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> a fiery Pegasus, And witch the world with noble <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORSEMANSHIP">horsemanship</a>. First <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">Part</a> Henry IV. act iii. sc. 5. King Henry. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a>, if thou think'st on Heaven's bliss, Hold up thy hand, make signal of thy hope. He dies, and makes no sign! <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">Second</a> Part Henry VI. act. iii. sc. iii. The same author, speaking ludicrously of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> debilitated with diseases, says, "Half of them dare not shake the snow from off their cascocks, lest they shake themselves to pieces." "I have seen the walls of Balcutha, but they were desolate. The flames had resounded in the halls: and the voice of the people is heard no more. The stream of Clutha was removed from its <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of the walls. The thistle shook there its lonely head: the moss whistled to the wind. The fox looked out from the windows: and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> grass of the wall waved round..." To draw a character is the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> stroke of description. In this Tacitus excels; his portraits are <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> and lively, not a feature wanting or misplaced. Shakespeare, however, exceeds Tacitus in liveliness; some characteristic circumstance being generally invented or laid hold of, which paints more to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> than many words. The following instances will explain our meaning, and at the same time prove our observation to be <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a>. Why should a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, whose blood is warm within, Sit like his grandsire cut in alabaster? Sleep when he <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WAKES">wakes</a>, and creep into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JAUNDICE">jaundice</a>, By being peevish? I tell thee what, Anthonio, (I <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOVE">love</a> thee, and it is my love that speaks), There are a sort of men, whose visages Do cream and mantle like a standing pond; And do a wilful stillness entertain, With purpose to be dress'd in an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> Of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>, gravity, profound conceit; As who should say, I am Sir Oracle, And when I ope my lips, let no dog bark! O my Anthonio! I do know of those, That therefore only are reputed wise, For saying nothing. Merchant of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, act i. sc. 1. Again: "Gratiano speaks an infinite <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of nothing, more than any man in all Venice: his reasons are two grains of wheat hid in two bushels of chaff; you shall seek all day ere you find them; and when you have them, they are not worth the search." Ibid. In the following passage a character is completed by a single stroke: Shallow. O the mad days that I have spent; and to see how many of mine old acquaintance are dead. Silence. We shall all follow, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUSIN">cousin</a>. Shallow. Certain, 'tis certain, very sure, very sure; Death (as the Psalmist saith) is certain to all: all shall die. How a good yoke of bullocks at <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAMFORD">Stamford</a> fair? Slender. Truly cousin, I was not there. Shallow. Death is certain. Is old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">Double</a> of your town living yet? Silence. Dead, Sir. Shallow. Dead! see, see: he drew a good bow: and dead. He <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> a fine shot. How a score of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-EWES">ewes</a> now? Silence. Thereafter as they be. A score of good ewes may be worth ten pounds. Shallow. And is old Double dead? Second part Henry IV. act iii. sc. 2. Describing a jealous husband: "Neither press, coffer, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHEST">chest</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a>, well, vault, but he hath an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a> for the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-REMEMBRANCE">remembrance</a> of such places, and goes to them by his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>. There is no hiding you in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>." Merry Wives of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINDSOR">Windsor</a>, act iv. sc. 3. Congreve has an inimitable stroke of this kind in his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a> of Love for Love: Ben <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEGEND">Legend</a>. Well, father, and how do all at home? how does <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Dick, and brother Val? Vol. XIV. Part II. Sir Sampson. Dick, body o' me, Dick has been dead these two years. I writ you word when you were at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEGHORN">Leghorn</a>. Ben. Mess, that's true; marry I had forgot. Dick's dead, as you say. Act iii. sc. 6. Falstaff speaking of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> Pistol: "He's no swaggerer, hostess; a tame cheater i'<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>; you may strock him as gently as a puppy greyhound; he will not swagger with a Barbary hen, if her feathers turn back in any show of resistance." Second part Henry IV. act ii. sc. 4. Ossian, among his other excellencies, is eminently successful in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>; and he never fails to delight his reader with the beautiful attitudes of his heroes. Take the following instances: "O Oscar! <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a> the strong in arm; but spare the feeble hand. Be thou a stream of many <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-TIDES">tides</a> against the foes of thy people; but like the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GALE">gale</a> that moves the grass to those who ask thine aid.—So Trenmor lived; such Trathal was; and such has Fingal been. My arm was the support of the injured; and the weak rested behind the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a> of my <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>." "We heard the voice of joy on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, and we thought that the mighty Cathmor came. Cathmor the friend of strangers! the brother of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>-haired Cairbar! But their souls were not the same; for the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> of heaven was on the bosom of Cathmor. His towers rose on the banks of Atha: <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> paths led to his halls: seven chiefs stood on these paths, and called the stranger to the feast. But Cathmor dwelt in the wood to avoid the voice of praise." "Dermid and Oscar were one: they reaped the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> together. Their friendship was strong as their steel; and death walked between them to the field. They rush on the foe like two rocks falling from the brow of Arden. Their swords are stained with the blood of the valiant: warriors faint at their name. Who is equal to Oscar but Dermid? who to Dermid but Oscar?" "Son of Comhal, replied the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>, the strength of Morni's arm has failed: I attempted to draw the sword of my youth, but it remains in its place: I throw the spear, but it falls short of the mark: and I feel the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of my shield. We decay like the grass of the mountain, and our strength returns no more. I have a son, O Fingal! his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> has delighted in the actions of Morni's youth; but his sword has not been fitted against the foe, neither has his fame begun. I come with him to battle, to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> his arm. His renown will be a sun to my soul, in the dark <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> of my departure. O that the name of Morni were forgot among the people! that the heroes would only say, Behold the father of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a>!" Some writers, through <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of imagination, fall into <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a>; some are guilty of downright absurdities; and some even rave like madmen. Against such <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> errors one cannot be more effectually warned than by collecting instances; and the first shall be of a contradiction, the most venial of all. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a> speaking of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a>, Interca NAR Intera magno misceri murmure pontum, Emissamque hyemem sensit Neptunus, et imis Stagna refusa vadis; gravior commotus, et alto Prospiciens, summâ placidum caput extulit usque. Æneid, i. 128. Again: When first young Maro, in his boundless mind, A <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> t'outlast immortal Rome <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>'d. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a> on Criticism, 30. The following examples are of absurdities. "Alii paliis è tormento catenis discerti sectique, dimidiatim corpore pugnabant sibi superstites, ac peremptioe partis ultores." Strada, Dec. ii. 2. Il pover huomo, che non sen' era accorto, Andava combattendo, ed era morto. Berni. He fled, but <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a>, left his life behind. Iliad, xi. 443. Full through his neck the weighty falchion sped: Along the pavement roll'd the mutt'<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> head. Odyssey, xxii. 365. The last article is of raving like one mad. Cleopatra speaking to the aspic, Welcome, thou kind deceiver, Thou best of thieves; who, with an easy <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KEY">key</a>, Dost open life, and unperceiv'd by us Ev'n steal us from ourselves; discharging so Death's dreadful office, better than himself; Touching our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a> so gently into slumber, That Death stands by, deceiv'd by his own image, And thinks himself but sleep. Dryden, All for Love, act v. Having discussed what observations occurred upon the thoughts or things expressed, we proceed to what more peculiarly concerns the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> or verbal dress. As words are intimately connected with the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> they represent, the emotions raised by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> and by the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> ought to be concordant. An elevated subject requires an elevated style; what is familiar, ought to be familiarly expressed: a subject that is serious and important, ought to be clothed in plain nervous language; a description, on the other hand, addressed to the imagination, is susceptible of the highest ornaments that sounding words and figurative <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> can bestow upon it. We shall give a few examples of the foregoing rules. A poet of any genius is not apt to dress a high subject in low words; and yet blemishes of that kind are found even in classical works. Horace, observing that men are satisfied with themselves, but seldom with their condition, introduces <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> indulging to each his own choice: Jam faciam quod vultis; <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ERIS">eris</a> tu, qui modo miles, Mercator; tu, consultus modo, rusticus: hinc vos, Vos hinc, mutatis discedite partibus, eia, Quid? statis? nolint. atqui licet esse beatis. Quid causae est, merito quin illis Jupiter ambas Iratus buccas inflat, neque se fore posthaec Tam facilem dicit, votis ut probeat aurem? Sat. i. 16. Jupiter in wrath puffing up both <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHEEKS">cheeks</a>, is a low and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NARRATION">Narration</a>, even ludicrous expression, far from suitable to the gravity and importance of the subject: every one must feel the discordance. The following compleat, sinking far below the subject, is no less ludicrous: Not one looks backward, onward still he goes, Yet ne'er looks forward farther than his nose. Essay on Man, ep. iv. 223. On the other hand, to raise the expression above the tone of the subject, is a fault than which none is more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a>. Take the following instances: Orcan le plus fidèle à servir ses desseins, Ne sous le ciel brûlant des plus noirs Africains. Bajazet, act iii. sc. 8. Les ombres par trois fois ont obscurci les cieux Depuis que le sommeil n'est entré dans vos yeux; Et le jour a trois fois chassé la nuit obscure Depuis que votre corps languit sans nourriture. Phaedra, act i. sc. 3. Assueris. Ce mortel, qui montra tant de zèle pour moi, Vit-il encore? Asaph. — Il voit l'astre qui vous éclaire. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESTHER">Esther</a>, act ii. sc. 3. Oui, c'est Agamemnon, c'est ton roi qui t'éveille; Viens, reconnais la voix qui frappe ton oreille. Iphigenia. No jocund <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> that <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a> drinks to-day, But the great cannon to the clouds shall tell; And the king's rowse the heav'n shall bruit again, Respeaking earthly <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAMLET">Hamlet</a>, act i. sc. 2. In the inner room I spy a winking <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-LAMP">lamp</a>, that weakly strikes The ambient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, scarce kindling into light. Souterne, Fate of Copina, act iii. In the Funeral Orations of the bishop of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEAUX">Meaux</a>, the following <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> are raised far above the tone of the subject; "L'Ocean etonné de se voir traversé tant de fois, en des appareils si <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a>, et pour des causes si differentes, &c." Pag. 6. "Grande reine, je satisfais à vos plus tendres desirs, quand je célèbre ce monarque; et son coeur qui n'a jamais vécu que pour lui, s'éveille, tout poudre qu'il est, et devient sensible, même sous ce drap mortuaire, au nom d'un époux si cher." Pag. 32. The following passage, intended, one would imagine, as a receipt to boil <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, is altogether <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURLESQUE">burlesque</a> by the laboured elevation of the diction: A massy cauldron of stupendous frame They brought, and plac'd it o'er the rising <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a>; Then heap the lighted wood; the flame divides Beneath the vase, and climbs around the sides: In its wide womb they pour the rushing stream: The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> water bubbles to the brim. Iliad, xviii. 495. In a passage at the beginning of the 4th book of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TELEMACHUS">Telemachus</a>, one feels a sudden bound upward without <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a>, which accords not with the subject: "Calypso," My waking thought admits no balmy rest, Nor the sweet bliss of soft oblivion share; But watchful woe distracts my aching <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, My heart the subject of corroding care: From haunts of men with wandering steps and slow I solitary steal, and soothe my pensive woe. Here every substantive is faithfully attended by some tumid epithet. We proceed to a second remark, not less important than the former. No person of reflection but must be sensible, that an incident makes a stronger impression on an eye witness, than when heard at second hand. Wri- ters of genius, sensible that the eye is the best avenue to the heart, represent every thing as passing in our sight; and, from readers or hearers, transform us as it were into spectators: a skilful writer conceals himself; and presents his personages: in a word, every thing becomes dramatic as much as possible. Plutarch, de gloria A- theniensium, observes, that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUCYDIDES">Thucydides</a> makes his reader a spectator, and inspires him with the same passions as if he were an eye witness. In the fine arts, it is a rule to put the capital objects in the strongest point of view; and even to present them oftenest than once, where it can be done. In history <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> is placed in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a>, and in the best light: an equestrian statue is placed in a centre of streets, that it may be seen from many places at once. In no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> is there greater opportuni- ty for this rule than in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>: ——— Sequitur pulcherrimus Astur, Astur equo fidens et versicoloribus armis. ——— Full many a lady I've ey'd with best regard, and many a time Th' <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> of their tongues hath into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONDAGE">bondage</a> Brought my too diligent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EAR">ear</a>: for several virtues Have I lik'd several women: never any With so full soul, but some defect in her Did quarrel with the noblest <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> she ow'd, And put it to the foil. But you, O you, So perfect, and so peerless, are created Of every creature's best. Tempest, act iii. sc. i. Orlando. — Whate'er you are That, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> inaccessible, Under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a> of melancholy boughs, Lose and neglect the creeping hours of time; If ever you have look'd on better days; If ever been where bells have knoll'd to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>; If ever sat at any good man's feast; If ever from your eyelids wip'd a tear, And known what 'tis to pity, and be pity'd; Let gentleness my strong enforcement be, In the which hope I blush, and hide my sword. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a> sen. True is it that we have seen better days, And have with holy <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELL">bell</a> been knoll'd to church; And sat at good men's feasts; and wip'd our eyes Of drops that sacred pity had engender'd; And therefore sit you down in gentleness, And take upon command what help we have, That to your wanting may be minist'red. As you like it. With thee conversing I forget all time; All seasons and their change, all please alike. Sweet is the breath of morn, her rising sweet, With <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARM">charm</a> of earliest birds; pleasant the sun When first on this delightful <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> he spreads His orient beams on herbs, tree, fruit, and flow'r Glist'ring with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEW">dew</a>; fragrant the fertile <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> After soft show'rs; and sweet the coming on Of grateful ev'n'ing mild, the silent night With this her solemn <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRD">bird</a>, and this fair <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, And these the gems of heav'n, her starry train: But neither breath of morn, when she ascends With charm of earliest birds, nor rising sun On this delightful land, nor <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERB">herb</a>, fruit, flow'r, Glist'ring with dew, nor fragrance after show'rs, Nor grateful ev'n'ing mild, nor silent night, With this her solemn bird, nor walk by moon Or glittering <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAR">star</a> light, without thee is sweet. Paradise Lost, book iv. l. 634. "What <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> ye, that ye <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> this proverb, The fathers have eaten sour <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a>, and the children's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> are set on edge? As I live, saith the Lord God, ye shall not have occasion to use this proverb in Israel. If a man keep my judgments to deal truly, he is just, he shall surely live. But if he be a robber, a shedder of blood: if he have eaten upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, and defiled his neighbour's wife: if he have oppressed the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> and needy, have spoiled by violence, have not restored the pledge, have lifted up his eyes to idols, have given forth upon usury, and have taken increase: shall he live? he shall not live: he shall surely die; and his blood shall be upon him. Now, lo, if he beget a son, that seeth all his father's sins, and considereth, and doth not such like; that hath not eaten upon the mountains, hath not lifted up his eyes to idols, nor defiled his neighbour's wife, hath not oppressed any, nor withheld the pledge, neither hath spoiled by violence, but hath given his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> to the hungry, and covered the naked with a garment: that hath not received usury nor increase, that hath executed my judgments, and walked in my statutes: he shall not die for the iniquity of his father; he shall surely live. The soul that sinneth, it shall die; the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son; the righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon him. Have I any <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> that the wicked should die, saith the Lord God; and not that he should return from his ways, and live?" <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EZEKIEL">Ezekiel</a> xvii. A concise comprehensive style is a great ornament in narration; and a superfluity of unnecessary words, not less than of circumstances, a great nuisance. A judicious selection of the striking circumstances, clothed in a nervous style, is delightful. In this style, Tacitus excels all writers, ancient and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a>. Instances are numberless: take the following specimen: "Cerbra hinc praelia, et scepsin in modum latrocinii: per saltus, per paludes; ut cuique fores aut virtus: te- <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a>, proviso, ob iram, ob prædam, jussu, et aliquando ignaris ducibus." Annal. lib. xii. § 39. After Tacitus, Ossian in that respect justly merits the place of distinction. One cannot go wrong for examples in any part of the book. If a concise or nervous style be a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, tautology must be a blemish; and yet writers, fettered by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>, are not sufficiently careful to avoid this slovenly practice: they may be pitied, but they cannot be justified. Take for a specimen the following instances, from the best poet, for versification at least, that England has to boast of: High on his helm celestial lightnings play, His beamy shield emits a living ray; Th' unweary'd blaze incessant streams supplies, Like the red star that fires the autumnal skies. Iliad. 5. Strength and omnipotence invest thy throne. Ibid. 576. So silent fountains, from a rock's tall head, In sable streams soft trickling waters shed. Ibid. ix. 19. His clanging armour rung. Ibid. xii. 94. Fear on their cheek, and horror in their eye. Ibid. xv. 4. The blaze of armour flash'd against the day. Ibid. xvii. 736. As when the piercing blasts of Boreas blow. Ibid. xix. 380. And like the moon, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> refultgent shield Blaz'd with long rays, and gleam'd athwart the field. Ibid. xix. 402. No—could one swiftness o'er the winds prevail, Or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> the pinions of the western gale, All were in vain— Ibid. xix. 604. The humid sweat from every pore descends. Ibid. xxiii. 829. We <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> this article with a curious inquiry. An object, however ugly to the sight, is far from being so when represented by colours or by words. What is the cause of this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>? With respect to painting, the cause is obvious: a good <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a>, whatever the subject be, is agreeable by the pleasure we take in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a>; and this pleasure overbalancing the disagreeableness of the subject, makes the picture upon the whole agreeable. With respect to the description of an ugly object, the cause follows. To connect individuals in the social state, no particular contributes more than language, by the power it possesses of an expeditious <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> of thought, and a lively representation of transactions. But <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> hath not been satisfied to recommend language by its utility merely: independent of utility, it is made susceptible of many beauties, which are directly felt, without any intervening reflection. And this unfolds the mystery; for the pleasure of language is so great, as in a lively description to overbalance the disagreeableness of the image raised by it. This, however, is no encouragement to choose a disagreeable subject; for the pleasure is incomparably greater where the subject and the description are both of them agreeable. The following description is upon the whole agreeable, though the subject described is in itself dismal: <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">Nine</a> times the space that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> day and night To mortal men, he with his horrid crew Lay. Lay vanquished, rolling in the fiery <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a>, Confound though immortal! but his doom Reserv'd him to more wrath; for now the thought Both of lost <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> and lasting pain Torments him: round he throws his baleful eyes That witness'd huge affliction and dismay, Mix'd with obdurate <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIDE">pride</a> and steadfast hate. At once as far as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a> ken he views The dismal situation waste and wild: A dungeon horrible, on all sides round As one great <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FURNACE">furnace</a> flamed; yet from those flames No light, but rather darkness visible Serv'd only to discover sights of woe, Regions of sorrow, doleful shades, where peace And rest can never dwell, hope never comes That comes to all; but torture without end Still urges, and a fiery deluge, fed With ever-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> sulphur unconsum'd! Such place eternal <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> had prepar'd For those rebellious. *Paradise Lost*, book i. 50. An unmanly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEPRESSION">depression</a> of spirits in time of danger is not an agreeable sight; and yet a fine description or representation of it will be relished: *K. Richard*. What must the king do now? must he submit? The king shall do it: must he be depos'd? The king shall be contented: must he lose The name of king? o' God's name let it go: I'll give my jewels for a set of beads; My gorgeous <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, for a hermitage; My gay apparel, for an almsman's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOWN">gown</a>; My figur'd goblets, for a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISH">dish</a> of wood; My sceptre for a palmer's walking <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFF">staff</a>; My subjects, for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of carved saints; And my <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, for a little <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a>; A little, little, grave,—an obscure grave. Or I'll be buried in the king's highway; Some way of common <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TREAD">tread</a>, where subjects feet May hourly trample on their sovereign's head; For on my heart they tread now, whilst I live; And, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BURY">bury</a>'d once, why not upon my head? *Richard II.*, act iii. sc. 6. Objects that strike terror in a spectator, have in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> and painting a fine effect. The picture, by raising a slight <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMOTION">emotion</a> of terror, agitates the mind; and in that condition every beauty makes a deep impression. May not <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTRAST">contrast</a> heighten the pleasure, by opposing our present security to the danger of encountering the object represented. The other shape, If shape it might be call'd that shape had none Distinguishable in member, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a>, or limb; Or substance might be call'd that shadow seem'd, For each seem'd either; <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> it stood as night, Fierce as ten furies, terrible as <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELL">hell</a>, And shook a dreadful dart. *Par. Lost*, book ii. 666. Now storming fury rose, And clamour such as heard in heaven till now Was never: arms on armour clashing bray'd Horrible <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCORD">discord</a>, and the maddling <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a> Of brazen <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHARIOTS">chariots</a> rage; dire was the noise Of conflict; overheard the dismal hiss Of fiery darts in flaming volleys flew, And flying vaulted either <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOST">host</a> with fire. So under fiery cope together rush'd Both battles main, with ruinous assault And unextinguishable rage: all heaven Resounded, and had earth been then, all earth Had to her centre shook. *Ibid.* book vi. 297. Ghost. ————But that I am forbid To tell the secrets of my prison-house, I could a tale unfold, whose lightest word Would <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARROW">harrow</a> up thy soul, freeze thy young blood, Make thy two eyes, like stars start from their spheres, Thy knotty and combined locks to part, And each particular hair to stand on end, Like quills upon the fretful porcupine: But this eternal blazon must not be To ears of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> and blood. *Hamlet*, act i. sc. 8. Gratiano. Poor Desdemona! I'm glad thy father's dead: Thy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATCH">match</a> was mortal to him; and pure grief Shore his old thread in twain. Did he live now, This sight would make him do a desperate turn: Yea, curse his better angel from his side, And fall to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-REPROBATION">reprobation</a>. *Othello*, act v. sc. 8. Objects of horror must be excepted from the foregoing <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a>; for no description, however lively, is sufficient to overbalance the disgust raised even by the idea of such objects. Every thing horrible ought therefore to be avoided in a description. *Narses*, the eunuch who rivalled <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELISARIUS">Belisarius</a> in heroism under the reign of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JUSTINIAN">Justinian</a>, emerged from obscurity A.D. 538. From the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the palace, and the administration of the private revenue, he was suddenly exalted to the head of an army. He is ranked among the few <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUNUCHS">eunuchs</a> who have rescued that unhappy name from the contempt and hatred of mankind. A feeble <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIMINUTIVE">diminutive</a> body concealed the soul of a statesman and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WARRIOR">warrior</a>. His youth had been employed in the management of the loom and distaff, in the cares of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a>, and the service of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a>; but, while his hands were busy, he secretly exercised the faculties of a vigorous and discerning mind. A stranger to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>, he studied in the palace to dissemble, to flatter, and to persuade; and as soon as he approached the person of the emperor, Justinian listened with surprise and pleasure to the manly counsels of his chamberlain and private <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a>. The talents of Narses were tried and improved in frequent embassies; he led an army into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, acquired a practical knowledge of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and presumed to strive with the genius of Belisarius. Twelve years after his return, the eunuch was chosen to achieve the conquest which had been left imperfect by the first of the Roman generals. Instead of being dazzled by vanity or emulation, he seriously declared, that unless he were armed with an adequate force, he would never consent to risk his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> and that of his sovereign. Justinian granted to the favourite what he might have denied to the hero: the Gothic war was rekindled from its ashes, and the preparations were not unworthy of the ancient majesty of the empire. Narses defeated the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOTHS">Goths</a>, the Franks, and the Alamanne. <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NARVA">Narva</a>; Alamanni; the Italian cities opened their gates to the conqueror; he entered the capital in triumph; and having established the seat of his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAVENNA">Ravenna</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> 15 years to govern Italy under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXARCH">Exarch</a>. His virtues, we are told, were stained with avarice; and in this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCIAL">provincial</a> reign he accumulated a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver which surpassed the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a> of a private fortune. His government was oppressive or unpopular; and the general discontent was expressed with freedom by the deputies of Rome. Before the throne of Justinian they boldly declared, that their Gothic servitude had been more tolerable than the despotism of a Greek eunuch; and that unless their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a> were instantly removed, they would consult their own happiness in the choice of a master. Thus was his disgrace the effect of the people's disaffection; and his death, though in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of old <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, was unseasonable and premature, since his genius alone could have repaired the last and fatal <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERROR">error</a> of his life. He died about the year 567, and, as some say, at the advanced age of 95; but this does not appear very probable. See Gibbon's Rom. Hist. vol. iv. 4to edit. p. 194, 298, &c.

MILVIUS

Pages 151-151

Molvius, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Mulvius, Pons; a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> on the Tiber, built by Aemilius Scaurus the censor, in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Sylla, at two miles distance from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, on the Via Flaminia, and repaired by Augustus. From this bridge the ambassadors of the Allobroges were brought back to Rome, by Cicero's management, and made a discovery of Catiline's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSPIRACY">conspiracy</a> (Sallust). Near it Maxentius was defeated by Constantine (Eutropius). Now called Ponte Molle. Milvius, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of Falco. See Falco, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MIMESIS

Pages 151-151

in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>, the imitating the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> and gestures of another person.

MIMI

Pages 151-151

Mimes, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a>, were buffoons <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> mimics, who entertained the people by taking off certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, using such gestures as suited the persons or subjects they represented. There were on the Roman stage <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> performers of this kind, called mimeae. The word is derived from μιμεῖν, I imitate. Some of the mimi acted their parts to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of the tibia; these they called mimauli. Mimi were also a kind of farces or ludicrous comedies, generally performed by one person. They had no acts, nor any exordium.—The mimi were introduced upon the Roman stage <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> after comedy and tragedy had arrived at their full perfection. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTOR">actor</a> wore no mask, but smeared his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOOT">soot</a>, was dressed in lambskin, wore garlands of ivy, and carried a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASKET">basket</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> and herbs, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>, and diverted the audience with apish tricks and ridiculous dances. This was the state of the mimai soon after their first introduction; but they underwent many alterations, which it would take up too much room to relate, and which are not of sufficient importance to justify a detailed account. See Pantomimes.

MIMOSA

Pages 151-151

the Sensitive Plant; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the mimosæ class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 3rd order, Lomentaceæ. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. The name mimosa, signifying "mimic," is given to this genus on account of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSIBILITY">sensibility</a> of the leaves, which, by their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, mimic <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> imitate, as it were, the motion of animals.

MINA

Pages 151-151
or Maneh, a species of money which properly signifies one part or ounce. It is observed that this word occurs only in the books of Kings, Chronicles, Ezra, and Ezekiel. This prophet (xlv. 12.) tells us, that the mina or maneh was valued at 60 shekels, which in gold make of our English money about 54½ pounds, and in silver almost seven pounds. Thus for the Hebrew maneh. But the Greek or Attic mina, which is probably that mentioned in the books of the Maccabees and in the New Testament, is valued at 100 drachmae, or about 21. 17s. sterling. There was also a lesser mina, which was valued at 75 drachmae.

MINAGNGHINIM

Pages 151-151

a pulsative <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> of music, among the Hebrews, which was a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> of wood, fitted with a handle; over this table was stretched.

MINCHA

Pages 151-152

in the Jewish customs, offerings of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAL">meal</a>, cakes, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> biscuits, made in the temple of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>. The Seventy have sometimes preserved this word in their translation; but instead of mincha they read <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANNA">manna</a>, which doubtless was the received <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRONUNCIATION">pronunciation</a> in their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. We find manna in the same <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, in Baruch i. 10. Levit. ii. 3. &c. See the Greek of Jerem. xvii. 26. Dan. ii. 46. 2 Kings viii. 5. xvii. 7. xx. 12. 2 Chron. vii. 7. Nehem. xiii. 5. 9. &c.

MINCHING-HAMPTON

Pages 152-152

a town of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GLOUCESTERSHIRE">Gloucestershire</a>, 20 miles from Bath and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a>, and near 90 from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, with a market on Tuesdays, and two <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> is pretty <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, being bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the Stroud, and on the south by the brook Avening; and has 12 hamlets belonging to it, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> called Amberley. Here is a good large rectory <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, built in form of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>. In 1811 the inhabitants amounted to 3246, many of whom are employed in the woollen manufacture. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2. 14. N. Lat. 51. 38.

MINCIUS

Pages 152-152

a river of the Transpadana in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>; running from, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rather transmitted through, the Lacus Benacus, from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> to south, into the Padus; but originally rising in the Rhetian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a>. Now Mincio or Menzo, running through the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANTUA">Mantua</a> into the Po.

MINDANAO

Pages 152-152
or MAGINDANAO, a large island of Asia in the East Indies, and one of the Philippines; 160 miles in length, and 120 in breadth. The interior parts contain several chains of lofty mountains, between which are extensive plains, where vast herds of cattle roam at large in the most delicious pastures. Several deep valleys also intersect, as it were, certain parts of the country, through which, during the rainy seasons, vast torrents pour from the mountains, and force their impetuous way to the sea. The rains and vapours which lodge in the plains diffuse themselves into meandering rivulets, and, collecting a variety of small streams in their course, approach the sea in the form of considerable rivers.—The sovereign of Magindanao is a powerful prince, and has several inferior chiefs, who acknowledge him as their head. Nevertheless, there are others of them who refuse submission to him, and are consequently in a continual state of war; so that peace, at least, does not appear to be one of the blessings of this island. The Spaniards, indeed, assert their right to the entire dominion of Magindanao; but it is mere assertion; for though they have forts, &c. on the island, it is by no means in a state of subjection to their nation. The air is esteemed salubrious, particularly in the vicinity of the sea. The heat there is not, in any degree, so intense as might be expected in a country which is situated on the very verge of the torrid zone. The prevalence of the easterly winds, in that part of the coasts which is washed by the Pacific ocean, renders the air cool and pleasant, the trade wind blowing incessantly on its shores. It acts, indeed, with so much power as to sweep the whole breadth of the island; and though in its passage it loses much of its strength, it retains a sufficient degree of force to afford refreshing breezes to the inhabitants of the western shore. The interior parts are much colder, from a very cloudy atmosphere, which frequently hangs over the summits of the mountains in thick and humid vapours. The soil, which is very exuberant, is suited to the cultivation of the whole vegetable tribes. Rice is produced in the greatest abundance; a pecul, or 133 pounds, may be purchased for a Spanish dollar. Every part of the island abounds with buffaloes, cows, hogs, goats, &c. It affords also great variety of fowls, and a species of duck, whose head is of a fine scarlet colour. Here is also a small breed of horses, remarkable for their spirit. The natives, however, principally employ buffaloes in the various branches of husbandry and agriculture. The city of Magindanao is situated on the southeast side of the island, has a river capable of admitting small vessels, and carries on a considerable trade with Manilla, Sooloo, Borneo and the Moluccas. Their exports are rice, tobacco, bees wax, and spices; in return for which they receive coarse cloths of Cermandel, China ware, and opium. The village or town of Samboingan is situated on the banks of a small rivulet, which empties itself immediately into the sea, and is agreeably shaded by groves of cocoa trees. The number of its inhabitants is about 1000, among which are included the officers, soldiers, and their respective families. In its environs there are several small look-out houses, erected on posts of twelve feet high, in all of which a constant guard is kept; so that it appears as if the Spaniards were in a continual state of enmity with the natives. The houses are built of those simple materials which are of very general use in the eastern seas. They are erected on posts, and built of bamboo, covered with mats; the lower apartments serve for their hogs, cattle, and poultry, and the upper ones are occupied by the family.

MINDELHEIM

Pages 152-152

a district of Germany, in Suabia, lying between the bishoprick of Augsburg and the abbacy of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KEMPTEN">Kempten</a>, which is 20 miles in length and 16 in breadth.

MINDEN

Pages 152-153

a considerable town of Germany, in the circle of Westphalia; and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a territory of the same name; seated on the river Weser, which renders it a trading <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. It formerly belonged to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>, who secularized the bishoprick. It is 27 miles east by south of Osnaburg, and 37 west of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HANOVER">Hanover</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 9. 5. N. Lat. 52. 22. Minden (the principality of), in Germany, lies in the circle of Westphalia, to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAVENSBURG">Ravensburg</a>, and along each side of the river Weser. It is about 22 miles <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, and Minden and Petershagen are the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> places. It was formerly a bishopric, but is now secularized; was afterwards ceded to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRANDENBURG">Brandenburg</a>, and is now annexed to the new <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of Westphalia.

MINDORA

Pages 153-153

an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, in the East Indies, and one of the Philippines, 50 miles in circumference, and separated from Luzon by a narrow channel. It is full of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, which abound in palm trees and all sorts of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>. The inhabitants are idolaters, and pay tribute to the Spaniards, to whom this island belongs.

MINE

Pages 153-158

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a deep pit under ground, from whence various kinds of minerals are dug out; but the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> is more particularly applied to those which yield <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>. Where <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> only are procured, the appellation of quarries is universally bestowed upon the places from which they are dug out, however deep they may be. The internal parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, as far as they have been yet investigated, do not consist of one uniform substance, but of various <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STRATA">strata</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> beds of substances, extremely different in their appearances, specific gravities, and chemical qualities, from one another. Neither are these strata similar to one another either in their <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> or appearance in different countries; so that even in the short <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of half a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a>, the strata <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> be found quite different from what they are in another <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. As little are they the same either in depth or solidity. Innumerable cracks and fissures, by the miners called lodes, are found in every one of them; but these are so entirely different in size and shape, that it is impossible to form any inference from their size in one place to that in another. In these lodes or fissures the metallic ore is met with; and, considering the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> uncertainty of the dimensions of the lodes, it is evident that the business of mining, which depends on that size, must in like manner be quite uncertain and precarious. Mr Price, in his treatise on the Cornish <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINES">mines</a>, observes, that "the comparative smallness of the largest fissures to the bulk of the whole earth is really wonderful. In the finest <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-POTTERY">pottery</a> we can make, by a microscopic view, we may discover numerous cracks and fissures, so small as to be impenetrable by any fluid, and impervious to the naked eye; as, by the laws of nature originally imposed by the Creator, it happens that <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> cannot <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> itself into <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> masses, without leaving fissures between them, and yet the very fissures are as necessary and useful as the strata through which they <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a>. They are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAINS">drains</a> that carry off the redundant moisture from the earth; which, but for them, would be too full of fens and bogs for animals to live or <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> to thrive on. In these fissures, the several ingredients which form lodes, by the continual passing of waters, and the menstrum of metals, are brought out of the adjacent strata, collected and conveniently lodged in a narrow channel, much to the advantage of those who search for and pursue them; for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> metals and minerals were more dispersed, and scattered thinly in the body of the strata, the trouble of finding and getting at them would be endless, and the expense of procuring them exceed the value of the acquisition. The insides of the fissures are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> coated over with a hard, crystalline, earthy substance or Mine-rind, which very often, in the breaking of hard ore, comes off along with it, and is commonly called the capels or walls of the lode: but Mr Price is of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that the proper walls of the lode are the sides of the fissure itself, and not the coat <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> mentioned, which is the natural <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a> upon those walls, furnished perhaps by the contents of the fissures, or from oozings of the surrounding strata. The breadth of a lode is easily known by the distance betwixt the two incrustated sides of the stones of ore; and if a lode yields any kind of ore, it is a better sign that the walls be regular and smooth, or at least that one of them be so, than otherwise; but there are not many of these fissures which have regular walls until they have been sunk <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> some fathoms. Thus the inner <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the fissure in which the ore lies, is all the way bounded by two walls of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, which are generally <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to one another, and include the breadth of the vein or lode. Whatever <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> of inclination some fissures make in the solid strata at their beginning, they generally continue to do the same all alone. Some are very uncertain in their breadth, as they may be small at their upper part and wide underneath, and vice versa. Their regular breadth, as well as their depth, is subject to great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a>; for though a fissure may be many fathoms wide in one particular place, yet a little further east or west it may not perhaps be one inch wide. This excessive variation happens generally in very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a> strata, when the vein or fissure is squeezed, as it were, through hard rocks which seem to compress and straiten it. A true vein or fissure, however, is never entirely obliterated, but always shows a string of metallic ore or of a veiny substance; which often serves as a leader for the miners to follow, until it sometimes leads them to a large and richly impregnated part. Their length is in a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> unlimited, though not the space best fitted for yielding metal.
