See Architecture. MINUTE is also used for a short memoir, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> sketch of a thing taken in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>. MINUTIUS Felix. See Felix. MINYÆ, a name given to the inhabitants of Orchomenos in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOEOTIA">Boeotia</a>, from Minyas <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. Orchomenos the son of Minyas gave his name to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the country; and the inhabitants still retained their original appellation, in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a> to the Orchomenians of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCADIA">Arcadia</a>. A colony of Orchomenians passed into Thessaly and settled in Iolchos; from which circumstance the people of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and particularly the Argonauts, were called Minyæ. This name they received, according to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of some, not because a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of Orchomenians had settled among them, but because the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> and noblest of them were descended from the daughters of Minyas. Part of the Orchomenians accompanied the sons of Codrus when they migrated to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IONIA">Ionia</a>. The descendants of the Argonauts, as well as the Argonauts themselves, received the name of Minyæ. They first inhabited <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEMNOS">Lemnos</a>, where they had been born from the Lemnian women who had murdered their husbands. They were driven from Lemnos by the Pelasgi, about 1160 before the Christian era, and came to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LACONIA">Laconia</a>, from whence they passed into Calliste with a colony of Lacedemonians.

MIQUELETS

Pages 322-322

a name given to the Spaniards who inhabit the Pyrenean <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> on the frontiers of Arragon and Catalonia, and live by robbing.

MIQUELON

Pages 322-322

a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> to the southwest of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> May in Newfoundland, ceded to the French by the peace of 1763, for drying and curing their fish. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 54° 30'. N. Lat. 47° 22'.

MIRABILIS

Pages 322-322

Marvel of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERU">Peru</a>; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the pentandra class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking with those of which the order is doubtful. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MIRACLE

Pages 322-327

in its original <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, is a word of the same import with wonder; but in its usual and more appropriate signification, it denotes "an effect contrary to the established <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> and course of things, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a sensible deviation from the known laws of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>." That the visible world is governed by stated general rules, or that there is an order of causes and effects established in every <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the system of nature which falls under our observation, is a fact which cannot be controverted. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the Supreme Being, as some have supposed, be the only real <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGENT">agent</a> in the universe, we have the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, that, in the particular system to which we belong, he acts by stated rules. If he employs inferior agents to conduct the various motions from which the phenomena result, we have the same evidence that he has subject- ed those agents to certain fixed laws, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called the laws of nature. On either <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a>, effects which are produced by the regular operation of these laws, or which are conformable to the established course of events, are properly called <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a>; and every <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a> to this constitution of the natural system, and the correspondent course of events in it, is called a miracle. If this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a> of a miracle be <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a>, no event can be deemed miraculous merely because it is strange, or even to us unaccountable; since it may be nothing more than a regular effect of some unknown <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a> of nature. In this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> earthquakes are rare; and for monstrous births perhaps no particular and satisfactory account can be given: yet an earthquake is as regular an effect of the established laws of nature as any of those with which we are most intimately acquainted; and under circumstances in which there would always be the same kind of production, the monster is nature's genuine issue. It is therefore necessary, before we can pronounce any effect to be a true miracle, that the circumstances under which it is produced be known, and that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> course of nature be in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> understood; for in all those <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> in which we are totally ignorant of nature, it is impossible to determine what is, or what is not, a deviation from its course. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">Miracles</a>, therefore, are not, as some have represented them, appeals to our <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a>. They suppose some antecedent knowledge of the course of nature, without which no proper judgment can be formed concerning them; though with it their reality may be so apparent as to prevent all possibility of a dispute. Thus, were a physician to cure a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLIND">blind</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of a cataract, by anointing his eyes with a chemical <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> which we had never before seen, and to the nature and effects of which we are <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> strangers, the cure would undoubtedly be wonderful; but we could not pronounce it miraculous, because, for any thing known to us, it might be the natural effect of the operation of the unguent on the eye. But were he to recover his patient merely by commanding him to see, or by anointing his eyes with spittle, we should with the utmost confidence pronounce the cure to be a miracle; because we know perfectly that neither the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> nor human spittle have, by the established constitution of things, any such power over the diseases of the eye. No one is now ignorant, that persons apparently dead are often restored to their families and friends, by being treated in the manner recommended by the Humane <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>. To the vulgar, and sometimes even to men of science, these effects appear very wonderful; but as they are known to be produced by physical agency, they can never be considered as miraculous deviations from the laws of nature. On the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, no one could doubt of his having witnessed a real miracle who had seen a person that had been four days dead come alive out of his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> at the call of another, or who had even beheld a person exhibiting all the symptoms of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> instantly resuscitated merely by being desired to live. Thus easy is it, in all cases in which the course of nature is understood, to determine whether any particular event be really a miracle; whilst in circumstances where we know nothing of nature and its course, even a true miracle, were it performed, could not be admitted as such, or carry any conviction to the mind of a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>. If miracles be effects contrary to the established constitution of things, we are certain that they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> never be performed on trivial occasions. The constitution of things was established by the Creator and Governor of the universe, and is undoubtedly the offspring of infinite <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> pursuing a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> for the best of purposes. From this plan no deviation can be made but by God himself, or by some powerful being acting with his permission. The plans devised by wisdom are steady in proportion to their perfection, and the plans of infinite wisdom must be absolutely perfect. From this consideration, some men have ventured to conclude, that no miracle was ever wrought, or can rationally be expected; but mature reflection must soon satisfy us that all such conclusions are hasty. Man is unquestionably the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> creature in this world, and apparently the only one in it who is capable of being made acquainted with the relation in which he stands to his Creator. We cannot, therefore, doubt, but that such of the laws of nature as extend not their operation beyond the limits of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> were established chiefly, if not solely, for the good of mankind; and if, in any particular circumstances, that good can be more effectually promoted by an occasional deviation from those laws, such a deviation may be reasonably expected. Were man, in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of his mental and corporeal powers, subjected to the laws of physical <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a>, the circumstances supposed would indeed never occur, and of course no miracle could be admitted. But such is not the nature of man. Without repeating what has been said elsewhere (See <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METAPHYSICS">Metaphysics</a>, Part III. Chap. V.) of necessity and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, we shall here take it for granted, that the relation between motives and actions is different from that between cause and effect in physics; and that, mankind have such command over themselves, as that by their voluntary conduct, they can make themselves in a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> degree either happy or miserable. We know likewise from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, that, by some means or other, almost all mankind were once sunk into the grossest ignorance of the most important truths; that they knew not the Being by whom they were created and supported; that they paid divine <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADORATION">adoration</a> to stocks, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, and the vilest reptiles; and that they were slaves to the most impious, cruel, and degrading superstitions. From this depraved state it was surely not unworthy of the common "Father of all" to rescue his helpless creatures, to enlighten their understandings that they might perceive what is <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, and to present to them motives of sufficient force to engage them in the practice of it. But the understandings of ignorant barbarians cannot be enlightened by arguments; because of the force of such arguments as regard moral science they are not qualified to judge. The philosophers of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> and Rome inculcated, indeed, many excellent moral precepts, and they sometimes ventured to expose the absurdities of the reigning <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>; but their lectures had no influence upon the multitude; and they had themselves imbibed such erroneous notions respecting the attributes of the Supreme Being, and the nature of the human <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>, and converted those notions into first principles, of which they would not permit. permit an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a>, that even among them a thorough reformation was not to be expected from the powers of reasoning. It is likewise to be observed, that there are many truths of the utmost importance to mankind, which unassisted reason could never have discovered. Amongst these we may confidently reckon the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-IMMORTALITY">immortality</a> of the soul, the terms upon which God will be reconciled to sinners; and the manner in which that all-perfect Being may be acceptably worshipped; about all of which philosophers were in such uncertainty, that, according to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a>, "Whatever is set right, and as it should be, in the present evil state of the world, can be so only by the particular interposition of God." An immediate <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVELATION">revelation</a> from Heaven, therefore, was the only method by which infinite wisdom and perfect goodness could <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REFORM">reform</a> a bewildered and vicious <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>. But this revelation, at whatever <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> we suppose it given, must have been made directly either to some chosen individuals commissioned to instruct others, or to every man and woman for whose benefit it was ultimately intended. Were every person instructed in the knowledge of his duty by immediate <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSPIRATION">inspiration</a>, and were the motives to practise it brought home to his mind by God himself, human nature would be wholly changed: men would not be masters of their own actions: they would not be moral agents, nor by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> be capable either of reward or of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>. It remains, therefore, that if God has been graciously pleased to enlighten and reform mankind, without destroying that moral nature which is essential to virtue, he can have done it only by revealing his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> to certain chosen instruments, who were the immediate instructors of their contemporaries, and through them have been the instructors of succeeding ages. Let us suppose this to have been actually the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, and consider how those inspired teachers could communicate to others every truth which had been revealed to themselves. They might easily, if it was part of their duty, deliver a sublime system of natural and moral science, and establish it upon the common basis of experiment and demonstration; but what foundation could they lay for those truths which unassisted reason cannot discover, and which, when they are revealed, appear to have no necessary relation to any thing previously known? To a bare <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AFFIRMATION">affirmation</a> that they had been immediately received from God, no rational being could be expected to assent. The teachers might be men of known veracity, whose simple assertion would be admitted as sufficient evidence for any fact in conformity with the laws of nature; but as every man has the evidence of his own consciousness and experience that revelations from heaven are deviations from these laws, an assertion so apparently extravagant would be rejected as false, unless supported by some better <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> than the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> affirmation of the teacher. In this state of things, we can conceive no evidence sufficient to make such doctrines be received as the truths of God, but the power of working miracles committed to him who taught them. This would, indeed, be fully adequate to the purpose. For if there were nothing in the doctrines themselves impious, immoral, or contrary to truths already known, the only thing which could render the teacher's assertion incredible, would be its implying such an intimate <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> with God as is contrary to the established course of things, by which men are left to acquire all their knowledge by the exercise of their own faculties. Let us now suppose one of those inspired teachers to tell his countrymen, that he did not desire them, on his ipse dixit, to believe that he had any preternatural communion with the Deity, but that for the truth of his assertion he would give them the evidence of their own senses; and after this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a> let us suppose him immediately to raise a person from the dead in their presence, merely by calling upon him to come out of his grave. Would not the only possible objection to the man's veracity be removed by this miracle? and his assertions that he had received such and such doctrines from God be as fully credited, as if it related to the most common occurrence? Undoubtedly it would; for when so much preternatural power was visibly communicated to this person, no one could have reason to question his having received an equal portion of preternatural knowledge. A palpable deviation from the known laws of nature, in one instance, is a sensible proof that such a deviation is possible in another; and in such a case as this, it is the witness of God to the truth of a man. Miracles, then, under which we include prophecy, are the only <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> evidence which can be given of divine inspiration. When a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, or any <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> truth, is to be revealed from heaven, they appear to be absolutely necessary to enforce its reception among men; and this is the only case in which we can suppose them necessary, or believe for a moment that they ever have been or will be performed. The history of almost every religion abounds with relations of prodigies and wonders, and of the intercourse of men with the gods; but we know of no religious system, those of the Jews and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> excepted, which appealed to miracles as the sole evidence of its truth and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>. The pretended miracles mentioned by Pagan historians and poets are not said to have been publicly wrought to enforce the truth of a new religion contrary to the reigning idolatry. Many of them may be clearly shown to have been mere natural events; (see <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGIC">MAGIC</a>). Others of them are represented as having been performed in secret on the most trivial occasions, and in obscure and fabulous ages <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> to the era of the writers by whom they are recorded. And such of them as at first view appear to be best attested, are evidently tricks contrived for interested purposes; to flatter power, or to promote the prevailing superstitions. For these reasons, as well as on account of the immoral character of the divinities by whom they are said to have been wrought, they are altogether unworthy of examination, and carry in the very nature of them the completest proofs of falsehood and imposture. (Α) Εν ταῖς ἐκείνων, ὡς ἂν ἦν ἀπὸ τῆς ἑτοῖμης συνέλευσι, ἐν τοῖς ἐκείνους καθαρίσασιν πολιτεύεται. Θεῖον μοιχεῖα ἐνδεχόμενον. But the miracles recorded of Moses and of Christ bear a very different character. None of them is represented as wrought on trivial occasions. The writers who mention them were eye witnesses of the facts; which they affirm to have been performed publicly, in attestation of the truth of their respective systems. They are indeed so incorporated with these systems, that the miracles cannot be separated from the doctrines; and if the miracles were not really performed, the doctrines cannot possibly be true. Besides all this, they were brought in support of revelations which opposed all the religious systems, superstitions, and prejudices, of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> in which they were given: a circumstance which of itself sets them, in point of authority, infinitely above the Pagan prodigies, as well as the lying wonders of the Romish <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. It is indeed, we believe, universally admitted, that the miracles mentioned in the book of Exodus and in the four Gospels, might, to those who <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> them performed, be sufficient evidence of the divine inspiration of Moses and of Christ; but to us it may be thought that they are no evidence whatever, as we must believe in the miracles themselves, if we believe in them at all, upon the bare authority of human testimony. Why, it has been sometimes asked, are not miracles wrought in all ages and countries? If the religion of Christ was to be of perpetual <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>, every <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> of men ought to have complete evidence of its truth and divinity. To the performance of miracles in every age and in every country, perhaps the same objections <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIE">lie</a> as to the immediate inspiration of every individual. Were those miracles universally received as such, men would be so overwhelmed with the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> rather than with the force of their authority, as hardly to remain masters of their own conduct; and in that case the very end of all miracles would be defeated by their frequency. The truth, however, seems to be, that miracles so frequently repeated would not be received as such, and of course would have no authority; because it would be difficult, and in many cases impossible, to distinguish them from natural events. If they recurred regularly at certain intervals, we could not prove them to be deviations from the known laws of nature, because we should have the same experience for the one <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of events as for the other; for the regular succession of preternatural effects, as for the established constitution and course of things. Be this, however, as it may, we shall take the liberty to affirm, that for the reality of the Gospel miracles we have evidence as convincing to the reflecting mind, though not so striking to vulgar <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a>, as those had who were <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> with Christ and his apostles, and actually saw the mighty works which he performed. To the admirers of Mr Hume's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> this assertion will appear an extravagant <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARADOX">paradox</a>; but we hope to demonstrate its truth from principles which, consistently with himself, that author could not have denied. He has indeed endeavoured to prove, that "no testimony is sufficient to establish a miracle;" and the reasoning employed for this purpose is, that "a miracle being a violation of the laws of nature which a firm and unalterable experience has established, the proof against a miracle, from the very nature of the fact, is as entire as any argument from experience can be; whereas our experience of human veracity, which (according to him) is the sole foundation of the evidence of testimony, is far from being uniform, and can therefore never preponderate against that experience which admits of no exception." This boasted and plausible argument has with equal candour and acuteness been examined by Dr Campbell*, who justly observes, that so far is experience from being the sole foundation of the evidence of testimony, that, on the contrary, testimony is the sole foundation of by far the greater part of what Mr Hume calls firm and unalterable experience; and that if in certain circumstances we did not give an implicit <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> to testimony, our knowledge of events would be confined to those which had fallen under the immediate observation of our own senses. For a short view of this celebrated controversy in which the Christian so completely vanquishes the philosopher, see the word <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ABRIDGMENT">ABRIDGMENT</a>. But though Dr Campbell has exposed the sophistry of his opponent's reasoning, and overturned the principles from which he reasons, we are persuaded that he might safely have joined issue with him upon those very principles. To us, at least, it appears that the testimony upon which we receive the Gospel miracles is precisely of that kind which Mr Hume has acknowledged sufficient to establish even a miracle. "No testimony (says he) is sufficient to establish a miracle, unless the testimony be of such a kind that its falsehood would be more miraculous than the fact which it endeavours to establish. When one tells me that he saw a dead man restored to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, I immediately consider with myself whether it be more probable that this person should either deceive or be deceived, or that the fact which he relates should really have happened. I weigh the one miracle against the other; and according to the superiority which I discover, I pronounce my decision, and always reject the greater miracle." In this passage every reader may remark what did not escape the perspicacious eye of Dr Campbell, a strange confusion of terms; but as all miracles are equally easy to the Almighty; and as Mr Hume has elsewhere observed, that "the raising of a feather, when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> wants ever so little of a force requisite for that purpose, is as real a miracle as the raising of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> or a ship into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>;" candour obliges us to suppose, that by talking of greater and less miracles and of always rejecting the greater, he meant nothing more, but that of two deviations from the known laws of nature he always rejects that which in itself is least probable. If, then, we can show that the testimony given by the apostles and other first preachers of Christianity to the miracles of their <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">Master</a> would, upon their supposition that those miracles were not really performed, have been as great a deviation from the known laws of nature as the miracles themselves, the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a> must be considered as evenly poised by opposite miracles; and whilst it continues so, the judgment must remain in a state of suspense. But if it shall appear, that in this case the false testimony would have been a deviation from the laws of nature less probable in itself than the miracles recorded in the Gospels, the balance will be instantly destroyed; and by Mr Hume's maxim we shall be obliged to reject the supposition of falsehood in the testimony. Miracle of the apostles, and admit the miracles of Christ to have been really performed. In this argument we need not waste time in proving that those miracles, as they are represented in the writings of the New <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a>, were of such a nature, and performed before so many witnesses, that no imposition could possibly be practised on the senses of those who affirm that they were present. From every page of the Gospels this is so evident, that the philosophical adversaries of the Christian faith never suppose the apostles to have been themselves deceived, but boldly accuse them of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> false witness. But if this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACCUSATION">accusation</a> be well founded, their testimony itself is as great a miracle as any which they record of themselves or of their Master. It has been shown elsewhere (see Metaphysics, No 138.), that by the law of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSOCIATION">association</a>, which is one of the laws of nature, mankind, in the very <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of learning to speak, necessarily learn to speak the truth; that <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> and relations are in the mind of every man so closely associated with the words by which they are expressed in his native tongue, and in every other <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of which he is master, that the one cannot be entirely separated from the other; that therefore no man can on any occasion speak falsehood without some effort; that by no effort can a man give consistency to an unpremeditated detail of falsehood, if it be of any length, and include a number of particulars; and that it is still less possible for several men to agree in such a detail, when at a distance from each other, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> questioned by their enemies. This being the case, it follows, if the testimony of the apostles to their own and their Master's miracles be false, either that they must have concerted a consistent scheme of falsehood, and agreed to publish it at every hazard; or that God, or some powerful agent appointed by him, must have dissolved all the associations formed in their minds between ideas of sense and the words of language, and arbitrarily formed new associations, all in exact conformity to each other, but all in direct contradiction to truth. One or other of these events must have taken <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; because, upon the supposition of falsehood, there is no other alternative. But such a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> and formation of associations as the latter implies, must, to every man who shall attentively consider it, appear to be as real a miracle, and to require as great an exertion of power, as the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESURRECTION">resurrection</a> of the dead. Nor is the supposed voluntary agreement of the apostles in a scheme of falsehood an event less miraculous. When they sat <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to fabricate their pretended revelation, and to contrive a series of miracles to which they were unanimously to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> for its truth, it is plain, since they proved successful in their daring enterprise, that they must have clearly foreseen every possible circumstance in which they could be placed, and have prepared consistent answers to every question that could be put to them by their most inveterate and most enlightened enemies; by the statesman, the lawyer, the philosopher, and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>. That such foreknowledge as this would have been miraculous, will not surely be denied; since it forms the very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> which we find it most difficult to allow even to God himself. It is not, however, the only miracle which this supposition would compel us to swallow. The very <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> of the apostles to propagate the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> of false miracles in support of such a religion as that which is taught in the New Testament, is as great a miracle as human imagination can easily conceive. When they formed this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, either they must have hoped to succeed, or they must have foreseen that they should fail in their undertaking; and in either case, they chose evil for its own sake. They could not, if they foresaw that they should fail, look for anything but that contempt, disgrace, and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a>, which were then the inevitable consequences of an unsuccessful endeavour to overthrow the established religion. Nor could their prospects be brighter upon the supposition of their success. As they knew themselves to be false witnesses and impious deceivers, they could have no hopes beyond the grave; and by determining to oppose all the religious systems, superstitions, and prejudices of the age in which they lived, they wilfully exposed themselves to inevitable misery in the present life, to insult, and imprisonment, to stripes and death. Nor can it be said that they might look forward to power and affluence when they should, through sufferings, have converted their countrymen; for so desirous were they of obtaining nothing but misery, as the end of their mission, that they made their own persecution a test of the truth of their doctrines. They introduced the Master from whom they pretended to have received these doctrines as telling them, "that they were sent forth as sheep in the midst of wolves; that they should be delivered up to councils, and scourged in synagogues; that they should be hated of all men for his name's sake; that the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> should deliver up the brother to death, and the father the child; and that he who took not up his cross and followed after him was not worthy of him." The very system of religion, therefore, which they invented and resolved to impose upon mankind, was so contrived, that the worldly prosperity of its first preachers, and even their exemption from persecution, was incompatible with its success. Had these clear predictions of the Author of that religion, under whom the apostles acted only as ministers, not been verified, all mankind must have instantly perceived that their pretence to inspiration was false, and that Christianity was a scandalous and impudent imposture. All this the apostles could not but foresee when they formed their plan for deluding the world. Whence it follows, that when they resolved to support their pretended revelation by an appeal to forged miracles, they wilfully, and with their eyes open, exposed themselves to inevitable misery, whether they should succeed or fail in their enterprise; and that they concerted their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> so as not to admit of a possibility of recompense to themselves, either in this life or in that which is to come. But if there be a law of nature, for the reality of which we have better evidence than we have for others, it is, that "no man can choose misery for its own sake," or make the acquisition of it the ultimate end of his pursuit. The existence of other laws of nature we know by testimony and our own observation of the regularity of their effects. The existence of this law is made known to us not only by these means, but also by the still clearer and more conclusive evidence of our own consciousness. Thus, then, do miracles force themselves upon our assent in every possible view which we can take of this interesting subject. If the testimony of the first preachers of Christianity was true, the miracles recorded in the Gospel were certainly performed, and the doctrines of our religion are derived from heaven. On the other hand, if that testimony was false, either God must have miraculously effaced from the minds of those by whom it was given all the associations formed between their sensible ideas and the words of language, or he must have endowed those men with the gift of prescience, and have impelled them to fabricate a pretended revelation for the purpose of deceiving the world, and involving themselves in certain and foreseen destruction. The power necessary to perform the one series of these miracles may, for any thing known to us, be as great as that which would be requisite for the performance of the other; and, considered merely as exertions of preternatural power, they may seem to balance each other, and to hold the mind in a state of suspense. But when we take into consideration the different purposes for which these opposite and contending miracles were wrought, the balance is instantly destroyed. The miracles recorded in the Gospels, if real, were wrought in support of a revelation which, in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of all by whom it is received, has brought to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> many important truths which could not otherwise have been made known to men; and which, by the confession of its adversaries, contains the purest moral precepts by which the conduct of mankind was ever directed. The opposite series of miracles, if real, was performed to enable, and even to compel, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of Jews, of the lowest <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> and of the narrowest <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, to fabricate, with the view of inevitable destruction to themselves, a consistent scheme of falsehood, and by an appeal to forged miracles to impose it upon the world as a revelation from heaven. The object of the former miracles is worthy of a God of infinite wisdom, goodness, and power. The object of the latter is absolutely inconsistent with wisdom and goodness, which are demonstrably attributes of that Being by whom alone miracles can be performed. Whence it follows, that the supposition of the apostles bearing false testimony to the miracles of their Master, implies a series of deviations from the laws of nature, infinitely less probable in themselves than those miracles: and therefore by Mr Hume's maxim, we must necessarily reject the supposition of falsehood in the testimony, and admit the reality of the miracles. So true it is, that for the reality of the Gospel miracles we have evidence as convincing to the reflecting mind, as those had who were contemporary with Christ and his apostles, and were actual witnesses to their mighty works.

MIRANDA-DE-EBRO

Pages 327-327

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in Old Castile, with a strong castle; seated in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> that produces excellent wine. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3° 10' N. Lat. 42° 52'.

MIRANDO-DE-DOURO

Pages 327-327
or Duero, a strong town of Portugal, and capital of the province of Tras-os-Montes, with a bishop's see. It is well fortified, and seated on a rock near the confluence of the rivers Douro and Fresno. W. Long. 5° 40' N. Lat. 41° 30'.

MIRANDOLA

Pages 327-327

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of the same name, situated between the duchies of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANTUA">Mantua</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODENA">Modena</a>; is well fortified, and has also a strong citadel and fort. It has been several times taken and retaken. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 11° 5' N. Lat. 44° 52'.

MIRIAM

Pages 327-327

sister of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-AARON">Aaron</a> and Moses, makes two <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> three remarkable appearances in Scripture. It was owing to her that her mother was employed by <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHARAOH">Pharaoh</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> as nurse to Moses. She put herself at the head of the women of Israel after their passage through the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RED_SEA"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, in order to sing the song which the men had sung before. She joined with her <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Aaron in murmuring against Moses, and was severely chastised for that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>; for she became leprous, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> separate from the rest without the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAMP">camp</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> days. She died before her brothers, though in the same year with them, and was buried at the public expense.

MIRROR

Pages 327-327

a name for a looking glass, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> any polished body, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> is to form the images of distant objects, by reflection of the rays of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>. See Reflection. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MIRRORS">Mirrors</a> are either <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANE">plane</a>, convex, or concave. The first reflect the rays of light in a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> exactly similar to that in which they <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> upon them, and therefore represent bodies of their <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> magnitude. The convex ones make the rays diverge much more than before reflection, and therefore greatly diminish the images of those objects which they show: while the concave ones, by collecting the rays into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FOCUS">focus</a>, not only magnify the objects they show, but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> burn very fiercely when exposed to the rays of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>; and hence they are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> known by the name of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> mirrors. See Burning Mirrors. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> times the mirrors were made of some kind of metal; and from a passage of the Mosaic writings we learn that the mirrors used by the Jewish women were made of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>. The Jews certainly had been taught to use that kind of mirrors by the Egyptians; from whence it is probable that brazen mirrors were the first kind used in the world. Any kind of metal, indeed, when well polished, will reflect very powerfully; but of all others silver reflects the most, though it has been in all countries too expensive a material for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> use. <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">Gold</a> also is very powerful; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, or even wood, gilded and polished, will <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> very powerfully as burning mirrors. Even polished <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a>, or straw nicely plaited together, will form mirrors capable of burning, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> on a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a>. Since the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of glass, and the application of quicksilver to it, became generally known, it hath been universally employed for those plane mirrors used as ornaments to houses; but in making reflecting telescopes, they have been found much inferior to metallic ones. It does not appear that the same superiority belongs to the metalline burning mirrors, considered merely as burning glasses; since the mirror with which M. Macquer melted platinum, though only 22 inches diameter, and which was made of quicksilvered glass, produced much greater effects than M. Vilette's metalline speculum, which considerably exceeded it in size. It is very probable, however, that this mirror of M. Vilette's was by no means so well polished as it ought to have been; as the art of preparing the metal for taking the finest polish has but lately been discovered and published in the Philosophical Transactions by Mr Mudge. See Glass-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRINDING">Grinding</a>.

MISADVENTURE

Pages 327-328

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, has an especial signification for the killing a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> partly by negligence, and partly by chance. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOMICIDE">HOMICIDE</a>. MISANTHROPY. (from μίσος, hatred, and ἄνθρωπος, a man); a general dislike <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> aversion to man, and mankind. In which <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> it stands opposed to philanthropy, or the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of mankind. MISCARRIAGE. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABORTION">ABORTION</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MIDWIFERY">MIDWIFERY</a>.

MISCHNA

Pages 328-328
or Misna, (from μίση, iteravit), a part of the Jewish Talmud. The Mischina contains the text; and the Gemara, which is the second part of the Talmud, contains the commentaries: so that the Gemara is, as it were, a glossary on the Mischina. The Mischina consists of various traditions of the Jews, and of explanations of several passages of Scripture; these traditions serving as an explication of the written law, and supplement to it, are said to have been delivered to Moses during the time of his abode on the Mount; which he afterwards communicated to Aaron, Eleazar, and his servant Joshua. By these they were transmitted to the 72 elders, by them to the prophets, who communicated them to the men of the great sanhedrim, from whom the wise men of Jerusalem and Babylon received them. According to Prideaux's account, they passed from Jeremiah to Baruch, from him to Ezra, and from Ezra to the men of the great synagogue, the last of whom was Simon the Just; who delivered them to Antigonus of Socho; and from him they came down in regular succession to Simeon, who took our Saviour in his arms; to Gamaliel, at whose feet Paul was educated; and last of all to Rabbi Judah the Holy, who committed them to writing in the Mischina. But Dr Prideaux, rejecting this Jewish fiction, observes, that after the death of Simon the Just, about 299 years before Christ, the Mischanical doctors arose, who, by their comments and conclusions, added to the number of those traditions which had been received and allowed by Ezra and the men of the great synagogue; so that towards the middle of the second century after Christ, under the empire of Antoninus Pius, it was found necessary to commit these traditions to writing; more especially, as their country had considerably suffered under Adrian, and many of their schools had been dissolved, and their learned men cut off; and therefore the usual method of preserving their traditions had failed. Rabbi Judah on this occasion being rector of the school at Tiberias, and president of the sanhedrim in that place, undertook the work, and compiled it in six books, each consisting of several tracts, which altogether make up the number of 63. Prud. Conner. vol. ii. p. 468, &c. edit. 9. This learned author computes, that the Mischina was composed about the 15th year of our Lord; but Dr Lightfoot says, that Rabbi Judah compiled the Mischina about the year of Christ 190, in the latter end of the reign of Commodus; or, as some compute, in the year of Christ 220. Dr Lardner is of opinion, that this work could not have been finished before the year 190, or later. Collect. of Jewish and Heathen Testimonies, &c. vol. i. p. 178. Thus the book called the Mischina was formed; a book which the Jews have generally received with the greatest veneration. The original has been published with a Latin translation by Surenhuis, with notes of his own, and others from the learned Maimonides, &c. in 6 vol. fol. Amsterd. A.D. 1698—1703. (See TALMUD). It is written in a much purer style, and is not near so full of dreams and visions as the Gemara.

MISDEMEANOUR

Pages 328-328

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, signifies a crime. Every crime is a misdemeanour; yet the law has made a distinction between crimes of a higher and a lower <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>; the latter being denominated misdemeanours, the former felonies, &c. For the understanding of which distinction, we shall give the following <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a> from Blackstone's Commentaries, vol. iv. 5. "A crime, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> misdemeanour, is an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> committed or omitted, in violation of a public law, either forbidding or commanding it. This general definition comprehends both crimes and misdemeanours; which, properly speaking, are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYNONYMOUS">synonymous</a> terms; though, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> usage, the word crime is made to denote such offences as are of a deeper and more atrocious dye; while smaller faults, and omissions of less <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, are comprised under the gentler name of misdemeanours only."

MISE

Pages 328-328

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a> books, is used in various senses: thus it sometimes signifies costs <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> expenses; in which <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> it is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> used in entering of judgments in actions personal. It is also used for the issue to be tried on the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> assize; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, joining of the mise upon the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, is putting in issue between the tenant and demandant, Who has the best or clearest right. Mise, also signifies a tax or tallage, &c. An honorary gift, or customary present from the people of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WALES">Wales</a> to every new <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of Wales, anciently given in cattle, wine, and corn, but now in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, being 5000l. or more, is denominated a mise; so was the usual tribute or fine of 3000 merks paid by the inhabitants of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> palatine of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHESTER">Chester</a> at the change of every owner of the said earldom, for enjoying their liberties. And at Chester they have a mise-book, wherein every town and village in the county is rated what to pay towards the mise. The 27 Hen. VIII. c. 26. ordains that lords shall have all such mises and profits of their lands as they had in times past, &c. Mise, is sometimes also corruptly used for mease, in law French mees, "a message;" as a mise <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, in some manors, is such a message or tenement as answers the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> a heriot at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of its owner.—2 Inst. §28.

MISENUM

Pages 328-328
or Misenus, in Ancient Geography; a promontory, port, and town in Campania, situated to the south-west of Baiae, in the Sinus Potentianus, on the north side. Here Augustus had a fleet, called Classis Misennensis, for guarding the Mare Inferum; as he had another at Ravenna for the Superum. On this peninsula a villa was built by Caius Marius, with a degree of elegance that gave great offence to the most austere among the Romans, who thought it ill suited to the character of so rough a soldier. Upon the same foundation Lucullus the plunderer of the eastern world, erected an edifice, in comparison of which the former house was a cottage; but even his magnificence was eclipsed by the splendour of the palace which the emperors raised upon the same spot. To these proud abodes

MISER

Pages 328-332

a parsimonious person who is at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> rich; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a wretch covetous to extremity, whom avarice has divested of all the charities of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and made even an enemy to himself. Of this most unaccountable of all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, many instances occur; some of them so extraordinary as almost to surpass <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a>. The following are here selected, as being of recent <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a>, perfectly authentic, and the last of them in particular exhibiting an assemblage of qualities the most singular perhaps that ever existed in the same person. Too little dignified to merit a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in regular biography, yet too curious a variety of human character to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> unnoticed in this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, the present seemed the only <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> under which it could with propriety be introduced. 1. In <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1790, died at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, literally of want, Mr Ostervald, a well known banker. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, originally of Neufchatel, felt the violence of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> of avarice (for surely it is rather a disease than a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> of the mind) so strongly, that within a few days of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, no importunities could induce him to buy a few pounds of meat for the purpose of making a little soup for him. "Tis true (said he), I should not dislike the soup, but I have no appetite for the meat; what then is to become of that?" At the time that he refused this nourishment, for fear of being obliged to give away two or three pounds of meat, there was tied round his neck a silken bag, which contained 800 assignats of 1000 livres each. At his outset in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, he drank a pint of beer which served him for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPPER">supper</a>, every night at a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> much frequented, from which he carried home all the bottle corks he could come at. Of these, in the course of eight years, he had collected as many as sold for 12 <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOUIS">louis</a> d'or, a sum that had laid the foundation of his future fortune, the superstructure of which was rapidly raised by his uncommon success in stock jobbing. He died possessed of three millions of livres (125,000 <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>). 2. The late John Elwes, Esq. was member for <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BERKSHIRE">Berkshire</a> in three successive parliaments. His family name was Meggot; and his father was a brewer of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> eminence, and distinguished by no peculiarity of character; but his mother, though she was left nearly 100,000l. by her husband, starved herself to death! At an early <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of life he was sent to Westminster school, where he remained for 10 or 12 years. During that time he certainly had not misapplied his talents; for he was a good classical scholar to the last; and it is a circumstance not a little remarkable, though well authenticated, that he never read afterwards, nor had he ever any knowledge in accounts; to which may in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> be attributed the total <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> he was always in as to his affairs. From Westminster school Mr Meggot removed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a>, where he soon entered upon pursuits more agreeable to him than <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>. The riding <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the academy there had then to boast perhaps of three of the best riders in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, Mr Worsley, Mr Elwes, and Sir Sidney Meadows. Of the three, Elwes was reckoned the most desperate; the young horses were always put into his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, and he was the rough rider to the other two. On his return to England, after an absence of two or three years, he was to be introduced to his uncle the late Sir Harvey Elwes, who was then living at Stoke in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a>, perhaps the most perfect <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> of human penury that ever existed. The attempts at saving <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> were in him so extraordinary, that Mr Elwes perhaps never quite reached them, even at the last period of his life.—Of what <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a> can do, Sir Harvey was an instance. At an early period of life he was given over for a consumption, and he lived till betwixt 80 and 90 years of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>. On his death, his fortune, which was at least 250,000l. fell to his nephew Mr Meggot, who by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> was ordered to assume the name and arms of Elwes. To this uncle, and this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, Mr Elwes succeeded when he had advanced beyond the 40th year of his age. For 15 years previous to this period, he was well known in the more fashionable circles of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. He had always a turn for play; and it was only late in life, and from paying always and not always being paid, that he conceived disgust at it. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> which he professed, "that it was impossible to ask a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> for money," he perfectly confirmed by the practice; and he never violated this feeling to the latest <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> of his life. The manners of Mr Elwes were such—so gentle, so attentive, so gentlemanly, and so engaging—that rudeness could not ruffle them, or strong ingratitude <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> their observance. He retained this peculiar feature of the old <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> to the last; but he had a praise beyond this: He had the most gallant disregard of his own person, and all care about himself that can be imagined. The instances in younger life, in the most imminent personal hazard, are innumerable; but when age had despoiled him of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a>, and might have rendered care and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> about himself <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a>, he knew not what they were: He wished no one to assist him: "He was as young as ever; he could walk; he could ride, and he could dance; and he hoped he should not give trouble even when he was old." He was at that time 75. It is curious to remark how he contrived to mingle small attempts at saving with objects of the most unbounded dissipation. After sitting up a whole night at play for thousands with the most fashionable and profligate men of the time, amidst splendid rooms, gilt sofas, wax lights, and waiters attendant on his call, he would walk out about four in the morning, not towards home, but into Smithfield, to meet his own cattle, which were coming to market from Thaydonhall, a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARM">farm</a> of his in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a>! There would this same man, forgetful of the scenes he had <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> left, stand in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>, bartering with a carcass <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BUTCHER">butcher</a> for a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SHILLING">shilling</a>! Sometimes when the cattle did not arrive at the hour he expected, he would walk on in the mire to meet them; and more than once has gone on foot the whole way to his farm without stopping, which was 17 miles from London, after sitting up the whole night. Had every man been of the mind of Mr Elwes, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of innkeepers must have perished, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POST">post</a>-chaises have been returned back to those who made them; for it was the business of his life to avoid both. He always travelled on horseback. To see him setting out on a journey, was a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> truly curious; his first care was to put two or three eggs, boiled, boiled hard, into his great coat pocket, or any scraps of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> which he found; baggage he never took; then mounting one of his hunters, his next attention was to get out of London into that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> where turnpikes were the fewest; then stopping under any hedge where grass presented itself for his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, and a little <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> for himself, he would sit <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> and refresh himself and his horse together. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> residence of Mr Elwes at this period of his life was in Berkshire, at his own seat at Marcham. Here it was he had two natural sons born, who inherit the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his property by a will made about the year 1785. The keeping of fox bounds was the only instance in the whole life of Mr Elwes of his ever sacrificing money to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>; and may be selected as the only period when he forgot the cares, the perplexities, and the regret, which his wealth occasioned. But even here everything was done in the most frugal manner. Scrub, in the Beaux Stratagem, when compared with Mr Elwes's huntsman, had an idle life of it. This famous huntsman might have fixed an epoch in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of servants: for in a morning, getting up at four o'clock, he milked the cows; he then prepared breakfast for Mr Elwes or any friends he might have with him; then slipping on a green coat, he hurried into the stable, saddled the horses, got the bounds out of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KENNEL">kennel</a>, and away they went into the field. After the fatigues of hunting, he refreshed himself by rubbing down two or three horses as quickly as he could; then running into the house to lay the cloth, and wait at dinner; then hurrying again into the stable to feed the horses—diversified with an interlude of the cows again to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, the dogs to feed, and eight hunters to litter down for the night. In the penury of Mr Elwes there was something that seemed like a judgment from heaven. All earthly comforts he voluntarily denied himself: he would walk home in the rain in London rather than pay a shilling for a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COACH">coach</a>; he would sit in wet clothes sooner than have a fire to dry them; he would eat his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> in the last stage of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUTREFACTION">putrefaction</a> sooner than have a fresh <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> from the butchers; and he wore a wig for above a fortnight, which his biographer <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> him pick up out of a rut in a lane where they were riding. This was the last extremity of laudable economy; for to all appearance it was the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a>-off wig of some beggar! Mr Elwes had now resided about 13 years in Suffolk, when the contest for Berkshire presented itself on the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>; and when, to preserve the peace of that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>, he was nominated by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Cran-ven. Mr Elwes, though he had retired from public business for some years, had still left about him some of the seeds of more <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> life, and he agreed to the proposal. It came farther enhanced to him, by the agreement, that he was to be brought in by the freeholders for nothing. All he did on the occasion was dining at the ordinary at <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">Reading</a>; and he got into parliament for 18 pence! Though a new man, Mr Elwes could not be called a young member; for he was at this time nearly 60 years old when he thus entered on public life. But he was in possession of all his activity; and, preparatory to his appearance on the boards of St Stephen's Chapel, he used to attend constantly during the races and other public meetings all the great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> where his voters resided. At the different assemblies he would dance among the youngest to the last, after riding over on horseback, and frequently in the rain, to the place of meeting. A gentleman who was one night standing by, observed on the extraordinary agility of so old a man.—O! that is nothing (replied another); for Mr Elwes, to do this, rode 20 miles in the rain, with his shoes stuck into his boots and his bag-wig in his pocket." The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of parliament made no <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> in the dress of Mr Elwes: on the contrary, it seemed at this time to have attained additional meanness; and nearly to have reached that happy climax of poverty, which has more than once drawn on him the compassion of those who passed by him in the street. For the speaker's dinners, however, he had one <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUIT">suit</a>, with which the speaker in the course of the sessions became very familiar. The minister likewise was well acquainted with it; and at any dinner of opposition still was his apparel the same. The wits of the minority used to say, "that they had full as much reason as the minister to be satisfied with Mr Elwes, as he had the same <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> with every body." At this period of his life Mr Elwes wore a wig. Much about the time when his parliamentary life ceased, that wig was worn out; so then, being older and wiser as to expense, he wore his own <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, which like his expenses was very small. All this time the income of Mr Elwes was increasing hourly, and his present expenditure was next to nothing; for the little pleasures he had once engaged in he had now given up. He kept no house, and only one old <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> and a couple of horses: he resided with his nephew: his two sons he had stationed in Suffolk and Berkshire, to look after his respective estates: and his dress certainly was no expense to him; for had not other people been more careful than himself, he would not have had it even mended. When he left London, he went on horseback to his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> seats with his couple of hard eggs, and without once stopping upon the road at any house. He always took the most unfrequented road, and used every shift to avoid turnpikes. Marcham was the seat he now chiefly visited; which had some reason to be flattered with the preference, as his journey into Suffolk cost him only twopence-halfpenny, while that into Berkshire amounted to fourpence! As Mr Elwes came into parliament without expense, he performed his duty as a member would have done in the pure days of our <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>. What he had not bought he never attempted to sell; and he went forward in that straight and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> path, which can alone satisfy a reflecting mind. Amongst the smaller memorials of the parliamentary life of Mr Elwes may be noted, that he did not follow the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of members in general by sitting on any particular side of the house, but sat as occasion presented itself on either indiscriminately; and he voted much in the same manner, but never rose to speak. In his attendance at the house, he was always early and late; and he never left it for dinner, as he had accustomed himself to fasting, sometimes for 24 hours in continuance. When he quitted parliament, he was, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> phrase, "a fish out of water!" The style of Mr Elwes's Elwes's life had left him no <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> scenes to which he could retire—his home was dreary and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a>—his rooms received no cheerfulness from fire; and while the outside had all the appearance of a "House to be Let," the inside was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a>; but he had his penury alone to thank for this, and for the want of all the little consolations which should attend old age, and smooth the passage of declining life. At the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> of 1785, he wished again to visit, which he had not done for some years, his seat at Stoke. But then the journey was a most serious object to him. The famous old servant was dead; all the horses that remained with him were a couple of worn-out brood mares; and he himself was not in that vigour of body in which he could ride 60 or 70 miles on the sustenance of two boiled eggs. The mention of a post chaise would have been a crime—"He afford a post chaise, indeed! where was he to get the money?" would have been his exclamation. At length he was carried into the country as he was carried into parliament, free of expense, by a gentleman who was certainly not quite so rich as Mr Elwes. When he reached Stoke—the seat of more active scenes, of somewhat resembling hospitality, and where his fox hounds had spread somewhat like vivacity around—he remarked, "he had expended a great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of money once very foolishly; but that a man grew wiser by time." The rooms at this seat, which were now much out of repair, and would have all fallen in but for his son John Elwes, Esq. who had resided there, he thought too expensively furnished, as worse things might have served. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> a window was broken, there was to be no repair but that of a little <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, or that of piecing in a bit of broken glass; which had at length been done so frequently, and in so many shapes, that it would have puzzled a mathematician to say "what <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> they described." To <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> fire, he would walk about the remains of an old greenhouse, or sit with a servant in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a>. During the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a> he would amuse himself with going into the fields to glean the corn on the grounds of his own tenants; and they used to leave a little more than common to please the old gentleman, who was as eager after it as any panter in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a>. In the advance of the season, his morning employment was to pick up any stray chip, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a>, or other things, to carry to the fire, in his pocket—and he was one <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> surprised by a neighbouring gentleman in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of pulling down, with some difficulty, a crow's nest for this purpose. On the gentleman wondering why he gave himself this trouble—"Oh, Sir, (replied old Elwes,) it is really a shame that these creatures should do so. Do but see what waste they make! They <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DON">don</a>'t care how extravagant they are!" As no gleam of favourite passion, or any ray of amusement, broke through this gloom of penury, his insatiable desire of saving was now become uniform and systematic. He used still to ride about the country on one of these mares—but then he rode her very economically, on the soft turf, adjoining the road, without putting himself to the expense of shoes, as he observed, "The turf was so pleasant to a horse's foot!" And when any gentleman called to pay him a visit, and the boy who attended in the stables, was profuse enough to put a little hay before his horse, old Elwes would slily steal back into the stable, and take the hay very carefully away. That very strong appetite which Mr Elwes had in some measure restrained during the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> sitting of parliament, he now indulged most voraciously, and on every thing he could find. To save, as he thought, the expense of going to a butcher, he would have a whole sheep killed, and so cat mutton to the—end of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a>. When he occasionally had his river drawn, though sometimes horse loads of small fish were taken, not one would he suffer to be thrown in again; for he observed, "He should never see them again!" <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAME">Game</a> in the last state of putrefaction, and meat that walked about his plate, would he continue to eat, rather than have new things killed before the old provision was finished. With this diet—the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARNEL">charnel</a> house of sustenance—his dress kept pace—equally in the last stage of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> dissolution. Sometimes he would walk about in a tattered brown-coloured hat, and sometimes in a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> woollen <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAP">cap</a>, like a prisoner confined for debt. His shoes he never would suffer to be cleaned, lest they should be worn out the sooner. But still, with all this self-denial—that penury of life to which the inhabitant of an alms house is not doomed—still did he think he was profuse, and frequently say, "He must be a little more careful of his property." His disquietude on the subject of money was now continual. When he went to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a>, he would put five or ten guineas into a bureau; and then, full of his money, after he had retired to rest, and sometimes in the middle of the night, he would come down to see if it was there. The <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of mortification at which Mr Elwes was now arrived was all but a denial of the common necessaries of life; and indeed it might have admitted a doubt, whether or not, if his manors, his fish ponds, and some grounds in his own hands, had not furnished a subsistence, where he had not any thing actually to buy, he would not, rather than have bought any thing, have starved.
