Strange as this may appear, it is not exaggerated.—He one day, during this period, dined upon the remaining part of a moor hen, which had been brought out of the river by a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-RAT">rat</a>! and at another ate an undigested part of a pike which a larger one had swallowed, but had not finished, and which were taken in this state in a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NET">net</a>. At the time this last circumstance happened, he discovered a strange kind of satisfaction; for he said to a friend, "Aye! this was killing two birds with one <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>!" In the room of all comment of all moral—let it be remarked, that at this time Mr Elwes was perhaps worth nearly eight hundred thousand pounds! and, at this period, he had not made his will, of course was not saving from any sentiment of affection for any person. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> of 1788 Mr Elwes passed at his house in Welbeck street, London; and he passed that summer without any other <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> than that of two maid servants; for he had now given up the expense of keeping any <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> domestic. His chief employment used to be that of getting up early in a morning to visit some of his houses in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>-le-bone, which during the summer were repairing. As he was there generally at four o'clock in a morning, he was of course on the spot before the workmen; and he used contentedly to sit down on the steps before the door, to scold them Miser. them when they did come. The neighbours who used to see him appear thus regularly every morning, and who concluded, from his apparel, that he was one of the workmen, observed, "there never was so punctual a man as the old carpenter." During the whole morning he would continue to run up and down stairs to see the men were not idle for an instant, with the same anxiety as if his whole <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> in life had been centered in the finishing of this house, regardless of the greater property he had at stake in various places, and for ever employed in the minute only of affairs. Indeed such was his anxiety about this house, the rent of which was not above 50l. a-year, that it brought on a fever which nearly cost him his life; but the fate which dragged him on thus strangely to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BURY">bury</a> him under the load of his own wealth, seemed as restless as it was unaccountable. In the muscular and unencumbered frame of Mr Elwes there was every thing that promised <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> length of life; and he lived to above 70 years of age without any natural disorder attacking him; but, as Lord <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACON">Bacon</a> has well observed, "the minds of some men are a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-LAMP">lamp</a> that is continually <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BURNING">burning</a>;" and such was the mind of Mr Elwes. Removed from those occasional public avocations which had once engaged his attention, money was now his only thought. He rose upon money—upon money he lay down to rest; and as his capacity sunk away from him by degrees, he dwindled from the real cares of his property into the perilous concealment of a few guineas. This little store he would carefully wrap up in various papers, and depositing them in different corners, would amuse himself with running from one to the other, to see whether they were all safe. Then forgetting, perhaps, where he had concealed some of them, he would become as seriously afflicted as a man might be who had lost all his property. Nor was the day alone thus spent—he would frequently rise in the middle of the night, and be heard walking about different parts of the house, looking after what he had thus hidden and forgotten. During the winter of 1789, the last winter Mr Elwes was fated to see, his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> visibly weakened every day; and from the unceasing wish to save money, he now began to fear he should die in want of it. Mr Gibson had been appointed his builder in the room of Mr Adams; and one day, when this gentleman waited upon him, he said with apparent concern, "Sir, pray consider in what a wretched state I am: you see in what a good house I am living; and here are five guineas, which is all I have at present; and how I shall go on with such a sum of money puzzles me to death. I dare say you thought I was rich; now you see how it is!" Mr George Elwes having now settled at his seat at Marcham in Berkshire, he was naturally desirous that, in the assiduities of his wife, his father might at length find a comfortable home. In London he was certainly most uncomfortable: but still, with these temptations before and behind him, a journey with any expense annexed to it was insurmountable. This, however, was luckily obviated by an offer from Mr Partis, a gentleman of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>, to take him to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> seat in Berkshire with his purse perfectly whole. But there was one circumstance still very distressing—the old gentleman had now nearly worn out his last coat, and he would not buy a new one; his son, therefore, with a pious fraud, contrived to get Mr Partis to buy him a coat and make him a present of it. Thus formerly having had a good coat, then a bad one, and at last no coat at all, he was kind enough to accept one from a neighbour. Mr Elwes carried with him into Berkshire five guineas and a half, and half a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>. Lest the mention of this sum may appear singular, it should be said, that previous to his journey he had carefully wrapped it up in various folds of paper, that no part of it might be lost. On the arrival of the old gentleman, Mr George Elwes and his wife did every thing they could to make the country a scene of quiet to him. But "he had that within" which baffled every effort of this kind. Of his heart it might be said, "there was no peace in Israel." His mind, cast away upon the vast and troubled ocean of his property, extending beyond the bounds of his calculation, returned to amuse itself with fetching and carrying about a few guineas, which in that ocean was indeed a drop. But nature had now carried on life nearly as far as she was able, and the sand was almost run out. The first symptom of more immediate decay was his inability to enjoy his rest at night. Frequently would he be heard at midnight as if struggling with some one in his chamber, and crying out, "I will keep my money, I will; nobody shall rob me of my property." On any one of the family going into his room, he would start from this fever of anxiety, and, as if waking from a troubled dream, again hurry into bed, and seem unconscious of what had happened. At length, on the 26th November 1789, expired this miserably rich man, whose property, nearly reaching to a million, extended itself almost through every county in England.

MISERICORDIA

Pages 332-332

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is an arbitrary fine imposed on any person for an offence; this is called misericordia, because the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AMERCEMENT">amercement</a> ought to be but small, and less than that required by <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MAGNA_CHARTA">magna <a cla</a>ss="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CHARTA">charta</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> a person be outrageously amerced in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> that is not of record, the writ called moderata misericordia lies for moderating the amercement according to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the fault. MISFORTUNE. An unlucky accident. Misfortune, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> chance, in Law, a deficiency of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a>; or committing of an unlawful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> by misfortune or chance, and not by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>. In such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, the will observes a total neutrality, and does not co-operate with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a>; which therefore wants one main ingredient of a crime. See Crime. Of this, when it affects the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of another, we have spoken under the article <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOMICIDE">HOMICIDE</a>; and in this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> have only occasion to observe, that if any accidental mischief happens to follow from the performance of a lawful act, the party stands excused from all guilt: but if a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> be doing any thing unlawful, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> ensues which he did not foresee or intend, as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of a man or the like, his want of foresight shall be no excuse; for, being guilty of one offence, in doing antecedently what is in itself unlawful, he is criminally guilty of whatever consequence may follow the first misbehaviour.

MISFEASANCE

Pages 332-333

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a> books, signifies a trespass. MISLETOE. See Viscum, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MISNOMER

Pages 333-333

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, a misnaming <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> mistaking a person's name. The Christian name of a person should always be perfect; but the law is not so strict in regard to surnames, a small mistake in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> be dispensed with to make good a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a>, and support the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of the party. See <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLEA">Plea</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDICTMENT">Indictment</a>.

MISPRISIONS

Pages 333-333

(a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> derived from the old French, mespris, a neglect <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> contempt), are, in the acceptation of our <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>, generally understood to be all such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> offences as are under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, but nearly bordering thereon; and it is said, that a misprision is contained in every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASON">treason</a> and felony whatsoever; and that, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> so please, the offender may be proceeded against for the misprision only. And upon the same principle, while the jurisdiction of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STAR_CHAMBER"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="vol19.html#article-STAR">star</a>-chamber subsisted, it was held that the king might remit a prosecution for treason, and cause the delinquent to be censured in that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>, merely for a high misdemeanor; as happened in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of Roger <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Rutland, in 43 Eliz. who was concerned in the earl of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a>'s rebellion. Misprisions are generally divided into two sorts; <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEGATIVE">negative</a>, which consist in the concealment of something which ought to be revealed; and positive, which consist in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> of something which ought not to be done. 1. Of the first, or negative kind, is what is called misprision of treason; consisting in the bare knowledge and concealment of treason, without any degree of assent thereto; for any assent makes the party a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> traitor; as indeed the concealment, which was construed aiding and abetting, did at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> law; in like manner as the knowledge of a plot against the state, and not revealing it, was a capital crime at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>, and other states of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. But it is now enacted by the statute 1 & 2 Ph. & Mar. c. 10. that a bare concealment of treason shall be only held a misprision. This concealment becomes criminal, if the party apprised of the treason does not, as soon as conveniently may be, reveal it to some judge of assize or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> of the peace. But if there be any probable circumstances of assent, as if one goes to a treasonable meeting, knowing beforehand that a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSPIRACY">conspiracy</a> is intended against the king; or, being in such <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> once by accident, and having heard such treasonable conspiracy, meets the same company again, and hears more of it, but conceals it; this is an implied assent in law, and makes the concealer guilty of actual high treason. Misprision of felony is also the concealment of a felony which a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> knows, but never assented to; for, if he assented, this makes him either principal or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACCESSORY">accessory</a>. And the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> of this, in a public officer, by the statute Westm. 1. 3 Edw. I. c. 9. is imprisonment for a year and a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>; in a common person, imprisonment for a less discretionary <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; and, in both, fine and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RANSOM">ransom</a> at the king's <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>: which pleasure of the king must be observed; once for all, not to signify any extrajudicial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> of the sovereign, but such as is declared by his representatives, the judges in his courts of justice; voluntas regis in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CURIA">curia</a>, non in camera. 2. Misprisions, which are merely positive, are generally denominated contempt or high misdemeanours; of which the principal is the mal-administration of such Misprisions high officers as are in public trust and employment. This is usually punished by the method of parliamentary impeachment; wherein such penalties, short of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, are inflicted, as to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PEERS">peers</a> shall seem proper; consisting usually of banishment, imprisonment, fines, or perpetual <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISABILITY">disability</a>. Hither also may be referred the offence of embezzling the public <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, called among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> peculatus; which the Julian law punished with death in a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>, and with deportation, or banishment, in a private person. With us it is not a capital crime, but subjects the committer of it to a discretionary fine and imprisonment.—Other misprisions are, in general, such contempts of the executive magistrate as demonstrate themselves by some arrogant and undutiful behaviour towards the king and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>: for a detail of which, vide Blackstone's Comment. iv. 22.

MISSAL

Pages 333-333

the Romish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a>-book, containing the several masses to be said on particular days. It is derived from the Latin word missa, which, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Christian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, signified every <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of divine <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>.

MISSIO

Pages 333-333

among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, was a full discharge given to a soldier after 20 years <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, and differed from the exactoratio, which was a discharge from duty after 17 years service. Every soldier had a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to claim his missio at the end of 20 years.

MISSION

Pages 333-333

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOLOGY">Theology</a>, denotes a power <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> to preach the gospel. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ gave his disciples their mission in these words, Go and teach all nations, &c. The Romanists reproach the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>, that their ministers have no mission, as not being authorized in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of their ministry, either by an uninterrupted succession from the apostles, or by <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a>, or by any extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of a vocation. Many among us deny any other mission necessary for the ministry than the talents necessary to discharge it. Mission is also used for an establishment of people zealous for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> of God and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SALVATION">salvation</a> of souls; who go and preach the gospel in remote countries and among infidels.

MISSIONARY

Pages 333-333

an ecclesiastic who devotes himself and his labours to some mission, either for the instruction of the orthodox, the conviction of heretics, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the conversion of infidels. See Jesuits.

MISSISSIPPI

Pages 334-334

one of the United States of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, is situated on the east side of the river of the same name, between 30° and 35° N. Lat. and 87° and 91° W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. It is about 350 miles long, and 150 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and has an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> of about 45,000 <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles. The southern parts on the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a> are low, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> marshy, and unhealthy; but the middle and northern parts are pretty well watered, and very fertile. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of culture are cotton and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> corn; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, however, are also raised. Lemons and other <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> thrive well. Horned cattle are raised in great numbers, but are sometimes destroyed by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WOLF">wolf</a> and couguar. Labour is generally performed by slaves. Natchez, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> town, and the only <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of trade, is about 300 miles above New <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORLEANS">Orleans</a>. There are some tanneries in the state, and some <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of woollen, cotton, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>. The principal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> are the Tombigbee, Pascagoula, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEARL">Pearl</a>, and Yazoo. This state was admitted into the Union in 1817. Its <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> the year before was 44,206, of whom 20,567 were slaves, and 191 free blacks. The Choctaws, Cherokees, and some other of the Indian tribes who have made considerable advances in civilization, reside in this state. The legislative power of this state is vested in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of representatives and a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>, chosen by all free <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> males of 21 years of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>.

MISSOURI

Pages 334-334

a territory of the United States of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, including the greater <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> formerly known under the name of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOUISIANA">Louisiana</a>. It extends from the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MISSISSIPPI">Mississippi</a> to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROCKY_MOUNTAINS">Rocky <a class=</a>"xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, and from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a> to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CANADA">Canada</a>. Its length from north to south is about 1400 miles, and its breadth from east to west 886, comprising an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> of 985,250 <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles. It is watered by the Missouri river and its numerous tributary streams, and by some other branches of the Mississippi. The surface is generally uneven, but not mountainous. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is rich and well watered; but, unlike that of the eastern parts of America, it produces little <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> wood, except on the banks of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>. Lime is abundant in this vast region; coal and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> ore were observed in many places; and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> is found in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> quantities. Near St <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> ore abounds, and is wrought to a great <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>. As the country extends through 20 degrees of latitude, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> is various; warm and unhealthy in the south; colder and more salubrious towards the north. There are as yet but a small <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> settlers in this country, the greater part of which is still occupied by <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> tribes.

MISSUS

Pages 334-334

in the Circensian games, were the matches in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> chariot races. The usual <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of missus or matches in one <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> was 24; though the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Domitian presented the people with 100. The last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATCH">match</a> was generally made at the expense of the people, who made a collection for the purpose; hence it was called missus ararius, a subscription plate.

MISTAKE

Pages 334-334

any wrong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> committed, not through an evil <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, but through an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERROR">error</a> of judgment.

MISUSER

Pages 334-334

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is an abuse of any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> benefit; as "He shall make fine for his misuser." Old Nat. Br. 149. By misuser a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> of a corporation may be forfeited; so also an office, &c.

MITCHELSTOWN

Pages 334-334

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POST">post</a> town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Cork and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUNSTER">Munster</a> in Ireland, where there is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> founded by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-KINGSTON">Kingston</a> for the support of 12 decayed gentlemen and 12 decayed gentlewomen, who have 40l. yearly, and handsome apartments.

MITELLA

Pages 334-335
BASTARD AMERICAN SANICLE; a genus of plants belonging to the decandria class, and in the natural method ranking under the 13th order, Succulenter. See Botany Index.

MITHRA

Pages 335-335

feasts of, in antiquity, were feasts celebrated among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MITHRAS">Mithras</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>. The most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> instance of this Mithras among the Romans occurs in an inscription dated in the third consulate of Trajan, or about the year of Christ 101. This is the dedication of an altar to the sun under the above name, thus <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a>, Deo Soli Mithrae. But the worship of Mithras was not known in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORIGEN">Origen</a>, who died about the year of Christ 253; though it was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> at Rome for more than a century before this time. The worship of Mithras was proscribed at Rome in the year 378, by order of Gracchus, prefect of the praetorium. According to M. Freret, the feasts of Mithras were derived from Chaldea, where they had been instituted for celebrating the entrance of the sun into the sign Taurus.

MITHRAS

Pages 335-335
or MITHRA, a god of Persia and Chaldea, supposed to be the sun. His worship was introduced at Rome. He is generally represented as a young man, whose head is covered with a turban after the manner of the Persians. He supports his knee upon a bull that lies on the ground, and one of whose horns he holds in one hand, while with the other he plunges a dagger in his neck.

MITHRIDATE

Pages 335-335

an old <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>; an antidote <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, in form of an electuary, supposed to serve either as a remedy or a preservative against poisons; so named from the inventor, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MITHRIDATES">Mithridates</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Pontus, who is said to have so fortified his body against poisons with antidotes and preservatives, that when he had a mind to dispatch himself he could not find any <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POISON">poison</a> that would take effect.

MITHRIDATES

Pages 335-336

the name of several kings of Pontus. See Pontus. MITHRIDATES VII., surnamed Eupator and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>, succeeded to the throne at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 11 years, about 123 years before the Christian era. The beginning of his reign was marked by ambition, cruelty, and artifice. He murdered his own mother, who had been left by his father co-heiress of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>; and he fortified his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> by drinking antidotes against the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POISON">poison</a> with which his enemies at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> attempted to destroy him. He early inured his body to hardship, and employed himself in the most manly exercises, often remaining whole months in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and making frozen snow and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of his repose. Naturally ambitious and cruel, he spared no pains to acquire himself power and dominion. He murdered the two sons whom his sister Laodice had by Ariarathes <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Cappadocia, and placed one of his own children, only eight years old, on the vacant throne. These violent proceedings alarmed Nicomedes king of Bithynia, who had married Laodice the widow of Ariarathes, and ultimately involved Mithridates in a quarrel with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. Mithridates never lost an opportunity by which he might lessen the influence of his adversaries; and the more effectually to destroy their power in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, he ordered all the Romans that were in his dominions to be massacred. This was done in one night, and no less than 150,000, according to Plutarch, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 80,000 Romans, as Appian mentions, were made the victims of his cruelty. This called aloud for vengeance. Aquilius, and soon after Sylla, marched against Mithridates with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. The former was made prisoner; but Sylla obtained a victory over the king's generals; and another decisive engagement rendered him <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of all <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IONIA">Ionia</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASIA_MINOR">Asia <a cl</a>ass="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a>. This ill fortune was aggravated by the loss of about 200,000 men, who were killed in the several engagements that had been fought; and Mithridates, weakened by repeated ill success by <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, sued for peace from the conqueror, which he obtained on hard terms. But he soon took the field again with an army of 140,000 infantry, and 16,000 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, consisting of his own forces and those of his son-in-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a> Tigranes king of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMENIA">Armenia</a>. With this army he made himself master of the Roman provinces in Asia; none dared to oppose his conquests; and the Romans, relying on his fidelity, had withdrawn the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of their armies from the country. The news of his warlike preparations were no sooner heard, than Lucullus the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a> marched into Asia; and without delay he blocked up the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAMP">camp</a> of Mithridates who was then besieging Cyzicus. The Asiatic monarch escaped from him, and fled into the heart of his kingdom. Lucullus pursued him with the utmost celerity; and would have taken him prisoner after a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, had not the avidity of his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> preferred the plundering of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MULE">mule</a> loaded with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> to the taking of a monarch who had exercised such cruelties against their countrymen. The appointment of Glabrio to the command of the Roman forces, instead of Lucullus, was favourable to Mithridates, who recovered the greatest part of his dominions. The sudden arrival of Pompey, however, soon put an end to his victories. A battle in the night was fought near the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a>. An universal overthrow ensued, and Mithridates, bold in his misfortunes, rushed through the thick ranks of the enemy at the head of 800 horsemen, 500 of whom perished in the attempt to follow him. He fled to Tigranes; but that monarch refused an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASYLUM">asylum</a> to his father-in-law, whom he had before supported with all the collected forces of his kingdom. Mithridates found a safe retreat among the Scythians; and though destitute of power, friends, and resources, yet he meditated the overthrow of the Roman empire, by penetrating into the heart of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> by land. These wild projects were rejected by his followers, and he sued for peace. It was denied to his ambassadors; and the victorious Pompey declared, that, to obtain it, Mithridates must ask it in person. He scorned to trust himself in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of his enemy, and resolved to conquer or to die. His subjects refused to follow him any longer; and revolting from him, made his son Pharmaces king. The son showed himself ungrateful to his father; and even, according to some writers, he ordered him to be put to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. This unnatural treatment broke the heart of Mithridates; he obliged his wife to poison herself, and attempted to do the same himself. It was in vain: the frequent antidotes he had taken in the early part of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, strengthened his constitution against the poison; and when this was unavailing, he attempted to stab himself. The blow was not mortal; and a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a> who was then present, at his own request, gave him the fatal stroke, about 64 years before the Christian era. Such were the misfortunes, abilities, and miserable end, of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, who MITRIDALES supported himself so <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> against the power of Rome, and who, according to the declarations of the Roman authors, proved a more powerful and indefatigable adversary to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Italy than the great <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HANNIBAL">Hannibal</a>, Pyrrhus, Perseus, or Antiochus. It is said that Mithridates conquered 24 nations, whose different languages he knew and spoke with the same ease and fluency as his own. As a man of letters he also deserves <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>. He was acquainted with the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, and even wrote in that dialect a treatise on <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>. His skill in physic is well known; and even now there is a celebrated antidote which bears his name, and is called mithridate.

MITRA

Pages 336-336

was a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAP">cap</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> covering for the head, worn by the Roman ladies, and sometimes by the men; but it was looked upon as a mark of effeminacy in the last, especially when it was tied upon their heads.

MITRE

Pages 336-336

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, is the workmen's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> for an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> that is <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> 45 degrees, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> half a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> one. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the angle be a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of a right angle, they call it a half mitre. To describe such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>, they have an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> called the mitre <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>; with this they strike mitre <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> on their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> or battens; and for despatch, they have a mitre box, as they call it, which is made of two pieces of wood, each about an inch thick, one nailed upright on the edge of the other; the upper piece hath the mitre lines struck upon it on both sides, and a kerf to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> the mitre <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a> readily, by only applying the piece into this box. MITRE is used by the writers of the Irish <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> for a sort of base <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, which was very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> there about the year 1270, and for 30 years before and as many after. There were besides the mitre several other pieces, called, according to the figures impressed upon them, rosaries, lionades, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAGLES">eagles</a>, and by the like names. They were imported from France and other countries, and were so much below the proper currency of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, that they were not worth so much as a halfpenny each. They were at length decreed in the year 1300, and good coins struck in their <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. These were the first Irish coins in which the sceptre was left out. They were struck in the reign of Edward, the son of our Henry III., and are still found among the other antiquities of that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. They have the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s head in a triangle full faced. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENNY">penny</a>, when well preserved, weighs 22 grains; the halfpenny 10½ grains.

MITTAU

Pages 336-336

the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURLAND">Courland</a>. It is strongly fortified; but was taken by the Swedes in 1701, and by the Muscovites in 1706. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 23° 51'. N. Lat. 56° 44'.

MITTIMUS

Pages 336-336

as generally used, hath two significations. 1. It signifies a writ for removing <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> transferring of records from one <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> to another. 2. It signifies a precept, or command in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, under the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> of the peace, directed to the gaoler or keeper of some prison, for the receiving and safe keeping of an offender <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with any crime, until he be delivered by due course of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>.

MITYLENE

Pages 336-336
or MYTELENE, in Ancient Geography, a celebrated, powerful, and affluent city, capital of the island of Lesbos. It received its name from Mitylene, the daughter of Macareus, a king of the country. It is greatly commended by the ancients for the stateliness of its buildings and the fruitfulness of its soil, but more particularly for the great men it produced: Pitacius, Alcaeus, Sappho, Terpander, Theophanes, Hellenicus, &c. were all natives of Mitylene. It was long a seat of learning; and, with Rhodes and Athens, it had the honour of having educated many of the great men of Rome and Greece. In the Peloponnesian war, the Mitylenians suffered greatly for their revolt from the power of Athens; and in the Mithridatic wars, they had the boldness to resist the Romans, and disdain the treaties which had been made between Mithridates and Sylla. See METELIN.

MIXTURE

Pages 336-336

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> assemblage of several different bodies in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a>. Chemical mixture is attended with many phenomena which are never observed in simple mixtures; such as <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, effervescence, &c. To chemical mixture belong the union of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALKALIES">alkalies</a>, the amalgamation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, solution of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUMS">gums</a>, &c. and upon it depend many of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> operations of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>. See that article, passim. Mixture, in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>, a medicine which differs from a julep in this respect, that it receives into its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> not only salts, extracts, and other substances dissoluble in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; but also earths, powders, and such substances as cannot be dissolved.

MIZEN

Pages 336-336

in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, is a particular mast <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> sail. The mizen mast stands in the sternmost <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the ship. In some <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> ships there are two of these; when that next the mainmast is called the main-mizen, and that next the poop the bonaventure mizen.

MIZRAIM

Pages 336-336
or MISRAIM, the dual name of Egypt, used in Scripture to denote the Higher and Lower Egypt, which see. It sometimes occurs singular, Mazzor: 2 Kings xix. Isaiah xix. Micah vii.

MNEMOSYNE

Pages 336-336

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Cœlus and Terra. She married <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, by whom she had the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSES">Muses</a>. The word mnemosyne signifies "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>;" and therefore the poets have rightly called Memory the mother of the Muses, because it is to that mental endowment that mankind are indebted for their progress in science.

MNIUM

Pages 336-336

MARSHMOSS; a genus of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> order of musci, belonging to the cryptogamia class of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MOAB

Pages 336-336

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a> Petraea; so called from Moab the son of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">Lot</a>, to whose posterity this country was allotted by divine appointment, Deut. xi. 9. It was originally occupied by the Emim, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of giants extirpated by the Moabites, ibid. Moab anciently lay to the south of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMMON">Ammon</a>, before Sihon the Amorite stripped both nations of a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of their territory, afterwards occupied by the Israelites, Numb. xxii.; and then Moab was bounded by the river Arnon to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, the Lacus <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASPHALTITES">Asphaltites</a> to the west;

MOAT

Pages 336-337
or DITCH, in Fortification, a deep trench dug round the rampart of a fortified place, to prevent surprises. The brink of the moat, next the rampart, is called the scarpe; and the opposite one, the counterscarpe. A dry moat round a large place, with a strong garrison, is preferable to one full of water; because the passage may be disputed inch by inch, and the besiegers, when lodged in it, are continually exposed to the bombs, grenades, and other fire works, which are thrown incessantly from the rampart into their works. In the middle of dry moats, there is sometimes another small one, called cunette; which is generally dug so deep till they find water to fill it. The deepest and broadest moats are accounted the best; but a deep one is preferable to a broad one: the ordinary breadth is about 20 fathoms, and the depth about 16. To drain a moat that is full of water, they dig a trench deeper than the level of the water, to let it run off; and then throw hurdles upon the mud and slime, covering them with earth or bundles of rushes, to make a sure and firm passage.

MOATAZALITES

Pages 337-337
or Separatists, a religious sect among the Turks, who deny all forms and qualities in the Divine Being; or who divest God of his attributes. There are two opinions among the Turkish divines concerning God. The first admits metaphysical forms or attributes; as, that God has wisdom, by which he is wise; power, by which he is powerful; eternity, by which he is eternal, &c. The second allows God to be wise, powerful, eternal; but will not allow any form or quality in God, for fear of admitting a multiplicity. Those who follow this latter opinion are called Moatazalites; they who follow the former, Sephalites. This sect is said to have first invented the scholastic divinity, and is subdivided into no less than 20 inferior sects, which mutually brand one another with infidelity.

MOBILE

Pages 337-337

Moveable, any thing susceptible of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> that is disposed to be moved either by itself or by some other <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> mobile or mover. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIMUM_MOBILE">Primum Mobile</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>, was a ninth heaven or sphere, imagined above those of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a> and fixed stars. This was supposed to be the first mover, and to carry all the lower spheres round along with it; by its rapidity communicating to them a motion whereby they revolved in 24 hours. But the diurnal revolution of the planets is now accounted for without the assistance of any such primum mobile. Perpetuum Mobile. See Perpetual Motion.

MOCHO

Pages 337-337

Moco, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Mokha; by some supposed to be the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSA">Musa</a> or Moza of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>, is a port and town on the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RED_SEA"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>, of considerable trade; contains about 10,000 inhabitants, Jews, Armenians, and Mohammedans; and it gives name to a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> extending along the most southern <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>; of which that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> which lies next the sea is a dry barren <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a>, in some places 10 or 12 leagues over; but bounded by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, which being well watered, enjoy an almost perpetual <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>; and besides coffee, the peculiar produce of this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, yields corn, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYRRH">myrrh</a>, frankincense, cassia, balm, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUMS">gums</a> of several sorts, mangos, dates, pomegranates, &c. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> here is so hot and sultry in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, especially when the south <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> blows, that it would be insupportable, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it was not mitigated by the cool breezes that generally blow from the mountains on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, or the Red and Arabic seas on the west and east. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> in winter is equal to that of our warmest summers; and it is very seldom that either <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> are seen. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Mocho is now the emporium for the trade of all <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIA">India</a> to the Red sea. The trade was removed hither from <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADEN">Aden</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the prophecy of a sheik, much revered by the people, who foretold that it would soon become a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of extensive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> notwithstanding its disadvantageous situation. The buildings here are lofty, and tolerably regular, having a pleasant aspect from <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECCA">Mecca</a>. The steeples of several mosques are very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, presenting themselves to view at a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> distance. Their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a> are well stored with beef, mutton, lamb, kid, camels and antelopes <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> fowls, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a> hens, partridges, and pigeons. The sea affords plenty of fish, but not savoury; which some think proceeds from the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> saltiness of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of their aliment. The markets are also stocked with fruit, such as grapes, peaches, apricots, quinces, and nectarines; although neither shrub nor tree is to be seen near the town, except a few <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a> trees. Frequently no rain falls here in two or three years, and seldom more than a shower or two in a year; but in the mountains, at the distance of about 20 miles from Mocha, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> is watered with a gentle shower every morning, which makes the valleys fertile in corn and the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>. The Arab inhabitants, though remarkably <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> and superstitious, are said to be extremely covetous and hypocritical; robbing, thieving, and committing <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIRACY">piracy</a>, without the least scruple or remorse. The English and Dutch companies have handsome houses here, and carry on a great trade in coffee, olibanum, myrrh, aloes, liquid storax, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> arsenic, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUM">gum</a> arabic, mummy, balm of Gilead, and other drugs. One inconvenience, however, they sustain from the violence and exactions of the Arabian princes; but the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s customs are easy, being fixed at three per cent. to Europeans. Of the coins at Mocha, the most current is the camassic, which rises and falls in value at the banker's <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a>: they are from 50 to 80 for a current dollar, which is but an imaginary <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, being always reckoned one and a half per cent. lower than Spanish dollars. MOCKING <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRD">BIRD</a>. See Turdus, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. MOCOCO. See Lemur, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">Mammalia</a> Index.

MODE

Pages 338-338

in Music, a regular disposition of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> and accompaniments, relative to certain <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> sounds upon which a piece of music is formed, and which are called the essential sounds of the mode. Our modes are not, like those of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, characterized by any sentiment which they tend to excite, but result from our system of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> alone. The sounds essential to the mode are in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> three, and form together one perfect chord. 1. The tonic <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KEY">key</a>, which is the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FUNDAMENTAL">fundamental</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> both of the tone and of the mode. 2. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMINANT">dominant</a>, which is a fifth from the tonic. 3. The mediant, which properly constitutes the mode, and which is a third from the same tonic. As this third may be of two kinds, there are of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> two different modes. When the mediant forms a greater third with the tonic, the mode is <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">major</a>; when the third is lesser, it is <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOR">minor</a>. See Music.

MODEL

Pages 338-340

in a general <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, an original pattern, proposed for any one to copy <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> imitate. This word is particularly used, in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, for an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> pattern made in wood, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a>, or other <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, with all its parts and proportions, in order for the better conducting and executing some <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, and to give an idea of the effect it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> have in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>. In all great buildings, it is much the surest way to make a model in relievo, and not to trust to a bare <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> or draught. There are also models for the building of ships, &c. and for extraordinary staircases, &c. They also <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> models in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a>; whence, in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ACADEMIES">academies</a>, they give the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> model to a naked <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> or woman, disposed in several postures, to afford an opportunity to the scholars to design them in various views and attitudes. Models in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of any <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> or artificial substance, are most usually made by means of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOULDS">moulds</a> composed of plaster of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. For the purpose of making these moulds, this kind of plaster is much more fit than any other substance, on account of the power it has of absorbing <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and soon condensing into a hard substance, even after it has been rendered so thin as to be of the consistence of cream. This happens in a shorter or longer <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> as the plaster is of a better or worse <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>; and its good or bad properties depend very much upon its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, to which, therefore, particular regard ought to be had. It is sold in the shops at very different prices; the finest being made use of for casts, and the middling sort for moulds. It may be very easily coloured by means of almost any kind of powder excepting what contains an alkaline <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>; for this would chemically decompose the substance of it, and render it unfit for use. A very considerable <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of chalk would also render it soft and useless, but lime hardens it to a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. The addition of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> size will likewise render it much harder than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> water is made use of. In making either moulds or models, however, we must be careful not to make the mixture too thick at first; for if this is done, and more water added to thin it, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> must always prove brittle and of a bad quality. The particular manner of making models (or casts, as they are also called) depends on the form of the subject to be taken. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> is easy, where the parts are elevated only in a slight degree, or where they form only a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> or obtuse <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> surface from which they project; but where the parts project in smaller <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>, or form curves inclined towards the principal surface, the work is more difficult. This observation, however, holds good only with regard to hard and inflexible bodies; for such as are soft may often be freed from the mould, even though they have the shape last mentioned. But though this be the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> with the soft original substance, it is not so with the inflexible model when once it is <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a>. The moulds are to be made of various degrees of thickness, according to the size of the model to be cast; and may be from half an inch to an inch, or, if very large, an inch and a half. Where a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of models are to be taken from one mould, it will likewise be necessary to have it of a stronger contexture than where only a few are required, for very obvious reasons. It is much more easy to make a mould for any soft substance than a rigid one, as in any of the viscera of the animal body; for the fluidity of the mixture makes it easily accommodate itself to the projecting parts of the substance; and as it is necessary to inflate these substances, they may be very readily extracted again by letting out the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> which distended them. When a model is to be taken, the surface of the original is first to be greased, in order to prevent the plaster from sticking to it; but if the substance itself is slippery, as is the case with the internal parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> body, this need not be done; when necessary, it may be laid over with lintseed <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> by means of a painter's <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRUSH">brush</a>. The original is then to be laid on a Pol's smooth <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, previously greased or covered with a cloth, to prevent the plaster sticking to it; then surround the original with a frame or ridge of glaziers putty, at such a distance from it as will admit the plaster to rest upon the table on all sides of the subject for about an inch, or as much as is sufficient to give the proper degree of strength to the mould. A suffi- cient quantity of plaster is then to be poured as uniformly as possible over the whole substance, until it be everywhere covered to such a thickness as to give a proper substance to the mould, which may vary in proportion to the size. The whole must then be suffered to remain in this condition till the plaster has attained its <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a>; when the frame is taken away, the mould may be <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVERTED">inverted</a>, and the subject removed from it: and when the plaster is thoroughly dry let it be well seasoned. Having formed and seasoned the moulds, they must next be prepared for the casts by greasing the inside of them with a mixture of olive oil and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-LARD">lard</a> in equal parts, and then filled with fine fluid plaster, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANE">plane</a> of the mould formed by its resting on the surface of the table covered to a sufficient thickness with coarse plaster, to form a strong basis or support for the cast where this support is requisite, as is particularly the case where the thin and membranous parts of the body are to be represented. After the plaster is poured into the mould, it must be suffered to stand until it has acquired the greatest degree of hardness it will receive; after which the mould must be removed: but this will be attended with some difficulty when the shape of the subject is unfavourable; and in some <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> the mould must be separated by means of a small <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALLET">mallet</a> and chisel. If by these instruments any parts of the model should be broken off, they may be cemented by making the two surfaces to be applied to each other quite wet; then interposing between them a little liquid plaster; and lastly, the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> smoothed after being thoroughly dry. Any small holes that may be made in the mould can be filled up with liquid plaster, after the sides of them have been thoroughly wetted, and smoothed over with the edge of a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a>. In many cases it is altogether impracticable to prepare a mould of one piece for a whole subject; and therefore it must be considered how this can be done in such a manner as to divide the mould into the fewest pieces. This may be effected by making every piece cover as much of the pattern as possible, without surrounding such projecting parts, or running into such hollows as would not admit a separation of the mould. It is impossible, however, to give any particular directions in this matter which can hold good in every instance, the number of pieces of which the mould is to consist being always determined from the shape of the pattern. Thus the mould of the human <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CALCULUS">calculus</a> will require no more than three pieces, but that of an os femoris could scarce have fewer than ten or twelve.—Where any internal pieces are required, they are first to be made, and then the outer pieces after the former have become hard. To make a mould upon a hard and dry substance, we must, in the first <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, rub the surface of it smoothly over with the mixture of oil and lard above mentioned. Such hollows as require internal pieces are then to be filled up with fluid plaster; and while it continues in this state, a wire loop must be introduced into it, by which, when hardened, it can be pulled off. The plaster should be somewhat raised in a pyramidal form around this wire, and afterwards cut smooth with a knife while yet in its soft state; preserving two or three angular ridges from the loop to the outer edge, that it may fix the more steadily in the outer piece of the mould to be afterwards made upon it. Let the outer piece then be well greased, to prevent the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> piece from adhering; the loop being enclosed with some glaziers putty, both to prevent the second piece from adhering and to preserve a hollow place for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CORD">cord</a>. To form the second or outside piece, mix a quantity of plaster proportioned to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of surface it is to cover and the intended thickness of the mould; when it is <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> beginning to thicken, or assumes such a consistence as not to run off very easily, spread it over the internal piece or pieces as well as the pattern, taking care at the same time not to go too far lest it should not deliver safely; and as the plaster becomes more tenacious, add more upon the pattern until it has become sufficiently thick, keeping the edges <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> and smooth like the edge of a board. The plaster should be spread equally upon all parts, which is best done by a painter's pallet knife or apothecary's bolus knife: but for this the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> should be somewhat less pliable than it is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> made. When the outside piece is hardened, the edges are to be pared smooth, and nearly made square with a small pointed knife. Little holes of a conical shape are to be made with the point of a knife about an inch distant from one another, according to the size of the piece. These are designed to receive the fluid plaster in forming the adjacent parts of the mould, and occasion <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> corresponding to the hollows; and are intended to preserve the edges of the different pieces steadily in their proper relative situations. The third piece is then to be formed in a manner similar to the second; greasing the edges of the former plentifully with <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HOG">hog</a>'s lard and oil, to prevent the pieces from adhering to each other. Thus the pattern is to be wholly enclosed, only leaving a proper orifice for pouring in the plaster to form the model; small holes being also bored in the mould opposite to the wire-loops fixed in the inside pieces, through which a cord is to be conveyed from the loop to confine such pieces during the time of casting. In some cases, however, it is not necessary that the mould should totally enclose the pattern; for instance, where a model is to be made of a pedestal, or a bust of any <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the human body. The bottom of such moulds being left open, there is accordingly ample room for pouring in the plaster. After the mould is completely formed, it is next to be dried either naturally or by a gentle artificial <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, and then seasoned in the following manner:—Having been made thoroughly dry, which, if the mould is large, will require two or three weeks, it is to be brushed over plentifully with linseed oil boiled with <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, finely levigated <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LITHARGE">litharge</a>, or oil of vitriol. The inside and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a> of the mould should be particularly well supplied with it. If the mould be large, it is needless to attend to the outside; but when the moulds are small, it will not be improper to boil them in the oil; by which means their pores are more exactly filled than could otherwise be done. After the moulds have undergone this operation, they are again set by to dry, when, being greased with olive oil and hog's lard, they are fit for use. If linseed oil be used for greasing the moulds, it will in a short time impart a disagreeable <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> to the casts. The mould being properly prepared and seasoned, nothing more is requisite to form the model than to pour the finest liquid plaster of Paris into it. After a layer of this, about half an inch in thickness, has been formed all round the mould, we may use the coarser kind to fill it up entirely, or to give to the model what thickness we please. Besides the models which are taken from inanimate subjects, it has been frequently attempted to take the exact resemblance of people while living, by using their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> as the original of a model, from whence to take a mould; and the operation, however disagreeable, has been submitted to by persons of the highest ranks in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. A considerable difficulty occurs in this, however, by reason of the person's being apt to shrink and distort his features when the liquid is poured upon him; neither is he altogether without danger of suffocation, unless the operator well understands his business. To avoid the former inconvenience, it will be proper to mix the plaster with warm instead of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> water, by which means the person will be under no temptation to shrink; and, to prevent any danger of a fatal accident, the following method is to be practised: Having laid the person horizontally on his back, the head must first be raised by means of a pillow to the exact position in which it is naturally carried when the body is erect; then the parts to be represented must be very thinly covered over with fine oil of almonds by means of a painter's brush; the face is then to be first covered with fine fluid plaster, beginning at the upper part of the forehead, and spreading it over the eyes, which are to be kept <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a>, that the plaster may not come in contact with the globe; yet not closed so strongly as to cause any unnatural wrinkles. Cover then the nose and ears, plugging first up the meatus auditorii, with cotton, and the nostrils with a small quantity of tow rolled up, of a proper size, to exclude the plaster. During the time that the nose is thus stopped, the person is to breathe through the mouth: in this state the fluid plaster is to be brought <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> low enough to cover the upper lip, observing to leave the rolls of tow projecting out of the plaster. When the operation is thus far carried on, the plaster must be suffered to harden; after which the tow may be withdrawn, and the nostrils left free and open for breathing. The mouth is then to be closed in its natural position, and the plaster brought down to the extremity of the chin. Begin then to cover that part of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAST">breast</a> which is to be represented, and spread the plaster to the outsides of the arms and upwards, in such a manner as to meet and join that which is previously laid on the face: when the whole of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> has acquired its due hardness, it is to be cautiously lifted, without breaking, or giving pain to the person. After the mould is constructed, it must be seasoned in the manner already directed; and when the mould is cast, it is to be separated from the mould by means of a small mallet and chisel. The eyes, which are necessarily shown closed, are to be carved, so that the eyelids may be represented in an elevated posture; the nostrils hollowed out, and the back part of the head, from which, on account of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, no mould can be taken, must be finished according to the skill of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a>. The edges of the model are then to be neatly smoothed off, and the bust fixed on its pedestal. The method of making models in the plaster of Paris is undoubtedly the most easy way of obtaining them. When models, however, are made of such large objects that the model itself must be of considerable size, it is vain to attempt making it in the way above described. Such models must be constructed by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> with some soft substance, as wax, clay, putty, &c. and it being necessary to keep all the proportions with mathematical exactness, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of a single model of this kind must be a work of great labour and expense as well as of time. Of all those which have been undertaken by human industry, however, perhaps the most remarkable is that constructed by General Psiffer, to represent the mountainous parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>. It is composed of 142 compartments, of different sizes and forms, respectively numbered, and so artfully put together, that they can be separated and replaced with the greatest ease. The model itself is 20½ feet <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> and 12 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and formed on a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> which represents two English miles and a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> by an English foot: comprehending part of the cantons of Zug, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZURICH">Zurich</a>, Schweitz, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-UNTERWALDEN">Unterwalden</a>, Lucern, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BERNE">Berne</a>, and a small part of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of Glarus; in all, an extent of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of 18½ leagues in length and 12 in breadth. The highest point of the model, from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of the centre (which is the lake of Lucerne), is about ten inches; and as the most elevated mountain represented therein rises 1475 toises or 9440 feet above the lake of Lucerne, at a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> calculation, the height of an inch in the model is about 900 feet.
