MONTAGUE

Pages 387-388

Edward Wortley, son of the former, passed through such variegated scenes, that a bare recital of them would savour of the marvellous. From Westminster school, where he was placed for <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, he ran away three several times. He exchanged clothes with a chimney-sweeper, and he followed for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOOTY">sooty</a> occupation. He next joined himself to a fisherman, and cried flounders in Rotherhithe. He then sailed as a cabin boy to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>; where he had no sooner arrived, than he ran away from the vessel, and hired himself to a driver of mules. After thus vagabondizing it for some time, he was discovered by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a>, who returned him to his friends in England. They received him with a joy equal to that of the father of the prodigal son in the gospel. A private <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> was employed to recover those <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of learning which a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of dissipation, of blackguardism, and of vulgarity, might have obliterated. Wortley was sent to the West Indies, where he remained some time; then returned to England, acted according to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of his birth, was chosen a member, and served in two successive parliaments. His expenses exceeding his income, he became involved in debt, quitted his native <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and commenced that wandering traveller he <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to the time of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. Having visited most of the eastern countries, he contracted a partiality for their manners. He drank little wine, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of coffee; wore a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARD">beard</a>; smoked much; and, even whilst at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, he was habited in the eastern style. He sat <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>-legged in the Turkish fashion through choice. With the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a>, the Arabic, the Chaldaic, and the Persian languages, he was as well acquainted as with his native tongue. He published several pieces. One on the "Rise and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">Fall</a> of the Roman Empire." Another an exploration of "The Causes of Earthquakes." As this <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> was remarkable for the uncommon incidents which attended his life, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of that life was no less marked with singularity. He had been early married to a woman who aspired to no higher a character than that of an industrious washerwoman. As the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> was solemnized in a frolic, Wortley never deemed her sufficiently the wife of his bosom to cohabit with her. She was allowed a maintenance. She lived contented, and was too submissive to be troublesome. Montague troublesome on account of the conjugal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a>. Mr Montague, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, was a perfect <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a> in his manners. He had wives of almost every <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. When he was with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALI">Ali</a> Bey in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, he had his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a> of Egyptian females, each striving who should be the happy she who could <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> the greatest ascendency over this Anglo-Eastern <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BASHAW">bashaw</a>. At Constantinople, the Grecian women had charms to captivate this unsettled wanderer. In Spain a Spanish brunette, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> the olive-complexioned <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a>, were solicited to partake the honours of the bridal <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a>. It may be asked what became of this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROUP">group</a> of wives? Mr Montague was continually shifting the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and consequently varying the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a>. Did he travel with his wives as the patriarch did with their flocks and herds? No such thing. Wortley, considering his wives as bad travelling companions, generally left them behind him. It happened, however, that news reached his ears of the death of the original Mrs Montague the washerwoman. Wortley had no issue by her; and without issue <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a>, a very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> estate would revert to the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> son of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Bute. Wortley owing the family no obligations, was determined, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> possible, to defeat their expectations. He resolved to return to England and marry. He acquainted a friend with his intentions; and he commissioned that friend to advertise for any young decent woman who might be in a pregnant state. Several ladies answered it. One out of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> was selected, as being the most eligible object. She waited with eagerness for the arrival of her expected bridegroom; but, behold, whilst he was on his journey, death very impertinently arrested him in his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CAREER">career</a>. <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MONTAGUE_ISLAND">Montague <a cla</a>ss="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">Island</a>, one of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBRIDES">Hebrides</a>, in the South <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> near <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDWICH">Sandwich</a> island. E. Long. 168° 37'. S. Lat. 17° 26'. Montaigne, Michel de, a French gentleman, was born in Perigord in 1533. His father educated him with great care, and made him learn Latin as other children learn their mother tongue. His tutors were Nicholas Gronchi, who wrote De Comitiis Romanorum; William Guerenti, who wrote on <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>; George Buchanan; and M. Anthony <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol15.html#article-MURET">Muret</a>. He was also taught Greek by way of recreation; and because some think that starting children out of their <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> spoils their understanding, he was awakened every morning with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of music. He was counsellor for a while in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> of Bordeaux; afterwards made mayor of Bordeaux. He published his Essays, so much known in the world, in 1580. Montaigne had a great deal of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WIT">wit</a> and subtlety, but no small share of conceit and vanity. The learned and ingenious are much divided in their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> about his works. He died in 1592. Montalcino, a small populous town of Italy in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a>, and in the territory of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SIENNA">Sienna</a>, with a bishop's see. It is seated on a mountain, 17 miles south-east of Sienna, and 44 south-east of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>. E. Long. 11° 30'. N. Lat. 43° 7'. Montalto, an episcopal town of Italy, in the Marca of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCONA">Ancona</a>; seated on the river Monacio, 10 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASCOLI">Ascoli</a>, and 45 south of Ancona. E. Long. 13° 30'. N. Lat. 42° 54'. Montanists, Christian heretics, who sprang up about the year 171, in the reign of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Marcus Aurelius. They were so called from their Montan leader, the heresiarch Montanus, a Phrygian by birth; whence they are sometimes styled Phrygians and Cata- phrygians. Montanus, it is said, embraced Christianity in hopes of rising to the dignities of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. He pretended to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSPIRATION">inspiration</a>; and gave out, that the Holy Ghost had instructed him in several <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a>, which had not been revealed to the apostles. Priscilla and Maximilla, two enthusiastic women of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHRYGIA">Phrygia</a>, presently became his disciples; and in a short time he had a great number of followers. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> being assembled together, condemned his prophecies, and excommunicated those who dispersed them. The Montanists, finding themselves exposed to the censure of the whole church, formed a schism, and set up a distinct <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> under the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of those who called themselves prophets. Montanus, in conjunction with Priscilla and Maximilla, was at the head of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a>. These sectaries made no <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> in the creed. They only held that the Holy Spirit made Montanus his organ for delivering a more perfect form of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> than what was delivered by the apostles. They refused <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> for ever to those who were guilty of notorious crimes, and believed that the bishops had no authority to reconcile them. They held it unlawful to fly in time of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a>. They condemned second marriages, allowed the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISSOLUTION">dissolution</a> of marriage, and observed three lents. The Montanists became separated into two branches, one of which were the disciples of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCLUS">Proclus</a> and the other of Æschines. The latter are <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with following the heterodoxy of Praxes and Sabellius concerning the Trinity. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MONTARGIS">Montargis</a>, a considerable town of France, in the department of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOIRET">Loiret</a>, situated on the river Loing, at the junction of the two <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a> which connect the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEINE">Seine</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOIRE">Loire</a>. It is 62 miles south of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, has some manufactories of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> and woollen, and is a place of considerable trade. E. Long. 2° 36'. N. Lat. 48° 1'. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MONTAUBAN">Montauban</a>, a considerable town of France, in the department of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">Lot</a>, seated on the river <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TARN">Tarn</a>, 20 miles north of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOULOUSE">Toulouse</a>. E. Long. 1° 27'. N. Lat. 43° 36'. Montbazon, a town of France, in the department of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDRE">Indre</a> and Loire, 135 miles south-west of Paris. E. Long. 0° 45'. N. Lat. 47° 17'. Montbéliard, a strong town of France, in the department of Haut <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, seated near the river <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOUBS">Doubs</a>, 45 miles north-east of Besançon. Its <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> in 1800 was 4000. E. Long. 6° 50'. N. Lat. 47° 31'. Montblanc, a town of Spain in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Catalonia, 15 miles north of Tarragon. E. Long. 1° 5'. N. Lat. 41° 20'. MONTESQUIEU

Pages 389-391
CHARLES DE SECONDAT, BARON, a most illustrious Frenchman, descended from an ancient and noble family of Guienne, was born at the castle of La Brede, near Bordeaux, in 1689. The greatest care was taken of his education; and at the age of 20 he had actually prepared materials for his Spirit of Laws, by well digested extracts from those immense volumes of civil law which he had studied, not barely as a civilian, but as a philosopher. He became a counsellor of the parliament of Bordeaux in 1714, and was received president à mortier two years after. In 1721 he published his Persian Letters; in which, under the screen of Oriental manners, he satirized those of France, and treated of several important subjects by delicate transient glances: he did not avow this publication; but was no sooner pointed out as the author, than zeal without knowledge, and envy under the mask of it, united at once against the Persian Letters. He was received into the French academy in 1728; and having previously quitted his civil employments, he entirely devoted himself to his genius, and was no longer a magistrate, but a man of letters. Having thus set himself at liberty, he travelled through Germany, Italy, Switzerland, Holland, and England, in which last country he resided three years, and contracted intimacies with the greatest men then alive; for Locke and Newton were dead. The result of his observations was, "that Germany was fit to travel in, Italy to sojourn in, England to think in, and France to live in." On his return he retired for two years to his estate at La Brede, where he finished his work On the Causes of the Grandeur and Declension of the Romans; which appeared in 1734. The reputation acquired by this last work only cleared the way for his greater undertaking, the Spirit of Laws, which was printed at Geneva in 2 vols. 4to, 1750. This was immediately attacked by the adversaries of his Persian Letters, in a multitude of anonymous pamphlets; containing all the reproaches to which a liberal mind is exposed from craft and ignorance. M. Montesquieu drew up a defence of this work; which for truth, moderation, and delicacy of ridicule, may be regarded as a model in its way. This great man was peaceably enjoying that fulness of esteem which his great merits had procured him, when he fell sick at Paris, and died on the 10th of February 1755.—The following character of this great man is drawn by Lord Chesterfield. "His virtues did honour to human nature, his writings justice. A friend to mankind, he asserted their undoubted and unalienable rights with freedom, even in his own country; whose prejudices in matters of religion and government he had long lamented, and endeavoured, not without some success, to remove. He well knew, and justly admired, the happy constitution of this country, where fixed and known laws equally restrain monarchy from tyranny, and liberty from licentiousness. His works will illustrate his name, and survive him, as long as right reason, moral obligation, and the true spirit of laws, shall be understood, respected, and maintained." As to his personal qualities, we are told by his eulogist, M. d'Alembert, that "he was of a sweet, gay, and even temper. His conversation was spirited, agreeable, and instructive. Nobody told a story in a more lively manner, or with more grace and less affectation. He had frequent absence of mind; but always awakened from it by some unexpected stroke that re-animated the languishing conversation. Though he lived with the great, he retired whenever he could to his estate in the country, and there met his books, his philosophy, and his repose. Surrounded at his leisure hours with peasants, after having studied man in the commerce of the world, he studied them in those simple Montezuma, or Moctezuma, was emperor or king of Mexico when Cortez invaded that country in 1518, invited thither, as he pretended, by the inhabitants, whose children Montezuma, in the blindness of his superstition, had sacrificed to his idols. The warlike animals on which the Spanish officers were mounted, the artificial thunder with which they were armed, the wooden castles on which they had crossed the ocean, the armour with which they were covered, the victories which they gained wherever they went; all these circumstances, added to that foolish disposition to wonder which always characterizes a simple people, so operated upon the minds of the Mexicans, that when Cortez arrived at the city of Mexico, he was received by Montezuma as his master, and by the inhabitants as a god. At first they fell down in the streets when a Spanish valet passed by; but by degrees the court of Montezuma grew familiar with the strangers, and ventured to treat them as men. Montezuma, unable to expel them by force, endeavoured to inspire them with confidence at Mexico by expressions of friendship, while he employed secret means to weaken their power in other quarters. With this view, one of his generals, who had private orders to that purpose, attacked a party of the Spaniards who were stationed at Vera Cruz; and, although his troops were unsuccessful, yet three or four of the Spaniards were killed. The head of one of them was carried to Montezuma. In consequence of this, Cortez did what has been reckoned one of the boldest political strokes that ever was performed. He ran to the palace, followed by fifty of his troops; and, by persuasion and threats, carried the emperor prisoner into the Spanish quarters. He afterwards obliged him to deliver up those who had attacked his troops at Vera Cruz; and, like a general who punishes a common soldier, he loaded Montezuma with chains. He next obliged him to acknowledge himself in public the vassal of Charles V.; and, in name of tribute for his homage, Cortez received 600,000 merks of pure gold. Montezuma soon afterwards fell a sacrifice to his submission to the Spaniards. He and Alvaro, the lieutenant of Cortez, were besieged in the palace by 200,000 Mexicans. The emperor proposed to show himself to his subjects, that he might persuade them to desist from the attack; but the Mexicans no longer considered him in any other light but as the slave of foreign conquerors. In the midst of his speech, he received a blow with a stone which wounded him mortally; and he expired soon after, A.D. 1520.—See Cortez. This unfortunate prince left two sons and three daughters, who embraced the Christian faith. The eldest received baptism, and obtained from Charles V. lands, revenues, and the title of count de Montezuma. He died in 1698; and his family is one of the most powerful in Spain. Montferrat, a province of Italy, with the title of a duchy; bounded on the east by the duchy of Milan, and part of the territory of Genoa; on the north, by the Vercellese and Canavese; on the west, by Piedmont properly so called; and on the south by the territory of Genoa, from whence it is separated by the Apennine mountains. It contains 200 towns and castles; and is very fertile and well cultivated, abounding in corn, wine, oil, and silk. It belongs to the king of Sardinia, and Casal is the capital town. It is capital of a country of the same name, which has been almost all purchased by the house of Austria. E. Long. 9. 51. N. Lat. 47. 22. It is seated in a fertile country, 25 miles north-east of Orensa, and 55 south-east of Compostella. W. Long. 7. 9. N. Lat. 42. 28. It was defended by the princess Ragotsky, wife of Count Tekeli, when besieged by an army of the imperialists, who were obliged to raise the siege in 1688. E. Long. 21. 55. N. Lat. 46. 26. Montgeron, Louis-Basile Carre de, was born at Paris in 1686: his father was master of requests. He was scarcely 25 years of age when he purchased the place of counsellor in parliament, where by his wit and external qualifications he gained considerable reputation. Deeply engaged in all the vices which flow from irreligion, he was converted by an extraordinary circumstance. He went on the 7th of September 1731 to the tomb of Deacon Paris, with an intention to examine, with the rigour of the severest critic, the miracles which were reported to be performed there. But, according to his own account, he felt himself suddenly beat to the earth by innumerable flashes of light with which he was surrounded. His incredulity was converted into flaming zeal, and he became the apostle of the saint whom he formerly ridiculed. From that moment he devoted himself to the fanaticism of conversions, with the same impetuosity of character with which he had run into the most shameful excesses. He had not long been the disciple of Jansenism when he suffered persecution. When the chamber of inquests was banished in 1732, he was sent into the mountains of Auvergne; which, instead During his exile, he formed the plan of collecting the proofs of the miracles wrought at the tomb of the abbé Paris, and of composing what he called a Demonstration of them. On his return to Paris, he prepared to execute this plan; and on the 29th of July 1737, he actually presented to the king at Versailles a volume in quarto superbly bound. This work he accompanied with a speech, which is a mixture of zeal and argument in a tolerable style. In consequence of this work, which some consider as a masterpiece of eloquence, and others as a mass of absurdities, he was committed to the Bastile. After a few months confinement, he was sent to an abbey of Benedictine monks in the diocese of Avignon; whence he was in a short time carried to Viviers. He was afterwards confined in the citadel of Valence, where he died, A.D. 1574, aged 68. The work which he presented to the king was entitled La vérité des Miracles opérées par l'intercession de M. Paris, &c., &c.—The critics, even to this day, seem to be guided in their opinion concerning this book either by hatred or by enthusiasm. "It would be extremely rash (says the abbé de St Pierre, in the second volume of his Annales, p. 593.) to maintain with the Molinists, that no miraculous cure was ever performed at the tomb of the abbé Paris; and to say with the Jansenists, that these cures were performed by a supernatural power, would be the height of fanaticism. The truth is, (adds the same author), that no miracle appears ever to have been performed at this tomb except in the cure of the human body; in all other cases, there would have been the want of that imagination on which the whole miracle depended." Thus, although Montgeron ventured to compare these prodigies with the miracles of Jesus Christ and his apostles, yet we find no person raised from the dead, no multiplication of loaves, no command obeyed by the elements, and no blind or deaf restored to their sight or hearing. It belongs to the Author of nature alone, or to those who have derived power from him, to work such miracles as are recorded by the evangelists, or in the history of the apostles. Montgeron added a second and third volume on the same subject: he left also in manuscript a work which he composed in prison contre les Incrédules. Religion, it must be confessed, has had much more powerful advocates. Fortunately Pascal and Bossuet are among the number; and it could well have wanted both Paris and Montgeron, whatever virtues they might possess in other respects.

MONTGOMERY

Pages 391-391

the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of the same name in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, 138 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, took its name from Roger de Montgomery <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Shrewsbury, who built the castle. It is called by the Welsh Tre Valdin, that is, Baldwin's town; having been built by Baldwin, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a> of the marches of Wales, in the reign of William I. The Welsh, after having put the garrison to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, demolished it in 1095; but Henry III. rebuilt it, and granted it the privileges of a free borough, with other liberties. It is a tolerably well built town, in a healthful situation and fertile <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, with 932 inhabitants in 1811.

MONTGOMERYSHIRE

Pages 391-391

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, 40 miles in length and 37 in breadth; bounded on the north by <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERIONETHSHIRE">Merionethshire</a> and Denbighshire, on the north-east and east by <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SHROPSHIRE">Shropshire</a>, on the south by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RADNORSHIRE">Radnorshire</a> and Cardiganshire, and on the west by Montgomeryshire, the last-mentioned county and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of Merionethshire. It is divided into six <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a>; has five market <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> and 47 parishes, and in 1811 contained 51,931 inhabitants. It lies in the three several dioceses of St Asaph, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANGOR">Bangor</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HEREFORD">Hereford</a>; but sends only two members to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, one for the county, and one for the town of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTGOMERY">Montgomery</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> is pleasant and salubrious; but this county, being extremely mountainous, is not very fertile, except in the valleys, which afford some corn and plenty of pasture; but the south, south-east, and north-east parts, being more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a>, are extremely fruitful, especially a pleasant vale, watered by the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEVERN">Severn</a>.

MONTH

Pages 391-393

the twelfth <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of a year. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">CHRONOLOGY</a>, No. 17. Month, in its proper acceptation, is that space of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> which the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a> takes up in passing from any certain point to the same again, which is called a periodical month; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> it is the space of time between two conjunctions of the moon with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, which is called a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYNODICAL">synodical</a> month. That space of time which the sun takes up in passing through one sign or 12th part of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZODIAC">zodiac</a>, is also called (but improperly) a month. So that there are two sorts of months; <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUNAR">lunar</a>, which are measured by the moon; and solar, which are measured by the sun. The lunar periodical month consists of 27 days 7 hours 43 minutes 5 seconds: The lunar synodical month is 29 days 12 hours 44 minutes 3 seconds and 11 thirds. A solar month contains, upon a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> calculation, 30 days 10 hours 29 minutes 5 seconds. The Jews, Greeks, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of lunar synodical months; but, to avoid fractions, they consisted alternately of 29 and 30 days. The former, the Romans called pleni, and the Greeks μεσης; the latter were termed pleni and μεσης. 1. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> months were ranged differently in their sacred and in their civil year. Order of the Sacred Year. | 1 Nisan | <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> | |---------|-------| | 2 Iair | April | | 3 Sivan | May | | 4 Thammuz| <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUNE">June</a> | | 5 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">Ab</a> | <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> | | 6 Elul | August | | 7 Tisri | September | | 8 Marschevan | October | | 9 Casleu | November | | 10 Thebet | <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> | | 11 Sebat | <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> | | 12 Adar | February | Order of the Civil Year. | 1 Tisri | September | |---------|-----------| | 2 Marschevan | October | | 3 Casleu | November | | 4 Thebet | December | | 5 Sebat | January | | 6 Adar | February | | 7 Nisan | March | | 8 Jair | April | | 9 Sivan | May | | 10 Thammuz | June | | 11 Ab | July | | 12 Elul | August | These months being lunar cannot exactly answer to our solar months; but every Jewish month must be conceived to answer to two of ours, and partake of both. As these 12 lunar months consisted only of 354 days, the Jews, in order to bring it nearer to the true year, took care every three years to intercalate a 13th month into the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, which they called Ve-adar, or the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> Adar. The new moon was always the beginning of the month; and it is said the Jews had people posted on elevated places, to give notice to the Sanhedrim as soon as she made her appearance: After this, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROCLAMATION">proclamation</a> was made by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRUMPET">trumpet</a>, and "the feast of the new moon, the feast of the new moon," resounded amongst the people. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Hebrew months were of 30 days each, excepting the last, which consisted of 35; so that the year contained 365 days, with an intercalary month at the end of 120 years, which, by absorbing the odd hours which remained at the conclusion of each year, brought it back nearly to its proper <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. This regulation of the year was borrowed from the Egyptians. 2. The months of the Athenian year, as we have before observed, consisted alternately of 29 and 30 days. The first month, according to Meton's reformation of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KALENDAR">kalendar</a>, began with the first new moon after the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> solstice, and was called Hecatombaeon, answering to the latter half of June, and the former half of July. The order of the months, with the number of days in each, are as follow: | Month | Days | |------------------------|------| | Hecatombaeon | 30 | | Metageitnion | 29 | | <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOEDROMION">Boedromion</a> | 30 | | Marmacterion | 29 | | Panepison | 30 | | Anthesterion | 29 | | Poseidion | 30 | | <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAMELION">Gamelion</a> | 29 | | Elaphebolion | 30 | | Munichion | 29 | | Thargelion | 30 | | Scirrophorion | 29 | Each month was divided into three decades of days called ἑξακοσίες. The first was called Μέση ἑξακοσία or ἑξακοσία, or the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECADE">decade</a> of the beginning of the month; the second was Μέση μεσαῖα, or the decade of the middle; and the third was Μέση ἐπιφανής, ἑξακοσία or ἑξακοσία, the decade of the expiring month. The first <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of the first decade was termed ἑξακοσία, because the first month began with the new moon; the second day was ἑξακοσία ἑξακοσία; the third ἑξακοσία ἑξακοσία, &c. The first day of the second decade was ἑξακοσία ἑξακοσία, the second ἑξακοσία ἑξακοσία, &c.—the days of this decade were also called ἑξακοσία ἑξακοσία, ἑξακοσία ἑξακοσία, &c. The first day of the third decade was ἑξακοσία ἑξακοσία; the second was ἑξακοσία ἑξακοσία, &c. i.e. the first, second, &c. after 20, because the last decade began on the 20th day. This decade was also counted by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVERSION">inversion</a> thus; ἑξακοσία ἑξακοσία the 21st, ἑξακοσία ἑξακοσία the 22d, ἑξακοσία ἑξακοσία the 23d, and so of the rest to the last day of the month, which was called ἑξακοσία ἑξακοσία, the old and the new, because one part of that day belonged to the old and the other to the new moon; but after the time of Demetrius, the last day of the month was called from him ἑξακοσία; it sometimes was named ἑξακοσία. The Grecian months, thus consisting of 29 and 30 days alternately, fell short of the solar year 11 days 6 hours. To remedy this defect, the cycle of four years, called ἑξακοσίες, was invented.—In this cycle, after the first two years, they added an intercalated month called ἑξακοσία, consisting of 22 days; and again, after the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EXPIRATION">expiration</a> of two years more, they inserted another month of 23 days, the fourth part of a day having in the space of four years amounted to a whole day. See YEAR. 3. The Roman year under <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a> consisted of 10 months only, and began with March, which contained 31 days; then followed April which had 30, May 31, June 30, Quintilis 31, Sextilis 30, September 30, October 31, November 30, December 30. These 10 months containing no more than 364 days, this account was in a short time found to be deficient. Numa Pompilius, therefore, took away one day from each of these six months, April, June, Sextilis, September, November, December; and to the six days thus obtained he added 51, which was the number that Romulus's year, in his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, wanted to make it perfect. Numa had now 57 days to dispose of; he therefore divided them, and constituted two other months, January and February; the former consisting of 29 and the latter of 28 days. The month of January, which he placed at the winter solstice, he made instead of March to begin the year. Thus Numa's year consisted of 355 days; but this being found 10 days 6 hours short of the solar year, he made use of the intercalation of 90 days at the expiration of eight years perpetually; which number, being made up of the 11 days and a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>, kept the year pretty well to its place. The beginning of the year in Julius Caesar's time had anticipated its true place 67 whole days: these he intercalated betwixt November and December: so that the year consisted, for this one time, of 15 months or 445 days. This reformation was called the Julian correction, and this year the year of confusion. At the end of 12 years, by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> of priests, who did not understand intercalation, 12 days had been intercalated for <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a>. This was observed by Augustus Caesar, and rectified, by ordering 12 years to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> without any intercalary days. The order and succession of months was the same as that of Numa: But January, March, May, Quintilis, Sextilis, October, and December, had each 31 days; April, June, September 30, and February, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> years, 28; but every fourth year or bisextile 29. This, with a very little <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>, is the account observed at present. Quintilis, in compliment to Julius Caesar was called July, because in this month he was born; and Sextilis, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of Augustus, was called August; both which names are still <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a>.—See YEAR. Each month by the Romans was divided into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KALENDS">kalends</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NONES">nones</a>, and ides, all of which were reckoned backwards. The kalends were the first day of the month. The nones fell on the seventh, and the ides on the 13th of March, May, July, October—but in all other months the nones were on the fifth, and the ides on the 13th. For the more easy comprehension of the Roman manner of dating, according to this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the months, here follows a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>. N. B. Every <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LEAP">leap</a> year, February consisting of 29 days, the 24th and 25th of that month are written sexto Kal. Mart.; hence leap year is called Bissextilis.

MONTIA

Pages 393-393

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the triandra class, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking with those of which the order is doubtful. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MONTINIA

Pages 393-393

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the dioecia class. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MONTMEDI

Pages 393-393

a small but strong town of France, in the department of the Meuse, seated on the river Chire, which divides it into the upper and lower <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>. It is 22 miles south-east of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEDAN">Sedan</a>, 27 south-west of Luxemburg, and 135 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5° 23'. N. Lat. 49° 32'.

MONTMORENCY

Pages 393-393

a town of France, in the department of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEINE">Seine</a> and Oise, remarkable for the tombs of the dukes of this name. It is seated on a hill, near a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> valley, fertile in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, especially excellent cherries. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2° 24'. N. Lat. 48° 59'.

MONTPELIER

Pages 393-393

one of the finest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of France, and the most considerable in the department of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HERAULT">Herault</a>, excepting Thoulouse, is situated in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3° 58'. N. Lat. 43° 37'. This town has been long famous for its salubrious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, and on this account has been the frequent <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> of invalids. But the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>, according to some Montpelier travellers, is considerably changed, having at times constant rains for three months together, and often very thick fogs. Its situation, though on an eminence, never could be healthy; for between it and the Mediterranean (which is about two leagues distant) it is one <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> marsh, covered with noxious vapours, which when the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> breeze sets in, blows directly on the town and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> adjacent; of the sad effects of which, its unhealthy inhabitants, with their meagre looks, are the most convincing proofs. This <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> stands upon a rising ground fronting the Mediterranean; on the other side is an agreeable plain, extending about the same distance towards the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of the Cevennes. It is reckoned well built, yet the streets are in general narrow and the houses dark. The city contained 33,913 inhabitants in 1800, many of whom are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>, and are sociable, gay, and good tempered. The trade of Montpelier is very extensive in wine, cordials, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, verdigris, and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALTPETRE">saltpetre</a>; and the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> and woollen goods are considerable. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a> are well supplied with fish, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POULTRY">poultry</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BUTCHER">butcher</a>'s meat, and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAME">game</a>, at reasonable <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RATES">rates</a>. The wine of the country is strong and harsh: <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a> is dear, and so is sweet wine of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FRONTIGNAN">Frontignan</a>, though made in the neighbourhood of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CETTE">Cette</a>. Liquors of various sorts are compounded and distilled at Montpelier. The environs are extremely pleasant, having on one side La <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">Place</a> de Peyrou, which forms a fine terrace. From thence on a clear <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, may be seen to the eastward the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALPS">Alps</a>, which form the frontiers of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>; to the south-west, the Pyrenean mountains, which form those of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, both at about 50 leagues distant; and to the southward a most extensive view of the Mediterranean. Not far from thence is a noble aqueduct, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> tier of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>; by this, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> is brought from a mountain at three leagues distance, into two basins in a small elegant temple at the west end of the town. Here also is a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> garden, where on certain days public lectures were formerly held on <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a>. On the other side of the town is the esplanade, a beautiful walk, bordered on each side by olive trees, from whence there is a pleasing prospect of the sea and the country adjacent to the town. Previous to the revolution, Montpelier had an university, an academy of sciences, and it was the see of a bishop.

MONTREAL

Pages 393-395

an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, in the river St Lawrence, ten leagues in length, and four leagues <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and about 65 miles above Quebec. It was taken from the French by generals <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AMHERST">Amherst</a> and Murray on the 8th of September 1760. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> of the island is exceedingly rich and good, producing all kinds of European <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> and vegetables in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> abundance, with variety of garden fruits. The south side is the most inhabited, and of course best cultivated; and besides the settlements, which are numerous, the island is adorned with villas, for the retirement of the more wealthy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> during the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> season. The town of MONTREAL, situated on this island, and formerly called Ville Marie, is the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CANADA">Canada</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, buildings, and strength; and besides possessing the advantage of a less rigorous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>, for delightfulness of situation is infinitely preferable to Quebec. It stands on the side of a hill, sloping to the south, with many agreeable villas upon it, which... Montreal, the island of St Helen, and the river (which is here about two miles broad), form a most charming landscape. It was formerly enclosed with walls, to protect it from the Indians, but these were levelled some years ago. Though the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> is not very broad from north to south, it covers a great length of ground from east to west, and is fully as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and populous as Quebec. The streets are regular, forming an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>; the houses well built, and in particular the public edifices, which far exceed those of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and commodiousness; the residence of the knights hospitalers being extremely magnificent.—There are several gardens, in which, however, the proprietors have consulted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> more than elegance, particularly those of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SISTERS">Sisters</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONGREGATION">Congregation</a>, the Nunnery <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">Hospital</a>, the Recollets, Jesuit Seminary, and Governor. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of inhabitants in 1827 was about 10,000. The gardens produce peaches, apricots, plums, currants, &c. By the situation of the place, the inhabitants are well supplied with all kinds of river fish, some of which are unknown to Europeans. They have likewise plenty of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> cattle, horses, hogs, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POULTRY">poultry</a>. The neighbouring shores supply them with a great variety of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAME">game</a> in the different seasons; and the island abounds with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> of good <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> and numerous rivulets. The trade in furs is considerable, and vessels of 200 tons can come up to the town. See Canada, Supplement. Montreal, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARAGON">Aragon</a>, with a castle, seated on the river Xiloca, 25 miles north-west of Terville, and 40 south-east of Calatada. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1. 2. N. Lat. 41. 9. Montreal, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, and in the valley of Mazara, with an archbishop's see; seated on a rivulet, five miles west of Palermo, and 50 north-east of Mazara. E. Long. 13. 31. N. Lat. 38. 14. Montreal, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Mount <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a>, a fortress of Germany, in the circle of the Lower <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a>, in the Prussian territories, seated on the river Moselle, 22 miles north-east of Triers. E. Long. 7. 6. N. Lat. 49. 59. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MONTROSE">Montrose</a>, a handsome town of North <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, in the shire of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGUS">Angus</a>, situated at the mouth of the river Esk, on the German ocean, 46 miles north-east of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>. The houses are neat, and many of them in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>. The most remarkable public buildings are, the town-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and an elegant episcopal chapel.—Montrose is a royal burgh, and a dukedom in the family of Graham. It stands between two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, the south and north Esk, over the latter of which there is a handsome <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>, and over the former there is one of wood. The salmon <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FISHERIES">fisheries</a> on these rivers are very extensive, and form a considerable branch of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>. The harbour is a fine semicircular basin defended by a handsome stone pier. A great number of trading vessels belong to this port. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of Montrose in 1811 amounted to 8955. W. Long. 2. 32. N. Lat. 56. 40. Montrose, Marquis of. See Graham; and Britain, No. 137, 138, 143, 265. Montserrat, a mountain of Spain, in Catalonia, one of the most singular in the world for situation, shape, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>. It stands single, towering over a hilly <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> like a pile of grotto <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> or Gothic spires; and its height so great, that to a beholder on the top the neighbouring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> appear to be sunk to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> with the plain. It is composed of steep rocks, which at a distance seem indented; whence it is said to have received the name Montserrat from the Latin word serru, a "<a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a>." It is impossible to describe the beauty, richness, and variety, of the landscapes discovered from the most elevated point; but the extensiveness of the prospect may be conceived by the reader, upon being told that the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINORCA">Minorca</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJORCA">Majorca</a>, which are at the distance of 6 leagues, are discovered from this elevation. Montserrat is particularly famous for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADORATION">adoration</a> that is paid to an image of the Virgin, which according to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a> was found in a cave in this mountain by some shepherds in the year 880. Over this image, Guthred <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARCELONA">Barcelona</a> caused a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> and chapel to be erected; but after remaining in this receptacle upwards of 700 years, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> II. and Philip III. built a magnificent church for its reception. Innumerable and astonishing <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a> are ascribed to this holy image. The convent or monastery is situated in a nook of the mountain; it seems as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> vast torrents of water, or some violent convulsion of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, had split the eastern <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> of Montserrat, and formed in the cleft a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATFORM">platform</a> to build the monastery upon. The river Llobregat rears at the bottom, and perpendicular walls of rock of prodigious height, rise from the water edge near half way up the mountain. Upon these masses of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> stone rests the small piece of level ground which the monks inhabit. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">Close</a> behind the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a>, and in some parts impending over it, huge cliffs shoot up in a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEMICIRCLE">semicircle</a> to a stupendous elevation: their summits are split into sharp cones, pillars, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a>, and other odd shapes, blanched and bare; but the interstices are filled up with forests of evergreen and deciduous trees and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. Fifteen hermitages are placed among the woods; nay, some of them on the very pinnacles of the rock, and in cavities hewn out of the loftiest of these pyramids. The monastery is one of the 45 <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> houses of the Spanish congregation of the order of St Benedict; their general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> is held every fourth year at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VALLADOLID">Valladolid</a>, where the deputies choose abbots and other dignitaries for the ensuing quadrennium. In this monastery, they elect for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a> a Catalan and a Castilian alternately. Their possessions are great, consisting of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> villages lying to the south of the mountain; but the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> has lately curtailed their income about 6000 livres a-year, by appropriating to his own use the best house in each village, some of which, with their tythes, are worth 200 dollars per annum. Their original foundation, in 866, gave them nothing but the mountain; and to donations and economy they owe the great increase of their landed <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>. They are bound to feed and harbour for three days all <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> pilgrims that come up and pay their homage to the Virgin; and the allowance is a luncheon of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> in the morning, as much more, with broth at noon, and bread again at night. Sometimes, on particular festivals, 7000 persons arrive in one <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>; but people of condition pay a reasonable price for what they eat.—The number of professed monks, according to Mr Swinburne, is 76 (according to M. Bourgeanne 60); of lay brothers, 28; and of singing boys 25; besides physician, surgeon, and servants. The church is a gloomy edifice; and the gilding is much sullied with the the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a> of 85 lamps of silver, of various forms and sizes, that hang round the cornice of the sanctuary. Funds have been bequeathed by different devotees for furnishing them with <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>. The choir above stairs is decorated with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of Christ, in good wooden carving. A gallery runs on each side of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCEL">chancel</a>, for the convenience of the monks. A large <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> grate divides the church from the chapel of the Virgin, where the image stands in a niche over the altar, before which burn four tapers in large silver candlesticks, the present of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Medina Celi. In the sacristy, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> leading to it, are presses and cupboards full of relics and ornaments of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, silver, and precious <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>; they point out, as the most remarkable, two crowns for the virgin and her son, of inestimable value; some large <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIAMOND">diamond</a> rings; an excellent <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CAMEO">cameo</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEDUSA">Medusa</a>'s head; the Roman emperors in alabaster; and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> of St Ignatius. But as no offerings to this miraculous statue can be rejected or otherwise disposed of, the shelves are crowded with most whimsical curiosities, viz. silver legs, fingers, breasts, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EAR">ear</a>-rings, watches, two-wheeled chaises, boats, carts, and such like trumpery. On different parts of the mountain, as already noticed, are a number of hermitages. Each of these solitary retreats, which at a distance seem destitute of every thing, has a chapel, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CELL">cell</a>, a well in the rock, and a little garden. The inhabitant of one of them, which is dedicated to St Benoet, has the privilege of making an annual entertainment on a certain day; on which day all the other hermits are invited, when they receive the sacrament from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the mountain <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VICAR">vicar</a>, and after divine <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> dine together. They meet also at this hermitage, on the days of the saints to which their several hermitages are dedicated, to say <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> and commune with each other. But at other times they live in a very solitary and recluse manner, perform various penances, and adhere to very rigid rules of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSTINENCE">abstinence</a>; nor do they ever eat <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>; nor are they allowed to keep within their walls either dog, cat, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRD">bird</a>, or any living thing, lest their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> should be withdrawn from heavenly to earthly affections. Most of these hermits are said to be persons of fortune and family, disgusted with the world, who have retired thither to devote themselves to meditation, self-denial, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTRITION">contrition</a>. Montserrat, one of the Caribbee isles, belonging to Great Britain. It is a very small, but very pleasant island, so called by Columbus from its resemblance to the famous mountain near Barcelona in Catalonia. It lies in W. Long. 61°. N. Lat. 16°. 50' having Antigua to the north-east, St Christopher's and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEVIS">Nevis</a> to the north-west, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUADALOUPE">Guadaloupe</a> lying south-south-east at the distance of about nine leagues. It is about nine miles in diameter, and is supposed to contain about 49,000 or 50,000 acres. The climate is warm, but less so than Antigua, and is esteemed very healthy. The surface is mountainous, but with pleasant, rich, and fertile valleys; the hills are covered with cedars and other fine trees. Here are all the animals as well as vegetables and fruits that are to be found in the other islands. The inhabitants raised formerly a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIGO">indigo</a>. The produce now is chiefly cotton, rum, and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>. There is no good harbour, but three tolerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a>, at <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLYMOUTH">Plymouth</a>, Old Harbour, and Ker's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">Bay</a>.

MONUMENT

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> destined to preserve the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>, &c. of the person who raised it, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the person for whom it was raised; such are a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MAUSOLEUM">mausoleum</a>, a triumphal <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYRAMID">pyramid</a>, &c.

MOON

Pages 395-399

(<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUNA">Luna</a>), in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, one of the heavenly bodies, usually ranked among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a>; but with more propriety accounted a satellite, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> secondary planet. Among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, the moon was an object of prime regard.—By the Hebrews she was more regarded than the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, and they were more inclined to worship her as a deity. The new moons, or first days of every <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a>, were kept as festivals among them, which were celebrated with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> of trumpets, entertainments, and sacrifice. (See Numb. xviii. 11, x. 16. 1 Sam. xx. 5—18.) People were not obliged on these days to rest. The feasts of new moons were a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINIATURE">miniature</a> representation of the feast of trumpets, which was held on the first of the month Tisri, which was the beginning of the civil year. The Jews not being acquainted with the physical causes of eclipses, looked upon them, whether of sun or moon, as signs of the divine displeasure. The Grecians looked upon the moon as favourable to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>; and the full moons, or the times of conjunction of sun and moon, were held the most lucky seasons for celebrating marriages; because they imagined the moon to have <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> influence over <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a>. The full moon was held favourable for any undertakings by the Spartans: And no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> could induce them to enter upon an expedition, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a> an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, or attack an enemy, till the full of the moon. The moon was supposed both by Greeks and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> to preside over child-birth. The patricians at Rome wore a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CRESCENT">crescent</a> on their shoes, to distinguish them from the other orders of men. This crescent was called Lunula. Some say it was of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a>, others that it was worked upon the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SHOE">shoe</a>, and others that it was only a particular kind of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FIBULA">fibula</a> or buckle. For the astronomical phenomena connected with the moon, see ASTRONOMY <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARVEST">Harvest</a>-Moon.—It is remarkable, that the moon, during the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a> in which she is full in harvest, rises sooner after sunsetting than she does in any other full moon week in the year. By doing so, she affords an immediate supply of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> after sunset, which is very beneficial to the farmers for reaping and gathering in the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; and therefore they distinguish this full moon from all the others in the year, by calling it the harvest-moon. Influence of the Moon on the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">Human</a> Body.—The famous Dr <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAD">Mead</a> was a believer in the influence of the sun and moon on the human body, and published a book to this purpose, entitled De Imperio Solis ac Lune in Corpore humano: but this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> has been exploded by most philosophers, as equally unreasonable in itself, and contrary to fact. As the most accurate and sensible <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAROMETER">barometer</a> is not affected by the various positions of the moon, it is not thought likely that the human body should be affected by them. Several learned and ingenious men, however, still consider Dr Mead's doctrine as far from being unfounded. Moon, Influence of, on the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-EARTH_S">Earth's</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">Atmosphere</a>.—It Moon has been the opinion of the vulgar in almost all ages and countries, that the changes which take <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the state of our atmosphere, or the changes of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, depend in a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> on certain situations of the moon. This particular opinion is alluded to by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a> (A), and is applied in the shepherd of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANBURY">Banbury</a>'s rules for judging of the weather (B). We have, under <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METEOROLOGY">Meteorology</a>, No. 92 to 92, given the result of some observations on the connection between the changes of the moon and those of the weather. It can scarcely be doubted that an opinion so generally received must be founded on something more than fancy or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a>; and indeed the observations of several eminent meteorologists within the last thirty years have contributed materially to favour this opinion. Independent of actual observation, it appears reasonable to infer, that a body so <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, and so near the earth, as the moon, whose gravitating influence on the earth's surface in producing the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLUX">flux</a> and reflux of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, cannot be altogether inactive with respect to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, a fluid much more susceptible of changes than the sea. We have already noticed (Meteorology, No. 14.) the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of Mr Luke Howard, on the moon's influence on the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a> of the barometer, and we are now to give a short account of what has been advanced on her general influence by the philosophers of the continent. Among these, Signor Toaldo may be said to have led the way. From observations made at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PADUA">Padua</a>, during fifty years, on the state of the weather that corresponded to certain changes of the moon, he found that these changes were always accompanied by good or bad weather; and he at length became enabled to foretel with some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of certainty what would be the state of the atmosphere that should follow any situation of the moon. There are ten situations of the moon, which, according to Toaldo, are capable of producing a sensible effect on the earth's atmosphere. These are the syzygies or new and full moon; the quadratures; the apsides, or apogee and perigee; the lunistices, or these <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> when the moon is nearest to our zenith and at the greatest distance from it; and the moon's equinoxes. There are three different relations of the moon's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> producing a corresponding <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of revolutions, each having a certain <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>, and each corresponding to some of the above ten situations, as it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> be seen by the following <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>. Revolutions. 1. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYNODICAL">Synodical</a>, in regard to the sun; continues 29 days 12 hours 44 minutes. - New moon. - First <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>. - Full moon. - Last quarter. 2. Anomalistic, in regard to the moon's course; continues 27 days 13 hours 43 minutes. - Apogee. - Perigee. 3. Periodical, in regard to the moon's passing the equator; continues 27 days 7 hours 43 minutes. Sig. Toaldo has calculated a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of probabilities that a change of weather will take place on the approach of any one of these ten situations, and these he has expressed in a tabular form as follows: | That a change will take place at | New moon | First quarter | Full moon | Last quarter | |----------------------------------|----------|--------------|-----------|-------------| | Perigee | | | | | | Apogee | | | | | | Ascending equinox | | | | | | Northern lunstice | | | | | | Descending equinox | | | | | | Southern lunstice | | | | | In general, each of the ten situations changes the weather that prevailed under the preceding situation, and it seldom happens that a change of weather takes place without a corresponding change in the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUNAR">lunar</a> situations. From the inequality of their revolutions, these situations are often combined, and by this union their effect in producing changes of the atmosphere is greatly increased, especially when a union takes place between the syzygues and apsides. Thus, That a change will follow | New moon with perigee | <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DITTO">Ditto</a> with apogee | Full moon with perigee | Ditto with apogee | |-----------------------|-------------------|------------------------|-------------------| | | | | | These combined situations are generally accompanied or followed by storms and tempests, especially when they take place near the moon's passage over the equator. This is more particularly the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> in the months of March and September, and we find that at the new and full moon in these months, the weather takes a certain character, by which it is distinguished for the succeeding three or six months. The same takes place at the solstices, especially at the winter solstice. The new moon does not always, however, produce a change of weather; and this want of effect is most likely to happen at those new moons which are most distant from the apsides. Though Toaldo considers it as perfectly ascertained that each succeeding situation of the moon alters that state of the atmosphere which had been produced by the preceding situation; it must, however, be observed that some situations of the moon favour good and others bad weather. Thus the perigee, the new and full moon, the passage over the equator, and the northern lunstice are favourable to bad weather, while the apogee... Bad years take place when the apsides of the moon <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> in the four <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> points of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZODIAC">zodiac</a>. Their intervals, therefore, are as four to five, eight to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a>, &c., or as the intervals of the passage of the apsides through the four cardinal points of the zodiac. Thus the year 1777 was, in general, a bad year; and in that year the apsides of the moon were in the equinoctial signs; and it is probable that the years in which the apsides fall in the signs Taurus, Leo, Virgo and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AQUARIUS">Aquarius</a>, will be good and moderate years, as the year 1776 really was; and in that year the apsides of the moon were in Taurus and Virgo. Every 18th year must be similar. We, however, cannot depend upon a return altogether the same, on account of the three different revolutions of the moon; and therefore it may happen, that the epoch of this extraordinary year may be retarded a year or perhaps two. Though approximations only are here given, this does not prevent their being useful to farmers, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they only pay <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to circumstances. Besides, various exceptions must be made for different parts of the earth; and it is difficult to determine these beforehand, as what regards this system is applicable to the whole globe; but when the result of the system has been improved by local observations, the conjectures for each <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> will be attended with more certainty. The 54th year must have a greater similarity to the first than to all the rest; because, at this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, the situations of the moon, in regard to the sun and the earth, are again found in the same points. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> which falls in nine successive years, is almost equal to that which falls in the next following nine. But this is not the case when we compare in like manner the quantity of rain which falls in six, eight, or ten years.* The observations of M. Lamarck, though they confirm the opinion of the moon's general influence on the atmosphere, do not agree with those of Tealdo, as to the situations of that luminary which correspond to the changes of the weather. He could not find that agreement between the syzygies and quadratures of the moon and a change of weather, which has been so much dwelt on by Tealdo; but he is of opinion, that we are to consider the declination of the moon as the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> cause of her influence on the atmosphere. Lalande had conceived the idea that when the moon entered the northern hemisphere, or had <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> declination, the weather was most likely to be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> and dry, and that when she passed to the south of the equator, it was likely to be rainy. The observations of Lamarck, however, tend to establish the contrary opinion. Lamarck considers the two following principles as established by his observations; viz. 1. That it is in the elevation of the moon above, and her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEPRESSION">depression</a> below the equator, that are to search for those regularly varied effects which she produces on our atmosphere. 2. That the determinable circumstances, which conspire --- (c) Luna revertentes cum primum colligit ignes, Si nigrum obscurum comprenderit aëra cornu; Maximus agricolis pelagoque parabitur imber. At si virgineum sufluerit ore ruborem, Ventus erit; vento semper rubet <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AURORA">aurora</a> Phœbe. Sin ortu in quarto (namque is certissimus auctor) Pura, neque obtusis per coelum cornibus ibit; Totus et ille dies, et qui nescitur <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">ab</a> illo Exactum <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AD">ad</a> mensem, pluvia ventoque careatur. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">Note</a> (n). Georg. I. 427. spire to increase or diminish the moon's influence in her different declinations, are her apogees and perigees, her conjunctions with and oppositions to the sun; and lastly, the solar solstices and equinoxes. Considering that every lunar month, or every revolution of the moon in the zodiac, may be divided into two distinct portions, each containing about fourteen days, and each giving occasion to a particular atmospheric <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, we may assume these as two circumstances of importance in meteorology, and we may call one the boreal or northern constitution, viz. that in which the moon passes through the six northern signs of the zodiac, and the other, the austral or southern constitution, viz. that in which she traverses the six southern signs. Lamarck is convinced by observation, that in these climates, during a boreal constitution, there chiefly prevail southerly, south-westerly, and westerly winds, though sometimes, in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, the winds <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> to the southeast. In general, during this constitution, the barometer exhibits only moderate elevations of the mercury; most <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> the season is rainy or moist, and the air loaded with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a>.
