In the succeeding rational or intellectual period, his understanding, which formerly crept in a lower, mounts into a higher sphere, canvasses the natures, judges of the relations of things, forms schemes, immortally deduces consequences from what is past, and from present as well as past collects future events. By this succession of states, and of correspondent culture, he grows up at length into a moral, a social, and a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> creature. This is the last period at which we perceive him to arrive in this his mortal <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CAREER">career</a>. Each period is introductory to the next succeeding one; each life is a field of exercise and improvement for the next higher one; the life of the fetus for that of the child, and all the lower for the infant for that of the child, and all the lower for the highest and best §.—But is this the last period of nature's progression? Is this the utmost <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of her plot, where she winds up the drama, and dismisses the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTOR">actor</a> into eternal oblivion? Or does he appear to be invested with supernumerary powers, which have not full exercise and scope even in the last scene, and reach not that maturity or perfection of which they are capable; and therefore point to some higher scene, where he is to sustain another and more important character than he has yet sustained? If any such there are, may we not conclude by analogy, or in the same way of anticipation as before, that he is destined for that after part, and is to be produced upon a more august and solemn stage, where his sublimer powers shall have proportioned action, and his nature attain its completion. If we attend to that curiosity, or prodigious thirst of knowledge, which is natural to the mind in every period of its progress, and consider withal the endless round of business and care, and the various hardships to which the bulk of mankind are chained down; it is farther evident, that in this present state it is impossible to expect the gratification of an appetite at once so insatiable and so noble. Our senses, the ordinary organs by which knowledge is let into the mind, are always imperfect, and often fallacious; the advantages of assisting or correcting them are possessed by few; the difficulties of finding out <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> amidst the various and contradictory opinions, interests, and passions of mankind, are many; and the wants of the creature, and of those with whom he is connected, numerous and urgent: so that it may be said of most men, that their intellectual organs are as much shut up and secluded from proper nourishment and exercise in that little circle to which they are confined, as the bodily organs are in the womb. Nay, those who to an aspiring genius have added all the assistances of art, leisure, and the most liberal <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, what narrow prospects can even they take of this unbounded scene of things from that little eminence on which they stand? and how eagerly do they still grasp at new discoveries, without any satisfaction or limit to their ambition? But should it be said, that man is made for action, and not for speculation, or fruitless searches after knowledge, we ask, For what kind of action? Is it only for bodily exercises, or for moral, political, and religious ones? Of all these he is capable; yet, by the unavoidable circumstances of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a>, he is tied down to the former, and has hardly any leisure to think of the latter, or, if he has, wants the proper instruments of exerting them. The love of virtue, of one's friends and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, the generous sympathy with mankind, and heroic zeal of doing good, which are all so natural to great and good Let it be considered, at the same time, that no possession, no enjoyment, within the round of mortal things, is commensurate to the desires, or adequate to the capacities of the mind. The most exalted condition has its abatements; the happiest conjuncture of fortune leaves many wishes behind; and after the highest gratifications, the mind is carried forward in pursuit of new ones without end. Add to all, the fond desire of immortality, the secret dread of non-existence, and the high unremitting <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a> of the soul <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> for perfection, joined to the improbability or the impossibility of attaining it here; and then judge whether this elaborate structure, this magnificent apparatus of inward powers and organs, does not plainly point out an hereafter, and intimate eternity to man? Does nature give the finishing touches to the lesser and ignoble instances of her skill, and raise every other creature to the maturity and perfection of his being; and shall she leave her principal workmanship unfinished? Does she carry the vegetative and animal life in man to their full vigour and highest destination; and shall she suffer his intellective, his moral, his divine life, to fade away, and be for ever extinguished? Would such abortions in the mortal world be congruous to that perfection of wisdom and goodness which upholds and adorns the natural? We must therefore conclude from this detail, that the present state, even at its best, is only the worm of man's being, in which the noblest principles of his nature are in a manner fettered, or secluded from a correspondent sphere of action; and therefore destined for a future and unbounded state, where they shall emancipate themselves, and exert the fulness of their strength. The most accomplished mortal, in this low and dark apartment of nature, is only the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of what he shall be when he takes his ethereal flight, and puts on immortality. Without a reference to that state, man were a mere <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABORTION">abortion</a>, a rude unfinished embryo, a monster in nature. But this being once supposed, he still maintains his rank of the masterpiece of the creation; his latent powers are all suitable to the harmony and progression of nature; his noble aspirations, and the pains of his dissolution, are his efforts towards a second birth, the pangs of his delivery into light, liberty, and perfection; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, his discharge from gaol, his separation from his fellow prisoners, and introduction into the assembly of those heroic spirits who are gone before him, and of their great eternal Parent. The fetters of his mortal coil being loosened, and his prison walls broke down, he will be bare and open on every side to the admission of truth and virtue, and their fair attendant happiness; every vital and intellectual spring will evolve itself with a divine elasticity in the free air of heaven. He will then peep at the universe and its glorious Author Immortal, through a dark grate or a gross medium, nor receive the reflections of his glory through the strait openings of sensible organs: but will be all eye, all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EAR">ear</a>, all ethereal and divine feeling. Let one part, however, of the analogy be attended to: That as in the womb we receive our original constitution, form, and the essential stamina of our being, which we carry along with us into the light, and which greatly affect the succeeding periods of our life; so our temper and condition in the future life will depend on the conduct we have observed, and the character we have formed, in the present life. We are here in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINIATURE">miniature</a> what we shall be at full length hereafter. The first rude sketch or outlines of reason and virtue must be drawn at present, to be afterwards enlarged to the stature and beauty of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a>. This, if duly attended to, must prove not only a guard, but an admirable incentive to virtue. For he who faithfully and ardently follows the light of knowledge, and pants after higher improvements in virtue, will be wonderfully animated and inflamed in that pursuit by a full conviction that the scene does not <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> with life—that his struggles, arising from the weakness of nature and the strength of habit, will be turned into triumphs—that his career in the track of wisdom and goodness will be both swifter and smoother—and those generous arduous with which he glows towards heaven, i.e., the perfection and immortality of virtue, will find their adequate object and exercise in a sphere proportionally enlarged, incorruptible, immortal. On the other hand, what an inexpressible damp must it be to the good man, to dread the total extinction of that light and virtue, without which life, nay, immortality itself, were not worth a single wish? Many writers draw their proofs of the immortality of the soul, and of a future state of rewards and punishments, from the unequal distribution of these here, life of present. It cannot be dissembled, that wicked men often escape the outward <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> due to their crimes, and do not feel the inward in that measure their demerit seems to require, partly from the callousness induced upon their nature by the habits of vice, and partly from the dissipation of their minds abroad by pleasure or business—and sometimes good men do not reap all the natural and genuine <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of their virtue, through the many unforeseen or unavoidable calamities in which they are involved. To the smallest reflection, however, it is obvious that the natural tendency of virtue is to produce happiness; that if it were universally practised, it would, in fact, produce the greatest sum of happiness of which human nature is capable; and that this tendency is defeated only by numerous individuals, who, forsaking the laws of virtue, injure and oppress those who steadily adhere to them. But the natural tendency of virtue is the result of that constitution of things which was established by God at the creation of the world. This being the case, we must either conclude, that there will be a future state, in which all the moral obliquities of the present shall be made straight; or else admit, that the designs of infinite wisdom, goodness, and power, can be finally defeated by the perverse conduct of human weakness.—But this last supposition is so extravagantly absurd, Motives to that the reality of a future state, the only other possible alternative, may be pronounced to have the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> of perfect demonstration. Virtue has present rewards, and vice present punishments annexed to it; such rewards and punishments as make virtue, in most cases that happen, far more eligible than vice: but, in the infinite variety of human contingencies, it may sometimes fall out, that the inflexible practice of virtue shall deprive a man of considerable advantages to himself, his family, or friends, which he might <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> by a well-timed piece of roguery; suppose by betraying his trust, voting against his conscience, selling his country, or any other crime where the security against discovery shall heighten the temptation. Or, it may happen, that a strict adherence to his honour, to his religion, to the cause of liberty and virtue, shall expose him, or his family, to the loss of every thing, nay, to poverty, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SLAVERY">slavery</a>, death itself, or to torments far more intolerable. Now what shall secure a man's virtue in circumstances of such <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>? What shall enforce the obligations of conscience against the allurements of so many interests, the dread of so many and so terrible evils, and the almost unsurmountable aversion of human nature to excessive pain? The conflict is the greater, when the circumstances of the crime are such as easily admit a variety of alleviations from necessity, natural affection, love to one's family or friends, perhaps in indigence: these will give it even the air of virtue. Add to all, that the crime may be thought to have few bad consequences,—may be easily concealed,—or imagined possible to be retrieved in a good measure by future good conduct. It is obvious to which side most men will lean in such a case; and how much need there is of a balance in the opposite <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a>, from the consideration of a God, of a Providence, and of an immortal state of retribution, to keep the mind firm and uncorrupted in those or like instances of singular trial or distress. But without supposing such peculiar instances, a general sense of a governing Mind, and a persuasion that virtue is not only befriended by him here, but will be crowned by him hereafter with rewards suitable to its nature, vast in themselves, and immortal in their duration, must be not only a mighty support and incentive to the practice of virtue, but a strong <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARRIER">barrier</a> against vice. The thoughts of an Almighty Judge, and of an impartial future reckoning, are often alarming, inexpressibly so, even to the stoutest offenders. On the other hand, how supporting must it be to the good man, to think that he acts under the eye of his friend, as well as judge! How improving, to consider from the present state as connected with a future one, and immortality of the soul, every relation in which he stands as a school of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> for his affections; every trial as the exercise of some virtue; and the virtuous deeds which result from both, as introductory to higher scenes of action and enjoyment! Finally, How transporting is it to view death as his discharge from the warfare of mortality, and a triumphant entry into a state of freedom, security, and perfection, in which knowledge and wisdom shall <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> upon him from every quarter; where each faculty shall have its proper object: and his virtue, which was often damped or defeated here, shall be enthroned in undisturbed and eternal empire? On reviewing this short system of morals, and the motives which support and enforce it, and comparing both with the Christian scheme, what light and vigour do they borrow from thence! How clearly and fully do Christianity lay open the connexions of our nature, both material and immaterial, and future as well as present! what an ample and beautiful detail does it present of the duties we owe to God, to society, and ourselves, promulgated in the most simple, intelligible, and popular manner; divested of every partiality of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>; and adapted to the general state of mankind! With what bright and alluring example does it illustrate and recommend the practice of those duties; and with what mighty sanctions does it enforce that practice! How strongly does it describe the corruptions of our nature; the deviations of our life from the rule of duty, and the causes of both! How marvellous and benevolent a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDEMPTION">redemption</a> does it unfold, by which those corruptions may be remedied, and our nature restored from its deviations to transcendent heights of virtue and piety! Finally, What a fair and comprehensive prospect does it give us of the administration of God, of which it represents the present state only as a small period, and a period of warfare and trial! How solemn and unbounded are the scenes which it opens beyond it! the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESURRECTION">resurrection</a> of the dead, the general judgment, the equal distribution of rewards and punishments to the good and the bad; and the full completion of divine wisdom and goodness in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FINAL">final</a> establishment of order, perfection, and happiness! How glorious then is that scheme of religion, and how worthy of affection as well as of admiration, which, by making such discoveries, and affording such assistances, has disclosed the unfading fruits and triumphs of virtue, and secured its interests beyond the power of time and chance. MORAL Sense, that whereby we perceive what is good, virtuous, and beautiful, in actions, manners, and characters. See Moral <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">Philosophy</a>. MORALITY. See Moral Philosophy. MORANT-Point, the most easterly point or promontory of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Jamaica, in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. W. Long. 75° 36'. N. Lat. 17° 56'.

MORASS

Pages 446-446

a marsh, fen, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> low moist ground, which receives the waters from above without having any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> to carry them off again. Sommer derives the word from the Saxon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERSE">merse</a>, "lake;" Salmasius from mare, "a collection of waters;" others from the German marast "a muddy <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>;" and others from marasso, of maricetum, a mariscus, i.e. rushes. See Draining, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">Agriculture</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. In Scotland, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of England, there is a particular kind of morasses called mosses, or <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEAT">peat</a>-mosses, whence the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> people dig their peat or turf for firing. See Moss.

MORAT

Pages 446-448
or Murten, a considerable town of Switzerland, Switzerland, capital of a bailiwick of the same name, belonging to the cantons of Bern and Friburg. It is seated on the lake Morat, on the road from Avenche to Bern, 10 miles west of Bern and 10 miles north-east of Friburg. The lake is about six miles long and two broad, and the country about it pleasant and well cultivated. The lakes of Morat and Neufchatel are parallel to each other, but the latter is more elevated, discharging itself by means of the river Broye into the lake of Neufchatel. According to M. de Luc, the former is 15 French feet above the level of Neufchatel lake; and both these lakes, as well as that of Biene, seem formerly to have extended considerably beyond their present limits, and from the position of the country appear to have been once united. Formerly the large fish named *saurus glans*, or the saloth, frequented these lakes, but has not been caught in them for a long time past. The environs of this town and lake were carefully examined by Mr Coxe, during his residence in Switzerland, who made several excursions across the lake to a ridge of hills situated betwixt it and Neufchatel. Here are many delightful prospects; particularly one from the top of Mount Vuilly, which, he says, is perhaps the only central spot from which the eye can at once comprehend the vast amphitheatre formed on one side by the Jura stretching from the environs of Geneva as far as Basle, and, on the other, by that stupendous chain of snowy Alps which extend from the frontiers of Italy to the confines of Germany, and is lost at each extremity in the horizon. Morat is celebrated for the obstinate defence it made against Charles the Bold, duke of Burgundy, and for the battle which afterwards followed on the 22d of June 1476, where the duke was defeated, and his army almost entirely destroyed*. Not far from the town, and adjoining to the high road, there still remains a monument of this victory. It is a square building, filled with the bones of Burgundian soldiers who were slain at the siege and in the battle; the number of which appears to have been very considerable. There are several inscriptions in the Latin and German languages commemorating the victory. *MORATA, OLYMPIA FULVIA*, an Italian lady, distinguished for her learning, was born at Ferrara, in 1526. Her father, after teaching the belles lettres in several cities of Italy, was made preceptor to the two young princes of Ferrara, the sons of Alphonsus I. The uncommon abilities he discovered in his daughter determined him to give her all the advantages of education. Meanwhile the princess of Ferrara studying polite literature, it was judged expedient that she should have a companion in the same pursuit; and Morata being called, she was heard by the astonished courtiers to declaim in Latin, to speak Greek, and to explain the paradoxes of Cicero. Her father dying, she was obliged to return home to take upon her the management of family affairs, and the education of her brother and three sisters; both which she executed with the greatest diligence and success. In the mean time Andrew Gruntler, a young German physician, had married her, and with him she went to Germany, taking her brother along with her, whom she instructed in the Latin and Greek tongues; and after staying a short time at Augsburg, went to Schweinfurt in Franconia, where her husband was born: but they had not been there long before that town was unhappily besieged and burnt; however, escaping the flames, they fled in the utmost distress to Hammelburg. This place they were also obliged to quit, and were reduced to the last extremities, when the elector Palatine invited Gruntler to be professor of physic at Heidelberg. He entered on his new office in 1554; but they no sooner began to taste the sweets of repose, than a disease, occasioned by the distresses and hardships they had suffered, seized upon Morata, who died in 1555, in the 29th year of her age; and her husband and brother did not long survive her. She composed several works, great part of which were burnt with the town of Schweinfurt; the remainder, which consist of orations, dialogues, letters, and translations, were collected and published under the title of *Olympia Fulviae Moratae, fiamine doctrinae, et planè divinae, opera omnia quae haecenium inveniri potuerint; quibus Caelii secundi curiosis epistolæ ac orationes accesserunt*. *MORAVIA*, a river of Turkey in Europe, which rises in Bulgaria, runs north through Servia by Nissa, and falls into the Danube at Semendria, to the eastward of Belgrade. *MORAVIA*, a marquisate of Germany, derives the name of Mohern, as it is called by the Germans, and of Morawa, as it is called by the natives, from the river of that name, which rises in the mountains of the county of Glatz, and passes through the middle of it. It is bounded to the south by Austria, to the north by Silesia, to the west by Bohemia, and to the east by Silesia and Hungary; being about 120 miles in length and 100 in breadth. Its surface is about 80,000 square miles. In 1775 its population, according to official returns, was 1,134,674, of whom 23,382 were Jews; but in 1801 has been computed to be 1,400,000 (Mentelle et Malte Brun). Olmutz, formerly the chief town, contains 11,000 inhabitants; Brunn, now the seat of government, contains 14,000; and there are several other considerable towns. A great part of this country is overrun with woods and mountains, where the air is very cold, but much wholesomer than in the low grounds, which are full of bogs and lakes. The mountains, in general, are barren; but the more champaign parts tolerably fertile, yielding corn, with plenty of hemp and flax, good saffron, and pasture. Nor is it altogether destitute of wine, red and white, fruits, and garden stuff. Moravia also abounds in horses, black cattle, sheep, and goats. In the woods and about the lakes there is plenty of wild fowl, game, venison, bees, honey, hares, foxes, wolves, beavers, &c. This country affords marble, alum, iron, sulphur, saltpetre, and vitriol, with mineral waters, and warm springs; but salt is imported. Its rivers, of which the March, Morawa, or Morau, are the chief, abound with trout, crayfish, barbels, eels, perch, and many other sorts of fish. The language of the inhabitants is a dialect of the Slavonic, differing little from the Bohemian; but the nobility and citizens speak German and French. Moravia was anciently inhabited by the Quadi, who were driven out by the Scavi. Its kings, who were once powerful and independent, afterwards became dependent on, and tributary to, the German emperors and kings. At last, in the year 928, the Moravian kingdom was parcelled out among the Germans, Poles, and Moravia and Hungarians. In 1886, that part of it properly called Moravia was declared a marquisate by the German king Henry IV. and united with Bohemia, to whose dukes and kings it hath ever since been subject. The states of the country consist of the clergy, lords, knights, and burgesses; and the diets, when summoned by the regency, are held at Brunn. The marquisate is still governed by its own peculiar constitutions, under the directorium in publicis et camerilibus, and the supreme judicatory at Vienna. It is divided into six circles, each of which has its captain, and contributes to its sovereign about one-third of what is exacted of Bohemia. Towards the expenses of the military establishment of the whole Austrian hereditary countries, its yearly quota is 1,856,490 florins. Seven regiments of foot, one of cuirassiers, and one of dragoons, are usually quartered in it. Christianity was introduced into this country in the 9th century; and the inhabitants continued attached to the church of Rome till the 15th, when they espoused the doctrine of John Huss, and threw off Popery; but after the defeat of the elector Palatine, whom they had chosen king, as well as the Bohemians, the emperor Ferdinand II. re-established Popery; though there are still some Protestants in Moravia. The bishop of Olmutz, who stands immediately under the pope, is at the head of the ecclesiastics in this country. The supreme ecclesiastical jurisdiction, under the bishop, is vested in a consistory. The commerce of this country is inconsiderable. Of what they have, Brunn enjoys the principal part. At Iglau and Trebitz are manufactures of cloth, paper, gunpowder, &c. There are also some iron works and glass houses in the country. The inhabitants of Moravia in general are open-hearted, not easy to be provoked or pacified, obedient to their masters, and true to their promises; but credulous of old prophecies, and much addicted to drinking, though neither such sots or bigots as they are represented by some geographers. The boors, indeed, upon the river Hank, are said to be a thievish, unpolished, brutal race. The sciences now begin to lift up their heads a little among the Moravians, the university of Olmutz having been put on a better footing; and a riding academy, with a learned society, has been lately established there. MORAVIAN BRETHREN. See HERNHUTTERS, and UNITAS FRATRUM.

MORAW

Pages 448-448
or MORAVA, a large river of Germany, which has its source on the confines of Bohemia and Silesia. It traverses the whole of Moravia, waters Olmutz and Hradisch, and receiving the Taya from the confines of Lower Hungary and Upper Austria, separates these two countries as far as the Danube, into which it falls.

MORBID

Pages 448-448

among physicians, signifies "diseased <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> corrupt;" a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> applied either to an unsound <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, or to those parts or humours that are affected by a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>.

MORBUS COMITIALIS

Pages 448-448

a name given to the epilepsy; because <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> on any <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> when the people were assembled in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMITIA">comitia</a> upon public business, any person suddenly seized with this disorder should <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> was dissolved, and the business of the comitia, however important, was suspended. See COMITIA.

MORDAUNT

Pages 448-448
CHARLES, earl of Peterborough, a celebrated commander both by sea and land, was the son of John Lord Mordaunt Viscount Avalon, and was born about the year 1638. In 1675 he succeeded his father in his honours and estate. While young he served under the admirals Torrington and Narborough in the Mediterranean against the Algerines; and in 1689 embarked for Africa with the earl of Plymouth, and distinguished himself at Tangier when it was besieged by the Moors. In the reign of James II. he voted against the repeal of the test act; and disliking the measures of the court, obtained leave to go to Holland to accept the command of a Dutch squadron in the West Indies. He afterwards accompanied the prince of Orange into this kingdom; and upon his advancement to the throne, was sworn of the privy-council, made one of the lords of the bedchamber to his majesty, also first commissioner of the treasury, and advanced to the dignity of earl of Monmouth. But in November 1692 he was dismissed from his post in the treasury. On the death of his uncle Henry earl of Peterborough in 1697, he succeeded to that title; and, upon the accession of Queen Anne, was invested with the commission of captain-general and governor of Jamaica. In 1703 he was sworn of the privy-council; and the same year declared general and commander in chief of the forces sent to Spain, and joint admiral of the fleet with Sir Cloudesley Shovel, of which the year following he had the sole command. His taking Barcelona with a handful of men, and afterwards relieving it when greatly distressed by the enemy; his driving out of Spain the duke of Anjou, and the French army, which consisted of 25,000 men, though his own troops never amounted to 10,000; his gaining possession of Catalonia, of the kingdoms of Valencia, Arragon, and the isle of Majorca, with part of Murcia and Castile, and thereby giving the earl of Galway an opportunity of advancing to Madrid without a blow; are astonishing instances of his bravery and conduct. For these important services his lordship was declared general in Spain by Charles III. afterwards emperor of Germany; and on his return to England he received the thanks of the house of lords. His lordship was afterwards employed in several embassies to foreign courts, installed knight of the Garter, and made governor of Minorca. In the reign of George I. he was general of all the marine forces in Great Britain, in which post he was continued by King George II. He died in his passage to Lisbon, where he was going for the recovery of his health, in 1735. His lordship was distinguished by various shining qualities: for, to the greatest personal courage and resolution, he added all the arts and address of a general; a lively and penetrating genius; and a great extent of knowledge upon almost every subject of importance within the compass of ancient and modern literature.

MORDELLA

Pages 448-448

a genus of insects of the coleoptera order. See Entomology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MORE

Pages 448-450

Sir Thomas, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> of England, the son of Sir John More, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a>, one of the judges of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENCH">Bench</a>, was born in the year 1480, in in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">Milk</a>-street <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. He was first sent to a school at St Anthony's in Threadneedle street; and afterward introduced into the family of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Moreton, who in 1497 sent him to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>. During his residence at the university he constantly attended the lectures of Linacre and Grocinus, on the Greek and Latin languages. Having in the space of about two years made considerable proficiency in academical learning, he came to New Inn in London, in order to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>; whence, after some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, he removed to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>'s Inn, of which his father was a member. Notwithstanding his application to the law, however, being now about 20 years old, he was so bigotted to monkish <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>, that he wore a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> shirt next his skin, frequently fasted, and often slept on a bare plank. In the year 1503, being then a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURGESS">burgess</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, he distinguished himself in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, in opposition to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> for granting a subsidy and three fifteenths for the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> of Henry VII.'s eldest <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>, Margaret, to the king of Scotland. The motion was rejected; and the king was so highly offended at this opposition from a beardless boy, that he revenged himself on Mr More's father, by sending him, on a frivolous pretence, to the Tower, and obliging him to pay 100l. for his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>. Being now called to the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a>, he was appointed law reader at Furnival's inn, which <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> he held about three years; but about this time he also read a public lecture in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of St Lawrence, Old Jewry, upon St Austin's treatise De Civitate Dei, with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> applause. He had indeed formed a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of becoming a Franciscan friar, but was dissuaded from it; and, by the advice of Dr Colet, married Jane, the eldest daughter of John <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COLT">Colt</a>, Esq., of Newhall in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a>. In 1508 he was appointed judge of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a>'s <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of London, was made a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> of the peace, and became very eminent at the bar. In 1516 he went to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a> in the retinue of Bishop Tonstal and Dr Knight, who were sent by King Henry VIII. to renew the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> with the archduke of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, afterwards <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V. On his return, Cardinal Wolsey would have engaged Mr More in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, and offered him a pension, which he refused. Nevertheless, it was not <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> before he accepted the place of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the requests, was created a knight, admitted of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRIVY_COUNCIL">privy <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, and in 1520 made <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a> of the exchequer. About this time he built a house on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>, at Chelsea, and married a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> wife. This wife, whose name was Middleton, and a widow, was old, ill tempered, and covetous; nevertheless Erasmus says, he was as fond of her as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> she were a young maid. In the 14th year of Henry VIII. Sir Thomas More was made speaker of the house of commons; in which capacity he had the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> to oppose the then powerful minister, Wolsey, in his demand of an oppressive subsidy; notwithstanding which, it was not long before he was made chancellor of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANCASTER">Lancaster</a>, and was treated by the king with singular familiarity. The king having once dined with Sir Thomas at Chelsea, walked with him near an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> in the garden, with his arm round his neck. After he was gone, Mr Roper, Sir Thomas's son-in-law, observed how happy he was to be so familiarly treated by the king: to which Sir Thomas replied, "I thank our lord, son Roper, I find his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> my very good lord indeed, and believe he doth as singularly favour me as any subject within this realm: howbeit, I must tell thee, I have no cause to be proud thereof; for if my head would win him a castle in France, it would not fail to go off." From this anecdote it appears, that Sir Thomas knew his grace to be a villain. In 1526 he was sent with Cardinal Wolsey and others, on a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> embassy to France, and in 1529, with Bishop Tonstal to Cambrai. The king, it seems, was so well satisfied with his services on these occasions, that in the following year, Wolsey being disgraced, he made him chancellor; which seems the more extraordinary, when we are told that Sir Thomas had repeatedly declared his disapprobation of the king's divorce, on which the great defensor fidei was so positively bent. Having executed the office of chancellor about three years, with equal <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> and integrity, he resigned the seals in 1533, probably to avoid the danger of his refusing to confirm the king's divorce. He now retired to his house at Chelsea; dismissed many of his servants; sent his children with their respective families to their own houses (for hitherto, he had, it seems, maintained all his children, with their families, in his own house, in the true style of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a>); and spent his time in study and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>: but the capricious <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a> would not suffer him to enjoy his tranquillity. Though now reduced to a private station, and even to indigence, his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of the legality of the king's marriage with <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a> Boleyn was deemed of so much importance, that various means were tried to procure his approbation; but all persuasion proving ineffectual, he was, with some others, attainted in the house of lords of misprision of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>, for encouraging <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> Barton, the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUN">nun</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>, in her treasonable practices. His innocence in this affair appeared so clearly, that they were obliged to strike his name out of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BILL">bill</a>. He was then accused of other crimes, but with the same effect; till, refusing to take the oath enjoined by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of supremacy, he was committed to the Tower, and, after 15 months imprisonment, was tried at the bar of the king's bench for high treason, in denying the king's supremacy. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> rested on the sole <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> of Rich the solicitor general, whom Sir Thomas, in his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>, sufficiently discredited; nevertheless the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JURY">jury</a> brought him in guilty, and he was condemned to suffer as a traitor. The merciful Harry, however, indulged him with simple decollation; and he was accordingly beheaded on Tower hill, on the 5th of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1535. His body, which was first interred in the Tower, was begged by his daughter Margaret, and deposited in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCEL">chancel</a> of the church at Chelsea, where a monument, with an inscription written by himself, had been some time before erected. This monument with the inscription is still to be seen in that church. The same daughter, Margaret, also procured his head after it had remained 14 days upon London <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a>, and placed it in a vault belonging to the Roper family, under a chapel adjoining to St Dunstan's church in Canterbury. Sir Thomas More was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of some learning, and an upright judge; a very <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, yet cheerful, and even affectedly witty. witty (a). He wanted not sagacity, where religion was out of the question; but in that his faculties were so enveloped, as to render him a weak and credulous enthusiast. He left one son and three daughters; of whom Margaret, the eldest, was very remarkable for her knowledge of the Greek and Latin languages. She married a Mr Roper of Wellhall in Kent, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of Sir Thomas More was published by Mr Hearne at Oxford in 1716. Mrs Roper died in 1544; and was buried in the vault of St Dunstan's in Canterbury, with her father's head in her arms. Sir Thomas was the author of various works, though his *Utopia* is the only performance that has survived in the esteem of the world; owing to the rest being chiefly of a polemic <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>: his answer to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUTHER">Luther</a> has only gained him the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> of having the best knack of any man in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, at calling bad names in good Latin. His English works were collected and published by order of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, in 1557; his Latin, at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a>, in 1563, and at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOUVAIN">Louvain</a>, in 1566.

MOREA

Pages 450-450

formerly called the *<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PELOPONNESUS">Peloponnesus</a>*, is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> to the south of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, to which it is joined by the isthmus of Corinth. Its form resembles a mulberry <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a>, and its name is derived from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of mulberry trees which it produces. It is about 140 miles in length, and 110 in breadth. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> is temperate, and the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> fertile, except in the middle, where it is full of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, and is watered by a great number of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>. It is divided into three provinces; Scania, Belvedera, and Brazzo-di-Maina. It was taken from the Turks by the Venetians in 1687; but they lost it again in 1715. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of the Morea is estimated by Dr Clarke at 300,000. See GREECE and PELOPONNESUS.

MOREL

Pages 450-450

the name of several celebrated printers to the kings of France, who, like the Stephens, were also men of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> learning. Frederic Morel, who was interpreter in the Greek and Latin tongues, as well as printer to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, was heir to Vascosan, whose <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> he had married.—He was born in Champagne, and he died in an advanced <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, 1583. His sons and grandsons trod in his steps; they distinguished themselves in literature, and maintained also the reputation which he had acquired by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a>. The edition of *St Gregory of Nyssa*, by his son <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CLAUDE">Claude</a> Morel, is held in great estimation by the learned. Morel, Frederic, son of the preceding, and still more celebrated than his father, was professor and interpreter to the king, and printer in ordinary for the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a>, Greek, Latin, and French languages. He was so devoted to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>, that when he was told his wife was at the point of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, he would not stir till he had finished the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> which he had begun. Before it was finished, he was informed that she was actually dead; *I am sorry for it*, (replied he coldly), *she was an excellent woman*. This printer acquired great reputation from the works which he published, which were very numerous and beautifully executed. From the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a> in the king's library, he published several treatises of St <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a>, Theodore, St Cyrille; and he accompanied them with a translation. His edition of the works of Ecumenius and Aretas, in 2 vols. folio, is much esteemed. In short, after distinguishing himself by his knowledge in the languages, he died <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 27, 1630, at the age of 78. His sons and grandsons followed the same profession. Morel, William, regius professor of Greek, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a> of the king's printing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> at Paris, died 1564. He composed a *Dictionnaire Grec-Latin Francais*, which was published in quarto in 1624, and some other works which indicate very extensive learning. His editions of the Greek authors are exceedingly beautiful. This great scholar, who was of a different family from the preceding, had a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> named John, who died in prison (where he had been confined for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a>) at the age of 20, and whose body was dug out of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a>, and burnt, Feb. 27, 1559. They were of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> of Tilleul, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MORTAIN">Mortain</a> in Normandy.

MORENA

Pages 450-450

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a district <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSIA">Mysia</a>, in the Hither <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>. A <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of which was occupied by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CLEON">Cleon</a>, formerly at the head of a band of robbers, but afterwards <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> Abrettens, and enriched with possessions, first by Antony, and then by Caesar.

MORESQUE

Pages 450-450

Moresk, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Morizko, a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, carving, &c. done after the manner of the Moors; consisting of several <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GROTESQUE">grotesque</a> pieces and compartments promiscuously intermingled, not containing any perfect <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, or other animal, but a wild resemblance of birds, beasts, trees, &c. These are also called arabesques, and are particularly used in embroideries, damask <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, &c. **Moresque Dances**, vulgarly called *Morrice dances*, are those altogether in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of the Moors, as sarabands, chacons, &c. and are usually performed with castanets, tambours, &c. There are few <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> places in England where the morrice dance is not known. It was probably introduced about, or a little before, the reign of Henry VIII. and is a dance of young men in their shirts, with bells at their feet, and ribbands of various colours tied round their arms and flung across their shoulders. **MORGAGNA**. See FATA.

MORGAGNI

Pages 450-451

John Baptist, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of medicine, first professor of anatomy in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PADUA">Padua</a>, and member of several of the most eminent <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a> of learned men in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, was born in the year 1682, at Forli, a town in the district of La Romagna in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. --- (a) This last disposition, we are told, he could not restrain even at his execution. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> being come, he ascended the scaffold, which seemed so weak that it was ready to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a>; whereupon, "I pray (said he) see me safe up, and for my coming <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> let me shift for myself." His prayers being ended, he turned to the executioner, and with a cheerful countenance said, "Pluck up thy spirits, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, and be not afraid to do thy office; my neck is very short, take heed therefore thou strike not awry for saving thy honesty." Then laying his head upon the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLOCK">block</a>, he bade him stay until he had put aside his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARD">beard</a>, saying, "That had never committed any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>." His parents, who were in easy circumstances, allowed him to follow that course in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> his genius dictated. He began his studies at the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-NATIVITY">nativity</a>; but soon after removed to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a>, where he obtained the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of Doctor of Medicine, when he had <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> reached the 16th year of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>. Here his peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for anatomy found an able preceptor in Valsalva, who bestowed on him the utmost <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>; and such was the progress he made under this excellent <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, that at the age of 20 he himself taught anatomy with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> reputation. Soon, however, the fame of his predictions, and the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of his pupils, excited the jealousy of the public professors, and gave rise to vindictive persecutions. But his abilities and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a> gained him a complete triumph over his enemies; and all opposition to him was finally terminated from his being appointed by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> of Bologna to fill a medical <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a>, which soon became vacant. But the duties of this office, although important, neither occupied the whole of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, nor satisfied his anxious desire to afford instruction. He still <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to labour in secret on his favourite subject, and soon after communicated the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of these labours to the public in his *Adversaria Anatomica*, the first of which was published in the year 1706, the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> and third in 1717, and the three others in 1719. The publication of this excellent <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> spread the fame of Morgagni far beyond the limits of the state of Bologna. Such was his reputation, that the wise republic of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> had no hesitation in making him an offer of the second chair of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of medicine in the university of Padua; then vacant by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of M. Molinetti; and, to ensure his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ACCEPTANCE">acceptance</a>, they doubled the emoluments of that appointment. While he was in this department, he published his treatise, entitled *Nova Institutionum medicarum idea*, which first appeared at Padua in the year 1712. From this work his former reputation suffered no diminution. And soon after he rose, by different steps, to be first professor of anatomy in that celebrated university. Although Morgagni was thus finally settled at Padua, yet he gave evident proofs of his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to Bologna, which he considered as his native <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> with respect to the sciences. He exerted his utmost efforts in establishing the academy of Bologna, of which he was one of the first associates; and he enriched their publications with several valuable and curious papers. Soon after this, the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> Societies of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> received him among their number. Not <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> after the publication of his *Adversaria Anatomica*, he began, much upon the same <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>, his *Epistolae Anatomicae*, the first of which is dated at Padua in the beginning of April 1726. The works of Morgagni which have already been mentioned, are to be considered, in a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, as strictly anatomical: but he was not more eminent as an anatomist, than as a learned and successful physician. In the year 1760, when he was not far distant from the 80th year of his age, he published his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and valuable work *De causis et sedibus morborum per anatomen indagatis*. This last and most important of all his productions <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> afford convincing <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> of his industry and abilities to latest posterity. Besides these works, he published, at different periods of his life, several miscellaneous pieces, which were afterwards collected into one volume, and printed under his own eye at Padua, in the year 1765. It does not appear that he had in view any future publications; but he intended to have favoured the world with a complete edition of all his works, which would probably have been augmented with many new observations. In this he was engaged when, on the 5th of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1771, after he had nearly arrived at the 90th year of his age, death put a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> to his long and glorious <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CAREER">career</a> in the learned world.

MORGES

Pages 451-451

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a> in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CANTON">canton</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BERNE">Berne</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of some trade, and situated on the lake of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a>, five miles from <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAUSANNE">Lausanne</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 6.42. N. Lat. 46.29.

MORGO

Pages 451-451

anciently *Amorgos*, an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the Archipelago, which produces wine, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, and corn. It is well cultivated, and the inhabitants are affable, and generally of the Greek <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. The best parts belong to a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a>. The greatest inconvenience in this island is the want of wood. It is 30 miles in circumference. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 26.15. N. Lat. 36.30.

MORIAH

Pages 451-451

one of the eminences of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>; on which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABRAHAM">Abraham</a> went to offer his son, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a> wanted to build the temple, which was afterwards executed by <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>: The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THRESHING">threshing</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a> of Arunah; originally narrow, so as scarce to contain the temple, but enlarged by means of ramparts; and surrounded with a triple wall, so as to add <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> strength to the temple, (Josephus). It may be considered as a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of Mount <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SION">Sion</a>, to which it was joined by a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> and gallery, (*Id.*).

MORILLES

Pages 451-451

a kind of mushroom, about the size of a walnut, pierced with holes like a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>-comb, and said to be good for creating an appetite. It is often used in sauces and ragouts.

MORINA

Pages 451-451

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the dian-dria class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 48th order, *Aggregate*. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MORINDA

Pages 451-451

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the pentandra class, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 48th order, *Aggregate*. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MORINORUM CASTELLUM

Pages 451-451

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, simply Castellum (Antonine); situated on an eminence, with a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> on its top, in the territory of the Morini. Now Mont Cassel, in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>.

MORISON

Pages 451-451

ROBERT**, physician and professor of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, was born at Aberdeen in 1620, bred at the university there, and taught <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> in it; but having a strong inclination to botany, made <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> progress in that science. The civil wars obliged him to leave his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; which, however, he did not do till he had first signalized his zeal for the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, and his courage, in a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> fought between the inhabitants of Aberdeen and the Presbyterian troops on the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> of Aberdeen, in which he received a dangerous wound on the head. As soon as he was cured of it, he went into France; and fixing at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, he applied assiduously to botany and anatomy. He was introduced to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORLEANS">Orleans</a>, who gave him the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> gardens at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLOIS">Blois</a>. He exercised the office till the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>; and afterwards went over to England in 1660. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II., to whom the duke of Orleans had presented him at Blois, sent for him to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and gave him the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of...

MORLACHIA

Pages 451-455

a mountainous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DALMATIA">Dalmatia</a>. The inhabitants are called Morlacks <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Morlacchi; they inhabit the pleasant valleys of Kotor, along the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Kerka, Cetina, Narenta, and among the inland <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of Dalmatia. The inhabitants are by some said to be of Walachian <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a>, as is indicated by their name; Morlachia being a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONTRACTION">contraction</a> of Mauro <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WALACHIA">Walachia</a>, that is, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> Walachia; and the Walachians are said to be descendants of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Roman colonies planted in these countries. This, however, is denied by the Abbé Fortis, who published a volume of travels into that country. He informs us that the origin of the Morlacchi is involved in the darkness of barbarous ages, together with that of many other nations, resembling them so much in customs and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, that they may be taken for one people, dispersed in the vast tracts from the Adriatic <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> to the Frozen ocean. With regard to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ETYMOLOGY">etymology</a> of the name, the Abbé observes, that the Morlacchi generally call themselves, in their own language, Vlassi; a national <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a>, of which no vestige is found in the records of Dalmatia till the 13th century. It signifies powerful men, or men of authority; and the denomination of Moro Vlassi, corruptly Morlacchi, as they are now called, may perhaps point out the original of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>. This word may possibly signify the conquerors that came from the sea; moor, in all the dialects of the Slavonian language, signifying the sea. With regard to the character of these people, we are informed that they are much injured by their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> neighbours. The inhabitants of the sea <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Dalmatia tell many frightful stories of their avarice and cruelty; but these, in our author's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, are all either of an ancient <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any have happened in latter times, they ought rather to be ascribed to the corruption of a few individuals, than to the bad disposition of the nation in general; and though thievish tricks are frequent among them, he informs us, that a stranger may travel securely through their country, where he is faithfully escorted, and hospitably treated. As to the Morlacchi themselves, they are represented as open and sincere to such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, that they would be taken for simpletons in any other country; and by means of this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> they have been so often duped by the Italians, that the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> of an Italian and the faith of a dog, are <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYNONYMOUS">synonymous</a> among the Morlacchi. They are very hospitable to strangers; and their hospitality is equally conspicuous among the rich and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a>. Morlack. The rich prepares a roasted lamb or sheep, and the poor with equal cordiality offers whatever he has; nor is this generosity confined to strangers, but generally extends itself to all who are in want. When a Morlack is on a journey, and comes to lodge at a friend's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, the eldest <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of the family, or the new married <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDE">bride</a>, if there happen to be one, receives and kisses him when he alights from his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> or at the door of the house; but a foreigner is rarely favoured with these <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> civilities; on the contrary the women, if they are young, hide themselves, and keep out of his way. The Morlacchi in general have little notion of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> economy, and readily consume in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a> as much as would be sufficient for several months, whenever any occasion of merriment presents itself. A <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, the holiday of the saint protector of the family, the arrival of relations or friends, or any other joyful incident, consumes of course all that there is to eat and to drink in the house. Yet the Morlack is a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> economist in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of his wearing apparel; for rather than spoil his new <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAP">cap</a>, he takes it off, let it <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> ever so hard, and goes bareheaded in the storm. In the same manner he treats his shoes, if the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> is dirty and they are not very old. Nothing but an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> impossibility hinders a Morlack from being punctual; and if he cannot repay the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> he borrowed at the appointed <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, he carries a small present to his creditor, and requests a longer term. Friendship is lasting among the Morlacchi. They have even made it a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> point, and tie the sacred bond at the foot of the altar. The Slavonian <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RITUAL">ritual</a> contains a particular benediction for the solemn union of two <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> or two female friends in the presence of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a>. The male friends thus united are called Pobratimi, and the female Povestrene, which means half-brothers and half-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SISTERS">sisters</a>. From those consecrated friendships among the Morlacchi and other nations of the same origin, it should seem that the sworn brothers arose; a denomination frequent enough among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> people of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> and in many parts of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between these and the Pobratimi of Morlachia consists not only in the want of the ritual <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>, but in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of the union itself. For, among the Morlacchi, the sole view is <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECIPROCAL">reciprocal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> and advantage; but such a brotherhood among the Italians is generally commenced by bad men, to enable them the more to hurt and disturb <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>. But as the friendships of the Morlacchi are strong and sacred, so their quarrels are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> unextinguishable. They <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> from father to son; and the mothers fail not to put their children in mind of their duty to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> their father if he has had the misfortune to be killed, and to show them often the bloody shirt and arms of the dead. And so deeply is revenge rooted in the minds of this nation, that all the missionaries in the world would not be able to eradicate it. A Morlack is naturally inclined to do good to his fellow creatures, and is full of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> for the smallest benefit, but implacable if injured or insulted. A Morlack who has killed another of a powerful family, is commonly obliged to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> himself by flight, and and to keep out of the way for several years. If during that time he has been fortunate enough to escape the search of his pursuers, and has got a small sum of money, he endeavours to obtain <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARDON">pardon</a> and peace; and, that he may treat about the conditions in person, he asks and obtains a safe conduct, which is faithfully maintained, though only verbally granted. Then he finds mediators: and, on the appointed <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, the relations of the two hostile families are assembled, and the criminal is introduced, dragging himself along on his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> and feet, the musket, pistol, or cutlass, with which he committed the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>, hung about his neck; and while he continues in that humble posture, one or more of the relations recites a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PANEGYRIC">panegyric</a> on the dead, which sometimes rekindles the flames of revenge, and puts the poor prostrate in no small danger. The Morlacks, whether they happen to be of the Roman or of the Greek <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, have very singular <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> about <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>: and the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> of their teachers daily augments this monstrous evil. They are as firmly persuaded of the reality of witches, fairies, enchantments, nocturnal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APPARITIONS">apparitions</a>, and sortileges, as if they had seen a thousand examples of them. Nor do they make the least doubt about the existence of vampires: and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> to them, as in Transylvania, the sucking the blood of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INFANTS">infants</a>. Therefore, when a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> dies suspected of becoming a vampire, or evodlak, as they call it, they cut his hams, and prick his whole body with pins; pretending, that after this operation he cannot walk about. There are even instances of Morlacchi, who, imagining that they may possibly thirst for children's blood after <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, entreat their heirs, and sometimes oblige them to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a>, to treat them as vampires when they die. A most perfect <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCORD">discord</a> reigns in Morlacehia, as it generally does in other parts, between the Latin and Greek <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a>, which their respective priests fail not to foment, and tell a thousand little scandalous stories of each other. The churches of the Latins are poor, but not very dirty; those of the Greeks are equally poor, and shamefully ill kept. Our author has seen the curate of a Morlack village sitting on the ground in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCHYARD">churchyard</a>, to hear the confession of women on their <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-KNEES">knees</a> by his side: a strange posture indeed! but a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of the innocent manners of those good people, who have the most profound veneration for their spiritual pastors, and a total dependence upon them; who, on their <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>, frequently make use of a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> rather <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a>, and correct the bodies of their offending flock with the cudgel. Innocence, and the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of pastoral ages, are still preserved among the Morlacchi, or at least many traces of them remain in the places farthest distant from our settlements. Pure cordiality of sentiment is not there restrained by other regards, and displays itself without any distinction of circumstances. A young handsome Morlack girl, who meets a man of her district on the road, kisses him affectionately, without the least imputation of impropriety; and M. Fortis has seen all the women and girls, all the young men and old, kissing one another as they came into the churchyard on a holiday; so that they looked as if they all belonged to one family. He often observed the same thing on the road, and at the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a> in the mar- ritime <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, where the Morlacchi came to sell their Merseeld commodities. The dress of the unmarried women is the most complex and whimsical, in respect to the ornaments of the head; for when married they are not allowed to wear anything else but a handkerchief, either <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> or coloured tied about it. The girls use a scarlet cap, to which they commonly hang a veil falling <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> on the shoulders, as a mark of their virginity.
