The first are only carcases dried by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, and by that means kept from <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUTREFACTION">putrefaction</a>: these are frequently found in the sands of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIBYA">Libya</a>. Some imagine, that these are the bodies of deceased people buried there on purpose to keep them entire without <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMBALMING">embalming</a>; others think they are the carcases of travellers who have been overwhelmed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a> of sand raised by the hurricanes frequent in those deserts. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> kind of mummies are bodies taken out of the catacombs near <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-CAIRO">Cairo</a>, in which the Egyptians deposited their dead after embalming. See Embalming. We have two different substances preserved for medicinal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> under the name of mummy, though both in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of the same origin. The one is the dried and preserved <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> bodies, embalmed with <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYRRH">myrrh</a> and spices; the other is the liquor running from such mummies, when newly prepared, or when affected by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> heat or damp. The latter is sometimes in a liquid, sometimes of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> form, as it is preserved in vials well stopped, or suffered to dry and harden in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>. The first kind of mummy is brought to us in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> pieces, of a lax and friable texture, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> and spogy, of a blackish <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and often damp and clammy on the surface: it is of a strong but disagreeable smell. The second kind of mummy, in its liquid state, is a thick, opaque, and viscous fluid, of a blackish colour, but not disagreeable smell. In its indurated state, it is a dry solid substance, or a fine shining <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> colour, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> texture, easily broken, and of a good smell; very inflammable, and yielding a scent of myrrh and aromatic ingredients while <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BURNING">burning</a>. This, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we cannot be content without medicines from our own bodies, ought to be the mummy used in the ships; but it is very scarce and dear; while the other is so cheap, that it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> always be most in use. All these kinds of mummies are brought from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>. But we are not to imagine, that any body breaks up the real Egyptian mummies, to sell them in pieces. pieces to the druggists, as they make a much better market of them in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> whole, when they can contrive to get them. What our druggists are supplied with, is the flesh of executed criminals, or of any other bodies the Jews can get, who fill them with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> bitumen, so plentiful in that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the world; and adding a little aloes, and two or three other cheap ingredients, send them to be baked in an oven, till the juices are exhaled, and the embalming <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> has penetrated so thoroughly that the flesh will keep and bear transporting into Europe. Mummy has been esteemed resolvent and balsamic: but whatever virtues have been attributed to it, seem to be such as depend more upon the ingredients used in preparing the flesh than in the flesh itself; and it would surely be better to give those ingredients without so shocking an addition. There are found in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a> a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> mummies, or human bodies preserved without the assistance of art. These <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIE">lie</a> in considerable numbers in some of the vast caverns in that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. They are dried with the flesh and skin shrunk up almost close to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a>, and are of a blackish colour. In the wars which several ages ago laid waste that country, it was common for parties of the weaker side to retire into these caves, where their enemies, if they found them out, suffocated them by burning straw, &c., at the mouth of the cavern, and then left the bodies; which, being out of the way of injuries from common accidents, have lain there ever since. Mummy, among gardeners, a kind of wax used in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAFTING">grafting</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTING">planting</a> the roots of trees, made in the following manner: Take one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> of black pitch, and a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of a pound of turpentine; put them together into an earthen pot, and set them on fire in the open air, holding something in your <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> to cover and quench the mixture in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, which is to be alternately lighted and quenched till all the nitrous and volatile parts be evaporated. To this a little common wax is to be added; and the composition is then to be set by for use. MUMPS. See Medicine <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

MUNDA

Pages 523-524

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> town of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANADA">Granada</a>, seated on the declivity of a hill, at the bottom of which runs a river. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 4° 13', N. Lat. 48° 15'. This <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> was anciently famous for a victory gained by Caesar over the two sons of Pompey, who had collected an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> in Spain after the defeat of their father at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHARSALIA">Pharsalia</a>. See (<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of) Rome. The Pompeys posted their army advantageously on a rising ground, whereof one side was defended by the city of Munda, and the other by a small river which watered the plain, and by a marsh: so that the enemy could not attack them but in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a>. Caesar likewise drew up his troops with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> art, and having advanced a little way from his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAMP">camp</a>, ordered them to halt, expecting the enemy would abandon their advantageous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POST">post</a>, and come to meet him. But as they did not stir, Caesar made as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he intended to fortify himself in that post; which induced the young general, who looked upon this as a sign of fear, to advance into the plain, and attack the enemy before they could secure themselves with any works. Pompey's army was by far the most numerous: for it consisted of 13 legions, 6000 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, and an incredible <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of auxiliaries, among whom were all the forces of Bocchus <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MAURITANIA">Mauritania</a>, commanded by his two sons, both youths of great valour and bravery. Caesar had 80 cohorts, three legions, to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WIT">wit</a>, the third, the fifth, and the tenth, and a body of 8000 horse. As the enemy drew near, Caesar betrayed a great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of uneasiness and concern, as if he were doubtful of the success, knowing he was to engage men no way inferior in valour and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> to his own, and commanded by officers who had on many occasions given signal proofs of their bravery and conduct. Cnecius, the elder of the two brothers, was generally looked upon as an able commander; and Labienus, who had revolted, esteemed scarce inferior to himself. However, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DICTATOR">dictator</a>, desirous to put an end to the civil <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, either by his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> that of his rivals, gave the signal for the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, and fell upon the enemy with his usual vigour and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>. At the first onset, which was dreadful, the auxiliaries on both sides betook themselves to flight, leaving the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> to decide their quarrel by themselves. Then the legionaries engaged with a fury hardly to be expressed; Caesar's men being encouraged by the hopes of putting an end to all their labours by this battle; and those of Pompey exerting themselves out of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> and despair, since most of them expected no <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>, as having been formerly pardoned. Never was victory more obstinately disputed. Caesar's men, who had been always used to conquer, found themselves so vigorously <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> by the enemy's legionaries, that they began to give ground; and though they did not turn their backs, yet it was manifest that shame alone kept them in their posts. All authors agree, that Caesar had never been in so great danger; and he himself, when he came back to his camp, told his friends, that he had often fought for victory, but this was the first <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he had ever fought for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. Thinking himself abandoned by fortune, which had hitherto favoured him, he had some thoughts of stabbing himself with his own <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, and by a voluntary death preventing the disgrace of a defeat: but returning soon to himself, and concluding it would be more to his reputation to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> by the enemy's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> at the head of his troops, than, in a fit of despair, by his own, he dismounted from his horse, and snatching a buckler from one of his legionaries, he threw himself like a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> in despair into the midst of the enemy, crying out to his men, Are you not ashamed to deliver your general into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of boys? At these words, the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> of the tenth legion, animated by the example of their general, fell upon the enemy with fresh vigour, and made a dreadful havoc of them. But in spite of their utmost efforts, Pompey's men still kept their ground, and, though greatly fatigued, returned to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> with equal vigour. Then the Carthagenians began to despair of victory; and the dictator, running through the ranks of his disheartened legionaries, had much ado to keep them together. The battle had already lasted from the rising to the setting of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, without any considerable advantage on either side. At length a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> accident decided the dispute in favour of the dictator. Bogud, a petty king of Mauritania, had joined Caesar soon after his arrival in Spain, with some squadrons of Numidian horse; but in the very very beginning of the battle, being terrified at the shouting of the soldiers, intermingled with groans, and the clashing of their arms, he had abandoned his post, and retired with the auxiliaries under his command to a rising ground at a small distance from the enemy's camp. There he <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> the whole <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> an idle spectator of the battle that was fought in the plain. But towards the evening, partly out of shame and partly out of compassion for his friend Caesar, he resolved to fall upon Pompey's camp; and accordingly flew thither with all the forces he had with him. Labienus, apprised of his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, hastened after him to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the camp; which Caesar observing, cried to his legionaries, Courage, fellow soldiers! the victory at length is ours; Labienus flies. This artifice had the desired effect; Caesar's men, believing that Labienus was truly fled, made a last effort, and charged the wing he commanded so briskly, that after a most obstinate dispute they put them to flight. Though the enemy's left wing was thus entirely defeated, the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> wing, where the elder Pompey commanded, still kept their ground for some time. Pompey dismounting from his horse, fought on foot like a private man in the first line, till most of his legionaries being killed, he was forced to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> himself by flight from falling into the enemy's hands. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">Part</a> of his troops fled back to their camp, and part took shelter in the city of Munda. The camp was immediately attacked, and taken sword in hand; and as for the city, Caesar, without loss of time, drew a line of circumvallation round it. This victory was gained on the 16th of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KALENDS">kalends</a> of April, i.e. according to our way of counting, on the 17th day of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a>, when the Dionysian festival, or the Liberalia, were celebrated at Rome; the very day, as Plutarch observes, in which Pompey the Great, four years before, had set out for the war. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> Pompey lost 30,000 men; among whom were the famous Labienus, Attius Varus, and 3000 Roman knights. Seventeen officers of distinction were taken, and all the enemy's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAGLES">eagles</a> and ensigns, together with Pompey's fasces, which he had assumed as governor of Spain. On Caesar's side, only 1000 men were killed and 500 wounded.

MUNDIC

Pages 524-524
or MARCASITE, an old name for pyrites of copper or iron. See Ores of Copper and Iron, Mineralogy Index.

MUNDINGOES

Pages 524-524

the name of a people who live on the sides of the river <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAMBIA">Gambia</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, and who are of a jet <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, strong, and well made. They have a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> sent over every year from one of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> de Verd <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> to christen and marry.

MUNDUS PATENS

Pages 524-524

the open world, in Roman antiquity, a solemnity performed in a small temple, of a round form like the world, dedicated to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIS">Dis</a> and the rest of the infernal gods. This temple was opened but three times in the year, viz. the 24th of August, the 4th of October, and the 7th of November. During these days, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> believed <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELL">hell</a> was open; on these days therefore they never offered <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, listed <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, put to <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> married.

MUNICH

Pages 524-524
Count dr., was the favourite of the czarina Ann, and was concerned in all the events of her reign. Being appointed general of her armies, he gained great advantages over the Crim Tartars, beat the Turks, A.D. 1739, in an engagement near Chocizim, and took that city together with Jassi the capital of Moldavia. He was afterwards prime minister to the czar Iwan VI. but in a short time after he was accused of employing the power which his office conferred on him to gratify his own ambition and private resentment. The empress Elizabeth brought him to trial, and he was condemned to lose his life, A.D. 1742. This sentence was mitigated to banishment into Siberia, whither many of the victims of his power had been exiled. He was recalled by Peter III. A.D. 1762, and declared field marshal. Upon the death of this prince, the empress Catharine II. appointed him director general of the ports of the Baltic. He died on the 8th of October 1767, at the age of 84.

MUNICIPAL

Pages 524-525

among us, is applied to the laws that obtain in any particular <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>. And those are called municipal officers who are elected to defend the interests of cities, to maintain their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> and privileges, and to preserve order and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> among the citizens; such as mayors, sheriffs, consuls, &c.

MUNICIPES

Pages 525-525

an appellation given by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> to the inhabitants of the municipia <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> municipal cities. See MUNICIPIUM.

MUNICIPIUM

Pages 525-525

in Roman antiquity, a corporation borough, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> enfranchised <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> or town, where the inhabitants enjoyed their own laws and customs, and at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> were honoured with the privileges of Roman citizens; but then this privilege generally reached no further than the bare <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a>. Some indeed, by particular merit, obtained the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of votes, which occasioned that distinction of municipium sine suffragio, and municipium cum suffragio.—The inhabitants of the municipium sine suffragio were called barely Romani, but those of the municipium cum suffragio were called <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CIRCUS">circus</a> Romani. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between proper citizens of Rome and the inhabitants of the municipium may be thus expressed. The proper citizens of Rome were, 1. Registered in the census; 2. Had the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of suffrage and of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> honours; 3. Were assessed in the poll-tax; 4. Served in the legions; 5. Used the Roman laws and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>; 6. Were called Quirites and populus Romanus; Whereas the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUNICIPES">municipes</a> enjoyed the three first of these privileges, but were denied the three last.

MUNITION

Pages 525-525

the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> with which a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is furnished in order for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> that which follows a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAMP">camp</a> for its subsistence. MUNITION Ships, are those that have stores on board in order to supply a fleet of men of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. In an engagement, all the munition ships and victuallers attending the fleet take their station in the rear of all the rest; they are not to engage in the fight, but to attend to such directions as are sent to them by the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a>.

MUNSTER

Pages 525-525

in Latin Monomia, and in Irish <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MOEN">Moen</a>, the most southerly <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>; bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEINSTER">Leinster</a> and Connaught, and on the east, west, and south, by the ocean. It contains the counties of Cork, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLARE">Clare</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KERRY">Kerry</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIMERICK">Limerick</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIPPERARY">Tipperary</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATERFORD">Waterford</a>; and 3,289,932 Irish plantation acres, 740 parishes, 63 baronies, and 26 boroughs. It is about 125 miles <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> and 120 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>; and its <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> town is Cork. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> name was Mumhan; and in latter ages it was divided into Desmond <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> South Munster, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORMOND">Ormond</a> or East Munster, and Thomond or North Munster. It lies between 51° 15' and 53° 0' N. Lat. and 7° 10' and 10° 40' W. Long. Munster, a bishopric of Germany in the circle of Westphalia, and territories of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>; bounded on the north by Emelden and Oldenburg, on the south by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Mark and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Westphalia, on the west by the county of Bentheim, and the United Provinces, and on the east by the bishoprics of Osnaburg and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PADERBORN">Paderborn</a> together with the county of Ravensberg. It is the largest of all the Westphalian bishoprics, being in length about 80 miles, and in breadth from 20 to 60, and contains 350,000 inhabitants. It is divided into 13 bailiwicks; and though in general but a barren <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, has some fruitful plains, with woods, and quarries of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. The inhabitants, excepting a few of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> and gentry, are all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a>; though Lutheranism had once a considerable footing here. The bishop, who was generally also <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTOR">elector</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLOGNE">Cologne</a>, has a revenue of about 70,000 pounds, and can maintain 8000 men. By an unjust <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, unknown in the rest of the empire, he is heir to all strangers who die in the country without children. In the matricula he is rated at 30 foot and 118 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>; or 832 florins annually in lieu of them. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> consists of 40 canons, who are all noble. Munster, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Germany, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a bishopric of the same name, and of all Westphalia, stands at the conflux of the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AA">Aa</a> with the Ems, in E. Long. 7° 49'. N. Lat. 52° 0'. It is of a circular form, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, and had strong fortifications which have been thrown <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>. The citadel, called the Brille, has been converted into a residence for the bishop. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> and chapter now elect the bishop; but till the beginning of the 13th century he was nominated by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>. This city has been rendered famous by three remarkable transactions. 1. By the peace concluded here in 1648, which put an end to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> of 30 years; occasioned by the persecuting spirit of bigotted Papists, who chose rather to plunge their country into all the calamities of war than allow <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>. By this peace, however, they consented, much against their inclinations, to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> them a toleration. 2. By the disorders and disturbances occasioned here in 1553, by a parcel of enthusiasts, headed by a taylor, called John of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of his birth, who turned out the magistrates, and took possession of the city, where they perpetrated the most horrid villanies and cruelties. 3. For the noble, though unsuccessful, efforts it made in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of its liberties against the tyranny and oppression of the above mentioned turbulent and bloody-minded bishop, Bernard van Galen. In this city are a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a> and other <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> houses, many of them stately piles, and surrounded with beautiful gardens.

MUNYCHIA

Pages 525-525
or Munichius Portus, in Ancient Geography, a village and port of Athens, nearer to the city, fortified in the same manner as the Piraeus, to the east of which it lay, or between it and the promontory Sunium, at the mouth of the Ilissus. Strabo says it was an eminence in form of a peninsula, at the feet of which stood three harbours, anciently encompassed with a wall, taking within its extent the Piraeus and other harbours full of docks, with the temple of Diana Munychia; taking its name from Mycinicus, the founder of the temple. Munychia, an anniversary solemnity observed at Athens, in honour of Diana, on the 16th of the month Munychion. Cakes were offered on the occasion, called μυκήτης.

MUNYCHION

Pages 525-525

the tenth <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of the Athenian year, containing 29 days, and answering to the latter <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of our <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> and the beginning of April. It was so called from the festival Munychia, which was observed in this month. See MONTH and MUNYCHIA. MUPHTI. See MUFTI. MURÆNA, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Eel; a genus of fishes, belonging to the order of apodes. See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>, MURAL.

MURAL

Pages 525-526

something belonging to a wall, which the Latins call murus.

MURAL ARCH

Pages 526-526

is a wall, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> walled <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a>, placed exactly in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANE">plane</a> of the meridian, i.e., upon the meridian line, for the fixing of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRANT">quadrant</a>, sextant, or other <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, to observe the meridian altitudes, &c., of the heavenly bodies. Tycho Brahe was the first who used a mural arch in his observations; after him Hevelius, Mr Flamstead, De la Hire, &c., used the same means. See <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">ASTRONOMY</a>.

MURANUM

Pages 526-526

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of the confines of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUCANIA">Lucania</a>. Now Morano; a citadel in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CALABRIA">Calabria</a> Citra, at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> of the Sybaris, midway between the Sinus Tarentinus to the east, and the Tuscan <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> to the west. Supposed to have risen from the ruins of Syphneum, a town of the Bruttii mentioned by Livy.

MURATORI

Pages 526-526
LEWIS, ANTHONY, a learned and celebrated Italian writer, born at Vigogna, in the territory of Bologna, in 1672. He early discovered an extreme fondness for the learned languages and sciences; and this was seconded by an excellent education. After having completed his first studies, he embraced the state of an ecclesiastic; and applied himself to polite literature, philosophy, theology, civil law, antiquities, and other sciences; by which means he became in a manner universally learned. He was scarcely 22 years of age when he was made librarian of the Ambrosian library at Milan. It 1700 the duke of Modena, his sovereign, recalled him, and made him his librarian, and keeper of the archives of his duchy. Muratori discharged this double employment during the rest of his life, and had no other benefit than the provostship of Santa Maria del Pomposa. The principal of his works are,—1. Anecdota, or a collection of pieces taken from the Ambrosian library, 2 vols 4to, with learned notes and dissertations. 2. A treatise on the perfection of the Italian poetry, 2 vols 4to. 3. Anecdota Graeca, 3 vols 4to. 4. A genealogical history of the house of Modena, 2 vols folio. 5. An excellent collection of the writers of the Italian history, 27 vols folio, with learned notes. 6. Another collection, under the title of Antiquitates Italicae. 7. A collection of ancient inscriptions, under the title of Novus Thesaurus, 6 vols folio. 8. The annals of Italy, 12 vols 4to, in Italian, &c. 9. Letters, dissertations, Italian poems, &c.

MURCIA

Pages 526-526

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, handsome, and populous town of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of the same name. It is a bishop's see, and contains six parishes. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> is a most superb edifice, with the stairs of the steeple so contrived that a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> may ride up to the top, either on horseback <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COACH">coach</a>. It is situated in a pleasant plain, which abounds in fine gardens about the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, and in which are the best <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> in Spain. It is seated on the river Segura, in W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 8° 36' N. Lat. 37° 48'.

MURDER

Pages 526-528
or Murther, in Law, is thus defined, or rather described, by Sir Edward Coke: "When a person, of sound memory and discretion, unlawfully killeth any reasonable creature in being, and under the king's peace, with malice aforethought, either express or implied." The best way of examining the nature of this crime will be by considering the several branches of this definition. 1. It must be committed by a person of sound memory and discretion: for lunatics or infants are incapable of committing any crime; unless in such cases where they show a consciousness of doing wrong, and of course a discretion or discernment between good and evil. 2. Next, it happens when a person of such sound discretion unlawfully killeth. The unlawfulness arises from the killing without warrant or excuse: and there must also be an actual killing to constitute murder; for a bare assault, with intent to kill, is only a great misdemeanor, though formerly it was held to be murder. The killing may be by poisoning, striking, starving, drowning, and a thousand other forms of death, by which human nature may be overcome. Of these the most detestable of all is poison; because it can of all others be the least prevented, either by manhood or forethought. And therefore, by the stat. 22 Hen. VIII. c. 9, it was made treason, and a more grievous and lingering kind of death was inflicted on it than the common law allowed; namely, boiling to death: but this act did not live long, being repealed by 1 Edw. VI. c. 12. There was also, by the ancient common law, one species of killing held to be murder, which may be dubious at this day, as there hath not been an instance wherein it has been held to be murder for many ages past, viz., bearing false witness against another, with an express premeditated design to take away his life, so as the innocent person be condemned and executed. The Gothic laws punished in this case both the judge, the witnesses, and the prosecutor; and, among the Romans, the lex Cornelia de sicariis, punished the false witnesses with death, as being guilty of a species of assassination. And there is no doubt but this is equally murder in foro conscientiae. conscientiae as killing with a sword; though the modern law (to avoid the danger of deterring witnesses from giving evidence upon capital prosecutions, if it must be at the peril of their own lives) has not yet punished it as such. If a man, however, do such an act, of which the probable consequence may be, and eventually is, death; such killing may be murder, although no stroke be struck by himself, and no killing may be primarily intended; as was the case of the unnatural son who exposed his sick father to the air against his will, by reason whereof he died; and of the harlot, who laid her child under leaves in an orchard, where a kite struck and killed it. So too, if a man have a beast that is used to do mischief; and be, knowing it, suffers it to go abroad, and it kills a man; even this is manslaughter in the owner; but if he have purposely turned it loose, though barely to frighten people, and make what is called sport, it is with us (as in the Jewish law) as much murder as if he had incited a bear or dog to worry them. If a physician or surgeon give his patient a potion or plaster to cure him, which, contrary to expectation, kills him, this is neither murder nor manslaughter, but misadventure; and he shall not be punished criminally, however liable he might formerly have been to a civil action for neglect or ignorance; but it hath been holden, that if it be not a regular physician or surgeon who administers the medicine, or performs the operation, it is manslaughter at the least. Yet Sir Matthew Hale very justly questions the law of this determination; since physic and salves were in use before licensed physicians and surgeons: wherefore he treats this doctrine as apocryphal, and fitted only to gratify and flatter licenciates and doctors in physic; though it may be of use to make people cautious and wary how they meddle too much in so dangerous an employment. In order also to make the killing murder, it is requisite that the party die within a year and a day after the stroke received, or cause of death administered; in the computation of which the whole day upon which the hurt was done shall be reckoned the first. 3. Farther: The person killed must be "a reasonable creature in being, and under the king's peace," at the time of the killing. Therefore to kill an alien, a Jew, or an outlaw, who are all under the king's peace or protection, is as much murder as to kill the most regular-born Englishman; except he be an alien-enemy, in the time of war. To kill a child in its mother's womb, is now no murder, but a great misprision; but if the child be born alive, and dieth by reason of the potion or bruises it received in the womb, it seems, by the better opinion, to be murder in such as administered or gave them. As to the murder of bastard children, see BASTARD. 4. Lastly, The killing must be committed "with malice aforethought," to make it the crime of murder. This is the grand criterion which now distinguishes murder from other killing: and this malice prepense, malitia praecogitata, is not so properly spite or malevolence to the deceased in particular, as any evil design in general; the dictate of a wicked, depraved, and malignant heart; un disposition à faire une mal chose: and it may be either express, or implied, in law. Express malice is when one, with a sedate deliberate mind and formed design, doth kill another, which formed de- sign is evidenced by external circumstances discovering that inward intention; as lying in wait, antecedent menaces, former grudges, and concerted schemes to do him some bodily harm. This takes in the case of deliberate duelling, where both parties meet avowedly with an intent to murder: thinking it their duty, as gentlemen, and claiming it as their right, to wanton with their own lives and those of their fellow creatures; without any warrant or authority from any power either divine or human, but in direct contradiction to the laws of both God and man; and therefore the law has justly fixed the crime and punishment of murder on them, and on their seconds also. Yet it requires such a degree of passive valour to combat the dread of even undeserved contempt, arising from the false notions of honour too generally received in Europe, that the strongest prohibitions and penalties of the law will never be entirely effectual to eradicate this unhappy custom, till a method be found out of compelling the original aggressor to make some other satisfaction to the affronted party, which the world shall esteem equally reputable as that which is now given at the hazard of the life and fortune, as well of the person insulted, as of him who has given the insult. Also, if even upon a sudden provocation one beats another, in a cruel and unusual manner, so that he dies, though he did not intend his death, yet he is guilty of murder by express malice; i.e. by an express evil design, the genuine sense of malitia: As when a park-keeper tied a boy that was stealing wood to a horse's tail, and dragged him along the park: when a master corrected his servant with an iron bar, and a schoolmaster stamped on his scholar's belly, so that each of the sufferers died; these were justly held to be murders, because the correction being excessive, and such as could not proceed but from a bad heart, it was equivalent to a deliberate act of slaughter. Neither shall he be guilty of a less crime who kills another in consequence of such a wilful act as shows him to be an enemy to all mankind in general; as going deliberately, and with an intent to do mischief, upon a horse used to strike, or coolly discharging a gun among a multitude of people. So if a man resolves to kill the next man he meets, and does kill him, it is murder, although he knew him not; for this is universal malice. And if two or more come together to do an unlawful act against the king's peace, of which the probable consequence might be bloodshed; as to beat a man, to commit a riot, or to rob a park, and one of them kills a man; it is murder in them all, because of the unlawful act, the malitia praecogitata, or evil intended beforehand. Also in many cases where no malice is expressed, the law will imply it: as, where a man wilfully poisons another, in such a deliberate act the law presumes malice, though no particular enmity can be proved. And if a man kills another suddenly, without any, or without a considerable provocation, the law implies malice; for no person, unless of an abandoned heart, would be guilty of such an act upon a slight or no apparent cause. No affront, by words or gestures only, is a sufficient provocation, so as excuse or extenuate such acts of violence as manifestly endanger the life of another. But if the person so provoked had unfortunately killed the other, by beating him in such a manner as showed Murder. only an intent to chastise and not to kill him, the law so far considers the provocation of contumacious behaviour, as to adjudge it only manslaughter, and not murder. In like manner, if one kills an officer of justice, either civil or criminal, in the execution of his duty, or any of his assistants endeavouring to conserve the peace, or any private person endeavouring to suppress an affray or apprehend a felon, knowing his authority or the intention with which he interposes, the law will imply malice, and the killer shall be guilty of murder. And if one intends to do another felony, and undesignedly kills a man, this is also murder. Thus if one shoots at A, and misses him, but kills B, this is murder; because of the previous felonious intent, which the law transfers from one to the other. The same is the case, where one lays poison for A, and B, against whom the prisoner had no malicious intent, takes it, and it kills him, this is likewise murder. So also, if one give a woman with child a medicine to procure abortion, and it operates so violently as to kill the woman, this is murder in the person who gave it. It were endless to go through all the cases of homicide, which have been adjudged, either expressly or impliedly, malicious: these therefore may suffice as a specimen; and we may take it for a general rule, that all homicide is malicious, and of course amounts to murder, unless where justified by the command or permission of the law; excused on a principle of accident or self-preservation; or alleviated into manslaughter, by being either the involuntary consequence of some act, not strictly lawful, or (if voluntary) occasioned by some sudden and sufficiently violent provocation. And all these circumstances of justification, excuse, or alleviation, it is incumbent upon the prisoner to make out, to the satisfaction of the court and jury, the latter of whom are to decide whether the circumstances alleged are proved to have actually existed; the former, how far they extend to take away or mitigate the guilt. For all homicide is presumed to be malicious, until the contrary appeareth upon evidence. The punishment of murder, and that of man-slaughter, were formerly one and the same; both having the benefit of clergy; so that none but unlearned persons, who least knew the guilt of it, were put to death for this enormous crime. But now, by several statutes, the benefit of clergy is taken away from murderers through malice prepense, their abettors, procurers, and counsellors. In atrocious cases it was frequently usual for the court to direct the murderer, after execution, to be hung upon a gibbet in chains near the place where the fact was committed; but this was no part of the legal judgment; and the like is still sometimes practised in the case of notorious thieves. This, being quite contrary to the express command of the Mosaic law, seems to have been borrowed from the civil law; which, besides the terror of the example, gives also another reason for this practice, viz. that it is a comfortable sight to the relations and friends of the deceased. But now, in England, it is enacted by statute 25 Geo. II. c. 37. that the judges, before whom any person is found guilty of wilful murder, shall pronounce sentence immediately after conviction, unless he sees cause to postpone it; and shall in passing sentence direct him to be executed on the next day but one (unless the same shall be Sunday, and then on the Monday following), and that his body be delivered to the surgeons to be dissected and anatomized; and that the judge may direct his body to be afterwards hung in chains, but in no wise to be buried without dissection. And, during the short but awful interval between sentence and execution, the prisoner shall be kept alone, and sustained with only bread and water. But a power is allowed to the judge, upon good and sufficient cause, to respite the execution, and relax the other restraints of this act. See farther, PARICIDE, and PETIT TREASON.

MURDERERS

Pages 528-528
or Murdering Pieces, in a ship, are small pieces of ordnance, either of brass or iron, which have chambers put in at their breeches. They are used at the bulk-heads of the fore-castle, half-deck, or steerage, in order to clear the deck, on the ship's being boarded by an enemy. MURENA. See Murena, Ichthyology Index.

MURENGERS

Pages 528-528

two officers of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> antiquity in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHESTER">Chester</a>, annually chosen out of the aldermen, to see the walls kept in repair, and to receive a certain toll for that purpose.

MUREX

Pages 528-528

a genus of animals belonging to the order of vermes testacea. See <a class="xref" href="../1815/vol6.html#article-CONCHOLOGY">Conchology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Murex, a caltrap <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, with sharp <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> projecting in every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, used by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> as a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> against the enemy's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>; so called, probably from some resemblance to the spines on the shell of the murex.

MURGI

Pages 528-528
or Murgis, in Ancient Geography, the last town of Bretica, next the Tarraconensis; the Urce of Ptolemy. Now Murzara, a port-town of Granada, on the Mediterranean. W. Long. 1° 5' N. Lat. 37° 6'.

MURIA

Pages 528-528

the Latin name of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>. See Soda, Muriate of, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. MURIATIC acid. See Chemistry Index. This acid, according to the views of Sir H. Davy, is composed of chlorine (the oxymuriatic acid of all chemists formerly, and of some still) and hydrogen.

MURINA

Pages 528-528
or Murines, a delicious sweet wine, medicated with spices, and the usual drink of the ladies of antiquity.

MURRAIN

Pages 528-528
or GARGLE, a contagious disease among cattle. See Farriery Index.

MURRAY

Pages 528-528
or Moray, the name of a district in the north of Scotland, which, in a former division of the kingdom, was denominated a province. This district includes the counties of Banff, Elgin and Nairn. The county of Elgin, the middle division of this district, is still known by the name of Morayshire.

MURRHINE

Pages 528-529

Murrhinus, Megger, in antiquity, an appellation given to a delicate sort of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARE">ware</a> brought from the east, whereof cups and vases were made, which added not a little to the splendour of the Roman banquets. Critics are divided concerning the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of the pocula <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> vasa murrhina, murrina, or murrea. Some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> have them to have been the same with our <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORCELAIN">porcelain</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">china</a> ware. The generality held them to have been made of some precious kind of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, which was found chiefly, as Pliny tells us, in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol8.html#article-PARTHIA">Parthia</a>, but more especially in Carmania. Arrian tells us, that there was a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of them made at Diospolis in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>. This he calls another sort of murrhina <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>; and it is evident, from all accounts, that the murrhina of Diospolis was a sort of glass ware, made in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of the porcelain or murrha of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIA">India</a>. There is some <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> in the accounts given by Pliny and Martial of the murrhina vasa. The first author says, that they would not bear hot liquors, but that only <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> ones were drank out of them. The latter, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, tells us, that they bore hot liquors very well. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> we <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> Pliny's account, their porcelain was much inferior to our's in this particular. Some conjecture them to have been of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGATE">agate</a>, others onyx, others of coral. Baronius, doubtless, was farthest out of the way, when he took them to be made of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYRRH">myrrh</a>, congealed and hardened. Some have supposed these vessels to be made of crystal, but this is contrary to the account of all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>. The Greeks had the words ἀγαθούς, for crystal, and ὄψις for myrrh, very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> among them; and therefore if these vessels had been made of either of these substances, they would in some places have called them <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMYRNA">smyrna</a> or crystalline. On the contrary, the most correct among them call them murrhina or morriona. The cups made of crystal, which were also in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> at those times were called crystallina, and these murrhina or murrhae, by way of keeping up the distinction; and Martial tells us that the stone they were made of was spotted or variegated, calling them pocula maculose murrhae. And Statius mentions the crystalline and murrhine cups in the same <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a>, but as different things, not the same. Arrian mentions also the λευκός πράσινος, which his interpreters censure as an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERROR">error</a> of the copies, and would alter into μύρρα, the name of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUM">gum</a> myrrh. Pompey is recorded as the first who brought these murrhine vessels out of the east, which he exhibited in his triumph, and dedicated to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> Capitolinus. But private persons were not <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> without them. So fond in effect did the Roman gentry grow of them, that a cup which held three sextaries was sold for 70 talents. T. Petronius, before his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, to spite Nero (or as Pliny expresses it, ut mensam ejus exhaeraret, to disinherit his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>), broke a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASON">bason</a>, trulla murrhina, valued at 300 talents, on which that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> had set his heart.

MUSA

Pages 529-529

the Plantain-tree; a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the polyandria class, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the eighth order, Scitamineae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. MUSÆUS, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Greek poet, was, according to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a> and Diodorus Siculus, an Athenian, the son of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORPHEUS">Orpheus</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the Eleusinian <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a> instituted at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CERES">Ceres</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, according to others, he was only the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Orpheus; but from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> resemblance which there was between his character and talents and those of his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, by giving a stronger outline to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> he was called his son, as those were styled the children of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a> who cultivated the arts of which he was the tutelar god. Musæus is allowed to have been one of the first poets who versified the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORACLES">oracles</a>. He is placed in the Arundelian marbles, epoch 15426 B.C., at which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> his hymns are said there to have been received in the celebration of the Eleusinian mysteries. Laertius tells us, that Musæus not only composed a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-THEOGONY">theogony</a>, but formed a sphere for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of his companions; yet as this honour is generally given to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIRON">Chiron</a>, it is more natural to suppose, with Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton, that he enlarged it with the addition of several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSTELLATIONS">constellations</a> after the conquest of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLEECE">fleece</a>. The sphere itself shows that it was delineated after the Argonautic expedition, which is described in the asterisms, together with several other more ancient histories of the Greeks, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of and without any thing later; for the ship Argo was the first <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> vessel which they had built; hitherto they had used round ships of burden, and kept within sight of the shore; but now, by the dictates of the oracle, and consent of the princes of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, the flower of that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> sail rapidly through the deep, and guide their ship by the stars. Musæus is celebrated by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a> in the character of hierophant, or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> of Ceres, at the head of the most illustrious mortals who have merited a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELYSIUM">Elysium</a>. Here he is made the conductor of Æneas to the recess where he meets the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a> of his father <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCHISES">Anchises</a>. A hill near the citadel of Athens was called Musæum, according to Pausanias, from Musæus, who used to retire thither to meditate and compose his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> hymns; at which place he was afterwards buried. The works which went under his name, like those of Orpheus, were by many attributed to Onomacritus. Nothing remains of this poet now, nor were any of his writings extant in the time of Pausanias, except a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYMN">hymn</a> to Ceres, which he made for the Lycomides. And as these hymns were likewise set to music, and sung in the mysteries by Musæus himself in the character of priest, he thence perhaps acquired from future times the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of musician, as well as of poet; the performance of sacred music being probably at first confined to the priesthood in these celebrations, as it had been before in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, whence they originated. However, he is not enumerated among ancient musicians by Plutarch; nor does it appear that he merited the title of son and successor to Orpheus for his musical abilities, so much as for his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, piety, and profound knowledge in religious mysteries.

MUSCA

Pages 529-529

the Fly; a genus of insects belonging to the order of diptera. See Entomology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Musca, a name given to such persons among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> as officiously thrust themselves into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of their superiors and those who despised them, by finding means of getting admittance to entertainments without invitation, and without a welcome: So that muscar were the same as parasites, who were frequently by the Greeks termed Musæi. See Parasite.

MUSCADINE

Pages 529-529

a rich wine, of the growth of Provence, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUEDOC">Languedoc</a>, Gividan, &c.—The word is supposed to be derived from <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MUSK">musk</a>; the wine being supposed to have a little of the smell of that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERFUME">perfume</a>; others from <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSCA">musca</a>, "a fly," because the flies are extremely fond of its <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a>; as the Latins had their nimum opimum, so called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">ab</a> opibus, from the bees which fed on it. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> for making muscadine at Frontignac, is the following: The muscadine grapes are allowed to be half dried on the vine; and as soon as they are gathered, they are trode and pressed, and the liquor is tanned, without letting it stand to ferment in the fat; the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEE">lee</a> which remains is supposed to produce the peculiar flavour of this wine.

MUSCHENBROECK

Pages 529-530
Peter de, a very distinguished natural philosopher and mathematician, was born Muschen, born at Utrecht a little before 1700. He was first professor in his own university, and afterwards invited to the chair at Leyden, where he died full of reputation and honours in 1761. He was a member of several academies; particularly the Academy of Sciences at Paris. He was the author of several works in Latin, which are frequently referred to, and all of which discover great penetration and exactness of the subjects of which he treats. He was also consummate in the knowledge of law.

MUSCI

Pages 530-530

MOSSES, one of the orders of the class cryptogamia; which see, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.—The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> took the moss of trees to be the effect of a disorder <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> discomposure of the texture of the bark; or at most a kind of little filaments arising from the bark: but the moderns find, by more accurate observation, that mosses are real distinct <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, whose seed, being extremely small, is enclosed in little capsules; which bursting of themselves, the seed is carried off by the winds; till, falling into the inequalities of the bark of trees, it is there stopped, takes root, and feeds at the expense of the tree, as mouldiness does on <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>, &c.

MUSCLE

Pages 530-530
or MUSSEL. See Mytilus, Conchology Index. MUSCOVY. See Russia. Muscovy Glass, or Glimmer, See Mica, Mineralogy Index.

MUSCULUS

Pages 530-530

a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> machine, made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> to cover and protect the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> while they approached and undermined the walls of besieged places, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> filled the ditches. It seems to have resembled the testudo in form, but was smaller in size. See Testudo.

MUSEIA

Pages 530-530

were Grecian festivals in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSES">Muses</a>, celebrated with games every fifth year, particularly by the Thespians. The Macedonians also observed a festival of the same name in honour of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> and the Muses, which lasted for <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> days, and was celebrated with stage plays, songs, and poetical compositions.

MUSES

Pages 530-531

certain fabulous deities among the Pagans, supposed to preside over the arts and sciences: for this reason it is usual for the poets, at the beginning of a poem, to invoke these goddesses to their aid. The Muses were originally only singers and musicians in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OSIRIS">Osiris</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> Egyptian <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACCHUS">Bacchus</a>, under the instruction and guidance of his son Orus; but in succeeding times they were called the daughters of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> and Mnemosyne or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMORY">Memory</a>. These are the only pagan divinities whose worship has been <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> through all succeeding changes in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> and sentiments of mankind. Professors of every liberal art in all the countries of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> still revere them; particularly the poets, who seldom undertake the slightest <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> without invoking their aid. Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton tells us, that the singing women of Osiris were celebrated in Thrace by the name of the Muses; and that the daughters of Pierius, a Thracian, imitating them, were celebrated by the same name. Diodorus Siculus informs us, that Alcman of Messene, a lyric poet who flourished in the 27th Olympiad, 670 years B.C. makes them the daughters of Uranus and Terra. It has been asserted by some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> writers, that at first they were only three in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>: but <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HESIOD">Hesiod</a>, and other profound mythologists, admit of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> (A). In his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYMN">hymn</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a>, Homer says, —By turns the nine delight to sing. And Hesiod, in his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-THEOGONY">Theogony</a>, names them all.—They are said severally to preside over some art or science, as music, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>. By some they are called virgins, because the virtues of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> appear unalterable: they are called muses from a Greek word which signifies to explain <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a>, because they have taught things the most curious and important to know, and which are above the comprehension of vulgar minds. Each of their names is said to include some particular allegory: Clio, for instance, has been thus called, because those who are praised in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> acquire immortal fame; Euterpe, on account of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> accruing to those who hear learned poetry; <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THALIA">Thalia</a>, implies for ever flourishing; Melpomene, that her <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MELODY">melody</a> insinuates itself into the inmost recesses of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>; Terpsichore marks the pleasure which those receive who are versed in the liberal arts; Erato seems to indicate, that the learned command the esteem and friendship of all mankind; Polyhymnia, that many poets are become immortal by the number of hymns which they have addressed to the gods; <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-URANIA">Urania</a>, that those whom she instructs elevate their contemplations and celebrity to the heavens and the stars; and lastly, the exquisite <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> of Calliope has acquired her that appellation, as the inventor and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUARDIAN">guardian</a> of eloquence and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a>. An epigram of Callimachus gives the attributes of the Muses in as many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>. Calliope the deeds of heroes sings; Great Clio sweeps to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> the strings; Euterpe teaches mimes their silent show; Melpomene presides o'er scenes of wo; Terpsichore the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLUTE">flute</a>'s soft pow'r displays; And Erato gives hymns the gods to praise; Polyhymnia's skill inspires melodious strains; Urania wise, the starry course explains; And gay Thalia's glass <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> out where folly reigns. This epigram does not, however, exactly correspond with the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of other poets, or of the ancient painters, in characterizing the attributes of the Muses. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> had numberless ingenious and fanciful ideas concerning the muses, which we have not room to recite. —"It seems (says the abbé Barthélemy) as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the first French poets, enchanted with the beauties of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, occasionally were led to invoke the nymphs of the woods, hills, caverns, and fountains; and that yielding to the prevailing <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for allegory, they gave them names relative to the influence..." fluence they might be supposed to have over the productions of the mind. At first three Muses only were admitted, Melete, Mneme, and Aoede: that is to say, the meditation or reflection necessary to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>; memory, which records illustrious deeds; and song, which accompanies their recital. In proportion as improvement was made in the art of versification, its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> and effects were personified, the number of the Muses increased, and the names they now received referred to the charms of poetry, its celestial origin, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of its <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, the pleasure and gaiety it inspires, the song and dance which add to it new charms, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> with which it is crowned. Afterwards were associated with them the Graces, whose employment it is to embellish poetry, and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOVE">Love</a> who is so frequently its object. These ideas took birth in a barbarous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, in Thrace, where <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORPHEUS">Orpheus</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINUS">Linus</a>, and their disciples, suddenly appeared in the midst of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a>. The Muses were honoured there on the Pierian mount; and extending their dominion, successively took their stations on Pindus, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARNASSUS">Parnassus</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELICON">Helicon</a>, and all those solitary places where the painters of nature, surrounded by the most pleasing images, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> the divine glow of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSPIRATION">inspiration</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYTHAGORAS">Pythagoras</a>, and afterwards <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a>, make the Muses the soul of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a> in our system; from whence the imaginary music of the spheres.

MUSEUM

Pages 531-548

a name which originally signified a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>, which took up at least one-fourth of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> was called the museum, on account of its being set apart for the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSES">Muses</a> and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the sciences. Here were lodged and entertained the men of learning; who were divided into many companies <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> colleges, according to the sciences of which they were the professors; and to Mushroom, each of these houses or colleges was allotted a handsome revenue. The foundation of this establishment is attributed to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILADELPHUS">Philadelphus</a>, who here placed his library. Hence the word museum is now applied to any <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> set apart as a repository for things that have an immediate relation to the arts. The museum at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, called the Ashmolean museum, is a noble pile of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, erected at the expense of the university, at the west end of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>, at which side it has a magnificent portal, sustained by pillars of the Corinthian order. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a>, which is to the street, extends about 60 feet, where there is this inscription over the entrance in gilt <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, Museum Ashmoleanum, schola naturalis historiae, officina chimica. It was begun in 1679, and finished in 1683, when a valuable collection of curiosities was presented to the university by Elias Ashmole, Esq. which were the same <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> reposed there: several accessions have been since made to the museum; among which are <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HIEROGLYPHICS">hieroglyphics</a>, and other Egyptian antiquities, an entire mummy, Roman antiquities, altars, medals, lamps, &c. and a variety of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> curiosities. For an account of the British museum, see <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">LONDON</a>, No 146. MUSHROOM. See FUNGI, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. To try the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MUSHROOMS">mushrooms</a>:—Take an onion, and strip the outer skin, and boil it with your mushrooms: <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the onion become blue or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, there are certainly dangerous ones amongst them; if it remain <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, they are good. MUSIC; THE art of combining sounds in a manner agreeable to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EAR">ear</a>. This <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> may be either simultaneous or successive: in the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, it constitutes <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a>; in the last, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MELODY">melody</a>. But though the same sounds, or intervals of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>, which give <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> when heard in succession, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> not always produce the same effect in harmony; yet the principles which constitute the simpler and more perfect kinds of harmony, are almost, if not entirely, the same with those of melody. By perfect harmony, we do not here <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> that plenitude, those complex modifications of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARMONIC">harmonic</a> sound, which are admired in practice; but that harmony which is called perfect by theoricians and artists; that harmony which results from the coalescence of simultaneous sounds produced by vibrations in the proportions of thirds, fifths, and octaves, or their duplicates. The principles upon which these various <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-COMBINATIONS">combinations</a> of sound are founded, and by which they are regulated, constitute a science, which is not only extensive but profound, when we would investigate the principles from whence these happy modifications of sound result, and by which they are determined; or when we would explore the sensations, whether mental or corporeal, with which they affect us. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> definitions of music are not proportioned in their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> to our present <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of that art; but M. Rousseau betrays a temerity highly inconsistent with the philosophical character, when from thence he infers, that their ideas were vague and undetermined. Every <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> susceptible of refinement and delicacy in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> or sentiment, must be conscious that there is a music in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> as well as in sound; and that the ideas of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECORUM">decorum</a>, of harmony and symmetry, are, if we may <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>, equally constituent of visible as of audible music. Those illustrious minds, whose comprehensive prospects in every science where taste and propriety prevail took in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> at a single glance, would behold with contempt and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a> those narrow and microscopic views of which alone their successors in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> have discovered themselves capacious. With these definitions, however, we are less concerned, as they bear no proportion to the ideas which are now entertained of music. Nor can we follow M. Rousseau, from whatever venerable sources his authority may be derived, in adopting his Egyptian <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ETYMOLOGY">etymology</a> for the word music. The established derivation from <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSA">Musa</a> could only be questioned by a paradoxical genius.
