The following is the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of the parishes of this county, according to the Statistical <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Scotland. | Parishes | Population in 1755 | Population in 1795-1798 | |----------|------------------|------------------------| | Ardclach | 1163 | 1186 | | Auldearn | 1951 | 1406 | | Calder | 882 | 1262 | | Nairn | 1698 | 2400 | Total: 5094 Increase: 360 Population in 1801, including part of some other Parishes. | Ardclach | 1256 | |----------|------| | Auldearn | 1401 | | Calder | 1179 | | Croy (Nairn <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a>) | 502 | | Moy do. | 34 | | Nairn town | 2215 | | Urquhart (do.) | 1610 | Total: 8257 In the returns for 1811 the population of Nairn is stated to be 8251. See Nairn, Supplement.

NAISSANT

Pages 660-660

in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, is applied to any animal issuing out of the midst of some ordinary, and showing only his head, shoulders, fore feet, and legs, with the tip of his tail; the rest of his body being hid in the shield, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> some <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> upon it; in which it differs from issuant, which denotes a living creature arising out of the bottom of any ordinary or charge.

NAISSUS

Pages 660-661

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of Dardania, a district of Mesia Superior, said to be the birthplace of Constantine the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>, which seems probable from his often residing at that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. Naissiani, the NAKED seeds, in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, those that are not enclosed in any pod <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>.

NAKIB

Pages 661-661

in the oriental dignities, the name of an officer who is a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a> to the cadiliskier, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, as he may be called, the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, appointed by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> signior. His office is to carry the standard of Mahomet.

NAKOUS

Pages 661-661

an Egyptian musical <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, made like two plates of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, and of all sizes, from two inches to a foot in diameter; they hold them by strings fastened to their middles, and strike them together so as to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. They are used in the Coptic churches and in the Mahometan processions.

NAME

Pages 661-662

denotes a word whereby men have agreed to express some idea; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> which serves to denote or signify a thing or subject spoken of. See WORD. This the grammarians usually call a noun, nomen, though their noun is not of quite so much <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> as our name. See NOUN. Seneca, lib. ii. de Beneficiis, observes, that there are a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of things which have no name; and which, therefore, we are forced to call by other borrowed names. Ingens est (says he) rerum copia sine nomine, quas cum propriis appellatibilibus signare non possumus, alienis accommodatis utimur: which may show why, in the course of this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DICTIONARY">dictionary</a>, we frequently give <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> senses to the same word. Names are distinguished into proper and appellative. Proper Names, are those which represent some individual thing or person, so as to distinguish it from all other things of the same <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; as, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCRATES">Socrates</a>, which represents a certain <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>. Appellative or General Names, are those which signify <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>; or which are common to several individuals of the same species; as, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, animal, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, oak, &c. Proper names are either called Christian, as being given at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a>; or surnames: The first imposed for distinction of persons, answering to the Roman praenomen; the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, for the distinction of families, answering to the nomen of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, and the patronymicum of the Greeks. Originally every person had but one name; as among the Jews, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a>, &c. among the Egyptians, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BUSIRIS">Busiris</a>; among the Chaldees, Nimus; the Medes, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTYAGES">Astyages</a>; the Greeks, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOMEDES">Diomedes</a>; the Romans, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a>; the Gauls, Divitius; the Germans, Ariovistus; the Britons, Cassibelans; the English, Hengist, &c. And thus of other nations, except the savages of Mount <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATLAS">Atlas</a>, whom Pliny and Marcellinus represent as anonymi, "nameless." The Jews gave the name at the circumcision, viz. eight days after the birth: the Romans, to females the same <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, to males the ninth; at which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> they held a feast, called nominalia. Since Christianity has obtained, most nations have followed the Jews, baptizing and giving the name on the eighth day after the birth; except our English <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>, who, till of late, baptized and gave the name on the birth day. The first imposition of names was founded on different views, among different people; the most common was to mark the good wishes of the parents, or to entitle the children to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a> a happy name seemed to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a>. Hence, Victor, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASTOR">Castor</a>, Faustus, Statorius, Probus, &c. Accordingly, we find such names, by Cicero called <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BONA">bona</a> nomina, and by Tacitus fausta nomina, were first enrolled and ranged in the Roman muster; first called to serve at the sacrifices, in the foundation of colonies, &c.—And, on the contrary, Livy calls Atius Umber, abominandi omnis nomen: and Plautus, on occasion of a person named Lyco, i.e. "greedy <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WOLF">wolf</a>," says; Vosmet nunc facile conjecturam easterum Quid id sit hominis, cui Lyco nomen fiet. Hence, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a> recommends it to men to be careful in giving happy names; and the Pythagoreans taught expressly, that the minds, actions, and successes of men, were according to their names, genius, and fate. Thus Panormitan, ex bono nomine ortur bona presumpsi; and the common proverb, Bonum nomen bonum <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OMEN">omen</a>; and hence the foundation of the onomantia. See ONOMANTIA. It is an observation deserving <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, says the abbé Barthelemy, that the greater <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of names found in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> are marks of distinction. They were given in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the qualities most esteemed in the heroic ages. From the word polemos, which signifies <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, have been formed Telipolonus and Archepolonus, the names of two heroes mentioned in the Iliad. The former name signifies able to support, and the latter, able to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a>, the labours of war. By adding to the word mache, or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, certain prepositions and different parts of speech, which modify the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> in a manner always <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a>, are composed the names Amphimachus, Antimachus, Promachus, Telomachus. Proceeding in the same way, with the word honorea, "strength or intrepidity," they formed the names Agapenor, "he who esteems valour;" Agenor, "he who directs it." From thoes, "swift," are derived, Alcathoes, Panthoes, Perithoes, &c. From nous, "mind or intelligence," come Astyques, Arsinoes, Autenoes, &c. From medes, "counsel," Agamedes, Eumedes, Lycomedes, Thrasymedes; and from elios, "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>," Amphieltes, Agacles, Iphicles, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATROCLUS">Patroclus</a>, Cleobulus, with many others. Hence Camden takes it for granted, that the names, in all nations and languages, are significative, and not simple sounds for <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> distinction's sake. This holds not only among the Jews, Greeks, Latins, &c., but even the Turks; among whom, Abdala signifies God's <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a>; Soliman, peaceable; Mahomet, glorified, &c. And the savages of Hispaniola, and throughout <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, who, in their languages, name their children, Glistering <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">Light</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">Sun</a>, Bright, Fine <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">Gold</a>, &c.; and they of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONGO">Congo</a>, by the names of precious <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, &c. To suppose names given without any meaning, however by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> their signification may be lost, that learned author thinks is to reproach our ancestors; and that contrary to the sense of Names of all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> writers. Porphyry notes, that the barbarous names, as he calls them, were very emphatical, and very concise; and accordingly it was esteemed a duty to be *sui nominis homines*: as Severus, Probus, and Aurelius, are called *sui nominis imperatores*. It was the usual way of giving names, to wish the children might discharge their names. Thus when Gunthram <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> of France named Clotharius at the font, he said, *Crescat puer, et hujus sit nominis executio*. The ancient Britons, Camden says, generally took their names from colours, because they painted themselves; which names are now lost, or remain hid among the Welsh. When they were subdued by the Romans, they took Roman names, some of which still remain corrupted; though the greatest part became extinct upon the admission of the English Saxons, who introduced the German names, as Crida, Penda, Oswald, Edward, &c.—The Danes, too, brought with them their names; as Sweyn, Harold, Knute, &c. The Normans, at the Conquest, brought in other German names, as originally using the German tongue; such as Robert, William, Richard, Henry, Hugh, &c. after the same manner as the Greek names Aspasius, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOETHIUS">Boethius</a>, Symmachus, &c. were introduced into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> upon the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the empire. After the Conquest, our <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, which had ever been averse to foreign names, as deeming them unlucky, began to take <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> names; as Matthew, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a>, Samson, &c. The various names anciently or at present obtaining among us, from what language or people soever borrowed, are explained by Camden in his Remains. As to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> when names began to be multiplied, and surnames introduced, &c. see <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURNAME">Surname</a>. Of late years it has obtained among us to give surnames for Christian names; which some dislike, on account of the confusion it may introduce. Camden relates it as an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that the practice first began in the reign of Edward VI. by such as would be godfathers, when they were more than half fathers. Upon which some were persuaded to change their names at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a>; which, it seems, is usual in other countries. —Thus, two sons of Henry II. of France, christened Alexander and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>, changed them at confirmation into Henry and Francis. In monasteries, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> assume new names at their admittance, to show they are about to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> a new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and have renounced the world, their family, and even their name: v. g. sister <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> of the Incarnation, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Henry of the Holy Sacrament, &c. The popes also changed their names at their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXALTATION">exaltation</a> to the pontificate; a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> first introduced by Pope Sergius, whose name till then, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLATINA">Platina</a> informs us, was Swine's-snout. But Onuphrius refers it to John XII. or XIII. and at the same time adds a different reason for it from that of Platina, viz. that it was done in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of St <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> and St Paul, who were first called Simon and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAUL">Saul</a>. Among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, those deified by the Heathen consecrations had new names given them; as Romulus was called Quirinus; Melicertes, Portunus or Portumnus, &c. New names were also given in adoptions, and sometimes by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TESTAMENT">testament</a>? thus L. Æmilius, adopted by Scipio, took the name of Seipio Africanus; and thus Augustus, who was at first called C. Octavius Thurinus, being adopted by the testament of Julius Caesar into his name and family, took the name of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAIUS">Caius</a> Julius Caesar Octavianus. Names were also changed at enfranchisements into new cities. Thus Lucumo, at his first being made free of Rome, took the name Lucius Tarquinius Priscus, &c.; and slaves when made free, usually assumed their masters names. Those called to the equestrian order, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they had base names, were always new named, *nominis ingeniorum veterumque Romanorum*. And among the primitive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, it was the practice to change the names of the catechumens: Thus the renegade <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUCIANUS">Lucianus</a>, till his baptism, was called Lucius. Towards the middle of the 13th century, it was the fancy of the wits and learned men of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, particularly in Italy, to change their baptismal names for classical ones. As Sannazarus, for instance, who altered his own plain name Jacopo to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIUS">Actius</a> Syncerius. Numbers did the same, and among the rest Platina the historian at Rome, who, not without a solemn <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CEREMONIAL">ceremonial</a>, took the name of Callimachus instead of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a>. Pope Paul II. who reigned about that time, unluckily chanced to be suspicious, illiterate, and heavy of comprehension. He had no idea that persons could wish to alter their names unless they had some bad <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, and actually scrupled not to employ imprisonment, and other violent methods to discover the fancied mystery. Platina was most cruelly tortured on this frivolous account: he had nothing to confess: so the pope, after endeavouring in vain to convict him of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a>, sedition, &c. released him after a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> imprisonment.

NAMPTWICH

Pages 662-662
or NANTWICH, a town of Chester in England, situated on the river Weaver, 14 miles S. E. from Chester, and 162 miles from London. It lies in the Vale Royal, and is one of the largest and best built towns in the county, the streets being very regular, and adorned with many gentlemen's houses. The inhabitants amounting in 1811 to 3999, trade in corn, cattle, cheese, fine white salt, and shoes. It is governed by a constable, &c. who are guardians of the salt springs. It is divided into two equal parts by the Weaver, which is navigable to Winsford bridge. The Chester canal, terminates in a large basin near this place. In this town were several religious foundations, now no more. The church is a handsome pile of building in the form of a cross, with an octangular tower in the middle.

NAMUR

Pages 662-663

a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, lying between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Sambre and Maese; bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by Brabant, on the east and south by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIEGE">Liege</a>, and on the west by Hainault. It is pretty fertile; has several forests, marble quarries, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, and pit coal; and is about 30 miles <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> and 20 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. Namur is the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> town. Namur, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, rich, and very strong town of the Netherlands, capital of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Namur, with a strong castle, several forts, and a bishop's see. It contains 15,400 inhabitants. The most considerable forts are, Fort William, Fort Maese, Fort Coquelet, and Fort Espinor. The castle is built in the middle of the town, on a craggy rock. It was besieged by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> William in 1695, who took it in the sight of an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of 100,000 French, though there were 16,000 men in the garrison. It was ceded to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a> in in 1713, but taken by the French in 1746; and restored by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AIX">Aix</a>-la-Chapelle. It was again taken by the French in 1794, and remained in their possession till 1814, when it was ceded to the king of the Netherlands. It is situated at the confluence of the rivers Maese and Sambre, in E. Long. 4° 57' N. Lat. 50° 25'.

NAN-KING

Pages 663-664

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Kiang-nan, is said to have been formerly one Nan-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, of the most beautiful and flourishing cities in the world. When the Chinese speak of its <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, they say, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> two horsemen should go out by the same gate, and ride round it on full speed, taking different directions, they would not meet before night. This account is evidently exaggerated; but it is certain, that Nan-king surpasses in extent all the other cities of China. We are assured that its walls are five leagues and a half in circumference. This city is situated at the distance of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> from the river <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-YANG_TSE_KIANG">Yang-tse-kiang</a>: it is of an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> which are within its circumference having prevented its being built on a regular <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>. It was formerly the imperial city; for this reason it was called Nan-King, which signifies, the Southern <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">Court</a>;" but since the six <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> tribunals have been transferred from hence to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PEKING">Peking</a>, it is called Kiang-ning in all the public acts. Nan-king has lost much of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> splendour: it had formerly a magnificent <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, no vestige of which is now to be seen; an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBSERVATORY">observatory</a> at present neglected, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, tombs of the emperors, and other superb monuments, of which nothing remains but the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-REMEMBRANCE">remembrance</a>. A third of the city is deserted, but the rest is well inhabited. Some <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a> of it are extremely populous and full of business; particularly the manufacture of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of cotton cloth, of which <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> quantities are imported into <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> under the name of Nan-kin. The streets are not so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> as those of Peking, they are, however, very beautiful, well paved, and bordered with rich shops. In this city resides one of those great mandarins called Tsong-giong, who takes cognizance of all important affairs, not only of both the governments of the province, but also of those of the province of Kiang-si. The Tartars have a numerous garrison here, commanded by a general of their own <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>; and they occupy a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of the city, separated from the rest by a plain wall. The palaces of the mandarins, whether Chinese <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Tartars, are in this city neither larger nor better built than those in the capital cities of other provinces. Here are no public edifices corresponding to the reputation of so celebrated a city, excepting its gates, which are very beautiful, and some temples, among which is the famous <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORCELAIN">porcelain</a> tower. It is 200 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and divided into <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> stories by plain boards within, and without by cornices and small projections covered with green varnished tiles. There is an ascent of 40 steps to the first story; between each of the others there are 21. The breadth and depth of the river Yang-tse-kiang formerly rendered the port of Nan-king very commodious; but at present <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> barks, or rather Chinese junks, never enter it: whether it be that it is shut up by sand-banks, or that the entrance of it has been forbidden, in order that navigators may insensibly lose all knowledge of it. In the months of April and May a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of excellent fish are caught in this river near the city, which are sent to court; they are covered with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ICE">ice</a>, and transported in that manner by barks kept entirely on purpose. Although this city is more than 200 leagues from Peking, these boats make such expedition, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NANKING">Nanking</a>, that they arrive there in eight or nine days. This city, though the capital of the province, has under its particular jurisdiction only eight cities of the third class. The number of its inhabitants is said to be 1,000,000 without comprehending the garrison of 40,000 men. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 119. 24. N. Lat. 32. 46.

NAN-TCHANG-FOU

Pages 663-663

the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of Kiang-si, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>. This <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> has no trade but that of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORCELAIN">porcelain</a>, which is made in the neighbourhood of Jao-tehou. It is the residence of a viceroy, and comprehends in its district eight cities; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> of which are of the third class, and only one of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a>. So much of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is cultivated, that the pastures left are scarcely sufficient for the flocks.

NANCI

Pages 663-663

a town of France, in the department of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEURTHE">Meurthe</a>, situated near the river Meurthe, and containing 29,740 inhabitants in 1820. It is divided into the Old and New <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">Towns</a>. The first is irregularly built, and contains the ducal <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>; the streets of the New Town are as straight as a line, adorned with handsome buildings, and a very fine <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>. The pri-matial <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> is a magnificent structure, and in that of the Cordeliers are the tombs of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> dukes. The <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> are cloths, woollen stuffs, silks, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-HATS">hats</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARE">ware</a>, &c. The town was very well fortified, but the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of France demolished the fortifications. It has been taken and retaken several times; but has belonged to France ever since 1736. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 6° 17'. N. Lat. 48° 41'.

NANCOWRY

Pages 663-663
or SOWRY, one of the Nicobar s="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands, lying at the entrance of the bay of Bengal. See NICOBAR.

NANI

Pages 663-663

JOHN BAPTIST, was born in 1616. His father was procurator of St Mark, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> to Rome. He was educated with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, and make considerable improvement. Urban VIII, a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> valuer of merit, soon perceived that of young Nani. He was admitted into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of senators in 1641, and was shortly after nominated ambassador in France, where he signalized himself by his compliant manners. He procured considerable succours for the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> of Candia against the Turks; and became, after his return to Venice, superintendant of the war office and of finances. He was afterwards ambassador to the empire; where he rendered those services to his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> which, as a zealous and intelligent citizen, he was well qualified to discharge. He was again sent into France in 1660 to solicit fresh succours for Candia; and on his return was appointed procurator of St Mark. He died November 5, 1768, at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 63, much regretted by his countrymen. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> had appointed him to write the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the Republic; which he executed to the satisfaction of the Venetians, although the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> was less admired by foreigners, who were not proper judges of the accuracy with which he stated the facts, of the purity of his diction, nor of the simplicity of his style; although it must be acknowledged that his narrative is much interrupted by too frequent parentheses. In <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> his history of Venice he has given an universal history of his times, especially with respect to the affairs of the French in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. This history, which is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> from 1613 to 1671, was printed at Venice in 2 vols 4to, in the years 1662 and 1679.

NANSIO

Pages 664-664

an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of the Archipelago, a little to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of the island of Santorino, 16 miles in circumference; but has no harbour. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> are nothing but bare rocks, and there are not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> sufficient to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> the fields. There is a vast <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of partridges, whose eggs they destroy every year to preserve the corn, and yet vast numbers of them are always produced. The ruins of the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a> are yet to be seen, and consist chiefly of marble columns. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 26. 20. N. Lat. 36. 15.

NANTES

Pages 664-664

an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a>, rich, and very considerable town of France, in the department of Lower <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOIRE">Loire</a>, containing 73,879 inhabitants in 1800. It is situated on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> side of the Loire, about 40 miles from its mouth, at the confluence of the Erdre. It is the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of the department, the see of a bishop, and the seat of several tribunals. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a> is pure, and the surrounding <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is rich and beautiful. Nantes is a town of extensive trade. Vessels under 100 tons ascend to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>; those above that size discharge their cargoes at Paimboeuf, 25 miles below, and have them conveyed up in boats. The <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> are cordage, canvas, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, calico, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, refined <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, bottle-glass, &c. By the Loire, this town has an extensive <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with the interior of France; and supplies <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORLEANS">Orleans</a> and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> with foreign commodities. The Spaniards trade here in wine, fine <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, oranges, and lemons; and they carry back cloth, stuffs, corn, and hard <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARE">ware</a>. The Dutch send <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> fish, and all sorts of spices; and in return have wine and brandy. The Swedes bring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>; and the English, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, tin, &c. It was in this place that Henry IV. promulgated the famous edict in 1598, called the Edict of Nantes, and which was revoked in 1685. Nantes was anciently, like almost every considerable city in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, very strongly fortified. <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> de <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DREUX">Dreux</a>, one of the dukes of Bretagne, surrounded it with walls, which have only been demolished within these few years. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> is an object of curiosity. It is near a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> and a half in length, being <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> across all the little <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> in the Loire, from north to south. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1. 45. N. Lat. 47. 13. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-NANTWICH">NANTWICH</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAMPTWICH">NAMPTWICH</a>. NAPÆA, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the polyadelphia class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 37th order, Columniferae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

NAPHTHA

Pages 664-664

an inflammable substance of the biminiuous kind. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERALOGY">Mineralogy</a>.

NAPHTHALI

Pages 664-664
or NEPHTHALI (Josh. xix.), one of the tribes of Israel; having Zabulon on the south, Asher on the west, the Jordan on the east, and on the north Antilibanus.

NAPIER

Pages 664-666

JOHN, baron of Merchiston in Scotland, inventor of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOGARITHMS">logarithms</a>, was the eldest son of Sir Archibald Napier of Merchiston, and born in the year 1550. Having given early discoveries of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> parts, his father was careful to have them cultivated by a liberal <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>. After going through the ordinary courses of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> at the university of St Andrew's, he made the tour of France, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and Germany. Upon his return to his native <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, his literature and other fine accomplishments soon rendered him conspicuous, and might have raised him to the highest offices of the state; but declining all civil employments, and the bustle of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>, he retired from the world to pursue literary researches, in which he made an uncommon progress, so as to have favoured mankind with sundry useful discoveries. He applied himself chiefly to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>; but at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> did not neglect that of the Holy Scriptures. In both these he hath discovered the most extensive knowledge and profound penetration. His <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSAY">essay</a> upon the book of the Apocalypse, indicates the most acute <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a>, and an uncommon strength of judgment; though time hath discovered, that his calculations concerning particular events hath proceeded upon fallacious <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATA">data</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> has been printed abroad in several languages; particularly in French at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROCHELLE">Rochelle</a> in the year 1593, 8vo, announced in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a>, as revised by himself. Nothing, says <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUCHAN">Buchan</a>, could be more agreeable to the Rochellers <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUGUENOTS">Huguenots</a> of France at this time, than the author's annunciation of the pope as antichrist, which in this book he has endeavoured to set forth with much zeal and erudition. But what has principally rendered his name famous, was his great and fortunate discovery of logarithms in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIGONOMETRY">trigonometry</a>, by which the ease and expedition in calculation have so wonderfully assisted the science of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a> and the arts of practical <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>. That he had begun about the year 1593 the train of inquiry which led him to that great achievement in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARITHMETIC">arithmetic</a>, appears from a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to Crugerus from Kepler in the year 1624; wherein mentioning the Canon Mirificus, he writes thus: "Nihil autem supra Neperianam rationem esse puto: et si Scotus quidem literis <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AD">ad</a> Tycholem, anno 1564, scriptis jam spem fecit Canonis illius mirifici;" which allusion agrees with the idle story mentioned by Wood in his Athene Oxon, and explains it in a way perfectly consonant to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of Napier as the inventor. When Napier had communicated to Mr Henry <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIGGS">Briggs</a>, mathematical professor in Gresham <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, his wonderful canon for the logarithms, that learned professor set himself to apply the rules in his Imitatio Neperiana; and in a letter to Archbishop Usher, in the year 1615, he writes thus: "Napier, baron of Merchiston, hath set my head and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> at work with his new and admirable logarithms. I hope to see him this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it please God; for I never <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> a book which pleased me better, and made me more wonder." The following passage from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of Lilly the astrologer is quoted by Lord Buchan, as giving a picturesque view of the meeting betwixt Briggs and the inventor of the logarithms at Merchiston near <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>. "I <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> acquaint you (says Lilly) with one memorable story related unto me by John Marr, an excellent mathematician and geometrician, whom I conceive you remember. He was <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> James I. and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. When Merchiston first published his logarithms, Mr Briggs, then reader of the astronomy lectures at Gresham college in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, was so much surprised with admiration of them, that he could have no quietness in himself until he had seen that noble person whose Napier whose only <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> they were: he acquaints John Marr therewith, who went into Scotland before Mr Briggs, purposely to be there when these two so learned persons should meet. Mr Briggs appoints a certain <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> when to meet at Edinburgh; but failing thereof, Merchiston was fearful he would not come. It happened one day as John Marr and the baron Napier were speaking of Mr Briggs: 'Ah, John (said Merchiston), Mr Briggs will not come.' At the very instant one knocks at the gate: John Marr hasted <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, and it proved to be Mr Briggs to his great contentment. He brings Mr Briggs up to the baron's chamber, where almost one <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> was spent, each beholding the other with admiration before one word was spoken. At last Mr Briggs began: 'Sir, I have undertaken this <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> journey purposely to see your person, and to know by what engine of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WIT">wit</a> or ingenuity you came first to think of this most excellent help into astronomy, viz. the logarithms; but, Sir, being by you found out, I wonder nobody else found it out before, when now being known it appears so easy.' He was nobly entertained by Baron Napier; and every summer after that, during the laird's being alive, this venerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, Mr Briggs, went purposely to Scotland to visit him." There is a passage in the life of Tycho Brahe by Gassendi, which may mislead an attentive reader to suppose that Napier's method had been explored by Herwart at Hoenburg: It is in Gassendi's Observations on a Letter from Tycho to Herwart of the last day of August 1599. "Dixit Hervartus nihil morari se solvendi cujusquam trianguli difficultatem; solere se enim multiplicationem, ac divisionem vice additiones solum, subtractiones 93 usupare (quod ad fieri posset, decuit postmodum suo logarithmorum Canone Neperus)." But Herwart here alludes to this work afterwards published in the year 1610, which solves triangles by prostapheresis; a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> totally different from that of the logarithms. Kepler dedicated his Ephemerides, to Napier, which were published in the year 1617; and it appears from many <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> in his letter about this time, that he held Napier to be the greatest man of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> in the particular department to which he applied his abilities. "And indeed (says our noble biographer), if we consider that Napier's discovery was not like those of Kepler or of Newton, connected with any analogies or coincidences which might have led him to it, but the fruit of unassisted reason and science, we shall be vindicated in placing him in one of the highest niches in the temple of Fame. Kepler had made many unsuccessful attempts to discover his canon for the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERIODIC">periodic</a> motions of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol11.html#article-HIT">hit</a> upon it at last, as he himself candidly owns, on the 15th of May 1618; and Newton applied the palpable tendency of heavy bodies to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> to the system of the universe in general; but Napier sought out his admirable rules by a slow scientific progress, arising from the gradual <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVOLUTION">evolution</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>." The last literary exertion of this eminent person was the publication of his Rabology and Promptuary in the year 1617, which he dedicated to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">Chancellor</a> Sexton; and soon after died at Merchiston on the 3rd of April O.S. of the same year, in the 68th year of his age and 23d of his happy invention.—The particular titles of his works published are: 1. A plain discovery of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVELATION">Revelation</a> of St John. 2. Mirifici ipsius cavonis constructio et logarithmorum, ad naturales ipsorum numeros habitudines. 3. Appendicis de alia atque praestantioris logarithmorum specie constituenda, in qua salicta unitas logarithmus est. 4. Rhodologiae, seu numerati-onis per virgulas, libri duo. 5. Propositiones quaedam eminentissimae, ad triangula sphaerica mira facultate re-solvenda. To which may be added, 6. His Letter to Anthony <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACON">Bacon</a> (the original of which is in the archbishop's library at Lambeth), entitled, "Secret inventions, profitable and necessary in these days for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, and notwithstanding strangers enemies to God's truth and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>;" which the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Buchan has caused to be printed in the Appendix to his Account of Napier's Writings. This letter is dated <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 2. 1596, about which time it appears the author had set himself to explore his logarithmic canon. This eminent person was twice married. By his first wife, who was a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Sir James Stirling of Keir, he had only one son named Archibald, who succeeded to the estate. By his <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> wife, a daughter of Sir James Chisholm of Cromlix, he had a numerous issue.—Archibald Napier, the only son of the first <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, was a person of fine parts and learning. Having more a turn to public business than his father had, he was raised to be a privy counsellor by James VI. under whose reign he also held the offices of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a>-depute, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>-clerk, and senator of the college of justice. By Charles I. he was raised to the peerage by the title of Lord Napier. Napier's Rods, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">Bones</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> invented by Baron Napier, whereby the multiplication and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> numbers is much facilitated. As to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">Construction</a> of Napier's Rods: Suppose the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> of multiplication to be made upon a plate of metal, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a>, or pasteboard, and then conceive the several columns (standing downwards from the digits on the head) to be cut asunder; and these are what we call Napier's rods of multiplication. But then there must be a good <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of each; for as many times as any <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> is in the multiplicand, so many rods of that <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> (i.e. with that figure on the top of it) must we have; though six rods of each species will be sufficient for any example in common affairs: there must be also as many rods of o's. But before we explain the way of using these rods, there is another thing to be known, viz. that the figures on every rod are written in an order different from that in the table. Thus the little <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> space or division in which the several products of every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLUMN">column</a> are written, is divided into two parts by a line across from the upper <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to the lower on the left; and if the product is a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGIT">digit</a>, it is set in the lower division; if it has two places, the first is set in the lower, and the second in the upper division; but the spaces on the top are not divided; also there is a rod of digits, not divided, which is called the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">index</a> rod, and of this we need but one single rod. See the figure of all the different rods, and the index, separate from one another, in Plate CCCLXIX. fig. 1. Multiplication by Napier's Rods. First lay down the index rod; then on the right of it set a rod, whose top is the figure in the highest <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of the multiplicand; next to this again, set the rod whose top is the next figure of the multiplicand; and so on in order to the first figure. Then is your multiplicand tabulated for all the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> digits; for in the same line of squares standing against every figure of the index rod, you have the product of that figure; and therefore you have no more to do but to transfer the products and sum them. But in taking out these products from the rods, the order in which the figures stand obliges you to a very easy and small addition; thus, begin to take out the figure in the lower <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>, or units place, of the square of the first rod on the right; add the figure on the upper part of this rod to that in the lower part of the next, and so on; which may be done as fast as you can look on them. To make this practice as clear as possible, take the following example. Example: To multiply 4768 by 385. Having set the rods together for the number 4768 (fig. 2) against 5 in the index, I find this number by adding according to the rule, | Against 8, this number | 23840 | |-----------------------|-------| | Against 3, this number | 38144 | Total product To make the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the rods yet more regular and easy, they are kept in a flat square box, whose breadth is that of ten rods, and the length that of one rod, as thick as to hold six (or as many as you please), the capacity of the box being divided into ten cells, for the different species of rods. When the rods are put up in the box (each species in its own <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CELL">cell</a> distinguished by the first figure of the rod set before it on the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> of the box near the top), as much of every rod stands without the box as shows the first figure of that rod; also, upon one of the flat sides without and near the edge, upon the left <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, the index rod is fixed; and along the foot there is a small ledge; so that the rods when applied are laid upon this side, and supported by the ledge, which makes the practice very easy; but in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> the multiplicand should have more than nine places, that upper face of the box may be made broader. Some make the rods with four different faces, and figures on each for different purposes. Division by Napier's Rods. First tabulate your divisor; then you have it multiplied by all the digits, out of which you may choose such convenient divisors as will be next less to the figures in the dividend, and write the index answering in the quotient, and so continually till the work is done. Thus 2179788, divided by 6123, gives in the quotient 356. Having tabulated the divisor 6123, you see that 6123 cannot be had in 21797; therefore take five places, and on the rods find a number that is equal or next less to 21797, which is 18369; that is, 3 times the divisor; wherefore set 3 in the quotient, and subtract 18369 from the figures above, and there will remain 3428; to which add 8, the next figure of the dividend, and seek again on the rods for it, or the next less, which you will find to be five times; therefore set 5 in the quotient, and subtract 30615 from 34288, and there will remain 3673; to which add 8, the last figure in the dividend, and finding it to be <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> six times the divisor, set 6 in the quotient.

NAPLES

Pages 666-677

a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, comprehending the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> countries of Samnium, Campania, Apulia, and Magna Graecia. It is bounded on all sides by the Mediterranean and Adriatic, except on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> east, where it terminates on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">Ecclesiastical</a> state. Its greatest length from south-east to north-west is about 280 English miles; and its breadth from north-east to south-west, from 96 to 120. The ancient <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> falls under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> ROME and ITALY; the present state of it, as well as of the rest of Italy, is owing to the conquests of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CHARLEMAGNE">Charlemagne</a>. When that monarch put an end to the kingdom of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOMBARDS">Lombards</a>, he obliged the dukes of Friuli, Spoletto, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENEVENTO">Benevento</a>, to acknowledge him as <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Italy; but allowed them to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> the same power and authority which they had enjoyed before his conquest. Of these three dukedoms Benevento was by far the most powerful and extensive, as it comprehended almost all the present kingdom of Naples; the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of Farther <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CALABRIA">Calabria</a> beyond the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Savuto of Bene and Peto, a few <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> cities in Hither Calabria, with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Acripoli, and the promontory in its neighbourhood called Capo di Licosa; and lastly, the dukedoms of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAETA">Gaeta</a>, Naples, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AMALFI">Amalfi</a>, which were very inconsiderable, and extended along the shore only about 100 miles, and were interrupted by the Gastaldato <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPUA">Capua</a>. This flourishing and extensive dukedom was at this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> governed by Arechis, who had married one of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Benevento's daughters, the last king of the Lombards, and had submitted, and taken the oath of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Charles. However, a few years after, he renounced his allegiance to the Franks, declared himself an independent sovereign, and was acknowledged as such by all the inhabitants of his duchy. To strengthen himself against Pepin king of Italy, who resided at <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAVENNA">Ravenna</a>, he enlarged and fortified the city of Benevento, and likewise built Salerno on the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, surrounding it with a very strong and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> wall. He engaged in several wars with the Greeks, whom he sometimes obliged to give him hostages; but having invaded the territories of the pope, whom Pepin could not assist, Charlemagne was prevailed on to return to Italy. Arechis, unable to oppose such a formidable enemy, sent his eldest son, Ronald, to Rome, with an offer of submission; but, at the instigation of the pope, Charles refused the offer, and detained his son prisoner; after which he ravaged the country, and made himself <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of Capua. Other deputies, however, proved more successful; and, in the year 787, a peace was concluded on these conditions: That Arechis and the Beneventans should renew their allegiance to the Franks; that he should pay a yearly tribute to Pepin; deliver up all his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a>; and give... gave his son Grimoald and his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> Adelgisa, with twelve others, as hostages for his fidelity; however, after many entreaties, Adelgisa was restored to her father. Charles had no sooner left Italy, than Arechis forgot all his engagements, and began to negotiate with Irene, empress of Constantinople, and her son Constantine, for expelling the Franks out of Italy. For himself, he desired the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the patriciate, and the dukedom of Naples with all its dependencies; and, in return, promised to acknowledge the Greek emperor as his sovereign, and to live after the manner of the Greeks. He required, however, to be supported by a Greek <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, and that his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>-in-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a> Adalgisus, son to Desiderius the last king of the Lombards, should be sent over into Italy, to raise a party among his countrymen. These conditions were readily accepted, on condition that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Romuald should be sent as an hostage; ambassadors were sent to Naples with the ensigns of the Patrician order, namely the mantle of cloth of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, the comb, and the sandals; but before the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> could be performed, Prince Romuald died, and soon after him his father; whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> was supposed to have been hastened by that of his son. After the death of Arechis, the Beneventans sent a most submissive embassy to Charlemagne, entreating him to send them Grimoald, the late king's son, and only lawful heir to his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>; threatening at the same time to revolt <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> their prince was denied them. Charles readily granted their request, and allowed Grimoald to depart, after he had agreed to the following conditions, viz. That he should oblige the Lombards to shave their beards; that, in writings, and on <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, the name of the king should be put before that of the prince; and that he should cause the walls of Salerno, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ACERENZA">Acerenza</a>, and Consia, to be entirely abolished.—The new king was received by his subjects with the utmost joy; and for some time <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> faithful to his engagements, excepting only the last article, which he either neglected or eluded. So far, however, was he from assisting the Greeks, that he gave notice of their machinations to Pepin king of Italy; raised an army to oppose his uncle Adalgisus; and being joined by Hildebrand duke of Spoletto, and Vinigise the general of Pepin, he attacked the Greeks in Calabria soon after they had landed, entirely defeated and took his uncle prisoner, and, as is said, put him to a cruel death. Yet in a short time Grimoald contracted an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> with the Greek emperor by marrying his niece Wanzia; and in the fifth year of his reign a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> broke out between him and Pepin, which continued for twelve years; at the end of which time a truce was concluded. Grimoald survived this pacification only three years, and was succeeded by his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a> Grimoald II. who submitted to Charlemagne after the death of Pepin; and from this time the Beneventans were looked upon as tributaries of the western emperors. As yet, however, the city of Naples did not own allegiance to the dukes of Benevento, but was held by the eastern emperors; and frequent wars took <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> between the Beneventans and Neapolitans. This happened to be the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> when Grimoald II. ascended the throne. He concluded a peace with them; which, however, was of no <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> continuance; for Theodore, governor of Naples, having granted protections to Daufurius a noble Beneventan, who had been concerned in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSPIRACY">conspiracy</a> against his prince, Grimoald marched against the city of Naples, and invested it by sea and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>. Theodore still refused to deliver up the traitor, and a general engagement both by land and sea was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>; in which the Neapolitans were defeated with so <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> slaughter, that the sea was stained with their blood for more than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> days. Theodore then consented to deliver up Daufurius, with 8000 crowns for the expense of the war; and Grimoald not only pardoned Daufurius, but received him into favour. The traitor, however, reflecting on the heinousness of his crime, was seized with remorse; and went a pilgrimage to the holy land, carrying a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> in his mouth, by way of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENANCE">penance</a>, which he never took out but at his meals. In the year 827, Grimoald was murdered by Radclhis <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNT">count</a> of Consta, and Sico Gastald of Acerenza, the latter of whom succeeded to the dukedom of Sico Benevento. Radclhis being soon after seized with remorse, became a monk; while Sico associated his son Sicardo with him in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>; and both, being of an ambitious and restless disposition, sought a pretence for attacking the Neapolitans. This was soon found, and the city was invested by sea and land. The walls were furiously battered; and part of them being <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, Sico prepared for a general assault. Stephen, at that time duke of Naples, pretended to submit; but, that he might prevent the city from being pillaged, entreated Sico to put off his entry till the morning, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time sent out his mother and his two children as hostages. Sico consented to his request; but next morning found the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> built up, and the Neapolitans prepared for their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>. Exasperated at their perfidy, he renewed his attacks with vigour, but without any success; the besieged defending themselves with the utmost obstinacy. At last, perceiving that they should not be able to hold out much longer, they consented to a peace on the following conditions, viz. That the Neapolitans should pay an annual tribute to the princes of Benevento, and consent of the transporting of the body of St Januarius from his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> without the walls of Naples to Benevento. These conditions being ratified, Sico returned with great honour to Benevento; but soon after renewed the war, under pretence that the Neapolitans had neglected to pay the stipulated sum; and hostilities continued till his death, which happened in 833. Sico was succeeded in the government of Benevento and by his son Sicardo, who had married the daughter of Roffrid his wife's brother, oppressed his subjects to such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> that they conspired against his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. He besieged Naples with a powerful army, and took possession of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ACERRA">Acerra</a> and Atella, both of which he fortified. But Bons, the Neapolitan duke, defended himself so vigorously, that the Beneventans were obliged to retire, and even to abandon Acerra and Atella, the fortifications of which were immediately demolished. At last Sicardo agreed to a peace for five years, on the intercession of Lothaire, emperor and king of Italy; but his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> was thought to have been the fear of the Saracens, whom the duke of Naples had called over from <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> to his assistance; for no sooner were Naples, they sent back than Sicardo attempted to delay the conclusion of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a>; but the emperor interposing his authority, a peace was concluded in the year 836, after the war had continued, with very little intermission, for 16 years. Soon after the conclusion of this peace, the Saracens landed at <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRINDISI">Brindisi</a>; and having made themselves masters of the place, ravaged all the neighbouring country. Sicardo marched against them with a numerous army; but the Saracens having dug a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of ditches which they slightly covered over, found means to draw the Beneventans in among them, whereby they were repulsed with great loss. However, Sicardo, having reinforced his army, marched again to attack them; but the Saracens, despairing of success, pillaged and burnt Brindisi, and then retired with their booty, and a great many captives to <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>. Sicardo, then, without any apparent provocation, attacked the city of Amalfi, levelled its walls with the ground, carried off all its wealth, and the body of its tutelar saint Triumphen. A great many of the inhabitants were transported to Salerno; and by promoting alliances between the inhabitants of both places, he endeavoured to unite Amalfi to his own principality as firmly as possible. During all these transactions, Sicardo had tyrannized over his subjects in such a manner, that at last he became intolerable. Among other acts of injustice, he imprisoned his own brother Siconolpus; compelled him to turn <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>; and afterwards sent him bound to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TARANTO">Taranto</a>, where he caused him to be shut up in an old tower that had been built for a cistern. By such acts of tyranny his <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a> were provoked to conspire against him; and in the year 839 he was murdered in his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TENT">tent</a>. On the death of Sicardo, Radelchis, his secretary or treasurer, was unanimously elected prince of Benevento; but Siconolphus, the last king's brother, having regained his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, formed a great party against the new prince. Radelchis did not fail to oppose him with a formidable army; and a most ruinous civil war ensued. Both parties by turns called in the Saracens; and these treacherous allies acted sometimes against one, and sometimes against the other; or, turned their arms against both, as seemed most suitable to their own <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>. Thus the war continued with the utmost animosity for 12 years, during which time the principality was almost entirely ruined; till at last the emperor <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> interposed, and obliged the competitors to agree to a partition of the principality. By this treaty, Radelchis promised to acknowledge Siconolphus and his successors as lawful princes of the principality of Salerno, which was declared to contain Taranto, Latiano, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CASSANO">Cassano</a>, Cossonzo, Laimo, Lucadia, Consia, Montella, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROTA">Rota</a>, Salerno, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SARNO">Sarno</a>, Ciraterium, Forcilo, Capua, Feano, Sora, and the half of the Gastaldate of Accerenza, where it joins Latiano and Consia. The boundary betwixt Benevento and Capua was fixed at St Angelo <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AD">ad</a> Cerros; Alli Peregrini was made the boundary betwixt Benevento and Salerno, and Staffilo betwixt Benevento and Consia. The monasteries of Monte Cassino and St Vincent were declared to be immediately under the protection of the emperor: both princes stipulated that no hostilities should be committed by either against the subjects of each other; and promised to join their forces Naples in order to drive out the Saracens. Soon after this pacification, however, both Radelchis and Siconolphus died; the former appointing his son Radelarius, or Radelcar, to succeed him; and the latter leaving an infant son, Sico, to the care of his godfather, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>. The war with the Saracens proved very unsuccessful; neither the united efforts of the princes, nor the full war assistance of the emperor Lewis himself, being able to with the Saracens expel the infidels; and in 854, Adelgise the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> son of Radelchis, who had now succeeded, on the death of his brother Radelcar, to the principality of Benevento, was obliged to pay them an annual subsidy. Two years after, Lando, count of Capua, revolted from the prince of Salerno, and could not be reduced. In the mean time, Sico, the lawful prince of Salerno, had been poisoned by Count Lando, and the principality usurped by Ademarius, the son of Peter above mentioned; but in 861, Ademarius himself was seized and imprisoned by Gaufurius, the son of Dauferius formerly mentioned. This was occasioned by his cruelty and rapaciousness, which entirely alienated the hearts of his subjects from him, and encouraged Gaufurius to become the head of the conspirators. The Saracens in the mean time committed terrible ravages throughout the Beneventan territories; which at last obliged Adelgise to enter into an alliance with Gaufurius, and both together sent a most humble embassy to the emperor Lewis, requesting him to take them under his protection. About the same time an embassy arrived from Constantinople, proposing a junction of the forces of the eastern and western empires against the infidels; upon which Lewis gave orders for assembling a formidable army. But in the mean time Adelgise fell off from his alliance, and made peace with the Saracens; nay, according to some, he encouraged them in their incursions, and it was at his desire that they invaded the duchy of Capua, and afterwards that of Naples, which they ravaged in a most barbarous manner. The Neapolitans, in conjunction with the duke of Spoleto and the count of Marsi, endeavoured to oppose them; but being defeated, the Saracens continued their ravages with redoubled fury, and retired to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARI">Bari</a>, which was their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> city, with an immense booty. In 866, Lewis arrived at Sora with his army: and having marched to Capua, was there joined by Landolph, the bishop and count, with a body of Capuans: but Landolph soon after persuading his countrymen to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESERT">desert</a>, Lewis marched against that city, which he took after a siege of three months, and almost totally destroyed. In the end of the year he was joined by Gaufurius with his quota of troops, having ordered the eyes of Ademarius to be put out in his absence. Lewis confirmed him in the principality, and marched with his army to Benevento, where Adelgise received him with great respect. Having reduced some inconsiderable places belonging to the Saracens, Lewis soon after invested Bari; but as the Saracens received continual supplies from their countrymen settled in Sicily, and besides were protected by the Neapolitans, he could not reduce the place till the year 871, though he had received considerable assistance from his brother Lotharius, and the Greek emperor had sent him a fleet of The expulsion of the Saracens was completed the same year by the taking of Tarento; after which the emperor returned with great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> to Benevento, resolving next to carry his arms into Sicily, and expel the infidels from thence also. But his future schemes of conquest were frustrated by a quarrel between him and Adelgise. The latter, pretending to have been insulted by the empress, and oppressed by the French, seized the emperor himself, and kept him prisoner for 40 days. His imprisonment would probably have been of much longer continuance, had not a body of Saracens arrived from Africa, who, being joined by such of their countrymen as had concealed themselves in Italy, laid siege to Salerno with an army of 30,000 men, ravaging the neighbouring country at the same time with the utmost barbarity. By this new invasion Adelgise was so much alarmed, that he set the emperor at liberty, but first obliged him to swear that he would not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> the insult that had been offered him, and that he would never return to Benevento. Lewis having then joined his forces to those of the prince of Salerno, soon obliged the Saracens to raise the siege of Salerno; but though they were prevented from taking that city, they entirely destroyed the inhabitants of Calabria, leaving it, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> of one of the historians of that time, "as desolate as it was at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a>." In the year 873, Lewis being absolved from his oath by the pope, went to Benevento, and was reconciled to Adelgise; but soon after this reconciliation he died, and the Saracens continued their ravages to such a degree that the inhabitants of Bari were constrained to deliver up their city to the Greeks. At the same time the Salernitans, Neapolitans, Cajetans, and Amalfitans, having made peace with the Saracens, were compelled to agree to their proposal of invading the territories of the Roman pontiff. His <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLINESS">holiness</a> exerted himself to the utmost, both with spiritual and temporal weapons, in order to defend his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>; but was at last reduced to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of becoming a tributary to the infidels, and promising to pay them a large sum annually.
