Besides bold thoughts and figures are never relished till the mind be heated and thoroughly engaged, which is not the reader's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> at the Commencement. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> introduces not a single simile in the first book of the Iliad, nor in the first book of the Odyssey. On the other hand, Shakespeare begins one of his plays with a sentiment too bold for the most heated imagination: <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEDFORD">Bedford</a>. Hung be the heav'ns with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, yield <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> to night! <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMETS">Comets</a>, importing change of times and states, Brandish your crystal tresses in the sky, And with them scourge the bad revolving stars, That have consented unto Henry's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>! Henry the Fifth, too famous to live <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>! England ne'er lost a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of so much worth. First <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> Henry VI. The passage with which Strada begins his history, is too poetical for a subject of that kind; and at any rate too <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> for the beginning of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> performance. 3. A third rule or observation is, That where the subject is intended for entertainment solely, not for instruction, a thing ought to be described as it appears, not as it is in reality. In running, for example, the impulse upon the ground is proportioned in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> to the celerity of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>; though in appearance it is otherwise, for a person in swift motion seems to skim the ground, and scarcely to touch it. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, with <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, describes quick running according to appearance; and raises an image far more lively than by adhering scrupulously to truth: Hos super adventit Volsca de gente Camilla, Agmen agens equitum, et florentes ære catervas, Bellatrix: non illa colo calathivse Minerve Foemineas assuetæ manus; sed prælia virgo Dura pati cursuque pedum prævertere rentos. Illa vel intactæ segestis per summa volaret <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMINA">Gramina</a>, nec teneras cursu lascisset aristas: Vel mare per medium, fluctu suspensa tumenti, Ferret iter, celere nec tingeret æquore plantas. Enicid, vii. 803. 4. In narration as well as in description, objects ought to be painted so accurately as to form in the mind of the reader distinct and lively images. Every useless circumstance ought indeed to be suppressed, because every such circumstance loads the narration; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a circumstance be necessary, however slight, it cannot be described too minutely. The force of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> consists in raising complete images, which have the effect to transport the reader as by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGIC">magic</a> into the very <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of the important <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, and to convert him as it were into a spectator, beholding every thing that passes. The narrative in an epic poem ought to rival a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> in the liveliness and accuracy of its representations: no circumstance must be omitted that tends to make a complete image; because an imperfect image as well as any other imperfect <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a>, is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> and uninteresting. We shall illustrate this rule by several examples, giving the first place to a beautiful passage from Virgil: Qualis populæ mores Philomela sub umbra Amisos queritur factus, quos durus orator Observans nido implures detraxit. Georg. lib. iv. 511. The poplar, ploughman, and unledged young, though not essential in the description, tend to make a complete image, and upon that account are an embellishment. Again: Hic viridem Æneas frondenti ex ilice metam Constituit, signum nautis. Æneid, v. 129. Horace addressing to Fortune: Te pauper ambit sollicita prece Ruris <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLONUS">colonus</a>: te dominam aquoris, Quicumque Bithynæ lacescit Carpathium pelagus carinâ. Carm. lib. i. ode 35. —Illum ex manibus hosticis Matrona bellantis tyranni Propiciens, et adulta virgo, Suspirat: Eheu, ne rudis agminum Sponsus lacescat regius asperum Tactu leonem, quem cruenta Per medias rapit ira cedes. Carm. lib. iii. ode 2. Shakespeare says, "You may as well go about to turn the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ICE">ice</a> by fanning in his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> with a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PEACOCK">peacock</a>'s feather." The peacock's feather, not to mention the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of the object, completes the image: an accurate image cannot be formed of that fanciful operation, without conceiving a particular feather; and one is at a loss when this is neglected in the description. Again, "The rogues slighted me into the river with as little remorse, as they would have drown'd a bitch's <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLIND">blind</a> puppies, fifteen i' th' litter." Old Lady. You would not be a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>? <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>. No, not for all the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> under heaven. Old Lady. 'Tis strange: a threepence bow'd would hire me, old as I am, to queen it. Henry VIII. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> ii. sc. 5. In the following passage, the action, with all its materi- He spake; and, to confirm his words, out flew Millions of flaming swords, drawn from the thighs Of mighty cherubim; the sudden blaze Far round illumina'd <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELL">hell</a>: highly they rag'd Against the Highest, and fierce with grasped arms, Clash'd on their sounding shields the din of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, Hurting defiance toward the vault of heav'n.

NARVA

Pages 686-686

a strong town of the Russian empire, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVONIA">Livonia</a>, with a castle and a harbour. It was taken by the Muscovites from the Danes in 1558, by the Swedes in 1581, and they defeated the Muscovites near it in 1700; but it was retaken by the Russians in 1704 by storm, and the inhabitants sent to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRACAN">Astracan</a>. It is seated on the river Narva, 95 miles south-west of Viborg, and 172 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGA">Riga</a>. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 29. o. N. Lat. 59. 8.

NASSAU-SIEGEN

Pages 686-686

a small principality of Germany in the Westerwalde, is in general a mountainous woody <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, with some arable and pasture ground, and a good breed of cattle. Its <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> are chiefly those of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>, having an iron mine in the neighbourhood of Siegen. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> John the Younger, in 1626, embraced the Roman Catholic <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, and endeavoured to introduce it into the country; but the principality, upon the extinction of the line of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NASSAU">Nassau</a>-Siegen in 1743, falling to the line of Nassau-Dietz, and therein to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STADTHOLDER">stadtholder</a> of the United Provinces, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a> were delivered from their apprehensions of Popish tyranny and bigotry. The prince, on account of these territories, has a seat and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> at the diets of the empire and circle in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of princes. His assessment in the matricula for Nassau-Siegen is 77 florins monthly; and towards the maintenance of the chamber judicatory, 50 rixdollars, six kruitzers and a half, each <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a>. The revenue of this principality is estimated at 100,000 rixdollars. NASSAU Dillenbourg, a principality of Germany, situated near the former. It has not much arable <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, but plenty of wood, good quarries of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, some silver and vitriol, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, with store of iron, for the working and smelting of which there are many forges and founderies in the country; and by these, and the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> of their iron, the inhabitants chiefly subsist. Calvinism is the religion of the principality, which contains five <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> and two boroughs, and belongs entirely to William V. prince of Orange, and Nassau hereditary stadtholder of the United Provinces, whose father succeeded to a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of it in 1739 on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Prince Christian, and to the rest in 1743 on the death of Prince William Hyacinth of Siegen. The prince, on account of this principality also and Dietz, has a seat and voice in the college of princes, at the diets of the empire and circle. His assessment in the matricula, for Nassau-Dillenbourg, is 102 florins monthly; and to the chamber judicatory, 59 rixdollars six and half kruitzers, each term. His revenue from this principality is computed at above 130,000 florins. Nassau-Hadamar, a country of Germany, which, till the year 1711, had princes of its own; but now belongs wholly to William V. prince of Orange. Nassau, prince of Orange. See Maurice.

NATES

Pages 686-686

in Anatomy, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> expressing those two fleshy exterior parts of the body, vulgarly called the buttocks. See Anatomy. NATES Cerebri, are two circular protuberances of the brain, situated on the back side of the medulla oblongata, near the cerebellum.

NATION

Pages 686-689

a collective <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a>, used for a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of people inhabiting a certain <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, confined within fixed limits, and under the same <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. NATIONAL DEBT: the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> owing by government. Our limits permit us to give but a very general sketch of this subject: However, as it is of considerable importance to every inhabitant of these kingdoms, we shall endeavour to give as clear and comprehensive a view of it as the bounds necessarily prescribed us <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> admit. In order to this, it may not be improper to refer back to the times that have gone before us, that we may the better discover the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of public revenues, the manner of their expenditure, and the causes of public debt. In that rude state of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> which precedes the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> and the improvements of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, when those expensive luxuries which commerce and manufactures can alone introduce, are altogether unknown; the person who possesses a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> revenue can spend <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> enjoy that revenue in no other way than by maintaining nearly as many people as it can maintain. Among our feudal <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> during which estates used to continue in the same family, sufficiently demonstrates the general disposition of nations people to live within their income. Though the rustic hospitality constantly exercised by the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> landlords may not to us in the present times seem consistent with that order which we are apt to consider as inseparably connected with good economy, yet we must certainly allow them to have been at least so far frugal as not <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> to have spent their whole income. Some <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of this money, perhaps, they spent in purchasing the few objects of vanity and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a> with which the circumstances of the times could furnish them: but some part of it they seem commonly to have hoarded. They could not well indeed do anything else but hoard whatever money they saved. To trade was disgraceful to a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>; and to lend money at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>, which at that time was considered as usury and prohibited by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>, would have been still more so. The same disposition to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> and to hoard prevailed in the sovereign as well as in the subjects. Among nations to whom commerce and manufactures are little known, the sovereign is in a situation which naturally disposes him to the parsimony requisite for accumulation. In that situation the expense even of a sovereign cannot be directed by that vanity which delights in the gaudy finery of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> of the times affords but few of the trinkets in which that finery consists. Standing armies are not then necessary; so that the expense even of a sovereign, like that of any other great <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a>, can be employed in scarce anything but bounty to his tenants and hospitality to his retainers. But bounty and hospitality very seldom <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> to extravagance: though vanity almost always does. All the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> sovereigns of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> accordingly had treasures. Every Tartar <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> in the present times is said to have one. In a commercial <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> abounding with every sort of expensive luxury, the sovereign, in the same manner as almost all the great proprietors in his dominions, naturally spends a great part of his revenue in purchasing those luxuries. His own and the neighbouring countries supply him abundantly with all the costly trinkets which compose the splendid but insignificant pageantry of a court. His ordinary expense becomes equal to his ordinary revenue, and it is well <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it does not frequently exceed it. The amassing of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a> can no longer be expected: and when extraordinary exigencies require extraordinary expenses, he must necessarily call upon his subjects for an extraordinary aid. The late <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a> and his father are the only great princes of Europe who, since the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Henry IV. of France in 1610, are supposed to have amassed any considerable treasure. The parsimony which leads to accumulation has become almost as rare in republican as in monarchical governments. The Italian republics, the United Provinces of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, are all in debt. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CANTON">canton</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BERNE">Berne</a> is the single republic in Europe which has amassed any considerable treasure. The other Swiss republics have not. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for some sort of pageantry, for splendid buildings at least and other public ornaments, frequently prevails as much in the apparently sober <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of a little republic as in the dissipated court of the greatest king. The want of parsimony in time of peace imposes the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of contracting debt in time of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. When war comes, there is no money in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a> but what is necessary for carrying on the ordinary expense of the peace establishment. In war an establishment of three or four times that expense becomes necessary for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the state, and consequently a revenue three or four times greater than the peace revenue. Supposing that the sovereign should have what he scarce ever has, the immediate means of augmenting his revenue in proportion to the augmentation of his expense; yet still the produce of the taxes, from which this increase of revenue must be drawn, will not begin to come into the treasury till perhaps ten or twelve months after they are imposed. But the moment in which war begins, or rather the moment in which it appears likely to begin, the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> must be augmented, the fleets must be fitted out, the garrisoned <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> must be put into a posture of defence: that army, that fleet those garrisoned towns, must be furnished with arms, ammunition, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>. An immediate and great expense must be incurred in that moment of immediate danger, which will not wait for the gradual and slow returns of the new taxes. In this exigency government can have no other resources but in borrowing. The same commercial state of society which, by the operation of moral causes, brings government in this manner into the necessity of borrowing, produces in the subjects both an ability and an inclination to lend. If it commonly brings along with it the necessity of borrowing, it likewise brings along with it the facility of doing so. A country abounding with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> and manufacturers, necessarily abounds with a set of people through whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> not only their own capitals, but the capitals of all those who either lend them money or trust them with goods, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> as frequently or more frequently than the revenue of a private <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, who without trade or business lives upon his income, passes through his hands. The revenue of such a man can regularly pass through his hands only once in a year. But the whole amount of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> of a merchant who deals in a trade of which the returns are very quick may sometimes pass through his hands two, three, or four times in a year. A country abounding with merchants and manufacturers, therefore, necessarily abounds with a set of people, who have it at all times in their power to advance, if they choose to do so, a very large sum of money to government. Hence the ability in the subjects of a commercial state to lend. The progress of the enormous debts which at present oppress, and will in the long-run probably ruin, all the great nations of Europe, has been pretty uniform. In England, after the Revolution, when new connexions with Europe introduced a new system of foreign politics, the expences of the nation not only in settling the new establishment, but in maintaining long wars, as principals, on the continent, for the security of the Dutch <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARRIER">barrier</a>, reducing the French <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a>, settling the Spanish succession, supporting the house of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, maintaining the liberties of the Germanic body, and other purposes, increased to an unusual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>: insomuch that it was not thought advisable to raise all the expences of any one year by taxes to be levied within that year, lest the unaccustomed <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of them should create murmurs among the people. It was therefore the policy of the times to anticipate the revenues of their posterity, by borrowing immense sums for the current <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the state, and to lay no more taxes upon the subject than would suffice to pay the annual interest of the sums so borrowed; by this means converting the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> debt into a new <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, transferable from one man to another at any time and in any <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>. This system indeed seems to have had its original in the state of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>, A.D. 1344; which government then owed about 60,000l. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>; and being unable to pay it, formed the principal into an aggregate sum, called metaphorically a mount or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a>, the shares whereof were transferable like our stocks, with interest at 5 per cent. the prices varying according to the exigencies of the state. National state. This laid the foundation of what is called the national debt; for a few long <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ANNUITIES">annuities</a> created in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. will hardly deserve that name. Nations, like private men, have generally begun to borrow upon what may be called personal credit, without assigning or mortgaging any particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUND">fund</a> for the payment of the debt; and when this resource has failed them, they have gone on to borrow upon assignments or mortgages of particular funds. What is called the unfunded debt of Great <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, is contracted in the former of those two ways. It consists partly in a debt which bears, or is supposed to bear, no interest; and which resembles the debts that a private man contracts upon account; and partly in a debt which bears interest, and which resembles what a private man contracts upon his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BILL">bill</a> or promissory <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>. The debts which are due either for extraordinary services, or for services either not provided for or not paid at the time when they are performed; part of the extraordinary of the army, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>, and ordnance, the arrears of subsidies to foreign princes, those of seamen's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WAGES">wages</a>, &c. usually constitute a debt of the first kind. Navy and exchequer bills, which are issued sometimes in payment of a part of such debts and sometimes for other purposes, constitute a debt of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> kind; exchequer bills <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> interest from the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> on which they are issued, and navy bills six months after they are issued. The bank of England, either by voluntarily discounting those bills at their current value, or by agreeing with government for certain considerations to circulate exchequer bills, that is, to receive them at par, paying the interest which happens to be due upon them, keeps up their value, and facilitates their circulation, and thereby frequently enables government to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> a very large debt of this kind. During the great recoinage in King William's time, when the bank of England thought proper to put a stop to its usual transactions, exchequer bills and tallies are said to have sold from 25 to 60 per cent. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCOUNT">discount</a>, owing partly, no doubt, to the supposed instability of the new government established by the Revolution, but partly too to the want of the support of the bank of England. When this resource is exhausted, and it becomes necessary, in order to raise money, to assign or mortgage some particular branch of the public revenue for the payment of the debt, government has upon different occasions done this in two different ways. Sometimes it has made this assignment or mortgage for a short <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of time only, a year or a few years, for example; and sometimes for perpetuity. In the one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, the fund was supposed sufficient to pay within the limited time both principal and interest of the money borrowed: In the other, it was supposed sufficient to pay the interest only, or a perpetual annuity <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to the interest; government being at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to redeem at any time this annuity upon paying back the principal sum borrowed. When money was raised in the one way, it was said to be raised by anticipation; when in the other, by perpetual funding, or, more shortly, by funding. In the reign of King William, when the debt began to be amassed, and during a great part of that of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>, before we had become so familiar as we are now with the practice of perpetual funding, the greater part of the new taxes were imposed but for a short period of time (for four, five, six, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years only), and a great part of the grants of every year consisted in loans upon anticipation of the produce of those taxes. The produce being frequently insufficient for paying within the limited term the principal and interest of the money borrowed, deficiencies arose; to make good which it became necessary to prolong the term. On the 31st of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1697, the funded and unfunded debts amounted to £21,515,742l. 13s. 8½d.; at the same time, 1714, they were £53,681,076l. 5s. 6½d. In 1755, before the breaking out of the war, they amounted to £72,289,673l.; and on the 5th of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1763, at the conclusion of the peace, they had accumulated to £122,603,336l. 8s. 2½d. of funded debt, and of unfunded £13,027,589l. 2s. 2½d. more. In 1775, they were very nearly 130 millions; and the last American war added upwards of 120 millions more to that enormous sum: to pay the interest of which, and the charges of management, amounting annually to nearly eight millions and a half, the extraordinary revenues elsewhere enumerated* (excepting only the land-tax and annual malt tax) are in the first <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> mortgaged and made perpetual by <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. Perpetual, we say; but still redeemable by the same authority that imposed them: which, if it at any time can pay off the capital, will abolish those taxes which are raised to discharge the interest. By this means, then, the quantity of property in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> is greatly increased in idea compared with former times; yet, if we coolly consider it, not at all increased in reality. We may boast of large fortunes, and quantities of money in the funds. But where does this money exist? It exists only in name, in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, in public <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, in parliamentary security: and that is undoubtedly sufficient for the creditors of the public to rely on. But then what is the pledge which the public faith has pawned for the security of these debts? The land, the trade, and the personal industry of the subject; from which the money must arise that supplies the several taxes. In these, therefore, and these only, the property of the public creditors does really and intrinsically exist; and of course the land, the trade, and the personal industry of individuals, are diminished in their true value <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> so much as they are pledged to answer. If A's income amounts to 100l. per annum; and he is so far indebted to B, that he pays him 50l. per annum for his interest; one half of the value of A's property is transferred to B the creditor. The creditor's property exists in the demand which he has upon the debtor, and nowhere else; and the debtor is only a trustee to his creditor for one half of the value of his income. In short, the property of a creditor of the public consists in a certain portion of the national taxes; by how much therefore he is the richer, by so much the nation, which pays these taxes, is the poorer. The only advantage that can result to a nation from public debts, is the increase of circulation, by multiplying the cash of the kingdom, and creating a new species of currency, assignable at any time and in any quantity; always therefore ready to be employed in any beneficial undertaking, by means of this its transferable <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>; and yet producing some profit even when National when it lies idle and unemployed. A certain proportion of debt seems to be highly useful to a trading people; but what that proportion is, it is not for us to determine. This much is indisputably certain, that the present magnitude of our national encumbrances very far exceeds all calculations of commercial benefit, and is productive of the greatest inconveniences. For, first, The enormous taxes that are raised upon the necessaries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> for the payment of the interest of this debt, are a hurt both to trade and manufactures, by raising the price as well of the artificer's subsistence as of the raw material, and of course, in a much greater proportion, the price of the commodity itself. Nay, the very increase of paper circulation itself, when extended beyond what is requisite for commerce or foreign <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a>, has a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> tendency to increase the price of provisions as well as of all other merchandise. For as its effect is to multiply the cash of the kingdom, and this to such an extent that much must remain unemployed, that cash (which is the universal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of the respective values of all other commodities) must necessarily sink in its own value, and everything grow comparatively dearer. Secondly, If part of this debt be owing to foreigners, either they draw out of the kingdom annually a considerable quantity of specie for the interest; or else it is made an argument to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> them unreasonable privileges in order to induce them to reside here. Thirdly, If the whole be owing to subjects only, it is then charging the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> and industrious subject, who pays his share of the taxes to maintain the indolent and idle creditor who receives them. Lastly, and principally, It weakens the internal strength of a state, by anticipating those resources which should be reserved to defend it in case of necessity. The interest we now pay for our debt would undoubtedly be sufficient to maintain the most vigorous war that any national motives could possibly require. If indeed our ancestors in King William's time had annually paid, so long as their exigencies lasted, a far less sum than we now annually raise upon their accounts, they would not in time of war have borne so great burdens as they have bequeathed to and settled upon their posterity in time of peace; and might have been eased the instant the exigence was over. On the whole, then, the national debt is undoubtedly a subject of vast importance, and as such it has been always considered; for much has been said and written upon it, and many schemes have been proposed at various times and by various persons for gradually removing it, it being considered by the most judicious as a most pernicious encumbrance to a commercial country. Some, we are aware, think it of vast utility; but this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> is too eccentric, and in our estimation too feebly supported, to be convincing. The public debt is indisputably a great grievance; and every lover of his country must surely wish to see it removed: the period, however, when this blessing shall take place, if indeed it ever arrive, must at least be very distant. We refer such as wish for farther information on this interesting topic, to those who have treated of it at full length, as Smith in his Wealth of Nations, and Sir John Sinclair in his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the Revenue. The writings of Dr Price likewise deserve considerable <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, especially as one of his plans for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a> of the debt has in fact been adopted, and in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> established, by the legislature: His three plans may be found in a pamphlet by William Morgan, entitled, A Review of Dr Price's Writings on the Subject of the Finances of this Kingdom. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-NATIVITY">Nativity</a>, or <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-NATAL">Natal</a> Day, the day of a person's birth. The word nativity is chiefly used in speaking of the saints; as, the nativity of St John the Baptist, &c. But when we say the Nativity, it is understood of that of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ, or the feast of Christmas. Nativity, nativitas, in ancient law books, signifies <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONDAGE">bondage</a> or servitude. Nativity, in Astrology, the theme or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of the heavens, and particularly of the twelve houses, at the moment when a person was born; called also the horoscope. Casting the nativity, or by calculation seeking to know how long the queen should live, &c. was made felony, an. 23. Eliz. c. 2. Nativó habendo, in Law, a writ directed to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a>, for a lord who claimed inheritance in any villain, when a villain was run away from him, for the apprehending and restoring him to the lord.

NATIX

Pages 689-689

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a name given by some old writers to the natrix.

NATOLIA

Pages 689-689

the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> name of the Lesser <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, being the most westerly <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a> in Asia, and consisting of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a>, which extends from the river <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUPHRATES">Euphrates</a> as far as the Archipelago, the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> of Marmora, the straits of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GALLIPOLI">Gallipoli</a> and of Constantinople, which separate it from <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> on the west. It is bounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BLACK_SEA"><a class=</a>"xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> sea, and on the south by the Mediterranean.

NATRIX

Pages 689-689

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, the name of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>-snake, called also torquata, from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> about its neck. See Ophiology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

NATRUM

Pages 689-689
or Natron, the nitre of the ancients, one of the fixed alkalies. See Soda, Chemistry Index. It is found in great abundance in many parts of Asia, where the natives sweep it up from the surface of the ground, and called soap earth. The earliest account we have of it is in the scriptures, where we find that the salt called nitre in those times would ferment with vinegar, and possessed a deterrent quality, so that it was used in baths and in washing. Solomon compares the singing of songs with a heavy heart, to the contrariety of vinegar and nitre: and Jeremiah says, that if the sinner wash himself with nitre, his sin is not cleansed off. These are properties that perfectly agree with this salt, but not at all with our saltpetre, which is the nitre of the moderns.

NATURAL

Pages 689-691

in general, something that relates to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. See Nature. Natural Children, are those born out of lawful wedlock. See <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASTARD">Bastard</a>. Natural Functions, are those actions whereby the aliments are changed and assimilated so as to become a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the body. Natural, in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, is used where animals, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, &c. are blazoned with the colours they naturally have, though different from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> colours. Natural <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">Beauty</a>. Natural <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">Note</a>, in Music, is used in opposition to flat and sharp notes, which are called <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> notes. See Note, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">Scale</a>, &c. Natural is also used for something coming immediately out of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of nature; in which <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> it stands opposed to fictitious <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> artificial, which signifies something wrought by art. See Artificial. Bishop Wilkins observes, that there appears a world of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between natural and artificial things, when viewed with microscopes. The first ever appear adorned with all imaginable elegance and beauty; the latter, though the most curious in their kind, infinitely rude and unshewn: the finest <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a> appears a rough <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>; and the most accurate engraving or embossment, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> done with a mattock or a trowel. Natural Beauty, or the beauty of natural objects, is that <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> or those qualities in the works of nature, or more properly of God, which are calculated to excite pleasing sensations in the minds of all such persons of true <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> as attentively observe them. It <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> not, we trust, be deemed improper or impertinent, therefore, to introduce a few observations on this subject, previous to our treating of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY">natural <a clas</a>s="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>.—To many, it is hoped, it will appear to be a very proper introduction to that important article. "That <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSIBILITY">sensibility</a> to beauty, which, when cultivated and improved, we <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> taste, is universally diffused through the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>;" and it is most uniform with respect to those objects, which being out of our power, are not liable to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a> from accident, caprice, or fashion. The verdant <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAWN">lawn</a>, the shady <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROVE">grove</a>, the variegated landscape, the boundless ocean, and the starry firmament, are contemplated with <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> by every attentive beholder. But the emotions of different spectators, though similar in kind, differ widely in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>; and to relish with full delight the enchanting scenes of nature, the mind must be uncorrupted by avarice, sensuality, or ambition; quick in her sensibilities; elevated in her sentiments; and devout in her affections. He who possesses such exalted powers of perception and enjoyment, may almost say, with the poet, I care not, Fortune! what you me deny; You cannot rob me of free Nature's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>; You cannot shut the windows of the sky, Through which <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AURORA">Aurora</a> shows her bright'ning <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a>; You cannot bar my constant feet to trace The woods and lawns, by living stream, at <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-EVE">eve</a>: Let <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> my nerves and finer fibres brace, And I their toys to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> children leave: Of fancy, reason, virtue, nought can me bereave. "Perhaps such ardent enthusiasm may not be compatible with the necessary toils and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> offices which <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a> has assigned to the generality of men. But there are none to whom some portion of it may not prove advantageous: and if it were cherished by each individual, in that degree which is consistent with the indispensable duties of his station, the felicity of human <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> would be considerably augmented. From this source the refined and vivid pleasures of the imagination are almost entirely derived: and the elegant arts owe their choicest beauties to a taste for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTEMPLATION">contemplation</a> of nature. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAINTING">Painting</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a> are express imitations of visible objects; and where would be the charms of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, if divested of the imagery and embellishments which she borrows from rural scenes? Painters, statuaries, and poets, therefore, are always ambitious to acknowledge themselves the pupils of nature; and as their skill increases, they grow more and more delighted with every view of the animal and vegetable world. But the pleasure resulting from admiration is transient; and to cultivate taste, without regard to its influence on the passions and affections, 'is to rear a tree for its blossoms, which is capable of yielding the richest and most valuable fruit.' Physical and moral beauty bear so intimate a relation to each other, that they may be considered as different gradations in the scale of excellence; and the knowledge and relish of the former should be deemed only a step to the nobler and more permanent enjoyments of the latter. "Whoever has visited the Leasowes, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARWICKSHIRE">Warwickshire</a>, must have felt the force and propriety of an inscription which meets the eye at the entrance into those delightful grounds. Would you then taste the tranquil <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a>? Be sure your bosoms be serene: Devoid of hate, devoid of strife, Devoid of all that poisons life: And much it 'vails you, in their <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, To graft the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of human <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>. "Now such scenes contribute powerfully to inspire that serenity which is necessary to enjoy and to heighten their beauties. By a secret contagion, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> catches the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> which she contemplates; and the frame within assimilates itself to that which is without. For, Who can forbear to smile with Nature? Can The stormy passions in the bosom roll, While every <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GALE">gale</a> is peace, and every grove Is <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MELODY">melody</a>? "In this state of sweet composure, we become susceptible of virtuous impressions, from almost every surrounding object. The patient ox is viewed with generous complacency; the guileless sheep with pity; and the playful lamb raises emotions of tenderness and love. We rejoice with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> and exemption from toil, while he ranges at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> through enamelled pastures; and the frolics of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COLT">colt</a> would afford unmixed delight, did we not recollect the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONDAGE">bondage</a> which he is soon to undergo. We are charmed with the song of birds, soothed with the buzz of insects, and pleased with the sportive motions of fishes, because these are expressions of enjoyment; and we exult in the felicity of the whole animated <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>. Thus an equal and extensive benevolence is called forth into exertion; and having felt a common <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> in the gratifications of inferior beings, we shall be no longer indifferent to their sufferings, or become wantonly instrumental in producing them. "It seems to be the intention of Providence, that the lower order of animals should be subservient to the comfort, convenience, and sustenance of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. But his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of dominion extends no farther; and if this right be exercised with mildness, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, the subjects of his power will be no less beneficent..." ed than himself. For various species of living creatures are annually multiplied by human art, improved in their perceptive powers by human culture, and plentifully fed by human industry. The relation, therefore, is <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECIPROCAL">reciprocal</a> between such animals and man; and he may supply his own wants by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of their labour, the produce of their bodies, and even the sacrifice of their lives, whilst he co-operates with all-gracious Heaven in promoting <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a>, the great end of existence. "But though it be true, that partial evil, with respect to different orders of sensitive beings, may be universal good; and that it is a wise and benevolent <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> of nature, to make destruction itself, within certain limitations, the cause of an increase of life and enjoyment; yet a generous person will extend his compassionate regards to every individual that suffers for his sake: and whilst he sighs Even for the kid or lamb that parts its life Beneath the bloody <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a>, he will naturally be solicitous to mitigate pain, both in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a> and degree, by the gentlest modes of inflicting it. "We are inclined to believe, however, that this sense of humanity would soon be obliterated, and that the heart would grow callous to every soft <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a>, were it not for the benevolent influence of the smiling face of nature. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNT">count</a> de Lauzon, when imprisoned by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV. in the castle of Pignerol, amused himself during a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> with catching flies, and delivering them to be devoured by a rapacious spider. Such an entertainment was equally singular and cruel; and inconsistent, we believe, with his former character, and his subsequent turn of mind. But his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CELL">cell</a> had no window, and received only a glimmering <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> from an aperture in the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a>. In less unfavourable circumstances, may we not presume, that instead of sporting with misery, he would have released the agonizing flies, and bid them enjoy that freedom of which he himself was bereaved? "But the taste for natural beauty is subservient to higher purposes than those which have been enumerated; and the cultivation of it not only refines and humanizes, but dignifies and exalts the affections. It elevates them to the admiration and love of that Being who is the author of all that is fair, sublime, and good in the creation. Scepticism and irreligion are hardly compatible with the sensibility of heart which arises from a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> and lively relish of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>, harmony, and order subsisting in the world around us: and emotions of piety must <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> up spontaneously in the bosom that is in unison with all animated nature. Actuated by this divine <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSPIRATION">inspiration</a>, man finds a fane in every grove; and glowing with devout fervour, he joins his song to the universal chorus, or <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSES">muses</a> the praise of the Almighty, in more expressive silence. Thus they "Whom Nature's works can <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARM">charm</a>, with God himself Hold <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONVERSE">converse</a>: grow familiar, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> by day, With his conceptions; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> upon his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>; And form to his the relish of their souls." On the whole, then, it certainly appears, that the advantages resulting from a taste for natural beauties are great and important: it is equally certain, that as it is useful, so it is a continual source of real enjoyment; for a more rational pleasure cannot possibly occupy the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> or captivate the affections of mankind, than that which arises from a due consideration of the works of nature. Pleasure, we know, is a necessary ingredient in human life, in order in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> to counterbalance the pains, the evils, and listless-nesses, which are at times perhaps unavoidable, and in order to render life tolerable. It is the part then of the moralist, and it has been frequently his business, to point out and recommend such pleasures as are highly gratifying, and are yet perfectly innocent. The Spectator, whose works will be admired as long as the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> in which they are written is understood, recommends strongly and elegantly the pleasure of a garden; and a later writer, of no common degree of merit, and of very considerable fame, has an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSAY">essay</a> on the same subject, from which we shall select a few observations, and so conclude the article. "Not he alone (says this elegant writer) is to be esteemed a benefactor to mankind, who makes an useful discovery; but he also who can point out and recommend an innocent pleasure. Of this kind are the pleasures arising from the observation of nature; and they are highly agreeable to every taste uncorrupted by vicious <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-INDULGENCE">indulgence</a>. Rural scenes of almost every kind are delightful to the mind of man. But the misfortune is, that the greater part are hurried on in the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CAREER">career</a> of life with too great rapidity to be able to give attention to that which solicits no <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>. The darkest habitation in the dirtiest street of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a>, where <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> can be earned, has greater charms with many than the groves of Hagley. "The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> of refined pleasure, the elegant Epicurus, fixed the seat of his enjoyment in a garden. He was of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that a tranquil spot, furnished with the united sweets of art and nature, was the best adapted to delicate repose. And even the severer philosophers of antiquity were wont to discourse in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a> of a spreading tree, in some cultivated plantation. It is obvious, on intuition, that nature often intended solely to please the eye in her vegetable productions. She decorates the floweret that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> beneath our feet in all the perfections of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> beauty. She has clothed the garden with a constant succession of various hues. Even the leaves of the tree undergo a pleasing vicissitude. The fresh verdure which they exhibit in the spring, the various shades which they assume in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> and russet tinge of autumn, and the nakedness of winter, afford a constant pleasure to a lively imagination. From the snowdrop to the moss rose the flower garden displays an infinite variety of shape and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. The taste of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORIST">florist</a> has been ridiculed as trifling; yet surely without reason. Did nature bring forth the tulip and the lily, the rose and the honeysuckle, to be neglected by the haughty pretender to superior reason? To omit a single social duty for the cultivation of a polyanthus were ridiculous as well as criminal; but to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> by the beauties lavished before us, without observing them, is no less ingratitude than stupidity. A bad heart finds little amusement but in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with the active world, where scope is given for the indulgence of

NATURAL HISTORY

Hence, taking the whole <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of known animals at 23,000, that of vegetables at 50,000 and that of minerals 267, the whole number of known species of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> objects <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> be 73,267. II. Though the classification of natural bodies is of hints for the highest importance towards making us acquainted studying with unknown species, and distinguishing them from those which we already know; this alone is not sufficient to form a naturalist. His <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> object should be to learn the habits, manners, and uses of the objects which he is studying; and he may perhaps be assisted in this object by the following observations. 1. In <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the natural <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the animal Zoology kingdom, it is necessary to ascertain both the distinctive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of each individual animal, and its peculiar habits, properties and uses. The naturalist first learns that the sheep, for instance, is in the class <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">mammalia</a>, being one of those animals that suckle their young; in the order pecora, because it is hoofed, and has no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> in the upper jaw; and that it is distinguished from other animals of the same order, by its having several blunt wedge-like incisive fore-teeth in the lower jaw only, hollow reclined horns, and no tusks. This information would satisfy many, who call themselves naturalists; but it is far from being all that is required; the philosophical investigator of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">Nature</a> inquires into its habits; as its food, its <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of gestation, its season of lambing, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> most suited to its <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> and vigour. He endeavours to learn what produces the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> in its <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLEECE">fleece</a>, whether climate, food, or some peculiarity in the breed; and is anxious to ascertain what variety is most disposed to fatten, and what food effects this speedily; with many other very useful particulars. The information of the first kind is of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, and even necessary in many <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>; but that of the latter is most useful. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> a traveller discovers an animal possessing any useful <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, or producing any useful drug, if he have not the first kind of information, he gives so confused and inaccurate a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of it, that others, mistaking the animal, discredit the author's account, and the world loses the benefit of his discovery. 2. <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, or the natural history of the vegetable Botany kingdom, in the usual acceptation of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a>, implies only (c) This number, drawn from the article Botany, compared with the three first volumes of Wildenow's edition of the Species Plantarum, and with Persoon's edition of the Systema Vegetabilium, of Linné, is certainly very far below the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>. Many years ago, the number of known species was reckoned at above twenty thousand, and there is reason to believe that it exceeds fifty thousand. Objects only the knowledge of the distinctive characters of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>; and he who knows the greatest number, and is most accurate in determining the different species, is accounted the best botanist. This however constitutes but a small <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the science; there is another distinct department, which may properly be termed the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> of botany, which is both more interesting and more useful. This includes the knowledge of the structure, or the anatomy of plants; and the knowledge of the uses, or functions of their various parts, as of the leaves, the bark, the pith, the roots, the juices, &c.; which is called the physiology of plants. It includes also an acquaintance with the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> and climate adapted to different vegetables, their <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of propagation, and the various uses to which their several parts or productions may be applied. Botany, in the first <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, which may be called practical botany, is subservient, and absolutely necessary to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the philosophy of botany; for no one that is unacquainted with the classification of plants can either convey to others his own information, or himself receive the benefit of that of others, respecting either the structure and economy or the habits and the uses of such plants, as may have been investigated. If medical virtues are discovered in any vegetable production; without the accuracy of the practical botanist, to ascertain and describe the particular plant which affords it, the discovery is often lost; or perhaps, what is worse, the virtues are attributed to a different plant, and it is only by repeated failures, and in some cases after much mischief, that the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERROR">error</a> is detected. It is evident that the same may happen to the agriculturist, the dyer, or any other artizan, who has discovered in the vegetable kingdom the means of improving his art, but has not botanical knowledge sufficient to give an accurate character of the plant, to which he is indebted for his discovery. 3. In <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERALOGY">Mineralogy</a>, or the natural history of the mineral kingdom, almost half the students are of that class, who content themselves with collecting, and being able to arrange systematically the minerals they meet with. But in this department of natural history, as well as the other two, which we have considered, something more than arrangement is required. It is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> who can analyze, and separate the component parts of mineral productions; who knows the art of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ASSAYING">assaying</a>, and who knows a priori the probable site of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARRY">quarry</a>, or a mine, and can tell the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of a stratum of coal, or of marble, that we may call a mineralogist. The natural history of the mineral kingdom includes <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOLOGY">geology</a>, or the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATA">data</a> upon which are founded the different theories of the formation of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. It includes the knowledge of those facts, upon which the art of mining, and the art of separating and purifying <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, is founded; and its object is to teach likewise the properties of those metals, as well as of the earths, and other mineral productions, when separated and in their simple state. With respect to the utility of the study of natural history, we have unavoidably given many instances of it, in considering the object of the science. We need therefore add but few others. The grazier knows the advantage of attending to the habits and distinctive marks of our <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> animals, and all. It is natural history, though not often studied scientifically, that teaches him what variety of sheep to prefer; by what means to obtain a variety of cows, remarkable for their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILK">milk</a>; how to choose the stock to the best adapted to his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, and what is the best food for them during winter. Much benefit is likely to accrue from the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> lately paid to the cultivation of what are termed the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> grasses. Instead of sowing his hay seeds indiscriminately, the grazier may select only such grasses as are, by observation, found to be most suited to his soil and cattle. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARMER">farmer</a>'s knowledge of the proper succession of crops, the best times for sowing them, when to weed, and with what to manure, as well as how to destroy both weeds and insects, is the knowledge of a naturalist; and surely he who is scientifically acquainted with the growth of plants, knowing what part the soil acts in vegetation, and what is the aliment most required by them, will have great advantage over the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> empirical farmer, who has no better reason for what he does, than that his father did the same before him. By studying the natural history of insects, we learn the habits of such as are noxious and injurious, and thence derive the means of destroying them. The minerologist has often enriched individual proprietors of land, and benefited his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, by the discovery of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINES">mines</a>; he is enabled to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> the planners of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a> by warning them of obstacles; and his knowledge has aided the physician in ascertaining the virtues of minerals, and of mineral waters. In the arts, a knowledge of natural history prevents that confusion, and those innumerable errors that must be committed, when the natural productions which are employed cannot be accurately discriminated from others. It is to the naturalist that we are many times indebted for the introduction of foreign animals and foreign plants into our own country. Wheat, oats, barley, and other vegetables, which are now become necessary to our existence, were not originally of British growth. The <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-POTATO">potato</a>, now so general and so useful, was first introduced into this country by Gerard, a noted botanist, and was for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> cultivated in his garden as a rarity. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANE">cane</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>-fruit tree, the farinaceous palms, the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, have all been transported by naturalists of the present <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, to regions where they never grew before. Besides the above, and many similar instances of advantage to be derived from studying the different branches of natural history, these two incalculable benefits necessarily arise to the student himself, from attending to the whole, or any part of the science; namely, a power of abstracting the mind, and reasoning methodically; and a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of contemplating the Creator in his works. Our limits do not permit us to enter further into the fertile topic of the utility and advantages of natural history. Its utility, in a moral and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> point of view, has been ably illustrated by Mr Ray, in his "<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WISDOM">Wisdom</a> of God;" by Mr Bingley, in the introduction. We have stated it to be one of the principal objects of natural history, to teach the mode of preserving specimens. This art, called by the French Taxidermie, is exceedingly curious, and would well deserve a much fuller consideration than we can here allot to it. We shall confine our attention on this subject entirely to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ANIMAL_KINGDOM">animal kingdom</a>, and even here we must be very <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIEF">brief</a>. The art of preparing and mounting the skins of animals appears to be pretty old; but it made no great progress before the 17th century, when Reaumur made some attempts to preserve the specimens from the attacks of insects. In the Journal de Physique for 1773, there is a memoir addressed to the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, by M. Kuckhan, on the methods of preparing birds, which is very curious, but is liable to many objections. In the same volume is a memoir by Mauduit, principally respecting the means of preserving animal specimens from the attacks of insects. His preservatives are of a poisonous nature; and, of course, their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> is dangerous, while they do not appear to have been attended with the expected success. The arsenical <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOAP">soap</a> of Becceur, much celebrated about the same time, is liable to similar objections. The latest, and probably the best <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> on this subject, is that published a few years ago by M. Nicolas; and from this the following observations are derived. The instruments employed in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> of specimens are much the same as those used by anatomists in their ordinary dissections, consisting of small knives or scalpels, forceps or pincers of various forms, probes, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEEDLES">needles</a>, and pins or wires. The preservatives employed by M. Nicolas to protect the specimens from insects, are principally of two kinds: 1. Sulphur, which he applies to the skins by means of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FUMIGATION">fumigation</a>, thus impregnating them with sulphurous acid; 2. A liquor for macerating the skins, another liquor for rubbing over the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, and a pomatum for anointing the inside of the skin. The first liquor is prepared by steeping a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> and a half of powdered oak bark, and four ounces of powdered <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a>, in twenty English pints of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, for two days, taking care to shake the mixture from time to time. The pomatum is prepared of a pound of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> soap, half a pound of caustic <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POTASH">potash</a>, four ounces of powdered alum, two English pints of water, four ounces of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETROLEUM">petroleum</a>, and the same of camphire. The soap, cut into small pieces, is put into an earthen pipkin, over a moderate fire; the water poured over it; and when the whole is formed into a sort of soft paste, the alum and then the oil are added; the whole well stirred together, removed from the fire, and when it is nearly cold the camphire is added; being before <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> rubbed <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a> with a little spirit of wine. The pomatum, thus prepared, must be kept in glass vessels, well stopp'd; and, when used, is to be lowered with water to the consistence of thin cream, and laid on the skins by means of a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRUSH">brush</a>. The liquor employed for preserving the fur is prepared by infusing an ounce of white soap shred very small, two ounces of camphire broken into very small pieces, the same of colocynth or bitter-apple grossly powdered, in two English pints of spirit of wine, for four or five days, shaking the vessel from time to time, after which the liquor is to be filtered through blotting-<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>. M. Nicolas has given directions for preparing and preserving specimens of all the various classes of animals. We shall, as far as our limits permit, briefly follow him through each. In skinning <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a>, he proposes to make an incision along the middle of the back, from the haunches to the shoulders, except in those animals whose skin is very thick and hard, or is set with spines, in which the opening must be made at the belly in the usual manner. In detaching the skin from the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, we must occasionally employ the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a>, and as we proceed, must insert tow between the skin and flesh, to prevent soiling the fur. When the whole body is detached, and the skin drawn down as far as the ankles, the nose, and the tip of the tail, the whole body is to be cut away except the head and extremities, which are left to give a better form and support to the specimen. All the fleshy and fatty parts, the brain, and the eyes, however, must be cut away, and nothing left but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a>, the spaces between which and the skin must be stuffed with tow cut fine, and a little soft clay must be put within the orbits, in order to fix the artificial eyes. Before stuffing, the skin is to be steeped for several days, from five to fifteen, according to the size of the animal, in the liquor first described, and after steeping, the inside is to be well anointed with the pomatum. When the legs and head are stuffed, the cavity of the skull filled with very dry moss, and the eyes fixed, wires are to be passed through the inside of the body, the extremities, and the head and tail, in the following manner. Three <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> wires of a moderate size, well annealed, at least twice as <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> as the animal, are to be twisted together for nearly half the length, and while one wire is left straight, the other two are to be bent at each end, so as to form a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>. When the skin is turned, ready for stuffing, these wires are to be placed within it in such a manner as that the straight wire shall <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through the head and tail, and the crossing wires through the extremities, coming out at the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a> of each foot; and in this way after the cavity is filled up with tow, and the open part neatly stitched, the specimen may be fixed on a board in its natural position. Nothing remains now but to impregnate the fur with the bitter liquor last described, which is done by means of a sponge, with which the whole outside is to be well washed, then covered with folds of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, and dried in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a>.
