And this its doctrine is agreeable not only to the sentiments of many of the wisest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, particularly Cicero, who holds, That sum cuique incommunum ferendum est, potius quam de alterius commodis detrahendum; but also to the Jewish law, as certified by King <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a> himself: "If a thief steal to satisfy his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> when he is hungry, he shall restore sevenfold, and shall give all the substance of his house;" which was the ordinary punishment for theft in that kingdom. And this is founded upon the highest reason: for men's properties would be under a strange insecurity, if liable to be invaded according to the wants of others; of which wants no man can possibly be an adequate judge but the party himself who pleads them. In England especially, there would be a peculiar impropriety in admitting so dubious an abuse: for by the laws such sufficient provision is made for the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> by the power of the civil <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGISTRATE">magistrate</a>, that it is impossible that the most needy stranger should ever be reduced to the necessity of thieving to support nature. The case of a stranger is, by the way, the strongest instance put to Baron Puffendorf, and whereon he builds his principal arguments: which, however they may hold upon the continent, where the parsimonious industry of the natives orders every one to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> or starve, yet must lose all their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> and efficacy in England, where <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> is reduced to a system, and interwoven in our very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>. Therefore our laws ought by no means to be taxed with being unmerciful, for denying this privilege to the necessitous; especially when we consider, that the king, on the representation of his ministers of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, hath a power to soften the law, and to extend mercy in cases of peculiar hardship. An advantage which is wanting in many states, particularly those which are democratical: and these have in its stead introduced and adopted, in the body of the law itself, a multitude of circumstances tending to Necessity alleviate its rigour. But the founders of our constitution thought it better to vest in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> the power of pardoning particular objects of compassion, than to countenance and establish theft by one general undistinguishing law.

NECHO

Pages 820-820
king of Egypt, began his reign 690 B.C. and was killed eight years after by Sabacon king of Ethiopia. Psammiticus his son succeeded him, and was the father, as Herodotus informs us, of Necho II., who reigned in the 616 B.C. This Necho II. is celebrated in history for attempting, though in vain, to cut a canal from the Nile to the Arabian gulf. He carried his arms as far as the Euphrates, and conquered the city of Carchemish. This prince is not only known in Scripture under the name of Necho, but also in profane history. He no sooner succeeded to the crown than he raised great land armies, and fitted out vast fleets, as well upon the Mediterranean as upon the s="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red sea: he gave battle to the Syrians near the city of Migdol; routed them, and made himself master of the city of Cadytis. The learned, however, are not agreed about this city Cadytis. Some will have it to be Cades in Arabia Petraea, others Jerusalem; and others say it is the city of Cedes, or Kedesb, in Galilee, in the tribe of Naphtali. The Scriptures acquaint us with the whole expedition of Necho in all its particulars, 2 Kings xxiii. 29. &c. and 2 Chr. xxxv. 20, 21, &c. In the year of the world 3394, this prince having drawn out his army into the field to make war with the Assyrians or Babylonians, and to take the city of Carchemish, otherwise called Circumcision, upon the Euphrates, Josiah king of Judah, who was a tributary to the king of Babylon, marched to oppose his passage. Necho, who had no designs against him, sent to tell him, "What have I to do with you, king of Judah? It is not against you that I am come forth, but against another people, against whom the Lord has commanded me to make war. Leave off therefore to set yourself against me, for fear the Lord should punish you for your resistance." But Josiah would not hearken to the remonstrances of Necho, but gave him battle at Megiddo, where he received the wound of which he died. The people of Jerusalem set up Jehoahaz for king of Judah, and Necho soon passed forward, without making any longer stay in Juden. But at his return from his expedition, which was very successful, he halted at Riblah in Syria; and sending for Jehoahaz king of the Jews, he deposed him, loaded him with chains, and sent him into Egypt. Then coming to Jerusalem, he set up Elia-kim, or Jehoiakim, in his place, and exacted the payment of 100 talents of silver and one talent of gold from the country. Jeremiah (xlvi. 2.) acquaints us that the city of Carchemish was taken from Necho by Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, in the fourth year of Jehoiakim king of Judah; so that Necho did not enjoy his conquest above four years. Josephus adds, that the king of Babylon pursuing his victory, brought under his dominion all the country which is between the Euphrates and Egypt, excepting Juden. Thus Necho was again reduced within the limits of his own country.

NECROLOGY

Pages 820-821

necrologium, formed of νεκρός, "dead," and λόγος, "discourse <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> enumeration," a book anciently kept in churches and monasteries, wherein were registered the benefactors of the same, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of their deaths, and the days of their commemoration; as also the deaths of the priors, abbots, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a>, canons, &c. This was otherwise called <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-CALENDAR">calendar</a> and obituary.

NECROMANCY

Pages 821-823

the art of revealing future events by a pretended <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with the dead. This superstitious and impious imposture appears to have had its origin at a very early <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, and to have been thence propagated in every <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> with the manners of which <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> has made us acquainted. The conquests of Sesostris might introduce it into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIA">India</a>; the Israelites would naturally borrow it from the people among whom they sojourned 400 years; and it would easily find its way into Phoenicia, from the vicinity of that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> of its <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-NATIVITY">nativity</a>. From the Egyptians and Phoenicians it was adopted, with the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> of paganism, by the Greeks; and it was imported into Rome with Grecian literature and Grecian manners. It was not however confined to the pagan nations of antiquity; it spread itself through all the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> nations of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and took such deep root as to be <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> retained even after those nations were converted to the Christian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>. Of its early antiquity we have complete <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> in the writings of Moses, where it is severely condemned as an abomination to the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>; and though it appears to have been even then spread into Phoenicia, we might yet conclude its birthplace to have been Egypt, because, at their exodus, the Israelites were corrupted only by Egyptian superstitions, and because necromancy seems to be one of those whoredoms which the prophet <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EZEKIEL">Ezekiel</a> represents his countrymen as having brought with them from Egypt, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to practise till they were carried captives into <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BABYLON">Babylon</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> from sacred we proceed to consult profane authors, we shall find them not only affirming Egypt to have been the birthplace of necromancy, but in some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> accounting for the origin of so impious a delusion. From Diodorus the Sicilian† we learn that the Grecian <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARON">Charon</a> the ferryman of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELL">hell</a>, of Styx, Coetus, the Elysian Fields, Tartarus, the judgment of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOS">Minos</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHADAMANTHUS">Rhadamanthus</a>, &c. with the whole scenery of the infernal regions, were imported from Egypt into <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Egyptians, and indeed all the people of the east, made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of caves for burying places, which were well suited to the solemn sadness of the surviving friends, and proper receptacles for those who were never more to behold the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>. In Egypt, many of those subterraneous cavities being dug out of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> rock, still remain, and command the admiration of travellers; and near to the pyramids in particular there are some apartments of a wonderful fabric, which though they extend in length 4400 feet, and are about 30 feet in depth, appear to have been, if not entirely dug, at least reduced to form by the chissel <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> pickaxe of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a>. From the practice of burying in such caverns sprung the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that the infernal mansions were situated somewhere near the centre of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, which by the Egyptians was believed to be not very distant from its surface‡. In these dreary mansions, it was very easy for such adepts as the priests of Egypt to fabricate <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EREBUS">Erebus</a>, Tartarus, the Elysian Fields, and all those scenes which were displayed before the initiated (see <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">Mysteries</a>), and by them described to the million of the people. As it was in those dark abodes that necromancy was practised, it would be no difficult <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> for such magicians as withstood Moses to impose so far upon the credulous vulgar, as to make them believe, that in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of their invocations they actually <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> the ghosts of their friends ascend out of the earth. It appears from the book of Exodus, that the Israelitish women were, even in the wilderness, well acquainted with the use of the mirror, which was therefore undoubtedly known to the Egyptians. But a mirror of a particular form and properly illuminated at the instant required, might be easily made to reflect, in a cavern from which all other light was carefully excluded, the image of the deceased, who was called upon by the necromancer; and we can readily conceive, that with respect to the question to be proposed, a person might be concealed, prepared to give such ambiguous answers as would satisfy the inquirer, and at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> of the oracle. The terrified imaginations of the spectators would aid the delusion, and make a very slight resemblance <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> for the ghost or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a> of their departed friend; or the necromancer might assign plausible reasons why a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SPECTRE">spectre</a>, after having dwelt for some time in the infernal regions, should lose something of its resemblance to the body which it animated. Such juggling tricks, though performed by artists less accomplished than Jannes and Jambres, have gained credit among people much more enlightened than the Egyptians can possibly have been when the science of necromancy was invented by their priests. That the Israelites, notwithstanding the prohibition of their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEGISLATOR">legislator</a>, continued to practise the rites of necromancy, is apparent from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAUL">Saul</a>'s transaction with the witch of Endor (see <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGIC">Magic</a>). From the same transaction, it is likewise apparent that the witches of Israel, and therefore in all <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> the necromancers of Egypt, pretended to evocate the ghosts of the dead by a demon or familiar spirit, which they had at their command to employ upon every emergency. This demon was called on; and therefore Saul desires his servants to find him a woman who was mistress of an ob (a). (a) The original, or radical, signification of this word occurs, in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOB">Job</a> xxxii. ver. 19.; where Elihu compares his belly to new bottles, which he calls oboth, the plural of ob. But as bottles were then made of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, new bottles filled with wine and ready to burst, as Elihu describes them, would of course be of a form nearly globular. It is probable that those wretched impostors had in their pay some persons who occasionally acted the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the demon, and when the execution of the plot required their agency, emitted, by means of a cavity dug for that purpose, a low hollow <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> from below the ground. Hence we find Isaiah, in his denunciations against Ariel*, saying, "Thou shalt be brought <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, and shalt speak out of the ground; and thy speech shall be low out of the dust, and thy voice shall be as of one that hath a familiar spirit (an ob) out of the ground, and thy speech shall whisper out of the dust." But though the Egyptian priests were undoubtedly the inventors of the whole mystery of necromancy, and though it was from them imported into Greece by the Selli or priests of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DODONA">Dodona</a>, it does not appear that the Grecian necromancers pretended to be masters of obs or familiar spirits. <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOPSUS">Mopsus</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORPHEUS">Orpheus</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINUS">Linus</a>, Eumolpus, &c. who either travelled into Egypt in quest of knowledge, or were actually natives of that country, instructed the early Greeks in this <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OCCULT">occult</a> science: but whatever might be the practice of these apostles themselves, their disciples professed to do all the feats of magic by performing certain rites, by offering certain sacrifices, by muttering a certain form of words, by charms, spells, and exorcisms. By these they pretended to evoke the dead as certainly as the Egyptians and Jews did by their familiar spirits. By a small display of critical learning this might be easily proved from the popular story of Orpheus and Eurydice, which certainly was founded on one of these necromantic deceptions exhibited in a cave near Dodona, where the priests had a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HADES">hades</a> or infernal mansion, in humble <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of those with which the first of them were well acquainted in Egypt. It is indeed evident, without the aid of criticism: no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of any letters is ignorant, that whatever superstitions of this kind prevailed among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> were borrowed from the Greeks. But we all know that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a> makes one of his shepherds, by means of certain herbs, poisons, and senseless charms, raise up ghosts from the bottoms of their graves; and Lucian has fabricated a story of this kind, which may be considered as an exact <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to the witch of Endor. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">Just</a> before the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHARSALIA">Pharsalia</a> he makes young Pompey travel by night to a Thessalian sorceress, and anxiously inquire of her the issue of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> necromancer, by a tedious <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of charms and incantations, conjures up the ghost of a soldier who had been lately slain. The phantom, after a long preamble, denounces a prediction much of the same kind with that which the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Israel received from Samuel at Endor; and though we have elsewhere shown, that nothing but the spirit of God could have foreseen the inevitable destruction of Saul, his sons, and his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, (see Necromancy.) Magic), it was very easy for any man of tolerable sagacity to foresee the defeat of Pompey's raw and undisciplined troops by the hardy veterans of the victorious Caesar. It would be endless to enumerate all the fallacious evocations of ghosts, and the ambiguous responses returned by those pretended spirits, of which we have accounts from the poets and historians of the celebrated nations of antiquity. We shall therefore proceed to mention a few which occur in the fabulous history of more modern nations, and then leave the subject to the meditation of our readers. In <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALLET">Mallet</a>'s Northern Antiquities, we have the following account of a necromantic exploit, between which, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> of the ancient heroes into hell, it is impossible not to remark a striking similitude. "Odin the sovereign of man arises. He saddles his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> Sleipner; he mounts, and is conveyed to the subterraneous abode of Hela. The dog which guards the gates of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> meets him. His <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAST">breast</a> and his jaws are stained with blood. He opens his voracious mouth to bite, and barks a long time at the father of magic. Odin pursues his way; and the infernal cavern resounds and trembles under his horse's hoofs. At length he reaches the deep abode of death, and stops near the eastern gate, where stands the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> of the prophetess. He sings with a voice adapted to call up the dead; he looks towards the world; he engraves Runic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> on her tomb; he utters mysterious words; and he demands an answer, until the prophetess is constrained to arise and thus utter the words of the dead.—Who is this unknown that <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DARES">dares</a> to disturb my repose, and drag me from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a>, in which I have been dead so long, all covered with snow, and moistened with the rains?" &c. The Gaelic <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRUIDS">druids</a> pretended to be masters of the same secret. This is evident from the name of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVINATION">divination</a>, not uncommon among the Scotch Highlanders so lately as in the beginning of the 18th century. By a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> excellently versed in the antiquities of that people, and a steady friend to the writer of this article, we have been informed, that not many years ago some of the Highlanders relied implicitly upon certain oracular responses, called in their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> toghairm. This word seems to be compounded of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TA">ta</a>, which in some parts of the Highlands is still used to denote a spirit or ghost, and gluirn, which signifies calling upon or invoking. Toghairm, therefore, in its original import, is necromancy in the most proper <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of that word. There were different kinds of toghairm, of which one was very lately practised in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SKYE">Skye</a>. The diviner covered himself with a cow's hide, and repaired at night to some deep-sounding cave, whither the person who consulted lar. Hence it may be inferred that the original import of ob was round or globular: but b and p being labials, are often changed into each other; and therefore, from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> ob is derived the Greek ob, oculus, oculus, video, and the Latin ops, a name under which the earth was worshipped. Upis was a name of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIANA">Diana</a> or the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>: the father of one of the Dianas was likewise Upis; but this Upis was undoubtedly the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>. Now the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between upis and opis is nothing; hence we are led to believe, that as they are all derived from ob, this word was employed by the early idolaters of Egypt to denote the first and greatest of Pagan gods, the sun. If so, those wretches who pretended to be mistresses of obs, were exactly the same kind of impostors with the Pythoneses of the Greeks. At the mouth of the cave he proposed aloud the questions of which he wanted solutions; and the man within pronounced the responses in a tone of voice similar to that with which the ons, or pretended demons of antiquity, gave from beneath the ground their oracular answers. That in the latter days of toghairm, the Gaelic diviners pretend to evocate ghosts, and from them to extort solutions of difficulties proposed, we have no positive evidence; but that such was the original pretence there can be little doubt, when we reflect either upon the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where this species of divination was practised, or upon the import of the word by which it was denominated. As we have been led to mention toghairm, we shall beg leave to make a few observations on another species of it, called toghairm an uisce, or "toghairm by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>." This too was last practised in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of Skye, by a man of the name of McCuillean, whose <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> had long been famous for the art. He lived near a beautiful cascade on a small river; and when consulted on any matter of consequence, he covered his whole body with a cow's hide, that necessary implement of Highland divination, and placed himself between the water of the cascade and the rock over which it flowed. Then another man with a heavy pole gave repeated strokes to the water, and the diviner behind it crying out now and then in Gaelic, "Is this a stock o' arm?" This operation was continued till McCuildean was perceived to be frantic or furious, when he was considered as in a condition to answer the most important questions. He was frequently consulted about futurity; and though he could not, in the proper sense of the word, be called a necromancer; his responses were listened to as proceeding from something more than <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a>. A degree of frenzy, either real or affected, seems to have accompanied the predictions of certain kinds of diviners in all ages; and we cannot help remarking the similarity between the madness of McCuildean and that of the Sibyl in the sixth book of the Aeneid; though we cannot suppose the one to have been borrowed from the other. That all these pretences, whether ancient or modern, to the power of divination by means of familiar spirits, or by the art of necromancy, were groundless as well as impious, it would be affronting the understandings of our readers to offer any <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>. Under the article MAGIC we have said enough on the subject, and perhaps more than enough, to those who know that demons, if they have any existence, and the departed spirits of good and bad men, are all under the control of Him who governs the intellectual as well as material world by fixed and equal laws.—These details of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>, however, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> not be useless, if, by showing how <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> and wretched a creature man becomes when left to his own inventions, they shall make any one grateful for the benefits of good <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, and the blessings of revealed <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>.

NECROPOLIS

Pages 823-823

a suburb of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>. It signifies "the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">City</a> of the Dead;" wherein there were <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, gardens, and superb mausoleums. Here Cleopatra is said to have applied the aspic to her <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, to prevent being led in triumph by Augustus, who endeavoured to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> her.

NECROSIS

Pages 823-823

necrosis, in Medicine, a complete mortification of any <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>; called also sideratio and sphacelus.

NECTANEBUS

Pages 823-823
or NECTANABIS, a king of Egypt, who defended his country against the Persians. His grandson of the same name made an alliance with Agesilaus king of Sparta, and with his assistance he quelled a rebellion of his subjects. Some time after he was joined by the Sidonians, Phoenicians, and inhabitants of Cyprus, who had revolted from the king of Persia. This powerful confederacy was soon attacked by Darius the king of Persia, who marched at the head of his troops. Nectanebus, to defend his frontiers against so dangerous an enemy, levied 20,000 mercenary soldiers in Greece, the same number in Libya, and 60,000 were furnished in Egypt. This numerous body was not equal to the Persian forces, and Nectanebus, defeated in a battle, gave up all hopes of resistance, and fled into Ethiopia, where he found a safe asylum. His kingdom of Egypt became from that time tributary to the king of Persia.

NECTAR

Pages 823-823

among <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> poets, the drink of the fabulous deities of the heathens; in contradistinction from their <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> food, which was called ambrosia.

NECTARINE

Pages 823-823

a fruit differing in nothing from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> peach, of which it is a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, but in having a smoother rind and a firmer pulp. See PERSICA.

NECTARIUM

Pages 823-824

from <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECTAR">nectar</a>, the fabled "drink of the gods," defined by Linnæus to be a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the corolla, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> appendage to the petals, appropriated for containing the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of vegetable <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> under a fluid form, that oozes from the plant, and is the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> food of bees and other insects. Notwithstanding this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a>, which seems to consider the nectarium as necessary a part of the corolla as the petals, it is certain that all <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> are not provided with this appendage, neither indeed is it essential to fructification. There is, besides, a manifest impropriety in terming the nectarium a part of the corolla. Linnæus might, Milne's Bot. Diet. with equal propriety, have termed it a part or appendage of the stamens, calyx, or pointal, as the appearance in question is confined to no particular part of the flower, but is as various in point of situation as of form. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> is, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> nectarium is exceedingly vague; and, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any determinate meaning can be affixed to it, is expressive of all the singularities which are observed in the different parts of flowers. The tube, or lower part of flowers with one petal, Linnæus considers as a true nectarium, because it is generally found to contain the sweet liquor formerly mentioned. This liquor Pontedera compares to that called amnios in pregnant animals, which enters the fertile or impregnated seeds; but that this is not at least Nectarium, least its sole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, is evident from this circumstance, that the honey or liquor in question is to be found in flowers where there are either no seeds, or those which, from the want of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> organs, cannot be impregnated. Thus the male flowers of nettle and willow, the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> flowers of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-side laurel and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> bryony, the male and female flowers of clutia, kiggelaria, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BUTCHER">butcher</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROOM">broom</a>, all abound with the honey or nectar alluded to. Vaillant was of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that the nectarium was an essential part of the corolla; for which reason he distinguished the singular appearances in fennel flower and columbine by the name of petals: the coloured leaves which are now termed the petals he denominates the flower cup. That the nectarium, however, is frequently distinct from the petals, is evident both from the well known examples <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> mentioned, as likewise from the flowers of monkshood, hellebore, isopyrum, fennel flower of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>, barreuwort, grass of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARNASSUS">Parnassus</a>, chocolate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NUT">nut</a>, cherleria, and sauvagesia. These general observations being premised, we proceed to take a nearer and more particular view of the principal diversities, both in form and situation, of this striking appendage to the flower. 1. In many flowers the nectarium is shaped like a spur or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORN">horn</a>; and that either in flowers of one petal, as valerian, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> milfoil (utricularia), butterwort, and calves-snout; or in such as have more than one, as larkspur, violet, fumitory, balsam, and orchis. 2. In the following <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, the nectarium is properly a part of the corolla, as lying within the substance of the petals: ranunculus, lily, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRIS">iris</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> imperial, water <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a>, mouse tail, ananas, or pine apple, dog's-tooth violet, pipe-ridge bush, vallisneria, hermannia, uvularia, and swertia. 3. The nectarium is frequently placed in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> or row within the petals, though entirely unconnected with their substance. In this situation it often resembles a cup, as in narcissus. A nectarium of this kind is said by Linnæus to crown the corolla. The following are examples: daffodil, sea daffodil, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAMPION">campion</a>, viscous cam- pion, swallow-wort, stapeia, cynanchum, nepenthes, cherleria, balsam-tree, African spiraea, witch-hazel, olax, and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>-flower. 4. In <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a>-cress, buckler, mus- tard, Barbados cherry, and monotropa, the nectarium is situated upon or makes part of the calyx. 5. The nectarium in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BASTARD">bastard</a> flower-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FENCE">fence</a> is seated upon the anthera or tops of the stamens; whence the name adenanthera, or glandular anthera, which has been given to this genus of plants. In the following <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIST">list</a> it is placed upon the filaments: bean-caper, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, fraxinella, marvel of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERU">Peru</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELL">bell</a>-flower, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>-wort, roella, and commelina. 6. In hyacinth, flowering-rush, stock <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> flower, and rocket, the nectarium is placed upon the seed-bud. 7. In honey-flower, orpine, buckwheat, collinsonia, la- threa, navelwort, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a>, clutia, kiggelaria, sea-side laurel, and African spiraea, it is attached to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> receptacle. Lastly, in ginger, nettle, dyer's weed, heart seed, costus, turmeric, grewia, bastard orpine, va- nelloa, show-tree, and willow, the nectarium is of a very singular <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a>, and cannot properly <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> under any of the foregoing heads. In discriminating the genera, the nectarium often furnishes an essential character. Plants which have the nectarium distinct from the petals, that is, not lodged within their substance, are Nectarium afflamed by Linnæus to be generally poisonous. The following are adduced as examples: monkshood, hel- bore, cumbine, fennel-flower, grass of Parnassus, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a>- ren-wort, oleander, marvel of Peru, bean-caper, succu- <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LENT">lent</a> swallow-wort, fraxinella, and honey-flower.

NECUIA

Pages 824-824

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, a name given by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Greeks to a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of mullein. The Greeks and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> both used the stalks of a peculiar kind of mullein, called thyrsalis by Nicander, for the making of wicks of lamps. We have a kind of mullein called tychnites, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a>-wick mullein, from the ἀγρόποιος of Dioscorides; but it is not certain that ours is the same plant. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> used the stalks of many different <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> for the wicks of their candles and lamps. The rush, stripped of its bark, was as <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> with them as with us for that purpose; and they also used the nettle, this mullein, and many other plants, whose stalks were composed of tough filaments, for the same purpose; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> them out like <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>, and when dry <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIPPING">dipping</a> them in melted resin, and other such inflammable substances. When thus prepared, they are readily inflammable, like our <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAMBEAU">flambeau</a>; and this mullein, having stalks more <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, and more firm than all the others, was used to make those lights with which they set fire to the funeral pile, for consuming the ashes of their dead friends.

NECYDALIS

Pages 824-824

a genus of insects belonging to the order of coleoptera. See Entomology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

NEE EXEAT REGNO

Pages 827-827

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is a writ to restrain a person from going out of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> without the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>'s license. F. N. B. 85. It may be directed to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a>, to make the party find surety that he <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> not depart the realm, and on refusal to commit him to prison: <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> it may be directed to the party himself; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he then goes, he may be fined. And this writ is granted on a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> being commenced against a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CHANCERY">chancery</a>, when the plaintiff fears the defendant will fly to some other <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; and thereby avoid the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EQUITY">equity</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>; which hath been sometimes practised: and when thus granted, the party must give bonds to the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the rolls, in the penalty of 100l. or some other <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> sum, for yielding obedience to it: or satisfy the court, by answer, affidavit, or otherwise, that he hath no <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of leaving the kingdom, and give security. NEFASTI dies, in Roman antiquity, an appellation given to those days wherein it was not allowed to administer justice, or hold courts. They were so called because non fuit licebat, the praetor was not allowed to pronounce the three solemn words or formulas of the law, do, dico, addico, I give, I appoint, I adjudge. These days were distinguished in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-CALENDAR">calendar</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> N. for nefastus; or N. P. Nefastus Primo, when the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> was only nefastus in the forenoon, or first <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>. The days of a mixed kind were called intercisi.

NEEDHAM

Pages 824-827

John Tuberville, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> the 10th of September in the year 1713. His parents were descended from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and noble families. His father, who had once possessed a considerable patrimony at Hilton, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Monmouth, was of the younger and Catholic branch of the Needham family: the head of the elder and Protestant branch was <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Kilmory, created viscount in the year 1625. The father of Mr Needham died young, and left but a small fortune to his four children. His eldest son, who is the subject of this article, prosecuted his studies under the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a> clergy of the English <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOUAY">Douay</a>, where he took orders, taught <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a> for several years, gave eminent proofs of sagacity and genius, and surpassed all the other professors of that seminary in the knowledge of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIMENTAL_PHILOSOPHY">experimental <a class="</a>xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>. In 1740, he was engaged by his superiors in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the English mission, and was entrusted with the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the school erected at Twyford, near <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WINCHESTER">Winchester</a>, for the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> of the Roman Catholic youth. In 1744, he was appointed professor of philosophy in the English college at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LISBON">Lisbon</a>, where, on account of his bad <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, he remained only 15 months. After his return, he passed several years at London and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, which were principally employed in microscopical observations, and in other branches of experimental philosophy. The results of these observations and experiments were published in the Philosophical Transactions of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> of London in 1749, and in a volume in 12mo at Paris in 1750; and an account of them was also given by M. de Buffon, in the first volumes of his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>. There was an intimate connexion between this illustrious French naturalist and Mr Needham: they made their experiments and observations together; Needham, gether; though the results and systems which they deduced from the same objects and operations were totally different. Mr Needham was admitted to a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in the Royal Society of London in the year 1747, and in the Antiquarian Society some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> after. From the year 1751 to 1767 he was chiefly employed in finishing the education of several English and Irish noblemen, by attending them as <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> in their travels through France, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and other countries. He then retired from this wandering <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> to the English seminary at Paris, and in 1768 was chosen by the Royal Academy of Sciences in that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> a corresponding member. When the regency of the Austrian <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, in order to the revival of philosophy and literature in that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> formed the project of an Imperial academy, which was preceded by the erection of a small literary society to prepare the way for its execution, Mr Needham was invited to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRUSSELS">Brussels</a> by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> Cobentzel and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> Ney, and was appointed successively <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a> of both these foundations. He held this place, together with some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> preferments in the Low Countries, until his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, which happened the 30th of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1781. "His piety, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEMPERANCE">temperance</a>, and purity of manners (we follow the expressions of the abbe Mann) were eminent; his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to the doctrines and duties of Christianity was inviolable. His zealous opposition to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> infidels was indefatigable, and even passionate. His probity was untainted. He was incapable of every <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of duplicity; his beneficence was universal, and his unsuspicious candour rendered him often a dupe to perfidy." These and other good qualities the panegyrist attributes to his deceased friend; and the learned authors of the Monthly Review, to whom Mr Needham was known, admit the justness of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PANEGYRIC">panegyric</a>. He was undoubtedly (say they), both an honest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> and a worthy citizen; but though his death be a real loss to the literary world, yet he died seasonably for himself; for had he lived to see <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> II. and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> making so free with the paint, patches, and trinkets of the mother <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, confiscating her lands, abolishing her <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a>, suppressing her holidays, introducing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> into her worship, erecting <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> conductors to disperse the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a> of the Vatican, and achieving many other things in this style of improvement, it would have vexed full sore his feeling heart. For this honest man was narrow even to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a> and bigotry in his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> system; and we never knew a man in whom there was such an unaccountable mixture of implicit <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> and philosophical curiosity as in Mr Needham. He was a keen and judicious observer of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, had a peculiar dexterity in confirming his observations by experiments, and he was always occupied (sometimes indeed with too much fancy and precipitation) in generalizing facts, and reducing them to his system. "His <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEN">pen</a> (says Abbe Mann) was neither remarkable for fecundity nor method: his writings are rather the great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of a subject expressed with energy, and thrown upon <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> in a hurry, than finished treatises." His works are well known both in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> and in France. Needham, a town in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a>, 73 miles from London, stands on the Orwell, 9 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IPSWICH">Ipswich</a>. Its <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> in 1811 was 1301. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">Needle</a>, a very common little <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> utensil made of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>, pointed at one end, and pierced at the other, used in sewing, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMBROIDERY">embroidery</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TAPESTRY">tapestry</a>, &c. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEEDLES">Needles</a> make a very considerable article in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, though there is scarce any commodity cheaper, the consumption of them being almost incredible.—The sizes are from No. 1, the largest, to No. 25, the smallest. In the manufacture of needles, German and Hungarian steel is of most repute. In the making of them, the first thing is to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> the steel through a coal fire, and under a hammer, to bring it out of its <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> into a cylindrical one. This done, it is drawn through a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> hole of a wire-<a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, and returned into the fire, and drawn through a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> hole of the iron smaller than the first; and thus successively from hole to hole, till it has acquired the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of fineness required for that species of needles; observing every time it is to be drawn, that it be greased over with <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-LARD">lard</a>, to render it more manageable. The steel, thus reduced to a fine wire, is cut in pieces of the length of the needles intended. These pieces are flattened at one end on the anvil, in order to form the head and eye: they are then put into the fire to soften them farther; and thence taken out and pierced at each <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> of the flat <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> on the anvil, by force of a pincerson of well-tempered steel, and laid on a leaden <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLOCK">block</a> to bring out, with another pincerson, the little piece of steel remaining in the eye. The corners are then filed off the square of the heads, and a little cavity filed on each side of the flat of the head; this done, the point is formed with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FILE">file</a>, and the whole filed over: they are then laid to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> hot on a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> narrow iron, crooked at one end, in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARCOAL">charcoal</a> fire; and when taken out thence, are thrown into a basin of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> to harden. On this operation a good <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> depends; too much heat burns them, and too little leaves them soft; the medium is learned by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>. When they are thus hardened, they are laid in an iron shovel, on a fire more or less brisk in proportion to the thickness of the needles; taking care to move them from time to time. This serves to temper them, and take off their brittleness; great care here too must be taken of the degree of heat. They are then straightened one after another with the hammer, the coldness of the water used in hardening them, having twisted the greatest part of them. The next <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> is the polishing them. To do this, they take 12,000 or 15,000 needles, and range them in little heaps against each other on a piece of new buckram sprinkled with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMERY">emery</a> dust. The needles thus disposed, emery dust is thrown over them, which is again sprinkled with <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> of olives; at last the whole is made up into a roll, well bound at both ends. This roll is then laid on a polishing <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, and over it a thick plank loaded with <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, which two men <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> backwards and forwards a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> and a half, or two days, successively; by which means the roll thus continually agitated by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the plank over it, the needles withinside being rubbed against each other with oil and emery, are insensibly polished. After polishing they are taken out, and the fifth washed off them with hot water and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOAP">soap</a>; they are then wiped in hot bran, a little moistened, placed with the needles in a round box, suspended in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CORD">cord</a>, which is kept stirring till the bran and needles be dry. The needles thus wiped in two or three different brans, Needle are taken out and put in wooden vessels, to have the good separated from those whose <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> or eyes have been broken either in polishing or wiping; the points are then all turned the same way, and smoothed with an emery <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> turned with a wheel. This operation finishes them, and there remains nothing but to make them into packets of 250 each. Needles were first made in England by a native of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, in 1545, but the art was lost at his death; it was, however, recovered by Christopher Greening in 1560, who was settled with his three children, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> John, and Thomas, by Mr Damar, ancestor of the present Lord <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILTON">Milton</a>, at Long Crendon in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BUCKS">Bucks</a>, where the manufactory has been carried on from that time to the present day. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIPPING">Dipping</a> Needle, or Inclinatory Needle, a magnetic needle, so hung, as that, instead of playing horizontally, and pointing out <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> and south, one end dips, or inclines to the horizon, and the other points to a certain degree of elevation above it. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIPPING_NEEDLE">dipping-needle</a> was invented in the year 1576, by one Robert Norman, a compass-maker at Wapping. The occasion of the discovery, according to his own account, was, that it being his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> to finish and hang the needles of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPASSES">compasses</a> before he touched them, he always found, that immediately after the touch, the north-point would <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a> or incline downward, under the horizon; insomuch that, to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a> the needle again, he was always forced to put a piece of wax on the south end as a counterpoise. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTANCY">constancy</a> of this effect led him at length to observe the precise <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of the dip, or to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> which the needle would make with the horizon; and this at London he found to be $7^\circ 52'$. In 1723 Mr Graham made a great many observations on the dipping-needle, and found the angle to be between $74$ and $75$ degrees. Mr Nairn, in 1772 found it to be somewhat above $72^\circ$. It is not certain whether the dip varies, as well as the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> direction, in the same place. The trifling <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between Mr Norman and Mr Nairne would <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> us to imagine that the dip was unalterable; but Mr Graham, who was a very accurate observer, makes the difference more considerable. It is certain, however, from a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of experiments and observations that the dip is variable in different latitudes, and that it increases in going northwards. It appears from a table of observations made with the marine dipping-needle in a voyage towards the north pole in 1733, that in lat. $60^\circ 18'$ the dip was $75^\circ$; and in lat. $70^\circ 45'$ it was $77^\circ 52'$; in lat. $80^\circ 12'$ it was $81^\circ 52'$; and in lat. $80^\circ 27'$ it was $82^\circ 2'$. Several authors have endeavoured to apply this discovery of the dip to the finding of the latitude; and Mr Bond attempted to apply it to the finding of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a> also; but for want of observations and experiments he could not make any progress. The affair was farther prosecuted by Mr Whiston, who published a treatise on the longitude, and for some time imagined it was possible to find it exactly by means of the dip of the needle: yet he at last despaired of it, for the following reasons; 1. The weakness of the magnetic power. 2. The concussion of the ship, which he found it exceedingly difficult to avoid so much as was necessary for the accuracy of the experiments. 3. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> objection was an irregularity in the motions of all magnetic needles, both horizontal and dipping, by which they, within the compass of about a degree, vary uncertainly backward and forward; even sometimes in a few hours time, without any evident cause. For a particular account of these variations, both of the horizontal and dipping needle, see the article <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VARIATION">Variation</a>. Mr Nairne made a dipping needle in 1772 for the Board of Longitude, which was used in the voyage towards the north pole. This is represented at fig. 2, Fig. 2. The needle <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AA">AA</a> is 12 inches long, and its axis, the ends BB of which are made of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, alloyed with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, rests on friction <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a> CCCC, of four inches diameter, each end on two friction wheels; which wheels are balanced with great care. The ends of the axis of the friction wheels are likewise of gold alloyed with copper, and moved in small holes made in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELL">bell</a> metal; and opposite to the ends of the axes of the needle and the friction wheels, are flat agates, set at DDD, finely polished. The magnetic needle vibrates within a circle of bell metal, EEEE, divided into degrees and half degrees; and a line, passing through the middle of the needle to the ends, points to the divisions. The needle of this instrument was balanced before it was made magnetic; but by means of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>, the ends of which are FFFF (contrived by the reverend Mr Mitchell) fixed on the axis of the needle, on the arms of which are cut very fine screws to receive small buttons, that may be screwed nearer or farther from the axis, the needles may be adjusted both ways to a great nicety, after being made magnetic, by reversing the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a>, and changing the sides of the needle. GG are two levels, by which the line of $0$ degrees of the instrument is set horizontal, by means of the four adjusting screws LLLL; H is the perpendicular axis, by which the instrument may be turned, that the divided <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> of the circle may <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a> the east or west; to this axis may be fixed an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">index</a> I, which points to an opposite line on the horizontal plate K when the instrument is turned half round; MMMM are screws which hold the glass cover to keep the needle from being disturbed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>. When this needle is constructed for <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, it is suspended by an universal <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> on a triangular stand, and adjusted vertically by a plumb line and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BUTTON">button</a> above the divided circle and the dovetail work at the upper go; and the divisions on the circle are adjusted so as to be perpendicular to the horizon by the same plumb line, and an adjoining screw; and when it is adjusted, a pointer annexed to a screw, which serves to move the divided circle, is fixed at the lowest go. Whenever the instrument is used to find the dip, it must be so placed that the needle may vibrate exactly in the magnetic meridian. Magnetic Needle, in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">Navigation</a>, a needle touched with a loadstone, and sustained on a pivot or centre; on which playing at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, it directs itself to certain points in or under the horizon; whence the magnetic needle is of two kinds, viz. horizontal or inclinatory. See the article Magnet. Horizontal needles are those equally balanced on each side of the pivot that sustains them, and which, playing horizontally with their two extremes, point out the north and south points of the horizon. For their application and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, see the article Compass. In the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of the horizontal needle, a piece of pure steel is provided; of a length not exceeding six inches, Needles, very thin, to take its verticity the better; and not pierced with any holes, or the like, for ornament sake, which prevent the equable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFUSION">diffusion</a> of the magnetic virtue. A perforation is then made, in the middle of its length, and a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAP">cap</a> or head soldered on, whose inner cavity is conical, so as to play freely on a style or pivot headed with a fine steel point. The north point of the needle in our hemisphere is made a little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> than the southern; the touch always destroying the balance, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> well adjusted before, and rendering the north end heavier than the south, and thus occasioning the needle to dip. The method of giving the needle its verticity or directive <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> has been shown already under the article MAGNET; but if, after touching, the needle be out of its equilibrium, something must be filed off from the heavier side, till it balance evenly. Needles in sea compasses are usually made of a rhomboidal or <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> form; we have given their structure already under the article COMPASS. The needle is not found to point precisely to the north, except in very few places; but deviates from it more or less in different places, and that too at different times; which deviation is called its declination or variation from the meridian. See the article VARIATION. Surgeons Needles are generally made crooked, and their points triangular; however, they are of different forms and sizes, and bear different names, according to the purposes they are used for. The largest are needles for amputation; the next, needles for wounds; the finest, needles for sutures. They have others, very short and flat, for tendons; others, still shorter, and the eye placed in the middle, for tying together of vessels, &c. Needles for couching cataracts are of various kinds; all of which have a small, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, and sharp point or tongue, and some with a sulcus at the point. Surgeons have sometimes used two needles in this operation; one with a sharp point for perforating the coats of the eye, and another with a more obtuse point for depressing or concaving the opaque crystalline <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LENS">lens</a>; but care should be taken in the use of any of these, that they be first well polished with cloth or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, before they are applied to the eye. Mr Warner observes, that the blade of the couching needle should be at least a third part larger than those generally used upon this occasion, as great advantages <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> be found in the depressing of the cataract, by the increased breadth of the blade of that instrument. The handle, also, if made somewhat shorter than usual, will enable the operator to perform with greater steadiness than he can do with a larger handled instrument. It is to be observed, that needles of silver pierce more easily in stitching <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ARTERIES">arteries</a> after an amputation, than those made of steel. Needle Fish. See SYNGNATHUS, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> Index. Needles, sharp pointed rocks north of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of Wight. They are situated at the western extremity of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, which is an acute point of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>, from which they have been disjoined by the washing of the sea. There were of these lofty <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> rocks formerly three, but about 14 years ago the tallest of them, called <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">Lot</a>'s Wife, which rose 120 feet above low water mark, and in its shape resembling a needle, being undermined by the constant efforts of the waves, was thrown <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, and totally disappeared.

NEEDS

Pages 827-827
or St Neots, six miles from Huntingdon, 58 miles from London, so called from the monument of a saint of that name in it, who was burnt by the Danes, is a large well built town, having a handsome strong church, with a very fine steeple, and a stone bridge over the Ouse. Its population in 1811 was 1933. NEEDWOOD forest, in Staffordshire, between the Trent, Dove, and Blythe, and near Uttoxeter, is said to exceed all the forests in England in the excellence of its soil and the fineness of its turf.

NEGAPATAN

Pages 827-827

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> on this side the Ganges, and on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Coromandel. It was first a colony of the Portuguese, but was taken from them by the Dutch, and now forms <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the British territory. It is situated in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 79. 10. N. Lat. 11. 15.

NEGATION

Pages 827-827

in Logic, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of the mind affirming one thing to be different from another; as that the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> is not <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>. See LOGIC.

NEGATIVE

Pages 827-828

in general, something that implies a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEGATION">negation</a>: thus we say, negative quantities, negative powers, negative signs, &c. NEGATIVE Sign. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the negative sign, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALGEBRA">algebra</a>, is attended with several consequences that at first sight are admitted with difficulty, and has sometimes given occasion to notions that seem to have no real foundation. This sign implies, that the real value of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> represented by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to which it is prefixed is to be subtracted; and it serves, with the positive sign, to keep in view what elements <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> parts enter into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of quantities, and in Negative what manner, whether as increments or decrements, (that is, whether by addition or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SUBTRACTION">subtraction</a>), which is of the greatest use in this art. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of this, it serves to express a quantity of an opposite <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> to the positive, as a line in a contrary position; a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> with an opposite <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>; or a centrifugal force in opposition to gravity; and thus often saves the trouble of distinguishing and demonstrating separately, the various <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of proportions, and preserves their <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a> in view. But as the proportions of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> depend on their magnitude only, without regard to their position, and motions and forces are said to be equal or unequal, in any given ratio, without regard to their directions; and, in general, the proportion of quantity relates to their magnitude only, without determining whether they are to be considered as increments or decrements; so there is no ground to imagine any other proportion of $-b$ and $+a$ (or of $-1$ and $1$) than that of the real magnitude of the quantities represented by $b$ and $a$, whether these quantities are, in any particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, to be added or subtracted. It is the same thing to subtract the decrement, as to add an equal increment, or to subtract $-b$ from $a-b$, as to add $+b$ to it: and because multiplying a quantity by a negative <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> implies only a repeated subtraction of it, the multiplying $-b$ by $-n$, is subtracting $-b$ as often as there are units in $n$; and is therefore <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to adding $+b$ so many times, or the same as adding $+nb$. But <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we infer from this, that $1$ is to $-n$ as $-b$ to $nb$, according to the rule, that unit is to one of the factors as the other <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACTOR">factor</a> is to the product, there is no ground to imagine, that there is any mystery in this, or any other meaning than that the real magnitudes represented by $1$, $n$, $b$, and $nb$ are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPORTIONAL">proportional</a>. For that rule relates only to the magnitude of the factors and product, without determining whether any factor, or the product, is to be added or subtracted. But this likewise must be determined in algebraic computations; and this is the proper use of the rules concerning the signs, without which the operation could not proceed. Because a quantity to be subtracted is never produced in composition by any repeated addition of a positive, or repeated subtraction of a negative, a negative <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> number is never produced by composition from the root. Hence $\sqrt{-1}$, or the square root of a negative, implies an imaginary quantity; and in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>, is a mark or character of the impossible cases of a problem, unless it is compensated by another imaginary symbol or supposition, when the whole <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> may have a real signification. Thus $1+\sqrt{-1}$, and $1-\sqrt{-1}$, taken separately, are imaginary, but their sum is $2$; as the conditions that separately would render the solution of a problem impossible, in some cases destroy each others effect when conjoined. In the pursuit of general conclusions, and of simple forms representing them, expressions of this kind must sometimes arise where the imaginary symbol is compensated in a manner that is not always so obvious. By proper substitutions, however, the expression may be transformed into another, wherein each particular <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> may have a real signification as well as the whole expression. The theorems that are sometimes briefly discovered by the use of this symbol, may be demonstrated without it by the inverse operation, or some other way; and though such symbols are of some use in the computations by the method of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLUXIONS">fluxions</a>, its <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> cannot be said to depend upon arts of this kind. See Algebra and Fluxions. NEGATIVE <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTRICITY">Electricity</a>. See the article Electricity, passim. See also Positive Electricity. NEGINOTH. This term is read before some of the Psalms, as Psalm lxvii. It signifies string instruments of music, to be played on by the fingers, or women musicians; and the titles of these Psalms where this word is found, may be thus translated, A psalm of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of music, who presides over the string instruments.

NEGOMBO

Pages 828-828

a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> port town of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, on the west <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Ceylon. It has a fort built by the Portuguese, which was taken from them by the Dutch in 1640. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 80° 25'. N. Lat. 17° 0'.

NEGRO

Pages 828-832

Homo peli nigra, a name given to a variety of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, who are entirely <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, and are found in the torrid zone, especially in that <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> which lies within the tropics. In the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEGROES">Negroes</a>, we meet with many various shades; but they likewise differ far from other men in all the features of their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a>. Round <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHEEKS">cheeks</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> cheek-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a>, a forehead somewhat elevated, a short, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, flat nose, thick lips, small ears, ugliness, and irregularity of shape, characterize their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> appearance. The negro women have the loins greatly depressed, and very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> buttocks, which gives the back the shape of a saddle. Vices the most notorious seem to be the portion of this unhappy <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>; illibleness, treachery, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a>, cruelty, impudence, stealing, lying, profanity, debauchery, nastiness, and intemperance, are said to have extinguished the principles of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>, and to have silenced the reproofs of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a>. They are strangers to every sentiment of compassion, and are an awful example of the corruption of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> when left to himself.
