His last signal ought not, and will not be forgotten, which was by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TELEGRAPH">telegraph</a>,— "That England expected every man would do his duty." He spoke in raptures concerning the event of the day only a short time before his dissolution, and sent word to Admiral Collingwood, desiring that he would make his affectionate farewell to all his brother seamen throughout the fleet. In this manner died, in the 47th year of his age, the greatest commander that perhaps ever adorned the British navy, leaving behind him a name dear to Great Britain, and an example of heroism which will inspire his companions in arms to emulate his virtues, that they too may live in the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-REMEMBRANCE">remembrance</a> of a grateful posterity. His singular <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of attack on this memorable occasion was communicated by his lordship to all his captains, who unanimously gave it as their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that it could not possibly fail of success, being concerted with such consummate <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>; and they even pledged their lives for the favourable result of it. His titles were, Viscount Nelson, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a> of Bronté.—The united <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> voted him a pension of £3000 a year, to continue during his own life and his two next heirs; the East

NEMEA

Pages 837-838

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, situated between Cleonae and Philus in Argolis; whether town, district, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other thing, uncertain; there a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROVE">grove</a> stood in which the Argives celebrated the Nemean games, and there happened all the fabulous circumstances of the Nemean lion. The district Nemea is called Bembinadica, (Pliny); a village, Bembina, standing near Nemen, (Strabo). Stephanus places Nemea in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIS">Elis</a>; though not in Elis, but on its borders; Pliny, erroneously in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCADIA">Arcadia</a>. In the adjoining mountain is still shown the den of the lion, distant 15 stadia from the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> Nemea, (Pausanias); in which stands a considerable temple of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> Nemeus and Cleonaeus, from the vicinity of these two places. This place gave name to the Nemean games, celebrated every third year.

NEMEAN GAMES

Pages 838-838

so called from <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEMEA">Nemea</a>, a village between the cities of Cleonae and Philus, where they were celebrated every third year. The exercises were chariot-races, and all the parts of the Pentathlum. These games were instituted in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of Opheltes <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Archemorus the son of Euphates and Creusa, and who was nursed by Hypsipela; who leaving him in a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEADOW">meadow</a> while she went to show the besiegers of Thebes a fountain, at her return found him dead, and a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERPENT">serpent</a> twined about his neck: whence the fountain, before called Langia, was named Archemorus; and the captains, to comfort Hypsipela, instituted these games.—Others ascribe their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a>, after his victory over the Nemean lion. Others allow, that they were instituted first in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of Archemorus; but interrupted, and revived again by Hercules. The victors were crowned with parsley, an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERB">herb</a> used at funerals, and feigned to have sprung from Archemorus's blood. The Argives presided at these games.

NEMEIN CONTRADICENTE

Pages 838-839

"none contradicting it;" a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> chiefly used in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> when any thing is carried without opposition.

NEMESIANUS

Pages 838-838

AURELIUS OLYMPIUS, a Latin poet who was born at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CARTHAGE">Carthage</a>, and flourished about the year 281, under the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARUS">Carus</a>, and his sons Carinus and Numerian: the last of which emperors was so fond of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, that he contested the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> with Nemesianus, who had written a poem upon <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> affairs. We have still remaining a poem of our author called Cynegeticon, and four eclogues: they were published by Paulus Manutius in 1538; by Barthelet in 1613; at <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a> in 1653; with the notes of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JANUS">Janus</a> Vitius. Giraldi hath preserved a fragment of Nemesianus, which was communicated to him by San-nazarius, to whom we are obliged for our poet's works: for having found them written in Gothic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, he procured them to be put into the Roman, and then sent them to Paulus Manutius. Although this poem hath acquired some reputation, it is greatly inferior to those of Oppian and Gratian upon the same subject; yet Nemesianus's style is <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> enough, and has some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of elegance. The world was so much possessed with an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of his poem in the eighth century, that it was read among the classics in the public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, particularly in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CHARLEMAGNE">Charlemagne</a>, as appears from a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> of the celebrated Hincmar bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHEIMS">Rheims</a>, to his nephew Hincmar of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAON">Laon</a>.

NEMESIS

Pages 838-838

in Pagan worship, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">Necessity</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, according to others, of Oceanus and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOX">Nox</a>, had the care of revenging the crimes which <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> left unpunished. She was also called Adrastea, because Adrastus <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARGOS">Argos</a> first raised an altar to her; and Rhamnusia, from her having a magnificent temple at Rhamnus in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTICA">Attica</a>. She had likewise a temple at Rome in the Capitol. She is represented with a stern countenance, holding a whip in one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of scales in the other.

NEMESIUS

Pages 838-838

a Greek <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> who embraced Christianity, and was made bishop of Emesa in Phoenicia, where he had his birth; he flourished in the beginning of the fifth century. There is a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of his extant, entitled De Natura Hominis, in which he refutes the fatality of the Stoics and the errors of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANICHEES">Manichees</a>, the Apollinarists, and the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUNOMIANS">Eunomians</a>; but he espouses the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORIGEN">Origen</a> concerning the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRE_EXISTENCE">pre-existence</a> of souls (A). This treatise was translated by Valla, and printed in 1535. Another version was afterwards made of it by Ellebedius, and printed in 1665; it is also inserted in the Bibliotheca Patrum, in Greek and Latin. Lastly, Another edition was published at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a> in 1671, folio, with a learned <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PREFACE">preface</a>, wherein the editor endeavours to prove, from a passage in this book, that (A) It is much more probable that he and Origen both brought their opinion with them from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, than that either of them borrowed it from the other. See <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METAPHYSICS">METAPHYSICS</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">Part</a> III. Chap. IV.

NEMOURS

Pages 839-839

a town in France, in the department of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEINE">Seine</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARNE">Marne</a>, containing 3469 inhabitants in 1800. It is seated on the river Loing, in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a> 2. 45. N. Lat. 48. 15.

NENAGH

Pages 839-839

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POST">post</a> and fair town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIPPERARY">Tipperary</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUNSTER">Munster</a>, 75 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>. It is situated on a branch of the river <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SHANNON">Shannon</a> which runs into Lough-Derg. Stand the ruins of an old castle called Nenagh-round. Also those of an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a> founded in the year 1200, for canons following the rule of St Augustin. It was dedicated to St John the Baptist, and was usually called Teachon, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> St John's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. In the reign of Henry III, a friary for conventual Franciscans was also founded here, and esteemed the richest foundation of that order in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>. Here is a barrack for two troops of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>. This town was burnt on St Stephen's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, 1348, by the Irish. The <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a> held here are four.

NENIA

Pages 839-839
or NENIA, in the ancient poetry, a kind of funeral song sung to the music of flutes at the obsequies of the dead. Authors represent them as sorry compositions, sung by hired women mourners called Prefice. The first rise of these Nenia is ascribed to the physicians. In the heathen antiquity, the goddess of tears and funerals was called Nemia; whom some suppose to have given that name to the funeral song, and others to have taken her name from it.

NEOCESARIA

Pages 839-839

(Pliny), a town of Pontus on the south <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the left side of the Lycaus. About the year 342, when Leontius and Sallustius were consuls, it was entirely ruined by a dreadful earthquake, no edifice having withstood the violence of the shock, except the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> and the bishop's habitation, who was saved, with the clergy and some other pious persons, while the rest of the inhabitants were buried in its ruins.

NEOMAGUS

Pages 839-839

(<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>); a town of Gallia Narbonensis, on the confines of the Tricastini. Now Nyons in Dauniane.

NEOMENIA

Pages 839-839
or Noumenia, a festival of the ancient Greeks, at the beginning of every lunar month, which, as the name imports, was observed upon the day of the new moon, in honour of all the gods, but especially Apollo, who was called Neomemos, because the sun is the fountain of light; and whatever distinction of times and seasons may be taken from other planets, Noumenia yet they are all owing to him as the original of those borrowed rays by which they shine. The games and public entertainments at these festivals were made by the rich, to whose tables the poor flocked in great numbers. The Athenians at these times offered solemn prayers and sacrifices for the prosperity of their country during the ensuing month. See Games. The Jews had also their neomenia, or feast of the new moon, on which peculiar sacrifices were appointed: and on this day they had a sort of family entertainment and rejoicing. The most celebrated neomenia of all others was that at the beginning of the civil year, or first day of the month Tisri, on which no servile labour was performed: they then offered particular burnt sacrifices, and sounded the trumpets of the temple. The modern Jews keep the neomenia only as a feast of devotion, which any one may observe or not as he pleases.

NEOPHYTES

Pages 839-839

"new <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>;" a name given by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> to those heathens who had newly embraced the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>; such persons being considered as regenerated, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> born anew by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> neophytes has been also used for new priests, or those <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> admitted into orders, and sometimes for the novices in monasteries. It is still applied to the converts made by the missionaries among the infidels.

NEPAL

Pages 839-839

a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-east of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATNA">Patna</a>, inclosed among the secondary branches of the Himmaeleh <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> from east to west, but scarcely exceeding a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of latitude in breadth. The height of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> above the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, as indicated by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAROMETER">barometer</a>, is not less than 4000 feet; yet <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLONEL">Colonel</a> Kirkpatrick found the thermometer on one occasion at 87°. But the neighbouring mountains afford the inhabitants every variety of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>, from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> of Russia. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> grounds are very healthy; in the valleys fever prevails; guttural tumours <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> goitres are found in both. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">Iron</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> abound in this country. Though <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> are found, the houses are built of brick, cemented with mud. The cattle are similar to those of Bengal, and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONEY">honey</a> is excellent. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is fertile, and besides wheat, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, yields the Zeoral a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of yam, and the Kuraila a kind of wild asparagus, which form a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the subsistence of the poorer inhabitants. The inhabitants consist principally of the two superior classes of Hindoos, and a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> called Newars, who are probably of Chinese or Tartar origin. The former, who compose the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, engross all situations of trust, and are found dispersed all over the country. The Newars are confined almost entirely to the valley of Nepal Proper. The latter are divided into several castes or orders. The total <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> is estimated at about half a million. The Newars are a peaceable and industrious people, of a middle size, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> shoulders and chests, very stout <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a>, round and flat faces, but open and cheerful. The Newar women change their husbands as often as they please on the slightest pretences. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> of the country is the same as the Hinduism of Bengal. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> is despotic. The trade is inconsiderable, being crushed by monopolies. Khatmandu, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, is supposed to contain about 50,000

NEPELUM

Pages 840-840

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the monocota class. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

NEPENTHES

Pages 839-840

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the gymnandra class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking among those of which the order is doubtful. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

NEPETTA

Pages 840-840

CATMINT, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Nep, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the didynamia class, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 42d order, Verticillata. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

NEPEW

Pages 840-840

a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> relative to uncle and aunt, signifying a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> sister's son; who, according to the civil <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>, is in the third <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSANGUINITY">consanguinity</a>, but according to the canon in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a>.

NEPHRITIC

Pages 840-840

something that relates to the kidneys. See Kidney. Nephritic Wood, (Lignum nephriticum), a wood of a very dense and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a> texture, and of a fine grain, brought to us from New <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> in small blocks, in its <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> state, and covered with its bark. This wood is said to be a good diuretic; and we are told it is used among the Indians in all diseases of the kidneys and bladder, and in suppression of urine, from whatever cause. It is also recommended in fevers, and in obstructions of the viscera. The way of taking it among the Indians is only an infusion in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. These uses are not however properly ascertained. See Guilandina, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Nephritic <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">Stone</a>. See Nephrite <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Jade, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERALOGY">Mineralogy</a> Index.

NEPHRITICS

Pages 840-840

in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHARMACY">Pharmacy</a>, medicines proper for diseases of the kidneys. See <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

NEPOS

Pages 840-840

CORNELIUS, a celebrated Latin biographer, who flourished in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Julius Caesar, and lived, according to St Jerome, to the sixth year of Augustus. He was an Italian, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we may <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> Cattullas, and born at Hostilia, a small town in the territory of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERONA">Verona</a>, in Cisalpine <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a>. Ausonius, however, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> have it that he was born in the Gauls. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEANDER">Leander</a> Alberti thinks Nepos's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> was Verona. Cicero and Atticus were friends of our author; who wrote the lives of the Greek historians, as he himself attests in that of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DION">Dion</a>, speaking of Philistus. What he says, also, in the lives of Cato and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HANNIBAL">Hannibal</a>, proves that he had also written the lives of the Latin captains and historians. He wrote some other excellent works which are lost. All that we have left of his at present is, "The Lives of the illustrious Greek and Roman Captains;" which were a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> time ascribed to Aemilius Probus, who published them, as it is said, under his own name, to insinuate himself thereby into the favour of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Theodosius; but, in the course of time, the fraud has been discovered, although several learned persons have confounded the two authors. This piece has been translated into French by the Sieur de Claveret, with a dedication to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of Longueville, in 1663; and again by M. le Gras, then of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> of the Oratory at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, 1729, 12mo. We have an excellent translation of it into English, by several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, which has gone through several editions.

NEPTUNE

Pages 840-841

in Pagan worship, the god of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, was the son of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SATURN">Saturn</a> and Vesta <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Ops, and the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a> and Pluto. He assisted Jupiter in his expeditions; on which that god, when he arrived at the supreme power, assigned him the sea and the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> for his empire. He was, however, expelled from heaven with <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APOLLO">Apollo</a> for conspiring against Jupiter; when they were both employed by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAOMEDON">Laomedon</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHRYGIA">Phrygia</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> the walls of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a>; but that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> dismissing Neptune without a reward, he sent a sea monster to lay waste the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, on which he was obliged to expose his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> Hestione. He is said to have been the first inventor of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORSEMANSHIP">horsemanship</a> and chariot <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACING">racing</a>; on which account <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MITHRIDATES">Mithridates</a> king of Pontus threw <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHARIOTS">chariots</a> drawn by four horses into the sea in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of this god; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> instituted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> races in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CIRCUS">circus</a> at his festival, during which all other horses left working, and the mules were adorned with wreaths of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>. In a contest with <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINERVA">Minerva</a> he produced a horse by striking the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> with his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIDENT">trident</a>; and on another occasion, in a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> of skill with Minerva and Vulcan, produced a bull, whence that animal was sacrificed to him. His favourite wife was <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-AMPHITRITE">Amphitrite</a>, whom he <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> courted in vain, till sending a dolphin to intercede for him, he met with success; on which he rewarded the dolphin by placing him among the stars. He had also two other wives, one of whom was called Salacia from the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; the other Venitia from the ebbing and flowing of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-TIDES">tides</a>. He had likewise many concubines, by whom he had a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of children. He is represented with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, with a garment of an azure or sea green: holding his trident in his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and seated in a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> shell drawn by sea horses: attended by the sea gods Palmon, Glaucus, and Phorcys, and the sea goddesses Thetis, Melita, and Panopca, and a long train of tritons and sea nymphs. This deity was known in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> by the name of Canobus or Canopus, and was worshipped as the numen aquarum or spirit of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NILE">Nile</a>. His <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMBLEM">emblem</a> was the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of certain vases or pitchers, with which the Egyptians filtrated the water of the sacred river, in order to purify and render it fit for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. From the mouth of each of these vases, which were <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> with <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HIEROGLYPHICS">hieroglyphics</a>, arose the head and sometimes the head and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> or woman. Such are the emblems which still remain of the Egyptian Neptune or Canobus; and it was by this emblem that the tutelar god of Egypt vanquished the god of Chaldea in the ridiculous manner mentioned by Ruffinus in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">Ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>. "The Chaldeans (says he) who adored the fire, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 26, carried their god into various countries that he might try his strength in contests with other gods. He vanquished, as we may easily conceive, the images made of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, silver, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, and wood, &c., by reducing them to ashes; and thus the worship of fire was everywhere established. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> of Canopus, unwilling, as became him, to admit the superiority of strange gods, contrived to make his god vanquish the god of Chaldea in a pitched <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>. The vases which were worshipped as the emblems of Canobus, being used for filtering the waters of the Nile, were of course perforated on all sides with very small holes. This faithful priest having stopped all the holes in one of these..." these with wax, and painted the vase of different colours for a reason which the reader <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> admit to be a good one, filled it up with water, and fitted to its mouth the head of an idol. This emblem of Canobus was then placed in a small fire brought by the Chaldeans as the emblem of their god; and thus the gods of Egypt and Chaldea were forced into battle. The contest, however, was of short <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> melting the wax made way for the water to run out, which quickly extinguished the fire; and thus Canobus vanquished the god of the Chaldeans." Ridiculous as this story is, it is perfectly suitable to the genius of Paganism, and the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> artifices of the Pagan priesthood; but we suspect that the historian laboured under one mistake, and substituted the Chaldeans instead of the Persians. See Polytheism.

NEREIDS

Pages 841-841

in the Pagan <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> nymphs, daughters of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEREUS">Nereus</a> and Doris.—The Nereids were esteemed very handsome; insomuch that Cassiopea, the wife of Cepheus <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Ethiopia, having triumphed over all the beauties of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and daring to vie with the Nereids, they were so enraged that they sent a prodigious sea monster into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and, to appease them, she was commanded by the oracle to expose her <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANDROMEDA">Andromeda</a>, bound to a rock, to be devoured by the monster. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> monuments, the Nereids are represented riding upon sea horses; sometimes with an entire <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> form, and at other times with the tail of a fish.

NEREIS

Pages 841-841

a genus of animals belonging to the order of vermes <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOLLUSCA">mollusca</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELMINTHOLOGY">Helminthology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

NEREUS

Pages 841-841

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a marine deity, was son of Oceanus and Thetis. He settled in the Aegean <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, was considered as a prophet, and had the power of assuming what form he pleased. He married his sister Doris, by whom he had 50 daughters called the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEREIDS">Nereids</a>, who constantly attended on <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a>, and when he went abroad surrounded his chariot.

NERIUM

Pages 841-841

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the pentandria class; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 30th order, Conforter. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> and Dying <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

NERO

Pages 841-842

CLAUDIUS DOMITIUS CESAR, a celebrated Roman <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>, son of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAIUS">Caius</a> Domitius Ahenobarbus and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGRIPPINA">Agrippina</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Germanicus. He was adopted by the emperor Claudius, A.D. 50, and four years after he succeeded him on the throne. In the beginning of his reign he showed several marks of the greatest kindness and condescension, affability, complaisance, and popularity. The object of his administration seemed to be the good of his people; and when he was desired to sign his name to a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIST">list</a> of malefactors that were to be executed, he exclaimed, Would to heaven I could not write! He hated flattery; and when the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> had liberally commended the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, he desired them to keep their praises till he deserved them. These promising virtues soon, however, proved to be <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a>: Nero soon displayed the real propensities of his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. He delivered himself from the sway of his mother, and at last ordered her to be murdered. This unnatural <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of barbarity might astonish some, but Nero had his devoted adherents; and when he declared that he had taken away his mother's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> himself from ruin, the senate applauded his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>, and the people signified their approbation. Many of his courtiers shared her unhappy fate; and Nero sacrificed to his fury <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> caprice all such as obstructed his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> or diverted his inclination. In the night he generally went from his <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> to visit the meanest taverns, and all the scenes of debauchery which Rome contained. In this nocturnal riot he was fond of insulting the people in the streets; and his attempts to offer violence to the wife of a Roman senator nearly cost him his life. He also turned <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTOR">actor</a>, and openly appeared on the Roman stage in the meanest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>. In his attempts to excel in music, and to conquer the disadvantages of a hoarse disagreeable <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>, he moderated his meals, and often passed the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> without eating. The Olympian games attracted his notice: he went into <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, and presented himself a candidate for the public <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>. He was defeated in wrestling; but the flattery of the spectators adjudged him the victory, and he returned to Rome with all the splendour and pomp of an eastern conqueror, drawn in the chariot of Augustus, and attended by a band of musicians, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ACTORS">actors</a>, and stage dancers from every <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the empire. These private and public amusements of the emperor were indeed innocent; his character only was injured, and not the lives of the people. His conduct, however, soon became more abominable: he disguised himself in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of a woman, and was publicly married to one of his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUNUCHS">eunuchs</a>. This violence to nature and decency was soon exchanged for another: Nero resumed his <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEX">sex</a>, and celebrated his nuptials with one of his meanest catamites: and it was on this occasion that one of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> observed that the world would have been happy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> Nero's father had had such a wife. But his cruelty was now displayed in a still higher <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, for he sacrificed to his wantonness his wife <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OCTAVIA">Octavia</a> Poppea, and the celebrated writers Seneca, Lucan, Petronius, &c. Nor did the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> escape his barbarity. He had heard of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a>; and as he wished to renew that dismal <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a>, he caused Rome to be set on fire in different places. The conflagration became soon universal, and during <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> successive days the fire <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a>. All was desolation: nothing was heard but the lamentations of mothers whose children had perished in the flames, the groans of the dying, and the continual <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of palaces and buildings. Nero was the only one who enjoyed the general consternation. He placed himself on the top of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> tower, and he sung on his lyre the destruction of Troy, a dreadful scene which his barbarity had realized before his eyes. He attempted to avert the public odium from his head by a pretended commiseration of the miseries of his subjects. He began to repair the streets and public buildings at his own expense. He built himself a celebrated palace, which he called his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. It was liberally adorned with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, with precious <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, and with every thing rare and exquisite. It contained spacious fields, artificial <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>, woods, gardens, orchards, and whatever exhibited a beautiful scene. The entrance of this edifice could admit a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> colossus of the emperor 120 feet high; the galleries were each a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and the whole was covered with gold. gold. The roofs of the dining halls represented the firmament, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> as well as in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>; and continually turned round night and day, showering <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> all sorts of perfumes and sweet waters. When this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> edifice, which, according to Pliny, extended all round the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, was finished, Nero said, that now he could lodge like a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. His profusion was not less remarkable in all his other actions. When he went <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> his nets were of gold and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>. He never appeared twice in the same garment; and when he took a voyage, there were thousands of servants to take care of his wardrobe. This continuation of debauchery and extravagance at last roused the people. Many conspiracies were formed against him; but they were generally discovered, and such as were <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACCESSORY">accessory</a> suffered the severest punishments. The most dangerous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSPIRACY">conspiracy</a> against Nero's life was that of Piso, from which he was saved by the confession of a slave. The conspiracy of Galba proved more successful, who, when he was informed that his plot was known to Nero, declared himself emperor. The unpopularity of Nero favoured his cause; he was acknowledged by all the Roman empire, and the senate condemned the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYRANT">tyrant</a> to be dragged naked through the streets of Rome, and whipped to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, and afterwards to be thrown down from the Tarpeian rock like the meanest malefactor. This, however, was not executed; for Nero prevented it by a voluntary death. He killed himself, A.D. 68, in the 32d year of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, after a reign of 13 years and eight months. Rome was filled with acclamations on the occasion; and the citizens, more strongly to indicate their joy, wore caps, such as were generally used by slaves who had received their freedom. Their vengeance was not only exercised against the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> of the deceased monster, but many of his friends were the object of the public resentment; and many were crushed to pieces in such a violent manner, that one of the senators, amid the universal joy, said that he was afraid they should soon have cause to wish for Nero. The tyrant, as he expired, requested that his head might not be cut off from his body, and exposed to the insolence of the populace, but that the whole might be burned on the funeral pile. His request was granted by one of Galba's freedmen, and his obsequies were performed with the usual ceremonies. Though his death seemed to be the source of general gladness, yet many of his favourites lamented his fall, and were grieved to see that their pleasures and amusements were stopped by the death of this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> of debauchery and extravagance. Even the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol8.html#article-PARTHIA">Parthia</a> sent ambassadors to Rome, to console with the Romans, and to beg that they would honour and revere the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of Nero. His statues were also crowned with garlands of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>; and many imagined that he was not dead, but that he would soon make his appearance and take vengeance on his enemies. It <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> be sufficient to observe, in finishing the character of this tyrannical monster, that the name of Nero is even now used emphatically to express a barbarous and unfeeling oppressor. Pliny calls him the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> enemy and fury of mankind; and so indeed he has been called by all writers, who exhibit Nero as a pattern of the most execrable barbarity and unpardonable wantonness. The same Pliny furnishes us with this singular anecdote of him: "Nero had ordered himself to be painted under the figure of a colossus, upon cloth or canvas, 120 feet in height." He adds, "that this preposterous <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a>, when it was finished, met with its fate from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a>, which consumed it, and involved likewise the most beautiful part of the gardens where it was placed in the conflagration."

NERVA

Pages 842-842

COCEIUS, a Roman <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> after Domitian, who was the last of the 12 Caesars. He was a native of Narnia in Umbria; his family, however, was originally of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CRETE">Crete</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DION">Dion</a> Cassius says he was born on the 17th of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a>, in the 18th year of Tiberius's reign, and of the Christian era the 32d. Nero in the 12th year of his reign made him praetor, and erected a statue for him in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> on account of his poems (for he was one of the best poets of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>), some of which were <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> to him. He was <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a> in 71 with Vespasian, and in 90 with Domitian. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> authors uniformly celebrate him as a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of a most mild and humane temper, of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> moderation and generosity, who looked on his office as emperor, not as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it was for his own advantage, but for that of his people; and whilst he reigned, which was however but for a short <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, he made the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> of his subjects his only end and pursuit. He narrowly escaped <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> under Domitian; was naturally of a weak and timorous disposition; and, as some say, addicted to excessive drinking. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> unanimously chose him emperor; and they had no cause to repent of their choice, for he was constantly attentive to what could make them happy; he was generous, merciful, and disinterested. An instance of his great lenity appears in his pardoning Calpurnius Crassus who conspired against him. In short, he omitted nothing that might contribute to the restoring of the empire to its former lustre: recalling those who had been banished for <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, and redressing all grievances that came to his knowledge. He however found his strength failing, and that it would be impossible for him to finish his designs, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which he adopted Trajan. After his death, which happened in the year 98, he was ranked among the gods. He was the first Roman emperor of foreign <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a>.

NERVES

Pages 842-842

in Anatomy, certain <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> glistening cords, proceeding from the brain and spinal marrow, and dividing into very small branches, which are sent off throughout all parts of the body; and which are found to be the organs of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>. See ANATOMY <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. NERVOUS FLUID. See ANATOMY Index.

NESSUS

Pages 842-844

in fabulous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, a celebrated Centaur, son of Ixion and a Cloud. He offered violence to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEJANIRA">Dejanira</a>, whom <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERCULES">Hercules</a> had intrusted to his care, with orders to carry her across the river Evenus. Hercules <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> the distress of his wife from the opposite shore of the river, and immediately he let fly one of his poisoned arrows, which struck the Centaur to the heart. Nessus, as he expired, gave the tunic he then wore to Dejanira, assuring her that from the poisoned blood which had flowed from his wounds, it had received the power of calling a husband away from unlawful loves. Dejanira received it with <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, and this mournful present caused the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Hercules.—A river which separates Thrace from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a>. It is also called Nessus, Nestos, and Nestus. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NESTOR">Nestor</a>, in fabulous history, a son of Neleus and Chloris, nephew to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PELIAS">Pelias</a> and grandson to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEPTUNE">Neptune</a>. He had eleven brothers, who were all killed with his father by Hercules. His tender <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> detained him at home, and was the cause of his preservation. The conqueror spared his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> and placed him upon the throne of Pylos. He married Euryclea the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Clymenus; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, according to others, Anaxibia the daughter of Atreus. He soon distinguished himself in the field of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>; and was present at the nuptials of Perithous, when a bloody engagement took <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> between the Lapithae and Centaurs. As <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Pylos and Messenia he led his subjects to the Trojan <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, where he distinguished himself among the rest of the Grecian chiefs, by eloquence, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, and uncommon <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a>. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> displays his character as the most perfect of all his heroes; and Agamemnon exclaims, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> he had 20 generals like Nestor, he should soon see the walls of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TROY">Troy</a> reduced to ashes. After the Trojan war Nestor retired to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, where he enjoyed in the bosom of his family the peace and tranquility which were due to his wisdom and to his age. The manner and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of his death are unknown: the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> are all agreed that he lived three generations of men; which length of time is supposed to be 300 years, though more probably only 90 years, allowing 30 years for each <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a>. From that circumstance, therefore, it was usual among the Greeks and the Latins, when they wished a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> and happy life to their friends, to wish them to see the years of Nestor. He had many children; two daughters, Pisidice, and Polycaeste; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> sons, Perseus, Stratius, Arethus, Echephrus, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PISISTRATUS">Pisistratus</a>, Antilochus, and Thrasymedes. Nestor was one of the Argonauts, according to Valerius Flaccus, v. 380, &c.—A poet of Lycaonia in the age of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Severus. He was father to Pisander, who under the emperor Alexander wrote some fabulous stories.—One of the body guards of Alexander. Nestor, whose <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a> name is not known, was a native of Russia, and the earliest historian of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>. He was born in 1056 at Biełozero; and in the 10th year of his age he assumed the monastic <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> in the convent of Petcherski at Kiof, and took the name of Nestor. He there made a considerable proficiency in the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>: but seems to have formed his style and manner rather from the Byzantine historians, Cedrenus, Zonaras, and Synecles, than from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> classics. The time of Nestor's death is not ascertained; but he is supposed to have lived to an advanced age, and to have died about the year 1115. His <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> is his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHRONICLE">Chronicle</a>, to which he has prefixed an introduction, which after a short sketch of the early state of the world, taken from the Byzantine writers, contains a geographical <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of Russia and the adjacent regions; an account of the Slavonian nations, their manners, their emigrations from the banks of the Danube, their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISPERSION">dispersion</a>, and settlement in the several countries wherein their descendants are now established. He then enters upon a chronological <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of the Russian annals, from the year 858 to about 1113. His style is simple and unadorned, such as suits a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> recorder of facts; but his chronological exactness, though it renders his narrative dry and tedious, contributes to ascertain the era and authenticity of the Nestorian events which he relates. It is remarkable (says Mr. Cox, from whom we have taken this narrative), that an author of such importance, whose name frequently occurs in the early Russian books, should have remained in obscurity above 600 years; and been scarcely known to his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> countrymen, the origin and actions of whose <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> he records with such circumstantial exactness. A copy of his Chronicle was given in 1668 by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Radziwiłł to the library of Königsburg, where it lay unnoticed till <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> the Great, in his passage through that town, ordered a transcript of it to be sent to Petersburg. But it still was not known as the performance of Nestor: for when <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MULLER">Muller</a> in 1732 published the first <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of a German translation, he mentioned it as the work of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a> Theodosius of Kiof; an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERROR">error</a> which arose from the following circumstance: The ingenious editor not being at that time sufficiently acquainted with the Slavonian tongue, employed an interpreter, who, by mistaking a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a>, supposed it to have been written by a person whose name was Theodosius. This ridiculous blunder was soon circulated and copied by many foreign writers, even long after it had been candidly acknowledged and corrected by Muller. Nestorians, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of ancient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, still said to be subsisting in some parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEVANT">Levant</a>; whose distinguishing tenet is, that <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> is not the mother of God. They take their name from <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NESTORIUS">Nestorius</a> bishop of Constantinople, whose doctrines were spread with much zeal through <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>. One of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> promoters of the Nestorian cause was Barsumas, created bishop of Nisibis, A.D. 435. Such was his zeal and success, that the Nestorians, who still remain in Chaldea, Persia, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASSYRIA">Assyria</a>, and the adjacent countries, consider him alone as their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARENT">parent</a> and founder. By him Phrozes the Persian monarch was persuaded to expel those Christians who adopted the opinions of the Greeks, and to admit the Nestorians in their place, putting them in possession of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> seat of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> authority in Persia, the see of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SELEUCIA">Seleucia</a>, which the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a> of the Nestorians has always filled even <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to our time.—Barsumas also erected a school at Nisibis, from which proceeded those Nestorian doctors who in the fifth and sixth centuries spread abroad their tenets through Egypt, Syria, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TARTARY">Tartary</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>. He differed considerably from Nestorius, holding that there are two persons in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ, as well as that the Virgin was not his mother, as God, but only as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. The abettors of this doctrine refuse the title Nestorians; alleging that it had been handed down from the earliest times of the Christian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. In the tenth century, the Nestorians in Chaldea, whence they are sometimes called Chaldeans, extended their spiritual conquests beyond Mount Imaus, and introduced the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> into Tartary properly so called, and especially into that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> called Karit, bordering on the northern part of China. The prince of that country, whom the Nestorians converted to the Christian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, assumed, according to the vulgar <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a>, the name of John after his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a>, to which he added Nestorians added the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRESBYTER">Presbyter</a>, from a principle of Nestorius' <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a>; whence it is said his successors were each of them called Prester John until the time of Genghis Khan. But Mosheim observes, that the famous Prester John did not begin to reign in that part of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> before the conclusion of the 11th century. The Nestorians formed so considerable a body of Christians, that the missionaries of Rome were industrious in their endeavours to reduce them under the papal yoke. Innocent IV. in 1246, and Nicolas IV. in 1278, used their utmost efforts for this purpose, but without success. Till the time of Pope Julius III., the Nestorians acknowledged but one patriarch, who resided first at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAGDAD">Bagdad</a>, and afterwards at Mosul; but a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> arising among them, in 1551 the patriarchate became divided, at least for a time, and a new patriarch was consecrated by that pope, whose successors fixed their residence in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORMUS">Ormus</a> in the mountainous part of Persia, where they still continue, distinguished by the name of Simon; and so far down as the last century, these patriarchs persevered in their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a> with the church of Rome, but seem at present to have withdrawn themselves from it. The great Nestorian pontiffs, who form the opposite party, and look with a hostile eye on this little patriarch, have since the year 1559 been distinguished by the general denomination of Elias, and reside constantly in the city of Mosul. Their spiritual dominion is very extensive, takes in a great part of Asia, and comprehends also within its circuit the Arabian Nestorians, and also the Christians of St Thomas, who dwell along the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Malabar. It is observed, to the lasting <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the Nestorians, that of all the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a> established in the East, they have been the most careful and successful in avoiding a multitude of superstitious opinions and practices that have infected the Greek and Latin churches. About the middle of the 17th century, the Romish missionaries gained over to their communion a small <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of Nestorians, whom they formed into a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> or church; the patriarchs or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> of which reside in the city of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMIDA">Amida</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIARBEKIR">Diarbekir</a>, and all assume the denomination of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a>. Nevertheless the Nestorians in general persevere to our own times in their refusal to enter into the communion of the Romish church, notwithstanding the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a> entreaties and alluring offers that have been made by the pope's legate to conquer their inflexible <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTANCY">constancy</a>.

NESTORIUS

Pages 844-845

from whom the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of Nestorian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> derive their name, was born in Germanica a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>. He received his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> at Antioch, where he was likewise baptized; and soon after his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a> he withdrew himself to a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> in the suburbs of that city. Upon his being admitted to the order of priesthood, he quickly acquired so <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reputation by the eloquence of his preaching, and the regularity of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, that by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Theodosius he was deemed a fit person to fill the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> see in the Christian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and was accordingly consecrated bishop of Constantinople in the year 429. In one of his first sermons after his promotion, he publicly declared his intention to make <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> upon heretics; and with that intolerant spirit which has so often disgraced the preachers of the mild <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a>, he called upon the emperor to free the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> from heretics, promising to give him heaven as a reward for his zeal. To this spiritual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> he added one, that, though Nestorius' carnal, he possibly judged of equal force: "Join with me (said he) in war against them, and I <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> assist you against the Persians." Although the wiser and better <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his audience were amazed to see a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, before he had tasted (as the historian expresses himself) the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> of his city, declare that he would persecute all who were not of his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>; yet the majority of the people approved of this discourse, and encouraged him to execute his purpose. Accordingly, five days after his consecration, he attempted to demolish the church in which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARIANS">Arians</a> secretly held their assemblies; and he succeeded so far in his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, that these people, growing desperate, set it on fire themselves, and consumed with it some of the neighbouring houses. This fire excited great commotions in the city, and Nestorius was ever afterwards called an incendiary. From the Arians he turned his <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a> against the Novatians, but was stopped in his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CAREER">career</a> by the interposition of the emperor. He then let loose his fury upon those Christians of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, Lydia, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARIA">Caria</a>, who celebrated the feast of Easter upon the 14th <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>; and for this unimportant deviation from the Catholic practice, many of those people were murdered by his agents both at Miletum and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SARDIS">Sardis</a>.—One cannot be sorry that such a relentless persecutor should himself be afterwards condemned as a heretic, for holding an opinion which no man who speaks <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> thinks with philosophic accuracy will now venture to controvert. This obnoxious tenet, which produced a schism in the church, and was condemned by a general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, was nothing more than that "the Virgin <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a> cannot with propriety be called the mother of God." The people being accustomed to hear this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>, were much inflamed against their bishop, imagining that he had revived the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERROR">error</a> of Paulus Samosatenus and Photinus, who taught that Jesus Christ was a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> man. The monks declared openly against him, and, with some of the most considerable men of Constantinople, separated themselves from his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNION">communion</a>. Several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISHOPS">bishops</a> wrote to him <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARNEST">earnest</a> persuasives to acknowledge that Mary was the mother of God; and when he would not comply, they procured his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONDEMNATION">condemnation</a> in the council of Ephesus, which deprived him of his see. He then retired to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> monastery at Antioch, whence he was taken four years afterwards by the emperor's order, and banished in 435 to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TARSUS">Tarsus</a>. That city being taken and destroyed by the Barbarians, he was removed to Panopolis, a city of Thebais; where he was not suffered to remain <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, but was compelled to go from <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to place, till, being in one of his journeys mortally bruised by a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> relieved him from the fury of his persecutors. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> we examine such of his writings as remain, we shall find that he was very unjustly condemned. It appears that he rejected the errors of Ebion, Paulus Samosatenus, and Photinus; that he maintained in express terms, that the divine Word was united to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> in Jesus Christ in the most strict and intimate <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> possible; that these two natures, in this state of union, make but one Christ and one person; that the properties of the Divine and human natures may both be attributed to this person; and that Jesus Christ may be said to have been born of a virgin, to have suffered and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NET">NET</a> Nestorius and died; but he never would admit that God could be said to have been born, to have suffered, or to have died.—When we consider that every person partakes of the substance of his mother, and that it is this which constitutes the parental and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FILIAL">filial</a> relation between them, it is indeed surprising that the expression "Mother of God" should ever have been admitted into the Christian church, or that any man who understands the meaning of the words should condemn Nestorius for not having used them.

NESTUS

Pages 845-845
or Nessus, a river which separates Thrace from Macedonia. It falls into the Aegean sea near the island Thasos. It is sometimes called Neuss and Nessus.

NET

Pages 845-846

a device for catching fish and fowl. See the article FISHERY. The taking fowls by nets is the readiest and most advantageous of all others, where numbers are to be taken. The making the nets is very easy, and what every true sportsman ought to be able to do for himself. All the necessary tools are wooden <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEEDLES">needles</a>, of which there should be several of different sizes, some round and others flat; a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of round pointed and flat scissors; and a wheel to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> off the thread. The pack-thread is to be of different strength and thickness, according to the sort of birds to be taken; and the general size of the meshes, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not for very small birds, is two inches from point to point. The nets should neither be made too deep nor too <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, for they are then difficult to manage; and they must be verged on each side with twisted thread. The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of the thread is too bright and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a>, and is therefore in many <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> to be altered. The most usual colour is the russet; which is to be obtained by plunging the net, after it is made, into a tanners' pit, and letting it <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIE">lie</a> there till it be sufficiently tinged: this is of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to the net, since it preserves the thread as well as alters the colour. The green colour is given by chopping some green wheat and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> it in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and then soaking the net in this green tincture. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> colour is given in the same manner with the decoction of celandine; which gives a pale straw-colour, which is the colour of stubble in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> nets are to be used on ploughed lands, the green on grass grounds, and the yellow on stubble lands. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">Day</a>-NET, among fowlers, a net generally used for taking such small birds as play in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> stoop either to prey, gig, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the like; as larks, linnets, buntings, &c. The time of the year for using this net is from August to November; and the best time is very early in the morning: and it is to be observed, that the milder the air, and the brighter the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> is, the better will be the sport, and of longer continuance. The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where this net should be laid, ought to be plain champaign, either on short stubbles, green leys, or flat meadows, near corn fields, and somewhat remote from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> and villages: you must be sure to let your net lie <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the ground, that the birds creep not out and make their escape.—The net is made of a fine packthread with a small mesh, not exceeding half an inch <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>; it must be three fathoms long, and but one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>: it must be verged about with a small but strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CORD">cord</a>; and the two ends extended upon two small long <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a>, suitable to the breadth of the net, with four stakes, tail-strings, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>.—This net is composed of two, which must be exactly alike; and are to be laid opposite to one another, so even and close, that when they are drawn and pulled over, the sides must meet and touch each other. You must stake this net <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> with strong stakes, very stiff on their lines, so that you may with a nimble touch <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> them to and fro at <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>; then fasten your drawing-cord or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>-lines (of which there must be a dozen at least, and each two yards long) to the upper end of the foremost staves: and so extend them of such a straitness, that with a little strength they may rise up in the nets and cast them over. Your nets being thus laid, place your gigs, or playing-wantons, about 20 or 30 paces beyond, and as much on this side your nets: the gigs must be fastened to the tops of long poles, and turned into the wind, so as they may play to make a noise therein. These gigs are a sort of toys made of long goose-feathers, like shuttle-cocks, and with little small tunnels of wood running in broad and flat swan-quills, made round like a small hoop; and so, with longer strings fastened to a pole, will, with any small wind or air, move after such a manner, that birds will come in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> flocks to play about them. When you have placed your gigs, then place your stake; which is a small stake of wood, to prick down into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, having in it a mortice-hole, in which a small and slender piece of wood, about two feet long, is fastened, so as it may move up and down at pleasure: and fasten to this longer stick a small line, which, running through a hole in the stick above-mentioned, and so coming up to the place where you are to sit, you may, by drawing the line up and down with your <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> hand, raise up the longer stick as you see occasion. Fasten a live lark, or such like <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BIRD">bird</a>, to this longer stick, which, with the line making it to stir up and down by your pulling, will entice the birds to come to your net.
