There is another stake, or enticement, to draw on these birds, called a looking-glass; which is a round stake of wood, as big as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>'s arm, made very sharp at the end, to thrust it into the ground: they make it very hollow in the upper <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>, above five fingers deep; into which hollow they place a three-square piece of wood about a foot long, and each two inches broad, lying upon the top of the stake, and going with a foot into the hollowness: which foot must have a great knob at the top, and another at the bottom, with a deep slenderness between; to which slenderness you are to fasten a small packthread, which, running through a hole in the side of the stake, must come up to the place where you sit. The three square piece of wood which lies on the top of the stake, must be of such a poise and evenness; and the foot of the socket so smooth and round, that it may whirl and turn round upon the least touch; winding the packthread so many times about it, which being suddenly drawn, and as suddenly let go, will keep the engine in a constant rotatory <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>: then fasten with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLUE">glue</a> on the uppermost flat squares of the three-square piece, about 20 small pieces of looking-glass, and paint all the square wood between them of a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> and lively <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>; which, in the continual motion, will give such a reflection, that the birds will play about to admiration until they are taken. Both this and the other stake are to be placed in the middle between the two nets, about two or three feet distance from each other; so that in the falling of the nets, the chords may not touch or annoy them: neither must they stand one before or after another; the glass being kept in a continual motion, and the bird very often fluttering. Having placed your nets in this manner, as also your gigs and stakes, go to the further end of your long drawing lines and stake lines; and having placed yourself, lay the main drawing line across your thigh, and, with your left, pull the stake line to show the birds; and when you perceive them to play near and about your nets and stakes, then pull the net over with both <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, with a quick but not too hasty motion; for otherwise your sport will be spoiled. See Plate CCCLXIX., where A shows the bodies of the main net, and how they ought to be laid. B, the tail lines, or the hinder lines, staked to the ground. C, the fore lines staked also to the ground. D, the bird stake. E, the looking-glass stake. G, the line which draws the bird stake. H, the line that draws the glass stake. I, the drawing double lines of the nets, which pulls them over. K, the stakes which stake down the four nether <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of the nets and the two tail lines. L, the stakes that stake down the fore lines. M, the single line, with the wooden <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BUTTON">button</a> to pull the net over with. N, the stake that stakes down the single line, and where the man should sit; and O, the gig. Net, Neat, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, something pure, and unadulterated with any foreign mixture. Thus wines are said to be net when not falsified or balderdashed; and coffee, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a>, &c. are net when the filth and ordure are separated from them. A <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIAMOND">diamond</a> is said to be net when it has no stains or flaws; a crystal, when transparent throughout. Net is also used for what remains after the tare has been taken out of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of any merchandise, i.e. when it is weighed clear of all package. See Tare. Thus we say, a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARREL">barrel</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COCHINEAL">cochineal</a> weighs 450 pounds; the tare is 50 pounds, and there remain net 400 pounds. Net Produce, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> used to express what any commodity has yielded, all tare and charges deducted. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> sometimes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the Italian words netto proceduto, for net produce.

NETHERLANDS

Pages 846-847

anciently called Belgia, but since denominated Low Countries <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Netherlands, from their low situation, are situated between 2° and 7° of east <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>, and between 50° and 53° 30' of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude: and are bounded by the German <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> on the north, Germany on the east, by Lorrain and France on the south, and by another <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of France and the British seas on the west; extending near 300 miles in length from north to south, and 200 miles in breadth from east to west. They consist of 17 provinces; 10 of which were called the Austrian and French Netherlands, and the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> the United Provinces. The whole united were erected into a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> at the peace of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1814. The greatest part of the Netherlands was conquered by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>; and that part which lies towards Nether-<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in their subjection till the decline of that empire; after which the Franks became masters of it; and under the French <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a>, it was part of the kingdom of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METZ">Metz</a> or Austrasia. Towards the end of the 15th century Maximilian of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, son of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Ferdinand III., acquired, by marrying the only <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a>, the duchies of Brabant, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBURG">Limburg</a>, and Luxemburg; the counties of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>, Burgundy, Hainault, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, Zeeland, and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAMUR">Namur</a>; and the lordship of Friesland. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> of Austria, son to Maximilian and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, married Jane the daughter of Ferdinand <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> of Arragon and of Isabella <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of Castile; by which means their son <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> inherited not only almost all <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> countries then lately discovered in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, but also those noble provinces of the Netherlands, and was chosen emperor under the name of Charles V. Towards the latter end of the 1527, he added to his dominions the temporalities of the bishoprick of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-UTRECHT">Utrecht</a> on both sides of the Yssel; and Henry of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a>, being distressed through <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with the duke of Guelderland, and tired with the continued rebellion of his own subjects, surrendered to the emperor the temporalities of his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a>, which was confirmed by the pope, and the states of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. In 1536, Charles V. bought of Charles of Egmond the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVERSION">reversion</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Guelderland and of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZUTPHEN">Zutphen</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> should die without issue. The same year the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRONINGEN">Groningen</a> took the oath of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a>, and submitted to Charles V. and in 1543 he put a garrison into the city of Cambrey, and built a citadel there. Having thus united the 17 provinces, as it were in one body, he ordered that they should continue for ever under the same prince, without being ever separated or dismembered; for which purpose he published in November 1549, with the consent and at the request of the states of all the provinces, a perpetual and irrevocable edict or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>, by which it was enacted, that in order to keep all those provinces together under one and the same prince, the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of representation, with regard to the succession of a prince or princess, should take <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> for ever both in a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> and collateral line, notwithstanding the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> laws of some provinces to the contrary. Charles had even a mind to incorporate these provinces with the Germanic body, and to make of them a circle of the empire, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of the circle of Burgundy, in order thereby to engage the princes of the empire to concern themselves for the preservation of those provinces. But the Netherlands, always jealous of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, did not seem to like that incorporation; and when they were demanded to pay their share towards the expenses of the empire, they refused it: whereupon the princes of Germany refused, in their turn, to take any part in the wars in Flanders, and looked upon those provinces as by no means belonging to the Germanic body. Philip of Austria and his son Charles, who were born in the Netherlands, had for these provinces that <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> affection which men <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> to have for their native country; and, knowing how jealous the inhabitants were of their liberty, and of the privileges granted to them by their former princes, they took great care to preserve them and suffered willingly that the states, who were the guardians of the people's liberty and privileges, should should in a manner share the supreme authority with them. Philip II., son to the emperor Charles V., had not the same affection for the Netherlands, nor those generous sentiments which his father had endeavoured to inspire him with. Being born in Spain of a Portuguese woman, he had no regard but for his native country; and, when he removed out of the Netherlands, he left them to the weak <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of a woman, to the proud and haughty spirit of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> de Grenville, and to the wild ambition of some lords of these provinces, who availing themselves of the imprudent conduct and continual blunders of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of Spain, found their private <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> in the disturbances they could not fail to produce. Philip II., also, instead of the mild and moderate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> which his predecessors had successfully employed on many occasions, as best suiting the genius and temper of the people, had recourse to the most violent and cruel proceedings; which, far from curing the evil, served only to exasperate it the more and render it incurable. The Spaniards, whom he sent thither, being born and educated in an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> monarchy, jealous of the liberties and envious of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> of the people, broke through all their privileges, and used them almost after the same manner as they had done the inhabitants of their new and ill-gotten dominions in America. This treatment occasioned a general insurrection. The counts <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOORN">Hoorn</a>, Egmont, and the prince of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a>, appeared at the head of it, and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUTHER">Luther</a>'s reformation gaining ground about the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> in the Netherlands, his disciples joined the malecontents: whereupon King Philip introduced a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INQUISITION">inquisition</a> in order to suppress them, and many thousands were put to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> by that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>, besides those that perished by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>; for these persecutions and encroachments had occasioned a civil war, in which several battles were fought. The counts Hoorn and Egmont were taken and beheaded; but the prince of Orange, retiring into Holland, with the assistance of England and France, preserved Holland and some of the adjacent provinces, which entered into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> for their mutual <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> at Utrecht in 1579, and they have ever since been styled the United Provinces; but the other provinces were reduced to the obedience of Spain by the duke of Alva and other Spanish generals. However, their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> privileges were in a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> restored; every <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> was allowed its great council or <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, whose concurrence was required to the making of laws, and raising <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> for the government, though these assemblies were too often obliged to follow the dictates of the court. The emperor <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> II. endeavoured to deprive them even of the form of their free <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>; and he might very probably have succeeded, had he not attempted at the same time a reformation of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. The Austrian Netherlands are wholly Catholic, and so bigotted to the Romish <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>, that though they had tamely submitted to many encroachments of the archducal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> on their civil <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a>, no sooner did the monarch encroach upon the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of the holy mother church than they resisted his authority, and claimed all their ancient privileges <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a>. The Spaniards continued possessed of almost eight of these provinces, until the duke of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARLBOROUGH">Marlborough</a>, general of the allies, gained the memorable victory of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAMILLIES">Ramillies</a>. After which <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRUSSELS">Brussels</a> the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, and great part of these provinces, acknowledged Charles VI. (afterwards emperor) their sovereign; and his daughter, the late empress queen, remained possessed of them till the war that followed the death of her father, when the French made an entire conquest of them, except part of the province of Luxembourg; but they were restored by the peace of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AIX">Aix</a>-la-Chapelle in 1748, and the French retained only Artois, the Cambressis, part of Flanders, part of Hainault, and part of Luxembourg. These provinces were overrun by the French in 1794, and formally ceded to them by the treaty of Campo Formio in 1797. They kept possession of them till 1814, when they were separated from France, and along with the seven Dutch provinces, formed into a kingdom under the prince of Orange, who assumed the title of king of the Netherlands. By the new constitution promulgated in 1815, the people of the two countries were to be represented in an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> called the States-General, whose sittings were to be held alternately in a town in Holland and a town in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELGIUM">Belgium</a>. The States consist of two chambers; the deliberations of the lower are public, those of the upper private. The constitution guarantees the liberty of the press, the right of petitioning, and the independence of the judges. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is generally fruitful, but differs in the several parts. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> also differs in the several provinces; in those towards the south it does not differ much from that of England, though the seasons are more regular. In the northern provinces the winter is generally very sharp, and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> sultry hot; but the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> and excessive <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> seldom continue above five or six weeks. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> is reckoned very wholesome, but is subject to thick fogs in winter, through the moistness of the country, which would be very noxious, were it not for the dry easterly winds, which, blowing off a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> continent for two or three months in the year, clear the air, and occasion very sharp frosts in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> and February; during which, the ports, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a> are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> shut up. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> of the country is low and flat; for, except some small hills and a few rising grounds in Utrecht and Guelderland, and in the parts lying towards Germany, there is no hill to be seen in the whole 17 provinces. This is the reason why they have been called the Low Countries. French Flanders abounds in grain, vegetables, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a> and cattle, but is in want of wood. For the Dutch Netherlands, see United Provinces.

NETHINIMS

Pages 847-847

among the Jews, the posterity of the Gibeonites, who were condemned by Joshua to be hewers of wood and drawers of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of God.

NETOPION

Pages 847-847

a name given by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> to a very fragrant and costly ointment, consisting of a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of the finest spicy ingredients. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HIPPOCRATES">Hippocrates</a>, in his Treatise on the Diseases of Women, frequently prescribes the netopion in diseases of the uterus; and in other places he speaks of its being poured into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EAR">ear</a> as a remedy for deafness; these compositions, by their attenuating qualities, dividing the viscous and thick humours. The word netopion is also sometimes used to express the unguentum Egyptianum, and sometimes simply for <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> of almonds.

NETTINGS

Pages 847-848

in a ship, a sort of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GRATES">grates</a> made of small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a> seized together with rope yarn <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> twine, and fixed NETTLE. See URTICA, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">SEA</a>-NETTLE. See <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEDUSA">MEDUSA</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELMINTHOLOGY">HELMINTHOLOGY</a> Index, and ANIMAL-Flower. NETTLE-TREE. See CELTIS, BOTANY Index.

NETTUNO

Pages 848-848

a handsome town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAMPAGNA">Campagna</a> di Roma. It is but thinly peopled, though seated in a fertile <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>. The inhabitants are almost all hunters. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 12° 57'. N. Lat. 41° 30'.

NEUCHATEL

Pages 849-850

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of the same name. There are several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> ruins near it, which show its former <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>; and there are two <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> churches, besides a castle where the governor resides. The town contains about 3000 inhabitants. It is situated partly on a small plain, between Mount <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JURA">Jura</a> and the lake of Neuchatel, which is 17 miles <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> and five <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>; the side of the harbour is the usual walk of the inhabitants. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">Part</a> of it too is built upon the side of the mountain; whence some of its streets are very steep. In this small <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> several public works have lately been executed, which Mr Coxe thinks are far beyond the revenues, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> even the wants, of such a little state. Among these he instances a superb causeway and a town-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> "built (says he) of such <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> materials, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it was intended to survive to the most distant posterity, and to rival the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a> of the much-famed Roman capitol." At the beginning of the 18th century, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> was very little followed in this town, owing to an absurd <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> which prevailed among the inhabitants, of its being disgraceful; but this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a> is now extinguished, and the town in a much more flourishing situation than before. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> article of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a> is wine, which is much esteemed; and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of printed linens and cottons have been established with considerable success. The flourishing state of Neuchattel is principally owing to the benefactions of Mr <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a> Pury, late banker of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LISBON">Lisbon</a>. He was born at Neuchattel in 1709; but having received his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> there, he quitted it in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> poverty, and repaired to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a>, where he served his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPRENTICESHIP">apprenticeship</a>, but in what line is not mentioned. From Geneva he went to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, where he acted as clerk to a dealer in precious <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, and acquired great reputation by estimating the value of diamonds at sight. After a long residence in England he went to Lisbon, where he carried on a very extensive commerce; and having been appointed court-banker, his fortune rapidly increased. His generosity, however, kept pace with his wealth; and he not only remitted large sums to Neuchattel while living, but left his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> his heir when he died. His contributions in all are estimated by Mr Coxe at 200,000l.; a considerable part of which has been employed in constructing the public works already mentioned. Neuchattel has a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> and little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>: the first is composed of 40 persons, with two masters of the keys; the little council consists of 24 members, comprehending the mayor, who is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a>. These two councils assemble regularly every <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a> likewise assemble every month, to consult on affairs belonging to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, and to fill up the places of ministers that die. They choose a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> every year, who is president of the general assemblies, which are called classes; and sometimes he is confirmed in this <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>. E. Long. 7. 10. N. Lat. 47. 5. Neuchattel, a sovereign county of Switzerland, bounded on the west by the Franche Compte, on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the bishopric of Basle, and on the east and south (a) We have given the detail in Mr Coxe's own words, as it appears to us to deserve <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> on account of the greatness of the project, which would have excited admiration had it been attempted by one enlightened by science and liberal arts, much more when it comes through the humble medium of a Russian <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEASANT">peasant</a>. It was never executed, as we are <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> informed by a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> who left St Petersburgh about the beginning of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1793; but the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a> remains, and is still shown. The same gentleman (we quote his own words) adds, "that every mechanic thinks it practicable; and that the general <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> is, that the empress would have built it, had she not found <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> for all her <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> in carrying on her warlike and diplomatic transactions with other courts." Neuchâtel south by the cantons of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BERNE">Berne</a> and Friburg. This principality of Neuchâtel and Vallengin extend from the lake of Neuchâtel to the borders of Franche Comté, being in length about 12 leagues, and six in breadth. The plain with the lower part of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> is occupied by the district of Neuchâtel, but Vallengin is totally enclosed by Jura. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">Parallel</a> chains of these mountains run from east to west, forming several valleys in the most elevated parts. The lower grounds of this chain consist of arable lands and vineyards; the higher of large tracts of forest, which in many parts have been cleared and converted into pasture grounds, intermixed with fields of barley and oats. The inhabitants are numerous, and remarkable for their genius, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITENESS">politeness</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> industry. It contains three cities, one town, 90 villages, and about 320 houses dispersed in the mountains. The inhabitants are all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROTESTANTS">Protestants</a>, except two Roman catholic villages: and in 1529 they entered into a strict <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> with the cantons of Berne, Friburg, Soleure, and Lucern. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> is healthy and temperate, but the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> not everywhere equally fertile: however, there are large vineyards, which produce <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> wine, which last is excellent. The pastures on the mountains feed a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of cattle; there are plenty of deer in the forests; the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> abound with fish. The mildness of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, and agreeable situation of the inhabitants in general in these districts is evident from the great increase of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> in the space of 32 years. In 1752 they contained only 28,017 subjects and 4318 aliens: but in 1784 the number was augmented to 31,576 subjects and 9754 aliens; being an increase of near a fourth part in that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. The facility with which the burgheership of Neuchâtel is acquired, may also be accounted one of the means of augmenting its population; for between the years 1760 and 1770, the magistrates admitted 41 persons to this privilege; from 1770 to 1780, 46; from 1780 to 1785, 51; in all 138; many of whom had children before they purchased their burgheership, and 38 of them were foreigners, either German, French, or Dutch. This country has experienced similar changes with the rest of Switzerland during the usurpation of the French.

NEUFCHATTEAU

Pages 850-850

a commercial town of France, in the department of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VOSGES">Vosges</a>, containing 2700 inhabitants. It formerly had an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> of the nuns of St Clair, a commandery of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALTA">Malta</a>, and several <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a> of monks and nuns. It is seated in a fertile <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, which produces corn, wine, and all the necessaries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, on the river Mouzon. E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5° 45'. N. Lat. 48° 20'.

NEURADA

Pages 850-850

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the decandria class, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 13th order, Succulenta. See Botany <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

NEUROPTERA

Pages 850-850

the name of one of the orders into which the class of insects is divided according to the Linnaean classification. See Entomology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

NEUTER

Pages 850-850

a person indifferent, who has espoused neither party, and is neither friend nor foe. A judge ought to be neuter in the causes he judges; in questions, where reason appears neuter, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> should ever incline to the side of the unhappy. Neuter, in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, denotes a sort of gender of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOUNS">nouns</a>, which are neither masculine nor <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMININE">feminine</a>. See Gender. The Latins have three kinds of genders, masculine, feminine, and neuter. In English, and other <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> tongues, there is no such thing as neuter nouns. See Noun. Verbs Neuter, by some grammarians called intransitive verbs, are those which govern nothing, and that are neither <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> nor <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSIVE">passive</a>. See Verb. When the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> expressed by the verb has no object to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> upon, but the verb alone supplies the whole idea of the action; the verb is said to be neuter: as, I <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a>, thou yawnest, he sneezes, we walk, ye run, they stand still. Some divide verbs neuter into, 1. Such as do not signify any action, but a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>; as albet, "it is <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>;"

NEVA

Pages 848-849

a river at Petersburg, in Russia. The views upon the banks exhibit the grandest and most lively scenes. The river is in most places broader than the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. It is deep, rapid, and transparent as crystal, and its banks are lined on each side with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> range of handsome buildings. On the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> side the fortress, the academy of sciences and that of art are the most striking objects; on the opposite side are the imperial <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADMIRALTY">admiralty</a>, the mansions of many Russian <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a>, and the English line, so called because (a few houses excepted) the whole row is occupied by the English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>. In <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a> of these buildings, on the south side, is the quay, which stretches for three miles, except where it is interrupted by the admiralty, and the Neva, during the whole of that space, has been lately embanked at the expense of the empress, by a wall, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARAPET">parapet</a>, and pavement of hewn <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANITE">granite</a>; a most elegant and durable monument of imperial magnificence. There is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> between the opposite sides of the river by a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> of pontoons, which, when any thing is apprehended from the force of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ICE">ice</a> rushing <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the stream, can be, and is, generally indeed, removed. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> depth of the river, it appears, prevents the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> bridge; and, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it could be built, there is no reason to suppose it could possibly resist the force of those vast shoals of ice which in the beginning of winter come down this rapid river. An attempt, however, has been made to remedy this inconvenience; and a Russian <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEASANT">peasant</a> has actually projected the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of throwing a wooden bridge of one <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> across it, which, in its narrowest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>, is 980 feet in breadth. As we think this is a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of very considerable importance, as well as of curiosity, we shall give the following copious account of the plan and its author, in Mr Coxe's own words; who tells us that the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a> had then executed a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a> 98 feet in length, which he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> and examined with considerable <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>. "The bridge is upon the same principle with that of Shaffhausen, excepting that the mechanism is more complicated, and that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> is not so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a>. I shall attempt to describe it by supposing it finished, as that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> convey the best idea of the plan. The bridge is roofed at the top, and covered at the sides; it is formed by four frames of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>, two on each side, composed of various beams <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> trusses, which support the whole machine. The road is not, as is usual, carried over the top of the arch, but is suspended in the middle. "The following proportions I noted down with the greatest exactness at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> when they were explained to me by the artist. Length of the abutment on the north end, 638 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAN">Span</a> of the arch, 980 feet Length of the abutment on the south end, 658 feet Length of the whole structure, including the abutments, 2296 feet The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANE">plane</a> of the road upon its first ascent makes an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> of five degrees with the ordinary surface of the river. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">Mean</a> level of the river to the top of the bridge in the centre, 168 feet <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DITTO">Ditto</a> to the bottom of the bridge in the centre, 126 feet Height of the bridge from the bottom to the top in the centre, 42 feet Height from the bottom of the bridge in the centre to the road, 7 feet Height from the bottom of ditto to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, 84 feet Height from the water to the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> of the arch, 56 feet So that there is a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of 35 feet between the road at the spring of the arch and the road at the centre; in other words, an ascent of 35 feet in half 980, or in the space of 490 feet, which is little more than eight-tenths of an inch to a foot. The bridge is broadest towards the sides, and diminishes towards the centre. In the broadest part it is 168 feet. In the centre or narrowest part, 42 feet. The breadth of the road is 28 feet. "The artist informed me, that to complete the bridge would require 49,650 <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> nails, 12,998 <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> trees, 5500 beams to strengthen them; and that it would cost 300,000 rubles or 60,000l. He speaks of this bold project with the usual warmth of genius; and is perfectly convinced that it would be practicable. I must own that I am of the same <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, though I hazard it with great diffidence. What a noble effect would be produced by a bridge striking across the Neva, with an arch 980 feet wide, and towering 168 feet from the surface of the water! The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of such a bridge seems almost chimerical; and yet upon inspection of the model we become reconciled to the idea. But whether the execution of this stupendous <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> may be deemed possible or not, the model itself is worthy of attention, and reflects the highest <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> on the inventive faculties of that unimproved genius. It is so compactly constructed, and of such uniform solidity, that it has supported 3540 pood, or 127,440 pounds, without having in the least swerved from its <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, which I am told is far more, in proportion to its size, than the bridge if completed would have occasion to sustain from the pressure of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">carriages</a> added to its own <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>. "The person who projected this plan is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> Russian peasant. This extraordinary genius was apprentice to a shopkeeper at Nishnei Novgorod; opposite to his dwelling was a wooden clock, which excited his curiosity. By repeated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> he comprehended the internal structure, and without any assistance formed one exactly similar in its proportion and materials. His success in this first <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSAY">essay</a> urged him to undertake the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of metal clocks and watches." The empress, hearing of these wonderful exertions of his native genius, took him under her protection, and sent him to England; from whence, on account of the difficulties attending his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, he soon returned to Russia. I saw a repeating watch of his workmanship at the Academy of Sciences: it is about the bigness of an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGG">egg</a>; in the inside is represented the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> of our Saviour, with the stone at the entrance, and the centinels upon duty: suddenly the stone is removed, the centinels <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> down, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGELS">angels</a> appear, the women enter the sepulchre, and the same chant is heard which is performed on Easter-<a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-EVE">eve</a>. These are trifling, although curious performances; but the very planning of the bridge was a most sublime <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a>. This person, whose name is Kollbin, bears the appearance of a Russian peasant: he has a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARD">beard</a>, and wears the common dress of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. He receives a pension from the empress, and is encouraged to follow the bent of his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> genius.

NEVEL

Pages 849-849
or NEBEL, in the Jewish antiquities, a kind of musical instrument. See NABLUM.

NEVERS

Pages 849-849

a town of France, in the department of Nievre, and situated in E. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3. 14. N. Lat. 46. 59. on the river <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOIRE">Loire</a>, which here receives the rivulet Nievre. It contained 12,150 inhabitants in 1805. It is a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> antiquity, supposed to be Cesar's Noviodunum in Aedui, where he erected magazines for his armies. Francis I. made it a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> and peerage in 1521, in favour of Francis of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CLEVES">Cleves</a>, to whom it came by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>. It devolved afterwards to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANTUA">Mantua</a>, and then to the Palatine family, who in 1651 sold it to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Mazarine. The cardinal obtained a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> and peer for his nephew <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> Mancini, in whose family it <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> till the late revolution. The town is fortified with walls, defended with many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> towers and deep ditches, and is the seat of a bishopric, suffragan of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENS">Sens</a>, as likewise of a bailiwick and chamber of accounts. There was a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> on the Loire, which was carried away by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ICE">ice</a>, and has been replaced by a wooden one. This town is famous for its manufacture of glass, earthen <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARE">ware</a>, cloth, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTLERY">cutlery</a>. In the centre of Nevers, on the summit of a hill, is built the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> dukes. It appears to have been constructed in the sixteenth century, and exhibits a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and delicacy of Gothic <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>. The apartments are hung with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TAPESTRY">tapestry</a> of 200 years old, which have an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GROTESQUE">grotesque</a> and rude magnificence.

NEVIS

Pages 850-850

one of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CARIBBEE_ISLANDS">Caribbee <a clas</a>s="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, lying about <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> leagues <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of Montserrat, and separated from St Christopher's by a narrow channel. It makes a beautiful appearance from the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, being a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> conical mountain covered with fine trees, of an easy ascent on every side, and entirely cultivated. The circumference is about 21 miles, with a considerable tract of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> ground all around. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> in the lower <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> is reckoned to be warmer than Barbadoes, but it is more temperate towards the summit. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is very fine in the lower part, but grows coarser as we ascend. The productions are nearly the same with those of St Christopher's. There are three pretty good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> bays, with small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> in their vicinity; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> Town, Moreton <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEWCASTLE">Newcastle</a>. This pleasant <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> was settled under the auspices of Sir Thomas Warner from St Christopher's. His successor, Governor Lake, was considered as the Solon of this little <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, in which he disposed of everything with such <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>, as procured him a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> reputation with the French as well as English. In the Dutch <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> they met with some disturbance from the French; but by being covered by an English squadron, the enemy were obliged to desist from their intended invasion, after a smart engagement in sight of the island. Sir William Stapleton sometimes resided here, and Sir Nathaniel Johnson constantly, at which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the inhabitants of Nevis were computed at 30,000. In the war immediately after the Revolution, they exerted themselves gallantly, and had two regiments of 300 men each. In that of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a> they behaved equally well, though they were less fortunate; for the French landing with a superior force, and having inveigled most of their slaves, they were forced to capitulate. About 4000 of these slaves the French carried away and sold to the Spaniards, to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> in their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINES">mines</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, after making due inquiry into the losses they had sustained, voted them about a third part of the sum which they had suffered. These losses by war, an epidemic <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a>, and repeated hurricanes, exceedingly diminished the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of the people. They are now thought not to exceed 2000 or 3000 whites, and 6000 blacks. There is here a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a> governor, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>, and an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a>, which is composed of three members from each of the five parishes into which the island is divided. The commodities are cotton and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>; and about 20 sail of ships are annually employed in this trade.

NEW STYLE

Pages 857-857

first used in England in 1753, was introduced into the western world by Pope Gregory XIII. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">CHRONOLOGY</a>, No. 24.

NEWBOROUGH

Pages 850-851
or NEWBURGH, in the isle of Anglesey, North Wales, distant from London 254 miles, though but a small town, situated over against Caernarvon in North Wales, about 17 miles southwest from Beaumaris, is governed by a mayor, two bailiffs and a recorder. Its Welsh name is Rhosseri, or Rhosseri.

NEWBURG

Pages 851-851

the name of several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of Germany, two of which are the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> towns of duchies of the same name; one in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a>, and the other in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALATINATE">Palatinate</a>.

NEWBURY

Pages 851-853

a town in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Berks in England, 16 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">Reading</a>, and 56 from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, arose on the decay of Spinham-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">Land</a>. Notwithstanding its name signifies New-Borough, it is as old almost as the Conquest. It made so much <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> cloth formerly, that in the reign of Henry VIII. here flourished John Winscomb, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called Jack-of-Newbury, one of the greatest clothiers that ever was in England, who kept 100 looms in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>; and in the expedition to Flowden Field against the Scots, marched with 100 of his own men, all armed and clothed at his own expense; and he built all the west <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. Also Mr Kensic, the son of a clothier here, though afterwards a merchant in London, left 4000l. to the town, as well as 750l. to Reading, to encourage the woollen manufactory. It makes a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of shalloons and druggets, but not near so much broad cloth now as formerly; yet it is a flourishing town, with spacious streets, and a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> market <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, in which is the guild-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALL">hall</a>. In the neighbourhood, on the banks of the Kennet, there is a stratum of petrified wood dug out for firing, where they frequently find trunks of large oaks yet undecayed, with petrified hazel nuts, fir cones, &c. with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> and horns of stags, antelopes, &c. tusks of boars, and heads of beavers. The river Kennet, which abounds with excellent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TROUT">trout</a>, eels, and cray-fish, runs through the town. It was made a corporation by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, and is governed by a mayor, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a>, aldermen, &c. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> in 1811 was 4808. <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEWCASTLE">NEWCASTLE</a>-under-Line, a town in England, in the county of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFFORD">Stafford</a>, on a branch of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRENT">Trent</a>, is 15 miles <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of Stafford, 33 south south-east of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WARRINGTON">Warrington</a>, and 149 from London: had a castle, now in ruins; and is so called from an older castle, which formerly stood two miles off, at Chesterton-under-Line. It was incorporated by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> Henry I. and again by Queen Elizabeth and King <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. and is governed by a mayor, two justices, two bailiffs, and 24 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>. The population in 1811 was 6175. The clothing trade flourishes here; but its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> manufactory is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-HATS">hats</a>, here being an incorporated <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of felt-makers. A great quantity of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARE">ware</a> is made near this place. NEWCASTLE-on-Tyne, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the county of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTHUMBERLAND">Northumberland</a> in England, 15 miles north of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURHAM">Durham</a>, 94 north of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>, 63 south by east of Berwick, 60 east of Carlisle, and 271 from London, stands at the end of the Piets wall, on the north side of the Tyne, Newcastle over which it has a stately <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> into the bishopric of Durham, in which its suburb called Gateside is situated; for the liberties of Newcastle extend no farther than the great <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> gate upon the bridge, which has the arms of the bishop of Durham carved on the east side and those of Newcastle on the west side. W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 1. 27. N. Lat. 55° 5'. It is admitted to have been a Roman station, though no <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> at present appears, except at Pandion-gate, whose superstructure is of different workmanship and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODEL">model</a> from any others of the town, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> being circular. The Carpenter's tower is also of Roman original. In the Saxons <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> it was called Moncaster, from the monks here, who all fled when it was depopulated by the Danes; and afterwards Newcastle, from a castle built here by William the Conqueror's son, Robert, in 1080, to defend the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> against the Scots, whose kings had this town before the Norman conquest, and sometimes resided here. Several monasteries and houses were built here soon after the castle; and it was greatly enlarged and enriched by a good trade to the coasts of Germany, and by the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> of its coal to other parts of England; for which, and for other merchandise, it is become the great emporium of the north of England, it being the nearest and largest town in those parts, next to York. In the reign of Edward I. it was burnt by the Scots; but a very rich burgher, who was taken prisoner, soon ransomed himself for a good sum of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, and began the first fortifications of the place, which he extended from Sandgate to Pampeldon, and thence to the Austin friars gate; which the townsmen finished, and encompassed with stout walls, which extended two miles, wherein are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> gates and many turrets, with several casemates <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOMB">bomb</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>. To which two other gates were added in more <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> times, viz. Bridge-gate and Sand-gate: the wall between them was afterwards removed to open the quay. Edward III. granted the corporation the duties and customs of the town for seven years, to enable them to complete the fortification. It is a borough at least as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> as King Richard II. who granted that a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> should be carried before the mayor; and King Henry VI. made it a town and county incorporate of itself, independent of Northumberland. Henry VII. built a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> here for the Franciscans. Besides which, it had several <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> foundations, several of which structures have been converted to companies halls and private residences. In the reign of Henry VIII. this place is said to have exceeded in the strength and magnificence of its works all the cities of England, and most places in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. The town is governed by a mayor, 12 aldermen, a recorder, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a>, town clerk, a clerk of the chambers, two coroners, eight chamberlains, a sword-bearer, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAILIFF">bailiff</a>, and seven sergeants at mace. Its situation, especially the most busy part of it towards the river, is very uneven, it being built on the declivity of a steep hill, and the houses very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a>. The castle overlooks the whole town. That part built by Robert was of great strength, and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, and surrounded by two walls; the square was 62 feet by 54, and the walls 13 feet thick, within which was a chapel. The outward fortifications are now defaced, and their site crowded with buildings. The tower remains entire, and situated on a lofty eminence, and its <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> entrance is to the south. This castle belongs to the county, and makes no part of the liberties.—It is Newcastle now the county prison, and in the great hall the judges hold the assizes. Here Baliol king of Scotland did homage to King Edward I. in 1292; as did Edward Baliol in 1334 to King Edward III. Here is a magnificent <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> and a customhouse; and a very fine quay. There is a handsome mansion house for the mayor, who is allowed 1000l. a-year, for his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, besides a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COACH">coach</a> and barge. The old bridge was carried away in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a>, and the present was erected about 1775, of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> noble elliptic arches. With the old bridge 22 houses were thrown <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, and six lives lost. It was originally built of wood; but having been destroyed by fire in 1248, was rebuilt of stone, and consisted of 12 arches, three of which on the north side were closed up, and served for cellars: this was again rebuilt about 1450, and was crowded with wooden buildings; but near the middle was a tower with an iron gate, used as a town prison. A strong <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> crossed the bridge, which was used as a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGAZINE">magazine</a>. On the south <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a> was a statue of King Charles II. The water which destroyed this bridge, on November 11, 1771, was upwards of 12 feet above high water mark in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-TIDES">tides</a>.—On removing the foundations of the piers of the old bridge to erect the present, by observations made, and medals found, part of it is supposed to have existed from the time of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. It is computed that above 6000 keelmen are employed here, who have formed themselves into a friendly <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>; and by their own contributions, built a noble <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">hospital</a> containing 50 chambers, for such of their fraternity as are <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a>, disabled, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> past their labour; and it is supported by the contribution of those that are in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>. The town is extremely populous; and notwithstanding the multitude of those employed in and about the coal pits, with which the town is in a manner surrounded, has abundance of poor; but it has also many wealthy inhabitants, and it is said they pay above 4000l. a-year to their relief. It is observed, that this town has the greatest public revenue in its own <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> as a corporation, of any town in England, it being computed at no less than 8000l. a-year. In 1774, the receipts of the corporation were 20,360l. 9s. 8d.; and their disbursements about 19,445l. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of inhabitants in 1811 was 27,587, exclusive of a number of seamen who cannot be accurately estimated. Here are four churches or chapels. That of St Nicholas is the mother church, a curious fabric, built <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a>-wise by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAVID">David</a> king of Scots, 240 feet long, 75 broad, and proportionably high, with a tower steeple 194 feet in height, of Gothic <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>; also St Andrew's, St John's, and All Saints, lately rebuilt on the site of the old structure, of a circular form. Here are also several meeting houses, and four <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> for 300 children; a fine hall for the surgeons, and a large prison called Newgate; also an hospital for lunatics, another for the lying-in of married women, as well as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUND">fund</a> raised for the relief of those who are delivered at their own houses. Here is a well endowed and large infirmary, and an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> room that attracts <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, containing every useful apartment, and a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a> room 93 feet by 40: The front is ornamented with six Ionic pillars, &c. In another part of the town is a new <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>. Here is a very neat set of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a>. A free <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a> school was granted by James I. from an old foundation. Newcastle of St <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>'s hospital, in the vestry room of whose chapel is the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> of the officers of the corporation. There were formerly several palaces in this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, viz., Pampered hall, Lumley place, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">Earl</a>'s Place, Northumberland house, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WESTMORELAND">Westmoreland</a> place, &c. The free masons have lately erected an elegant hall, richly ornamented, to hold their lodge in, near High friar <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a>, capable of holding above 4000 of that ancient fraternity. Here is an hospital for 39 decayed freemen and their widows; and another for three clergymen's widows and three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> widows. The Maidens hospital, built in 1753, is endowed with 2400l. for six maiden women and six poor men. Dr Thomlin, a prebendary of St Paul's, and rector of Whicham in the bishopric of Durham, gave a library of above 6000 valuable books to the corporation, and settled a rent <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of 3l. a-year for ever for buying new ones; and Sir Walter Blacket, formerly one of its representatives in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, built a neat repository for them, and settled 23l. a-year for ever on a librarian. The upper or north part of the town, inhabited by the politer sort of people, is much pleasanter than that part next the river, and has three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a>, well built, and spacious streets. The river all the way up from Shields to Newcastle is broad, the channel safe, and the tide flows with a strong current to the town, and far beyond it. In the beginning of the civil wars, this town was taken and plundered by the Scotch fanatics, who here sold their king, Charles I. for 200,000l. in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and security for as much more. The glass works are very curious, and have more business of the fine sort than most other places: the duty on this article drawn by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> is said to amount to 200,000l. annually. Besides, it has a considerable manufacture of broad and narrow cloths, and several <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOAP">soap</a> boilers; and this place is famous for grindstones, for which there is such a demand, that scarce a ship stirs without them; from whence came the proverb, "That a Scotsman and a Newcastle grindstone travel all the world over." Ships fit for the coal trade are built here to perfection, with great strength. Here is a considerable manufactory of hardware and wrought iron, after the manner of that at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHEFFIELD">Sheffield</a>.—Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a> are on Tuesdays and Saturdays. Its <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a> in August, which last nine days, and October 29th, which last nine days. By an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of Queen Mary, the price of the carriage of goods hither from London by waggons was settled at 2d. per lib. London alone is said to consume at least 766,857 chaldrons of its coal every year; but as for the fish vendied in that city by the name of Newcastle salmon, it is more properly called Berwick salmon, the fresh salmon being taken near 50 miles farther, as far as the Tweed, and brought on the backs of horses to Shields, where it is cured, pickled, and sent on board for London. It is worth remembering, that at the assizes here in 1743, two old men were subpœna'd hither as witnesses from a neighbouring village, viz. one 135 years of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and his son 95, both hearty, and having their sight and hearing; and that in 1744, one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a> Turnbull died in this town aged 112, who had had four wives, the last of whom he had married when he was near 100 years old. The annual amount of the revenue of customs at this port, which Mr Brand in his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Newcastle states at 41,000l. is now very considerably up wards of 70,000l. The coals carried out of it annually (on an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a> from 1785 to 1791) were nearly 4,48,000 Newcastle chaldrons; the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of which is 1,187,200 tons. The following are the exports of coals from the Tyne for the years annexed. | Years | Coals, Chaldrons | Over <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> | Plantation | |-------|-----------------|----------|------------| | 1802 | 494,488 | 41,157 | 2844 | | 1803 | 505,137 | 42,808 | 1516 | | 1804 | 579,929 | 48,737 | 3852 | | 1805 | 552,827 | 47,213 | 2360 | The number of persons employed in the coal trade of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Tyne and Wear in 1792 exceeded 64,000. The manufacture of earthen ware is greatly increased, and carried on to great perfection in its neighbourhood, in seven potteries; and their produce exported hence to foreign parts, as well as to the different ports of this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>; some of which potteries constantly employ upwards of 100 persons, men, women, and children. New works of considerable <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> for the manufacture of iron have been established; as also a very capital manufactory for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, milled lead, &c. Independent of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> and white lead, the quantity of lead exported from the river Tyne during four years was as follows. | Years | Tons | Cts. | |-------|------|-----| | 1802 | 8609 | 18 | | 1803 | 6364 | 6 | | 1804 | 10352| 2 | | 1805 | 9163 | 3 | The trade with the West <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIA">India</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> is increasing, and may in time become very considerable; as the port has great advantages, in being able to supply on the cheapest terms many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> wanted in those islands; such as coals, grindstones, lime, bricks, tiles, iron wares, &c.; and is most advantageously situated for the re-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a> of the West India produce to the ports on the Baltic, to Germany, the United Provinces, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>, and part of France; and moreover, the risk of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, and the rate of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSURANCE">insurance</a>, not being greater than between those islands and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-LIVERPOOL">Liverpool</a>, and some other ports on the western <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of this kingdom. The population of Newcastle in 1811 was 271,877, and it is daily increasing in inhabitants and opulence. It has long been noted for hospitality and good living. Great improvements have been made in the town, by opening new streets, and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PAVING">paving</a> the principal ones, in the same manner as in London. To the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIST">list</a> of public edifices of modern erection, and mentioned above, viz. the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> assembly rooms, and the elegant theatre, which were built by subscription, and the superb <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> church of All Saints, built at a very great expense by the parishioners, may be added a commodious riding house, built also by subscription.

NEWCASTLE

Pages 854-855
Duke of. See Cavendish. NEW ENGLAND. See ENGLAND, New. NEW FOREST of Hampshire in England, is a tract of at least 40 miles in compass, which had many populous towns and villages, and 36 mother churches, till it was destroyed and turned into a forest by William the Conqueror. There are nine walks in it; and to every one a keeper, under a lord warden, besides two rangers, and a bow-bearer. As this large tract lay many ages open and exposed to invasions from foreigners, King Henry VIII. built some castles in it: and it has now several pretty towns and villages. It is situated in that part of Hampshire which is bounded on the east by Southampton river, and on the south by the British channel. It possesses advantages of situation, with respect to the convenience of water carriage and nearness to the dock yards, superior to every other forest, having in its neighbourhood several ports and places of shelter for shipping timber, among which Lymington is at the distance of only two miles, Bexley about half a mile, and Redbridge three or four miles from the forest; and the navigation to Portsmouth, the most considerable dock yard in this kingdom, is only about 30 miles from the nearest of those places. This is the only forest belonging to the crown of which the origin is known. Doomsday-book contains the most distinct account of its afforestation by William the Conqueror: the contents of every field, farm, or estate afforested, in hides, carucates, or virgates, by which the extent of land was then computed, together with the names of the hundreds and villages, and of the former proprietors (which are for the most part Saxon), the rent or yearly value of each possession, and the tax which had been paid for it to the crown during the reign of Edward the Confessor, before the inhabitants were expelled, and that part of the country laid waste, are all to be found in that most curious and venerable record. New Forest. Wishing to discover the original extent of the forest, we extracted, for our own information, all that relates to it in that ancient survey. The extract is far too voluminous for insertion. The names of many of the places having been changed since that time, it is difficult to ascertain with precision what were then the limits of the forest. The oldest perambulation we have met with is among the Pleas of the Forest, in the eighth year of King Edward I., preserved in the Chapter-house at Westminster. The boundaries there described include all the country from Southampton river on the east to the Avon on the west, following the sea coast as far as the southern boundary between those rivers, and extending northwards as far as North Chalkeford, or North Charford, on the west, and to Wade and Orebrugg, or Owerbridge, on the east; and the greatest part, if not the whole, of that extensive district, is mentioned in Doomsday book to be the forest belonging to the crown. Another perambulation was however made in the 29th of the same king, which leaves out a great part of the country contained within the former.
