This perambulation, which is preserved in the Tower of London, confines the forest to limits which, as far as we can trace them, appear to have been followed in the 22d year of Charles II., when the forest was again perambulated. By the Charta de Foresta, all lands not belonging to the crown which had been afforested by Henry II., Richard I., or King John, were to be disafforested; but as no provision was made for the reduction of the more ancient afforestations, it is easy to account for the great diminution of this forest in the reign of Edward I., who was not a prince likely to submit to any encroachment on his rights. The perambulation of the 22d of Charles II., is the last which we find on record: it contains the present legal bounds of the forest, and was given to the surveyors as their guide, in taking the plan which they have made lately by direction. From that plan, with the approbation of the lords commissioners of his majesty's treasury, an engraving was made. According to the last-mentioned perambulation and the plan, the forest extends from Godshill on the north-west to the sea on the south-east, about 20 miles; and from Hardley on the east to Ringwood on the west, about 15 miles; and contains within those limits about 92,365 acres statute measure. The whole of that quantity, however, is not forest land, or now the property of the crown: there are several manors and other considerable freehold estates within the perambulation, belonging to individuals, to the amount of about 24,797 acres; about 625 acres are copyhold or customary lands belonging to his majesty's manor of Lyndhurst; about 1004 acres are lease-hold under the crown, granted for certain terms of years, and forming part of the demised land revenue, under the management of the surveyor-general of crown lands; about 901 acres are purprestures or encroachments on the forest; about 1193 acres more are enclosed lands held by the master-keepers and groom-keepers, with their respective lodges; and the remainder, being about 63,845 acres, are woods and waste lands of the forest. To perpetuate the spot where William Rufus was killed by the glance of an arrow shot at a stag, a triangular stone was erected in 1745. George III. visited Newfoundland situated this spot in 1789. In August 1782, a curious ancient golden cross was found here by a labouring man digging turf. It weighed above an ounce of gold, and had on one side an engraving of our Saviour, and on the other, the ladder, spear, nails, and other emblems of his sufferings. New s="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland. See Holland, New. New lass="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York. See York, New. New s="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZEALAND">Zealand. See Zealand, New. New Year's Gifts, presents made on the first day of the new year. Nomin Marcellus refers the origin of this custom among the Romans to Tatusius king of the Sabines, who reigned at Rome conjointly with Romulus, and who having considered as a good omen a present of some branches cut in a wood consecrated to Strema, the goddess of strength, which he received on the first day of the new year, authorized this custom afterwards, and gave to these presents the name of strema. However this may be, the Romans on that day celebrated a festival in honour of Janus, and paid their respects at the same time to Juno; but they did not pass it in idleness, lest they should become indolent during the rest of the year. They sent presents to one another of figs, dates, honey, &c. to show their friends that they wished for a happy and agreeable life. Clients, that is to say, those who were under the protection of the great, carried presents of this kind to their patrons, adding to them a small piece of silver. Under Augustus, the senate, the knights, and the people, presented such gifts to him, and in his absence deposited them in the capitol. Of the succeeding princes some adopted this custom and others abolished it; but it always continued among the people. The early Christians condemned it, because it appeared to be a relic of Paganism and a species of superstition; but when it began to have no other object than that of being a mark of veneration and esteem, the church ceased to disapprove it.

NEWFOUNDLAND

Pages 855-856

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, belonging to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, lying between 46° 50' and 51° 30' N. Lat. and between 53° 30' and 58° 22' W. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. The form is that of an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> triangle, the base <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> south side being 80 leagues in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>; the east side is the longest; and the whole circumference about 150 leagues. It is bounded on the north by the straits of Belleisle, which separate it from <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LABRADOR">Labrador</a>; on the east and south it hath the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATLANTIC_OCEAN">Atlantic ocean</a>, and on the west the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of St Lawrence. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> is rather severe; and the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, at least on the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, which is all that we know of it, is <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> and barren. A few <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a> vegetables, with strawberries and raspberries, are all its produce. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> within <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> is mountainous, and abounds with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>; there are several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> which are plentifully stored with various sorts of fish, abundance of deep bays, and many good ports. St John's and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACENTIA">Placentia</a> are the two <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> settlements, and at each of these there is a fort; the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of people who remain here in the winter hath been computed at 4000. The French, by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-UTRECHT">Utrecht</a>, were permitted to fish from <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BONAVISTA">Bonavista</a> on the east side round the north of the island to Point Rich on the west; and by the treaty of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, they are allowed the isles of St Pierre and Miquelon, upon which they are to dry their fish, but not to erect fortifications of any kind. The great importance of this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> arises from its fishery, which is in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> carried on by the inhabitants at the several harbours, which are about 20 in number, who take vast quantities of cod near the coast, which they bring in and cure at their leisure, in order to have it ready for the ships when they arrive. But the great and extensive fishery is on the banks at some distance from the island. The great <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> lies 20 leagues from the nearest point of land, from the latitude 41° to 49°, stretching 300 miles in length and 75 in breadth.—To the east of this lies the False Bank; the next is styled Vert, or the Green Bank, about 240 miles long, and 120 over; then Banquero, about the same size; the shoals of Sand Island, Whale Bank, and the Bank of St <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>'s, with several others of less <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, all abounding with fish. The cod are caught only by a hook; an expert fisher <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> take from 150 to 300 and upwards in a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>; for the fish never bite in the night: the labour is very great. The season is from May to October, in the height of which there are from 500 to 700 sail upon the banks at a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. The fish caught in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> months are best; they are cured in very different ways. Some are styled <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> fish, others mud fish, which are stowed and salted in the hold, and will not keep long; but the best and most valuable are the dried cod. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> taken is prodigious: yet in some seasons and in different places varies considerably, as the fish frequently change their stations. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> ships, as they are called, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIE">lie</a> upon the banks, with the help of their boats take and cure their own fish, and as soon as they are full sail for a market. The sack ships proceed directly to the island, where they purchase fish from the inhabitants either by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BARTER">barter</a> or bills of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a>. The principal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a> for cod are <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and the West Indies. The value of this fishery is computed at some hundred thousand pounds annually; employing, besides several hundred ships, some thousands of seamen, and affording a maintenance to a number of tradesmen of different occupations, by which many large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> on the west side of England accumulate much wealth, and at the same time contribute in many respects to the benefit of the public. The great utility of this fishery was very early seen, and very vigorously pursued; for in the beginning of the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> James I., we had two hundred and fifty sail employed therein. It is computed, that three quintals of wet fish make one quintal of dried cod. Besides, the livers of every hundred quintals make a hogshead of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>; and exclusive of these there are many lesser advantages that go in diminution of the expense. The fishery, as we have said above, produces differently in different seasons; but it is judged to be a very good one when it produces 300,000 quintals of fish and 3000 barrels of oil, both equally saleable and valuable commodities. As every ship carries twelve, and each of their boats eight men, and as these return home in six months, there cannot be a more noble nursery for seamen. The artificers and traders employed in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, victualling, and repairing these vessels, are very numerous in the respective ports from which they sail. These circumstances justify the particular <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> paid by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> to this branch of the public <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>; in respect to which that they may be well informed, an annual and very distinct account, by which the whole is seen at one view, is delivered by the proper officer to the governor of Newfoundland, that is, to the commodore of his majesty's squadron. Mr Pennant, in the appendix to his Arctic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, gives us, from what appears to be very good authority, the following account of this island. "Within the circuit of 60 miles of the southern part, the country is hilly, but not mountainous. The hills increase in height as they recede from the sea; their course is irregular, not forming a chain of hills, but rising and falling abruptly. The coasts are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and the shores most remarkably bold. The same may be said of almost every part of this vast island. The country is much wooded, and the hills (such as have not flat tops to admit the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> to stagnate on them) are clothed with birch, with hazel, spruce, fir, and pine, all small; which is chiefly owing to the inhabitants taking off the bark to cover the fish stages. This <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> is so indented by the fine and deep bays of Placentia, St <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONCEPTION">Conception</a>, and Trinity, that it may be penetrated in all parts, which is done for the sake of fowling, or the procuring of spars for <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a>, oars, &c. The island is on all sides pierced with deep bays, which peninsulate it in many places by isthmuses most remarkably narrow.—The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> on the south-west side, near the sea, are very high, and terminate in lofty headlands; such are Chapeau Rouge, a most remarkably high promontory, Cape St Mary's, and Cape le Hune. Such in general is the formation of the island; on the north-east, most of the hills in the interior part of the country terminate pyramidically, but form no chain. The interior parts of the country consist chiefly of morasses, or dry barren hummocks, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> land, with frequent <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a> or ponds, and in some places covered with stunted <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> spruce. The rivers of Newfoundland are unfit for <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, but they are of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in floating <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the wood with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> floods. Still the rivers and the brooks are excellent guides for the hunters of beavers and other animals, to penetrate up the country, which as yet has never been done deeper than 30 miles. Near the brooks it is that timber is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> met with, but seldom above three or four miles inland, and in valleys; the hills in the northern district being naked and barren. "In some parts of Newfoundland there is timber sufficiently large for the building of merchant ships: the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HULK">hulk</a> is made of juniper, and the pine furnishes masts and yards; but as yet none has been found large enough for a mast for a large <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTER">cutter</a>. The fishery is divided into two seasons; that on the shore, or the shore season, commences about the 25th of April, and ends about the 10th of October; the boats fish in from four to 20 fathoms of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. The most important, the bank fishing-season, begins the 10th of May, and continues till the last of September, and is carried on in 30 to 45 fathoms deep of water. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BANKING">Banking</a> vessels have sailed from St John's to the bank as early as the 12th of April. At first they use pork or birds for a bait; but as they catch fish, they supply themselves with a shell Newfound-fish called clams, which is found in the belly of the cod. The next bait is the lobster; after that the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERRING">herring</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANCE">lance</a>, which last till <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUNE">June</a>, when the capelan comes on the coast, and is another bait. In August the squid comes into use, and finally the herring again. The greatest number of cod fish taken by a single fisherman in the season has been 12,000, but the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a> is 7,000. The largest fish which has been taken was four feet three inches long, and weighed 46 pounds. A banking vessel of 10,000 fish ought to be filled in three weeks, and so in proportion; and 80 quintals (11215 each) for a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> in the same time. "In 1785, 541 English vessels fished on the bank, a number exceeding that of the French. A heap of dried fish, 20 feet long and ten wide, and four deep, contains 300 quintals. Such a heap settles, in the course of 48 hours after it is made, about 1/2. An extraordinary splitter will split five quintals of fish in an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>. The average in that time is two. There is no fishing during winter, on account of the inclemency of the season. It is supposed that the fish in a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> quit the banks before that time, as in general they are very scarce when the fishing vessels go upon the banks early in the spring. "There are a few small towns on the coasts, which have gardens sown with English <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a>; but many of the inhabitants quit the country in winter. "An <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a> or some sea officer is generally governor of Newfoundland."

NEWMARKET

Pages 856-856

in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CAMBRIDGESHIRE">Cambridgeshire</a>, 13 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, 13 from St Edmundsbury, and 60 from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, is a town with one <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> street, the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> side in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a>, the south side in Cambridgeshire. It is a healthy <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> thoroughfare in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> from London to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a>; but stands mostly by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> races every year in April and October, here being the finest course in England; on which there is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a> when he comes to the races, which was built by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. The king gives a plate <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> two every year, besides those given by the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>; and wagers are laid upon the horses, which are seldom under 500l. and often above 1000l. Here are two coffeehouses, at which, every night and morning during the races, there is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAMING">gaming</a>, as there is also at the houses of the nobility and gentry. Here are also cock matches. Here is a little chapel, which is a chapel of ease to the mother <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> at Ditton; and another in the Suffolk side, which is parochial. The town was burnt in 1683, but soon rebuilt; and in 1811 contained 1917 inhabitants.

NEWROSS

Pages 856-856

a borough town in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEXFORD">Wexford</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEINSTER">Leinster</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, 67 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>. This town was formerly walled, and some of the gates still remain. It lies on the river <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARROW">Barrow</a>, which is here very deep, and ships of burden can come up to the quay even when the tide is out. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, but the customhouse and quay are both small, and sometimes overloaded many feet. It is one of the staple ports for exporting <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, yet its trade is but inconsiderable; beef and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a> are the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> exported. Here is a barrack for a troop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, and a good ferry into the county of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KILKENNY">Kilkenny</a>. Near this town is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a>-school. It is also a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POST">post</a> town, and gives <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">earl</a> to the family of Gore. It was formerly fortified, and adorned

NEWSPAPERS

Pages 856-857

periodical publications, daily, weekly, &c., for the purpose of communicating to the world every thing of importance, whether <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> literary, &c., which is going on. They have tended much to the dissemination of learning, and have served many other valuable purposes; and while they are carried on with candour, impartiality, and ability, they are unquestionably a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> national benefit. When this, however, is not the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, and it often happens, they disgrace their authors, and are highly injurious to the public. They were first published in England, August 22, 1642. Journal de Scavans, a French <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, was first published in 1665, though one was printed in England, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of the Public Intelligence, by Sir Roger L'Estrange, 1663, which he dropped, on the publication of the first <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> Gazette. Newspapers and pamphlets were prohibited by <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROCLAMATION">proclamation</a> 1680. Though at the Revolution prohibitions of this kind were done away, and the press set at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, yet newspapers were afterwards made objects of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-TAXATION">taxation</a>, and for this purpose were first stamped in 1713. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of them, however, gradually increased; and there were printed in the whole <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> during the years 1775, 12,680,000; 1776, 12,830,000; 1777, 13,159,642; 1778, 13,240,059; 1779, 14,106,842; 1780, 14,217,371; 1781, 14,397,622; 1782, 15,272,519. They are now still more numerous. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a> number of newspapers printed in England at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the reign of George II. was 9,464,790. The number in 1792, was 14,935,639; in 1792, it was 15,055,760. Chalmers' <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a> of Ruddiman, p. 442.

NEWTON

Pages 857-861

SIR <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">ISAAC</a>, one of the greatest philosophers and mathematicians the world has ever produced, was the only child of Mr John Newton of Colesworth, not far from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANTHAM">Grantham</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-LINCOLNSHIRE">Lincolnshire</a>, who had an estate of about 120l. per annum, which he kept in his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. He was born at that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> on Christmas <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> 1642. His father dying when he was young, his mother's <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, a clergyman of the name of Ayscough, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Askew, who lived near her, and directed all her affairs after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Mr Newton, put her son to school at Grantham. When he had finished his school learning, his mother took him home, intending, as she had no other child, to have the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>; and that he, as his father had done, should occupy his own estate. But his uncle happening to find him in a hay loft at Grantham working a mathematical problem, and having otherwise observed the boy's mind to be uncommonly bent upon learning, he prevailed upon her to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> with him; and she sent Newton to Trinity <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, where her brother, having himself been a member of it, had still many friends. Isaac was soon taken notice of by Dr Isaac <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARROW">Barrow</a>; who, observing his bright genius, contracted a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> friendship for him. M. de Fontenelle tells us, "That in learning <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a> he did not <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> Euclid, who seemed to him too plain and simple, and unworthy of taking up his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. He understood him almost before he read him; and a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> of his eye upon the contents of his theorems was sufficient to make him <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of them. He advanced at once to the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a> of Des Cartes, Kepler's <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPTICS">Optics</a>, &c. It is certain that he had made his great discoveries in geometry, and laid the foundation of his two famous works, the Principia and Optics, by the time he was 24 years of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>." In 1664, he took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of bachelor of arts; and in 1668 that of master, being elected the year before, fellow of his college. He had before this time discovered the method of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLUXIONS">fluxions</a>; and in 1669 he was chosen professor of mathematics in the university of Cambridge, upon the resignation of Mr Barrow. The same year, and the two following, he read a course of optical lectures in Latin, in the public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> of the university; an English translation of which was printed at <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> in 1728, in 8vo, as was the Latin original the next year in 4to. From the year 1671 to 1679, he held a correspondence by letters with Mr Henry Oldenburg secretary of the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>, and Mr John Collins fellow of that society; which letters contain a variety of curious observations. Concerning the origin of his discoveries, we are told that as he sat alone in a garden, the falling of some apples from a tree led him into a speculation on the power of gravity; that as this power is not diminished at the remotest distance from the centre of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> to which we can rise, it appeared to him reasonable to conclude, that it must extend much farther than was usually thought; and pursuing this speculation, by comparing the periods of the several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a> with their distances from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, he found, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any power like gravity held them in their courses, its strength must decrease in the duplicate proportion of the increase of distance. This inquiry was dropped; but resumed again, and gave rise to his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> the treatise which he published in 1687, under the name of Mathematical Principles of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">Philosophy</a>; a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> looked upon as the production of a celestial intelligence rather than of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. The very same year in which this great work was published, the university of Cambridge was attacked by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> James II. when Mr Newton was one of its most zealous defenders, and was accordingly nominated one of the delegates of that university to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>; and the next year he was chosen one of their members for the convention <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>, in which he sat till it was dissolved. In 1696, Mr Montague, then <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> of the exchequer, and afterwards <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALIFAX">Halifax</a>, obtained for him the king the office of warden of the mint; in which employment he was of signal <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, when the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> was called in to be recurred. Three years after, he was appointed master of the mint; a place of very considerable profit, which he held till his death. In 1699, he was elected one of the members of the Royal Academy of Sciences at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>. In 1701, he was a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> Newton time chosen member of parliament for the university of Cambridge. In 1724, he published his Optics; which is a piece of philosophy so new, that the science may be considered as entirely indebted to our author. In 1735, he was knighted by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a>. In 1757, he published his Arithmetica Universalis. In 1711, his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALYSIS">Analysis</a> per Quantitatem <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">Series</a>, Fluxiones et Differentias, &c., was published by William Jones, Esq. In 1712, several letters of his were published in the Commercium Epistolicum. In the reign of George I, he was better known at court than before. The princess of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, afterwards queen consort of England, used frequently to propose questions to him, and to declare that she thought herself happy to live at the same time with him, and have the pleasure and advantages of his conversation. He had written a treatise of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">chronology</a>, which he did not think of publishing; but the princess desired an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a>, which she would never part with. However, a copy of it stole abroad, and was carried into France, where it was translated and printed, with some observations, which were afterwards answered by Sir Isaac. But, in 1728, the Chronology itself was published at London in quarto; and was attacked by several persons, and as zealously defended by Sir Isaac's friends. The main <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of it was to find out, from some tracts of the most ancient Greek <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>, what was the position of the colours with respect to the fixed stars, in the time of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIRON">Chiron</a> the centaur. As it is now known that these stars have a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a> of one degree in 72 years, if it be once known through what fixed stars the colours passed in Chiron's time, by taking the distance of these stars from those through which it now passes, we might determine what <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of years has elapsed since Chiron's time. As Chiron was one of the Argonauts, this would fix the time of that famous expedition, and consequently that of the Trojan <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>; the two great events upon which all ancient chronology depends. Sir Isaac places them 500 years nearer the birth of Christ than other chronologers have done. This great man had all along enjoyed a settled and equal state of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> to the age of 80, when he began to be afflicted with an incontinence of urine. However, for the five following years, he had great intervals of ease, which he procured by the observance of a strict regimen. It was then believed that he certainly had the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>; and when the paroxysms were so violent, that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> drops of sweat ran <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a>, he never uttered the least complaint, or expressed the smallest degree of impatience; but, as soon as he had a moment's ease, would smile and talk with his usual cheerfulness. Till then he always read and wrote several hours in a day. He had the perfect <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of all his senses and understanding till the day before he died, which was on the 20th of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1726-7, in the 87th year of his age. He lay in state in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a> chamber at Westminster, and on the 28th of March his body was conveyed into Westminster <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a>; the pall being supported by the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">lord</a> chancellor, the dukes of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MONTROSE">Montrose</a> and Roxburgh, and the earls of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PEMBROKE">Pembroke</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUSSEX">Sussex</a>, and Macclesfield. The bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROCHESTER">Rochester</a> read the funeral service, being attended by all the clergy of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. The corpse was interred <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> at the entrance into the choir, where a noble monument is erected to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>. Sir Isaac was of a middling stature, and in the latter part of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> somewhat inclined to be fat. His countenance was pleasing, and at the same time venerable. He never made use of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECTACLES">spectacles</a>, and lost but one tooth during his whole life. His temper is said to have been so equal and mild, that no accident could disturb it. Of this the following remarkable instance is related. Sir Isaac had a favourite little dog, which he called <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIAMOND">Diamond</a>; and being one day called out of his study into the next room, Diamond was left behind. When Sir Isaac returned, having been absent but a few minutes, he had the mortification to find, that Diamond having thrown down a lighted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a> among some papers, the nearly finished labour of many years was in flames, and almost consumed to ashes. This loss, as Sir Isaac was then very far advanced in years, was irretrievable; yet without once striking the dog, he only rebuked him with this exclamation, "Oh! Diamond! Diamond! thou little knowestest the mischief thou hast done!" He was a great lover of peace, and would rather have chosen to remain in obscurity than to have the calm of life ruffled by those storms and disputes which genius and learning always draw upon those that are peculiarly eminent for them. In contemplating his genius it presently becomes a doubt, which of these endowments had the greatest share, sagacity, penetration, strength or diligence: and after all, the mark that seems most to distinguish it is, that he himself made the justest estimation of it, declaring, that, if he had done the world any service, it was due to nothing but industry and patient thought; that he kept the subject under consideration constantly before him, and waited till the first dawning opened gradually, by little and little, into a full and clear <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>. It is said, that when he had any mathematical problems or solutions in his mind, he would never quit the subject on any account. Dinner has been often three hours ready for him before he could be brought to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>; and his man often said, when he has been getting up in a morning, he has sometimes begun to dress, and with one leg in his breeches sat down again on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BED">bed</a>, where he has remained for hours before he got his clothes on. From his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of peace, no doubt, arose that unusual kind of horror which he had for all disputes; a steady unbroken <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, free from those frequent recoilings inseparably incident to others, was his peculiar felicity; he knew it, and he knew the value of it. No wonder then that controversy was looked on as his bane. When some objections, hastily made to his discoveries concerning light and colours, induced him to lay aside the design he had of publishing his optic lectures, we find him reflecting on that dispute, into which he was unavoidably drawn thereby, in these terms: "I blamed my own imprudence for parting with so real a blessing as my quiet, to run after a shadow." It is true this shadow (as Mr Fontenelle observes) did not escape him afterwards, nor did it cost him that quiet which he so much valued, but proved as much a real <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> to him as his quiet itself; yet this was a happiness of his own making: he took a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>, from these disputes, not to publish any more about that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> till he had put it above the reach of controversy, by the exactest experiments and the strictest demonstrations; and accordingly it has never been called in question since. In the same temper, af- ter he had sent the manuscript of his Principia to the Royal Society, with his consent to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a> of it by them, upon Mr Hook's injuriously insisting that himself had demonstrated Kepler's problem before our author, he determined, rather than be involved again in a controversy, to suppress the third book, and was very hardly prevailed upon to alter that resolution. It is true, the public was thereby a gainer; that book, which is indeed no more than a corollary of some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPOSITIONS">propositions</a> in the first, being originally drawn up in the popular way, with the design to publish it in that form; whereas he was now convinced that it would be best not to let it go abroad without a strict demonstration. After all, notwithstanding his anxious care to avoid every occasion of breaking his intense application to study, he was at a great distance from being steeped in philosophy: on the contrary, he could lay aside his thoughts, though engaged in the most intricate researches, when his other affairs required his attendance; and as soon as he had leisure, resume the subject at the point where he had left off. This he seems to have done not so much by any extraordinary strength of memory, as by the force of his inventive <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a>, to which every thing opened itself again with ease, if nothing intervened to ruffle him. The readiness of his <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> made him not think of putting his memory much to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a>: but this was the offspring of a vigorous intrepidity of thought, out of which he was but a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> man. He spent therefore, the prime of his age in those abstruse researches, when his situation in a college gave him leisure, and even while study was his proper profession. But as soon as he was removed to the mint, he applied himself chiefly to the business of that office; and so far quitted mathematics and philosophy, as not to engage in any pursuits of either kind afterwards. The amiable <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a> is represented as standing foremost in the character of this great man's mind and manners. It was in reality greater than can be easily imagined, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> be readily believed; yet it always <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> so without any <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a>, though the whole world, says Fontenelle, conspired against it; and let us add, though he was thereby robbed of his invention of fluxions. Nicholas Mercator publishing his Logarithmotechnia in 1668, where he gave the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-QUADRATURE">quadrature</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HYPERBOLA">hyperbola</a> by an infinite series, which was the first appearance in the learned world of a series of this sort drawn from the particular <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the curve, and that in a manner very new and abstracted; Dr Barrow, then at Cambridge, where Mr Newton, at that time about 26 years of age, resided, recollected that he had met with the same thing in the writings of that young <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a>; and there not confined to the hyperbola only, but extended, by general forms, to all sorts of curves, even such as are <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a>; to their quadratures, their rectifications, and their centres of gravity; to the solids formed by their rotations, and to the surfaces of those solids; so that, when their determinations were possible, the series stopped at a certain point, or at least their sums were given by stated rules; and, if the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> determinations were impossible, they could yet be infinitely approximated; which is the happiest and most refined method, says Mr Fontenelle, of supplying the defects of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> knowledge that man's imagination could possibly invent. To be master of so fruitful and general a theory was a mine of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> to a geometrician; but it was a greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> to have been the discoverer of so surprising and ingenious a system. So that Mr Newton finding, by Mercator's book, that he was in the way to it, and that others might follow in his track, should naturally have been forward to open his treasures, and secure the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, which consisted in making the discovery; but he contented himself with his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a> which he had found, without regarding the glory. What an idea does it give us of his unparalleled modesty, when we see him declaring, that he thought Mercator had entirely discovered his secret, or that others would, before he was of a proper age for writing? His MS. upon infinite series was communicated to none but Mr John Collins and the lord Brounker; and even that had not been complied with, but for Dr Barrow, who would not suffer him to indulge his modesty so much as he desired. It is further observed, concerning this part of his character, that he never talked either of himself or others, nor ever behaved in such a manner as to give the most malicious censurers the least occasion even to suspect him of vanity. He was candid and affable, and always put himself upon a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> with his company. He never thought either his merit or his reputation sufficient to excuse him from any of the common offices of social life; no singularities, either natural or affected, distinguished him from other men. Though he was firmly attached to the church of England, he was averse to the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a> of the non-conformists. He judged of men by their manners; and the true schismatics, in his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, were the vicious and the wicked. Not that he confined his principles to natural <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, for he was thoroughly persuaded of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVELATION">revelation</a>; and amidst the great variety of books which he had constantly before him, that which he studied with the greatest application was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIBLE">Bible</a>: and he understood the nature and force of moral certainty as well as he did that of a strict demonstration. Sir Isaac did not neglect the opportunities of doing good, when the revenues of his patrimony, and a profitable employment, improved by a prudent economy, put it in his power. We have two remarkable instances of his bounty and generosity; one to Mr M'Laurin, professor of mathematics at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, to whom he offered £20. per annum, and the other to his niece Barton, on whom he settled an annuity of £100. When decency upon any occasion required expense and show, he was magnificent without prodiging it, and with a very good <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>; at all other times, that pomp which seems great to low minds only, was utterly retrenched, and the expense reserved for better uses. He never married, and perhaps he never had leisure to think of it. Being immersed in profound studies during the prime of his age, and afterwards engaged in an employment of great importance, and even quite taken up with the company which his merit drew to him, he was not sensible of any vacancy in life, or of the want of a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol5.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a> at home. He left £32,000l. at his death; but made no will, which Mr Fontenelle tells us was because he thought a legacy was no gift. As to his works, besides what were published in his lifetime, there were found after his death, among his papers, several discourses upon subjects of antiquity, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">chemistry</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-NEWTONIAN_PHILOSOPHY">Newtonian philosophy</a>, the doctrine of the universe, and particularly of the heavenly bodies, their laws, affections, &c., as delivered by Sir Isaac Newton. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> Newtonian philosophy is applied very differently; whence <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> confused notions relating thereto. Some authors under this philosophy include all the corpuscular philosophy, considered as it now stands corrected and reformed by the discoveries and improvements made in several parts thereof by Sir Isaac Newton. In which <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> it is that Graveshane calls his elements of physics, Introductio <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AD">ad</a> Philosophiam Newtonianam. And in this sense the Newtonian is the same with the new philosophy; and stands contradistinguished from the Cartesian, the Peripatetic, and the ancient Corpuscular. Others, by Newtonian philosophy, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> the method or order which Sir Isaac Newton observes in philosophizing; viz. the reasoning and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> of conclusions directly from phenomena, exclusive of all previous hypotheses; the beginning from simple principles; deducing the first powers and laws of nature from a few select phenomena, and then applying those laws, &c., to account for other things. And in this sense the Newtonian philosophy is the same with the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIMENTAL_PHILOSOPHY">experimental philosophy</a>, and stands opposed to the ancient corpuscular. Others, by Newtonian philosophy, mean that wherein physical bodies are considered mathematically, and where geometry and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a> are applied to the solution of the appearances of nature. In which sense the Newtonian is the same with the mechanical and mathematical philosophy. Others again, by Newtonian philosophy, understand that part of physical knowledge which Sir Isaac Newton has handled, improved, and demonstrated, in his Principia. Others, lastly, by Newtonian philosophy, mean the new principles which Sir Isaac Newton has brought into philosophy; the new system founded thereon; and the new solutions of phenomena thence deduced; or that which characterizes and distinguishes his philosophy from all others.—Which is the sense wherein we shall chiefly consider it. As to the history of this philosophy, we have nothing to add to what has been given in the preceding article. It was first made public in the year 1687, by the author, then a fellow of Trinity College, Cambridge, and in the year 1713, republished with considerable improvements.—Several authors have since attempted to make it plainer; by setting aside many of the more sublime mathematical researches, and substituting either more obvious reasonings or experiments in lieu thereof; particularly Whiston in his Praelect. Phys. Mathemat. Graveshane in Element. et Instit. and Dr <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PEMBERTON">Pemberton</a> in his View. The whole of the Newtonian philosophy, as delivered by the author, is contained in his Principia or Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy. He founds his system on the following definitions: 1. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of the same, arising from its density and bulk conjunctly.—Thus <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> density, in a double space, is quadruple in quantity; in a triple space, sextuple in Newtonian quantity, &c. 2. The quantity of motion is the measure of the same, arising from the velocity and quantity of matter conjunctly. This is evident, because the motion of the whole is the motion of all its parts; and therefore in a body double in quantity, with equal velocity, the motion is double, &c. 3. The vis insita, or innate force of matter, is a power of resisting, by which every body, as much as it lies, endeavours to persevere in its present state, whether it be of rest, or moving uniformly forward in a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> line.—This <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a> is proved to be just, only by the difficulty we find in moving any thing out of its place; and this difficulty is by some reckoned to proceed only from gravity. They contend, that in these <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> where we can prevent the force of gravity from acting upon bodies, this power of resistance becomes insensible, and the greatest quantities of matter may be put in motion by the very least force. Thus there have been balances formed so exact, that when loaded with 200 <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> in each <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a>, they would turn by the addition of a single drachm. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> 400lb. of matter was put in motion by a single drachm, i.e. by \(\frac{1}{3}\) part of its own quantity: and even this small weight, they say, is only necessary on account of the inaccuracy of the machine: so that we have no reason to suppose, that, if the friction could be entirely removed, it would take more force to move a ton weight than a grain of sand. This objection, however, is not taken notice of by Sir Isaac: and he bestows on the resisting power above mentioned the name of vis inertiae; a phrase which is perhaps not well chosen, and with which inferior writers have endeavoured to make their readers merry at the expense of Newton. A force of inactivity, it has been said, is a forceless force; and analogous to a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, and a tempestuous calm. But objections of more importance have been made to the whole of this doctrine than those which merely respect the term vis inertiae. “An endeavour to remain at rest (we are told) is unnecessary, whilst nothing attempts to disturb the rest. It is likewise impossible to be conceived, as it implies a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a>. A man, by opposing force to force, may endeavour not to be moved; but this opposition is an endeavour of not to move, not with a design to move, but by counteracting another force to prevent being moved. An endeavour not to move therefore cannot exist in bodies, because it is absurd; and if we <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> to fact, we shall find every body in an actual and constant endeavour to move.” It has been likewise observed, and we think justly, that “if bodies could continue to move by any innate force, they might also begin to move by that force. For the same cause which can move a body with a given velocity at one time, could do it, if present, at any other time; and therefore if the force by which bodies continue in motion were innate and essential to them, they would begin to move of themselves, which is not true.” Newton indeed says that this innate force is the cause of motion under certain circumstances only, or when the body is acted upon by a force impressed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">ab</a> extra. But if this impressed force do not continue as well Newtonian as begin the motion, if it cease the instant that Philosophy, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> is over, and the body continue to move by its vis inertiae, why is the body ever stopped? "If in the beginning of the motion the body, by its innate force, overcomes a certain resistance of friction and air, in any following times, the force being undiminished, it will overcome the same resistance forever. These resistances, therefore, could never change the state of a moving body, because they cannot change the quantity of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> force. But this is contrary to universal <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>." For these reasons we are inclined to think that bodies are wholly <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSIVE">passive</a>; that they endeavour nothing; and that they continue in motion not by any innate force or vis insita, but by that force, whatever it be, which begins the motion, and which, whilst it remains with the moving body, is gradually diminished, and at last overcome by opposite forces, when the body of course ceases to move. 4. An impressed force is an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> exerted upon a body, in order to change its state, either of rest or of moving uniformly forward in a right line.—This force consists in the action only; and remains no longer in the body when the action is over. For a body maintains every new state it acquires by its vis inertiae only. It is here implied, and indeed fully expressed, that motion is not continued by the same power that produced it. Now there are two grounds on which the truth of this doctrine may be supposed to rest. "First, On a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> that the impressed force does not remain in the body, either by showing the nature of the force to be transitory and incapable of more than its first action; or that it acts only on the surface, and that the body escapes from it; or that the force is somewhere else, and not remaining in the body. But none of these direct proofs are offered. "Secondly, It may rest on an indirect proof, that there is in the nature of body a sufficient cause for the continuance of every new state acquired; and that therefore any adventitious force to continue motion, though necessary for its production, is superfluous and inadmissible. As this is the very ground on which the supposition stands, it ought to have been indubitably certain that the innate force of the body is sufficient to perpetuate the motion it has once acquired, before the other <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGENT">agent</a>, by which the motion was communicated, had been dismissed from the office. But the innate force of body has been shown not to be that which continues its motion; and therefore the proof, that the impressed force does not remain in the body, fails. Nor indeed is it in this case desirable to support the proof, because we should then be left without any reason for the continuance of motion*:" When we mention an impressed force, we mean such a force as is communicated either at the surface of the body or by being diffused through the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a>. 5. A centripetal force is that by which bodies are drawn, impelled, or any way tend towards a point, as to a centre.—The quantity of any centripetal force may be considered as of three kinds, absolute, accelerative, and motive. 6. The absolute quantity of a centrifugal force is the measure of the same, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROPORTIONAL">proportional</a> to the efficacy of the cause that propagates it from the centre, through the Newtonian spaces round it. 7. The accelerative quantity of a centripetal force is the measure of the same, proportional to the velocity which it generates in a given time. 8. The motive quantity of a centripetal force is a measure of the same, proportional to the motion which it generates in a given time. This is always known by the quantity of a force equal and contrary to it, that is just sufficient to hinder the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> of the body. [Merged from SCHOLIA, p.861] I. Absolute, true, and mathematical time, of itself, Of time, and from its own nature, flows equably, without regard to any thing <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a>, and, by another name, is called <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>. Relative, apparent, and common time, is some sensible and external measure of duration, whether accurate or not, which is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> used instead of true time; such as an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>, a day, a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a>, a year, &c. II. Absolute space, in its own nature, without regard to any thing external, remains always similar and immovable. Relative space is some moveable <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIMENSION">dimension</a> or measure of the absolute spaces; and which is vulgarly taken for immovable space. Such is the dimension of a subterraneous, an aerial, or celestial space, determined by its position to bodies, and which is vulgarly taken for immovable space; as the distance of a subterraneous, an aerial, or celestial space, determined by its position in respect of the earth. Absolute and relative space are the same in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> and magnitude; but they do not remain always numerically the same. For if the earth, for instance, moves, a space of our air which, relatively and in respect of the earth, remains always the same, will at one time be one part of the absolute space into which the earth passes; at another time it will be another part of the same; and so, absolutely understood, it will be perpetually mutable. III. Place is a part of space which a body takes Place up; and is, according to the space, either absolute or fixed relative. Our author says it is part of space; not the situation, nor the external surface of the body. For the places of equal solids are always equal; but their superficies, by reason of their dissimilar figures, are often unequal. Positions properly have no quantity, nor are they so much the places themselves as the properties of places. The motion of the whole is the same thing with the sum of the motions of the parts; that is, the translation of the whole out of its place is the same thing with the sum of the translations of the parts out of their places; and therefore the place of the whole is the same thing with the sum of the places of the parts; and for that reason it is internal, and in the whole body. IV. Absolute motion is the translation of a body Of Motion from one absolute place into another, and relative motion the translation from one relative place into another. Thus, in a ship under sail, the relative place of a body is that part of the ship which the body possesses, or that part of its cavity which the body fills, and which therefore moves together with the ship; and relative rest is the continuance of the body in the same part of the ship, or of its cavity. But real absolute. Newtonian absolute rest is the continuance of the body in the Philosophy same part of that immoveable space in which the ship itself, its cavity, and all that it contains, is moved. Wherefore, if the earth is really at rest, the body which relatively rests in the ship will really and absolutely move with the same velocity which the ship has on the earth. But if the earth also moves, the true and absolute motion of the body will arise partly from the true motion of the earth in immoveable space; partly from the relative motion of the ship on the earth; and if the body moves also relatively in the ship, its true motion will arise partly from the true motion of the earth in immoveable space, and partly from the relative motions as well of the ship on the earth as of the body in the ship; and from these relative motions will arise the relative motion of the body on the earth. As if that part of the earth where the ship is, was truly moved towards the east, with a velocity of 1001 parts; while the ship itself with a fresh <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GALE">gale</a> is carried towards the west, with a velocity expressed by 10 of these parts; but a sailor walks in the ship towards the east with one part of the said velocity: then the sailor will be moved truly and absolutely in immoveable space towards the east with a velocity of 1001 parts: and relatively on the earth towards the west, with a velocity of 9 of those parts. Absolute time, in astronomy, is distinguished from relative, by the equation or correction of the vulgar time. For the natural days are truly unequal, though they are commonly considered as equal, and used for a measure of time: astronomers correct this inequality for their more accurate deducing of the celestial motions. It may be that there is no such thing as an equable motion whereby time may be accurately measured. All motions may be accelerated or retarded; but the true or equable progress of absolute time is liable to no change. The duration or perseverance of the existence of things remains the same, whether the motions are swift or slow, or none at all; and therefore ought to be distinguished from what are only sensible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> thereof, and out of which we collect it by means of the astronomical equation. The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of which equation for determining the times of a phenomenon is evinced, as well from the experiments of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENDULUM">pendulum</a> clock as by eclipses of the satellites of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>. As the order of the parts of time is immutable, so also is the order of the parts of space. Suppose those parts to be moved out of their places, and they will be moved (if we may be allowed the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>) out of themselves. For times and spaces are, as it were, the places of themselves as of all other things. All things are placed in time as to order of succession; and in space as to order of situation. It is from their essence or nature that they are places; and that the primary places of things should be moveable is absurd. These are therefore the absolute places; and translations out of those places are the only absolute motions. But because the parts of space cannot be seen, or distinguished from one another by the senses, therefore in their stead we use sensible measures of them. For, from the positions and distances of things from any body, considered as immoveable, we define all place; and then with respect to such places, we estimate all motions, considering bodies as transferred from some Newtonian places into others. And so, instead of absolute places and motions, we use relative ones; and that without any inconvenience in common affairs: but in philosophical disquisitions we ought to abstract from our senses, and consider things themselves distinct from what are only sensible measures of them. For it may be, that there is no body really at rest, to which the places and motions of others may be referred. But we may distinguish rest and motion, absolute and relative, one from the other, by their properties, causes, and effects. It is a property of rest, that bodies really at rest do rest in respect of each other. And therefore, as it is possible, that in the remote regions of the fixed stars, or perhaps far beyond them, there may be some body absolutely at rest, though it be impossible to know from the position of bodies to one another in our regions, whether any of these do keep the same position to that remote body; it follows, that absolute rest cannot be determined from the position of bodies in our regions. It is a property of motion, that the parts which retain given positions to their wholes do partake of the motion of their wholes. For all parts of revolving bodies endeavour to recede from the axis of motion; respect to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> impetus of all the parts. Therefore if surrounding bodies are moved, those that are relatively at rest within them will partake of their motion. Upon which account the true and absolute motion of a body cannot be determined by the translation of it from those only which seem to rest; for the external bodies ought not only to appear at rest, but to be really at rest. For otherwise all included bodies, beside their translation from near the surrounding ones, partake likewise of their true motions; and though that translation was not made, they would not really be at rest, but only seem to be so. For the surrounding bodies stand in the like relation to the surrounded, as the exterior part of a whole does to the interior, or as the shell does to the kernel; but if the shell moves, the kernel will also move, as being part of the whole, without any removal from near the shell. A property near akin to the preceding is, that if a place is moved, whatever is placed therein moves along with it; and therefore a body which is moved from a place in motion, partakes also of the motion of its place. Upon which account all motions from places in motion, are no other than parts of entire and absolute motions; and every entire motion is composed of the motion of the body out of its first place, and the motion of this place out of its place; and so on, until we come to some immoveable place, as in the above-mentioned example of the sailor. Wherefore entire and absolute motions can be no otherwise determined than by immoveable places. Now, no other places are immoveable but those that from infinity to infinity do all retain the same given positions one to another; and upon this account must ever remain unmoved, and do thereby constitute what we call immoveable space. The causes by which true and relative motions are distinguished one from the other, are the forces impressed Newtonian pressed upon bodies to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATE">generate</a> motion. True motion is neither <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATED">generated</a> nor altered, but by some force impressed upon the body moved; but relative motion may be generated or altered without any force impressed upon the body. For it is sufficient only to impress some force on other bodies with which the former is compared, that by their giving way, that relation may be changed, in which the relative rest or motion of the other body did consist. Again, True motion suffers always some change from any force impressed upon the moving body; but relative motion does not necessarily undergo any changes by such force. For if the same forces are likewise impressed on those other bodies with which the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> is made, that the relative position may be preserved; then that condition will be preserved, in which the relative motion consists. And therefore any relative motion may be changed when the true motion remains unaltered, and the relative may be preserved when the true motion suffers some change. Upon which account true motion does by no means consist in such relations. The effects which distinguish absolute from relative motion are, the forces of receding from the axis of circular motion. For there are no such forces in a circular motion purely relative; but in a true and absolute circular motion, they are greater or less according to the quantity of the motion. If a vessel hung by a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CORD">cord</a>, is so often turned about that the cord is strongly twisted, then filled with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and let go, it will be whirled about the contrary way; and while the cord is untwisting itself, the surface of the water will at first be plain, as before the vessel began to move; but the vessel, by gradually communicating its motion to the water, will make it begin sensibly to revolve, and recede by little and little from the middle, and ascend to the sides of the vessel, forming itself into a concave figure; and the swifter the motion becomes, the higher will the water rise, till at last, performing its revolutions in the same times with the vessel, it becomes relatively at rest in it. This ascent of the water shows its endeavour to recede from the axis of its motion; and the true and absolute circular motion of the water, which is here directly contrary to the relative, discovers itself, and may be measured by this endeavour. At first, when the relative motion in the water was greatest, it produced no endeavour to recede from the axis; the water showed no tendency to the circumference, nor any ascent towards the sides of the vessel, but remained of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANE">plane</a> surface; and therefore its true circular motion had not yet begun. But afterwards, when the relative motion of the water had decreased, the ascent thereof towards the sides of the vessel proved its endeavour to recede from the axis; and this endeavour showed the real circular motion of the water perpetually increasing, till it had acquired its greatest quantity, when the water rested relatively in the vessel. And therefore this endeavour does not depend upon any translation of the water in respect of the ambient bodies; nor can true circular motion be defined by such translations. There is only one real circular motion of any one revolving body, corresponding to only one power of endeavouring to recede from its axis of motion, as its proper and adequate effect; but relative motions in one and the same body are innumerable, according to the various relations it bears to external bodies; and, like other relations, are altogether Newtonian, destitute of any real effect, otherwise than they may perhaps participate of that only true motion. And therefore, in the system which supposes that our heavens, revolving below the sphere of the fixed stars, carry the planets along with them, the several parts of those heavens and the planets, which are indeed relatively at rest in their heavens, do yet really move. For they change their position one to another, which never happens to bodies truly at rest; and being carried together with the heavens, participate of their motions, and, as parts of revolving wholes, endeavour to recede from the axis of their motion. Wherefore relative quantities are not the quantities themselves whose names they bear, but those sensible measures of them, either accurate or inaccurate, which are commonly used instead of the measured quantities themselves. And then, if the meaning of words be determined by their use, by the names time, space, place, and motion, their measures are properly to be understood; and the expression will be unusual and purely mathematical, if the measured quantities themselves are meant. It is indeed a matter of great difficulty to discover, and effectually to distinguish, the true motions of particular bodies from those that are only apparent: because the parts of that immovable space in which those motions are performed, do by no means come under the observation of our senses. Yet we have some things to direct us in this intricate affair; and these arise partly from the apparent motions which are the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of the true motions, partly from the forces which are the causes and effects of the true motions. For instance, if two globes kept at a given distance one from the other by means of a cord that connects them, were revolved about their common centre of gravity; we might, from the tension of the cord, discover the endeavour of the globes to recede from the axis of motion, and from thence we might compute the quantity of their circular motions. And then, if any equal forces should be impressed at once on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALTERNATE">alternate</a> faces of the globes to augment or diminish their circular motions, from the increase or decrease of the tension of the cord we might infer the increment or decrement of their motions; and thence would be found on what faces those forces ought to be impressed, that the motions of the globes might be most augmented; that is, we might discover their blindermost faces, or those which follow in the circular motion. But the faces which follow being known, and consequently the opposite ones that precede, we should likewise know the determination of their motions. And thus we might find both the quantity and determination of this circular motion, even in an immense <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VACUUM">vacuum</a>, where there was nothing external or sensible with which the globes might be compared. But now, if in that space some remote bodies were placed that kept always a given position one to another, as the fixed stars do in our regions; we could not indeed determine from the relative translation of the globes among those bodies, whether the motion did belong to the globes or to the bodies. But if we observed the cord, and found that its tension was that very tension which the motions of the globes required, we might conclude the motion to be in the globes, and the bodies to Newtonian be at rest; and then, lastly, from the translation of the Philosophy, globes among the bodies, we should find the determination of their motions.
